catalog_formula_sheets.name: Conic Sections Formula Sheet
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: By definition of parabola, distance from point $P(x, y)$ to focus $S(a, 0)$ equals perpendicular distance to directrix $x + a = 0$: $SP = PM \implies \sqrt{(x - a)^2 + y^2} = |x + a|$. Squaring both sides: $(x - a)^2 + y^2 = (x + a)^2 \implies x^2 - 2ax + a^2 + y^2 = x^2 + 2ax + a^2 \implies y^2 = 4ax$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Fundamental locus of a point moving such that its distance from focus equals its distance from directrix ($e = 1$).

content_json.title: Conic Sections Formula Sheet

sections.title: Conic Sections Formula Sheet - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.title: Standard Parabola Definition and Anatomy
formulas.derivation: By definition of parabola, distance from point $P(x, y)$ to focus $S(a, 0)$ equals perpendicular distance to directrix $x + a = 0$: $SP = PM \implies \sqrt{(x - a)^2 + y^2} = |x + a|$. Squaring both sides: $(x - a)^2 + y^2 = (x + a)^2 \implies x^2 - 2ax + a^2 + y^2 = x^2 + 2ax + a^2 \implies y^2 = 4ax$.
formulas.description: Standard Parabola Definition and Anatomy
formulas.explanation: Fundamental locus of a point moving such that its distance from focus equals its distance from directrix ($e = 1$).

formulas.latex: y = m x + \frac{a}{m} \quad (m \ne 0) \implies \text{Tangent to } y^2 = 4ax \text{ at } \left(\frac{a}{m^2}, \frac{2a}{m}\right)
formulas.title: Tangent to Parabola in Slope Form
formulas.derivation: Substitute line $y = mx + c$ into $y^2 = 4ax$: $(mx + c)^2 = 4ax \implies m^2 x^2 + (2mc - 4a)x + c^2 = 0$. For tangency, the quadratic must have equal roots ($\Delta = 0$): $(2mc - 4a)^2 - 4m^2 c^2 = 0 \implies 4m^2 c^2 - 16amc + 16a^2 - 4m^2 c^2 = 0 \implies -16amc + 16a^2 = 0 \implies c = a/m$. Hence $y = mx + a/m$.
formulas.description: Tangent to Parabola in Slope Form
formulas.explanation: Equation of any tangent line to parabola $y^2 = 4ax$ with known slope m.

formulas.latex: y = m x - 2am - a m^3 \implies \text{Normal to } y^2 = 4ax \text{ at } (am^2, -2am)
formulas.title: Normal to Parabola in Slope Form
formulas.derivation: Tangent at parametric point $t$ has equation $yt = x + at^2 \implies y = \frac{1}{t}x + at$. Slope of tangent is $m_T = 1/t$. The normal is perpendicular to tangent, so its slope is $m = -t \implies t = -m$. Normal in point form: $y - 2at = -t(x - at^2)$. Substitute $t = -m$: $y - 2a(-m) = m(x - a(-m)^2) \implies y + 2am = mx - am^3 \implies y = mx - 2am - am^3$.
formulas.description: Normal to Parabola in Slope Form
formulas.explanation: Notice this is cubic in m: from any external point $(h, k)$, at most three normals can be drawn to a parabola.

formulas.title: Standard Ellipse and Eccentricity Relation
formulas.derivation: By focal property $SP + S'P = 2a$: $\sqrt{(x - ae)^2 + y^2} + \sqrt{(x + ae)^2 + y^2} = 2a$. Rearranging and squaring twice eliminates the radicals: $x^2(1 - e^2) + y^2 = a^2(1 - e^2)$. Setting $b^2 = a^2(1 - e^2)$ yields standard form $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$. Solving for $e$ gives $e = \sqrt{1 - b^2/a^2}$.
formulas.description: Standard Ellipse and Eccentricity Relation
formulas.explanation: Symmetric closed conic section where the sum of distances from any point on ellipse to two foci is constant 2a.

formulas.latex: y = m x \pm \sqrt{a^2 m^2 + b^2} \implies \text{Tangent to } \frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1
formulas.title: Tangent to Ellipse in Slope Form
formulas.derivation: Substitute $y = mx + c$ into $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1 \implies b^2 x^2 + a^2(mx + c)^2 = a^2 b^2 \implies (b^2 + a^2 m^2)x^2 + 2a^2 mc x + (a^2 c^2 - a^2 b^2) = 0$. Condition for tangency ($\Delta = 0$): $(2a^2 mc)^2 - 4(b^2 + a^2 m^2)a^2(c^2 - b^2) = 0 \implies c^2 = a^2 m^2 + b^2 \implies c = \pm \sqrt{a^2 m^2 + b^2}$.
formulas.description: Tangent to Ellipse in Slope Form
formulas.explanation: Tangency condition: $c^2 = a^2 m^2 + b^2$. For any slope m, exactly two parallel tangents exist to an ellipse.

formulas.latex: x^2 + y^2 = a^2 + b^2 \implies \text{Director Circle of Ellipse}
formulas.title: Director Circle of Ellipse (Locus of Perpendicular Tangents)
formulas.derivation: Let perpendicular tangents pass through point $(h, k)$. Tangent equation: $(k - mh)^2 = a^2 m^2 + b^2 \implies m^2(h^2 - a^2) - 2mhk + (k^2 - b^2) = 0$. Since tangents are perpendicular, product of slopes is $m_1 m_2 = -1$. By Vieta's formula: $\frac{k^2 - b^2}{h^2 - a^2} = -1 \implies k^2 - b^2 = -(h^2 - a^2) \implies h^2 + k^2 = a^2 + b^2$. Replacing $(h, k)$ with $(x, y)$ gives $x^2 + y^2 = a^2 + b^2$.
formulas.description: Director Circle of Ellipse (Locus of Perpendicular Tangents)
formulas.explanation: Locus of points from which the two tangents drawn to the ellipse are perpendicular to each other.

formulas.title: Standard Hyperbola and Eccentricity Relation
formulas.derivation: By focal definition $|SP - S'P| = 2a$: $\sqrt{(x - ae)^2 + y^2} - \sqrt{(x + ae)^2 + y^2} = \pm 2a$. Squaring twice eliminates radicals, yielding $x^2(e^2 - 1) - y^2 = a^2(e^2 - 1)$. Setting $b^2 = a^2(e^2 - 1)$ gives $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \\frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$. Solving for $e$ yields $e = \sqrt{1 + b^2/a^2} > 1$.
formulas.description: Standard Hyperbola and Eccentricity Relation
formulas.explanation: Open, two-branched conic section where the absolute difference of distances to two foci is constant 2a.

formulas.latex: y = m x \pm \sqrt{a^2 m^2 - b^2} \implies \text{Tangent to } \frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1 \quad (|m| > b/a)
formulas.title: Tangent to Hyperbola in Slope Form
formulas.derivation: Substitute $y = mx + c$ into $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1 \implies b^2 x^2 - a^2(mx + c)^2 = a^2 b^2 \implies (b^2 - a^2 m^2)x^2 - 2a^2 mc x - a^2(c^2 + b^2) = 0$. Condition for tangency ($\Delta = 0$): $(-2a^2 mc)^2 - 4(b^2 - a^2 m^2)(-a^2)(c^2 + b^2) = 0 \implies c^2 = a^2 m^2 - b^2 \implies c = \pm \sqrt{a^2 m^2 - b^2}$. Real tangents require $a^2 m^2 \ge b^2$.
formulas.description: Tangent to Hyperbola in Slope Form
formulas.explanation: Condition of tangency: $c^2 = a^2 m^2 - b^2$. Slopes must satisfy $|m| > b/a$ to touch the hyperbola.

formulas.latex: x^2 + y^2 = a^2 - b^2 \quad (a > b) \implies \text{Director Circle of Hyperbola}
formulas.title: Director Circle of Hyperbola
formulas.derivation: Let perpendicular tangents pass through $(h, k)$: $(k - mh)^2 = a^2 m^2 - b^2 \implies m^2(h^2 - a^2) - 2mhk + (k^2 + b^2) = 0$. Since $m_1 m_2 = -1$: $\frac{k^2 + b^2}{h^2 - a^2} = -1 \implies k^2 + b^2 = -h^2 + a^2 \implies h^2 + k^2 = a^2 - b^2$. For director circle to be real, $a > b$. If $a < b$, no pair of perpendicular tangents exists.
formulas.description: Director Circle of Hyperbola
formulas.explanation: Real locus of perpendicular tangents exists only when $a > b$; collapses to a point when $a = b$ (rectangular hyperbola).

formulas.title: Asymptotes of Hyperbola
formulas.derivation: Solve for $y$: $y = \pm \frac{b}{a}\sqrt{x^2 - a^2} = \pm \frac{b}{a} x \sqrt{1 - \frac{a^2}{x^2}}$. Expanding by binomial theorem for large $x$: $y = \pm \frac{b}{a} x \left(1 - \frac{a^2}{2x^2} - \dots\right) = \pm \frac{b}{a} x + O(1/x)$. As $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$, the hyperbola approaches the straight lines $y = \pm \frac{b}{a} x$ asymptotically.
formulas.description: Asymptotes of Hyperbola
formulas.explanation: Lines tangent to the hyperbola at infinity; angle between asymptotes is $2\tan^{-1}(b/a)$.

formulas.latex: x y = c^2 \implies \text{Rectangular Hyperbola with asymptotes as axes and } e = \sqrt{2}
formulas.title: Rectangular Hyperbola in Cartesian Coordinates
formulas.derivation: Rotate standard hyperbola $x^2 - y^2 = a^2$ (which has $a = b \implies e = \sqrt{1 + a^2/a^2} = \sqrt{2}$) by $-45^\circ$: $X = \frac{x - y}{\sqrt{2}}, Y = \frac{x + y}{\sqrt{2}}$. Substitute: $\left(\frac{x - y}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{x + y}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 = a^2 \implies -2xy = a^2 \implies xy = c^2$ where $c^2 = a^2/2$.
formulas.description: Rectangular Hyperbola in Cartesian Coordinates
formulas.explanation: Asymptotes are mutually perpendicular coordinate axes ($x=0$ and $y=0$), giving constant eccentricity $e = \sqrt{2}$.

formulas.title: Tangent to General Conic at Point (x1, y1)

variables.T = 0: notation replacing x^2 with x x_1, 2x with x + x_1, etc.

formulas.derivation: Differentiate general second degree conic $x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0$ implicitly: $2x + 2y y' + 2g + 2f y' = 0 \implies y' = -\frac{x + g}{y + f}$. Slope at $(x_1, y_1)$ is $m = -\frac{x_1 + g}{y_1 + f}$. Equation: $y - y_1 = -\frac{x_1 + g}{y_1 + f}(x - x_1) \implies (y - y_1)(y_1 + f) + (x - x_1)(x_1 + g) = 0 \implies x x_1 + y y_1 + g(x + x_1) + f(y + y_1) + c = 0$.
formulas.description: Tangent to General Conic at Point (x1, y1)
formulas.explanation: Universal rule of replacement ($T = 0$) for writing tangent equations to any second-degree conic at boundary point $(x_1, y_1)$.

content_json.derivation: By definition of parabola, distance from point $P(x, y)$ to focus $S(a, 0)$ equals perpendicular distance to directrix $x + a = 0$: $SP = PM \implies \sqrt{(x - a)^2 + y^2} = |x + a|$. Squaring both sides: $(x - a)^2 + y^2 = (x + a)^2 \implies x^2 - 2ax + a^2 + y^2 = x^2 + 2ax + a^2 \implies y^2 = 4ax$.
content_json.explanation: Fundamental locus of a point moving such that its distance from focus equals its distance from directrix ($e = 1$).

catalog_formula_sheets.name: Sets Formula Sheet
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: Divide $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ by $a$: $x^2 + \frac{b}{a}x = -\frac{c}{a}$. Complete square by adding $\left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2$: $\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 = \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}$. Taking square roots gives $x + \frac{b}{2a} = \pm \frac{\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} \implies x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Yields the two exact roots of any general quadratic polynomial. The term $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$ governs the nature of the roots.

content_json.title: Sets Formula Sheet

sections.title: Sets Formula Sheet - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.title: Quadratic Formula for roots of ax^2 + bx + c = 0
formulas.derivation: Divide $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ by $a$: $x^2 + \frac{b}{a}x = -\frac{c}{a}$. Complete square by adding $\left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2$: $\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 = \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}$. Taking square roots gives $x + \frac{b}{2a} = \pm \frac{\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} \implies x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$.
formulas.description: Quadratic Formula for roots of ax^2 + bx + c = 0
formulas.explanation: Yields the two exact roots of any general quadratic polynomial. The term $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$ governs the nature of the roots.

formulas.title: Vieta's Formulas for Quadratic Equations
formulas.derivation: Since $\alpha, \beta$ are roots: $a(x - \alpha)(x - \beta) = a(x^2 - (\alpha + \beta)x + \alpha\beta) = ax^2 - a(\alpha + \beta)x + a\alpha\beta = ax^2 + bx + c$. Equating coefficients: $-a(\alpha + \beta) = b \implies \alpha + \beta = -b/a$, and $a\alpha\beta = c \implies \alpha\beta = c/a$.
formulas.description: Vieta's Formulas for Quadratic Equations
formulas.explanation: Directly links polynomial coefficients to root sums and products without solving the equation explicitly.

formulas.title: Difference of Roots Formula
formulas.derivation: Using identity $(\alpha - \beta)^2 = (\alpha + \beta)^2 - 4\alpha\beta = \left(-\frac{b}{a}\right)^2 - 4\frac{c}{a} = \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{a^2} = \frac{\Delta}{a^2}$. Taking principal square root gives $|\alpha - \beta| = \frac{\sqrt{\Delta}}{|a|}$.
formulas.description: Difference of Roots Formula
formulas.explanation: Measures the horizontal distance between the x-intercepts of the parabola $y = ax^2 + bx + c$.

formulas.title: Discriminant Characterization of Roots
formulas.derivation: Follows directly from the radical term $\sqrt{\Delta}$ in the quadratic formula. If $\Delta > 0$, $\sqrt{\Delta} \in \mathbb{R}^+$, yielding two distinct real values. If $\Delta = 0$, $\sqrt{\Delta} = 0$, giving coincident root $-b/(2a)$. If $\Delta < 0$, $\sqrt{\Delta} = i\sqrt{-\Delta}$, producing non-real conjugate pair $\frac{-b \pm i\sqrt{4ac - b^2}}{2a}$.
formulas.description: Discriminant Characterization of Roots
formulas.explanation: Determines whether the parabola intersects the x-axis at 2 points, touches at 1 vertex, or never intersects.

formulas.title: Condition for Exactly One Common Root Between Two Quadratics

variables.a_i, b_i, c_i: coefficients of a1 x^2 + b1 x + c1 = 0 and a2 x^2 + b2 x + c2 = 0

formulas.derivation: Let $\alpha$ be common root: $a_1 \alpha^2 + b_1 \alpha + c_1 = 0$ and $a_2 \alpha^2 + b_2 \alpha + c_2 = 0$. By cross-multiplication: $\frac{\alpha^2}{b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1} = \frac{\alpha}{c_1 a_2 - c_2 a_1} = \frac{1}{a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1}$. Eliminating $\alpha$: $\alpha = \frac{c_1 a_2 - c_2 a_1}{a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1}$, so $\alpha^2 = \frac{(c_1 a_2 - c_2 a_1)^2}{(a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1)^2} = \frac{b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1}{a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1} \implies (c_1 a_2 - c_2 a_1)^2 = (a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1)(b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1)$.
formulas.description: Condition for Exactly One Common Root Between Two Quadratics
formulas.explanation: Necessary and sufficient algebraic condition for two distinct quadratic equations to share a common solution.

formulas.latex: \Delta \ge 0, \quad a \cdot f(k) > 0, \quad -\frac{b}{2a} > k \implies \text{Both roots greater than } k
formulas.title: Location of Roots: Both roots greater than real number k
formulas.derivation: For both roots $\alpha, \beta > k$: (1) Real roots require $\Delta \ge 0$. (2) Parabola opens up ($a>0$) means $f(k) > 0$; opens down ($a<0$) means $f(k) < 0$, unified as $a \cdot f(k) > 0$. (3) The vertex $x = -b/(2a) = (\alpha + \beta)/2$ must lie strictly to the right of $k$: $-b/(2a) > k$.
formulas.description: Location of Roots: Both roots greater than real number k
formulas.explanation: Standard IIT-JEE test for restricting both roots of a quadratic polynomial to the right of a given real value k.

formulas.latex: a \cdot f(k) < 0 \implies k \text{ lies strictly between the roots}
formulas.title: Location of Roots: Number k lies strictly between roots
formulas.derivation: If $k$ lies between $\alpha$ and $\beta$, the vertex value must have opposite sign to $f(k)$ compared to $a$. If $a > 0$, parabola is below x-axis between roots $\implies f(k) < 0 \implies a f(k) < 0$. If $a < 0$, parabola is above x-axis between roots $\implies f(k) > 0 \implies a f(k) < 0$. Note: $\Delta > 0$ is automatically guaranteed since $a f(k) < 0 \implies b^2 - 4ac > 0$.
formulas.description: Location of Roots: Number k lies strictly between roots
formulas.explanation: Simplest root-location check: a single inequality $a f(k) < 0$ guarantees real distinct roots with k strictly between them.

formulas.title: Maximum or Minimum Value of Quadratic Function

variables.a: lead coefficient (min if a > 0, max if a < 0)

formulas.derivation: Let $f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$. Setting derivative to zero: $f'(x) = 2ax + b = 0 \implies x = -b/(2a)$. Evaluating at critical point: $f(-b/2a) = a\left(\frac{b^2}{4a^2}\right) + b\left(-\frac{b}{2a}\right) + c = \frac{b^2 - 2b^2 + 4ac}{4a} = -\frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a} = -\frac{\Delta}{4a}$. Second derivative $f''(x) = 2a$, so minimum if $a > 0$, maximum if $a < 0$.
formulas.description: Maximum or Minimum Value of Quadratic Function
formulas.explanation: Gives the absolute extremum of a quadratic polynomial. Range of $f(x)$ is $[-\Delta/4a, \infty)$ if $a > 0$ and $(-\infty, -\Delta/4a]$ if $a < 0$.

formulas.latex: a S_n + b S_{n-1} + c S_{n-2} = 0 \quad \text{where } S_n = p \alpha^n + q \beta^n
formulas.title: Newton's Sums Theorem for Powers of Roots

variables.S_n: linear combination of n-th powers of roots

formulas.derivation: Since $\alpha$ and $\beta$ satisfy $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$: $a\alpha^2 + b\alpha + c = 0$ and $a\beta^2 + b\beta + c = 0$. Multiply by $p\alpha^{n-2}$ and $q\beta^{n-2}$ respectively: $a(p\alpha^n) + b(p\alpha^{n-1}) + c(p\alpha^{n-2}) = 0$ and $a(q\beta^n) + b(q\beta^{n-1}) + c(q\beta^{n-2}) = 0$. Adding both equations yields $a(p\alpha^n + q\beta^n) + b(p\alpha^{n-1} + q\beta^{n-1}) + c(p\alpha^{n-2} + q\beta^{n-2}) = 0 \implies aS_n + bS_{n-1} + cS_{n-2} = 0$.
formulas.description: Newton's Sums Theorem for Powers of Roots
formulas.explanation: Extremely powerful JEE Advanced shortcut for computing high-power root expressions like $\alpha^{10} -  eta^{10}$ without calculating roots.

formulas.title: Sum of Cubes of Quadratic Roots
formulas.derivation: From algebraic identity $(\alpha+\beta)^3 = \alpha^3 + \beta^3 + 3\alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta)$, rearrange: $\alpha^3 + \beta^3 = (\alpha+\beta)^3 - 3\alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta)$. Substitute $\alpha+\beta = -b/a$ and $\alpha\beta = c/a$: $\alpha^3 + \beta^3 = (-b/a)^3 - 3(c/a)(-b/a) = -\frac{b^3}{a^3} + \frac{3bc}{a^2} = \frac{3abc - b^3}{a^3}$.
formulas.description: Sum of Cubes of Quadratic Roots
formulas.explanation: Allows fast computation of third-order symmetric root expressions using solely equation coefficients.

formulas.title: Condition for Positive Definite Quadratic Expression
formulas.derivation: Completing square: $f(x) = a\left[\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 - \frac{\Delta}{4a^2}\right]$. The squared term is $\ge 0$. For $f(x)$ to remain strictly positive for all $x$, the parabola must open upwards ($a > 0$) and its minimum vertex value $-\Delta/(4a)$ must be strictly positive, which requires $-\Delta > 0 \implies \Delta < 0$.
formulas.description: Condition for Positive Definite Quadratic Expression
formulas.explanation: Guarantees that a quadratic expression never crosses or touches zero, remaining strictly positive across all real numbers.

formulas.latex: c x^2 + b x + a = 0 \implies \text{roots are } \frac{1}{\alpha}, \frac{1}{\beta}
formulas.title: Transformation of Equations: Reciprocal Roots
formulas.derivation: Let $y = 1/x \implies x = 1/y$. Substitute into $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$: $a(1/y)^2 + b(1/y) + c = 0 \implies \frac{a}{y^2} + \frac{b}{y} + c = 0$. Multiply through by $y^2$: $c y^2 + b y + a = 0$. The roots of this transformed equation are $y_1 = 1/\alpha$ and $y_2 = 1/\beta$.
formulas.description: Transformation of Equations: Reciprocal Roots
formulas.explanation: Reversing the coefficients of a polynomial immediately inverts all its roots.

content_json.derivation: Divide $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ by $a$: $x^2 + \frac{b}{a}x = -\frac{c}{a}$. Complete square by adding $\left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2$: $\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 = \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}$. Taking square roots gives $x + \frac{b}{2a} = \pm \frac{\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} \implies x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$.
content_json.explanation: Yields the two exact roots of any general quadratic polynomial. The term $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$ governs the nature of the roots.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: Solid State Formula Sheet
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: Hooke's law states stress $\sigma$ is directly proportional to strain $\epsilon$, giving $Y = \sigma / \epsilon$. Work done in stretching is $W = \int_0^{\Delta L} F(x)dx = \int_0^{\Delta L} \frac{YA}{L}x dx = \frac{1}{2}\frac{YA}{L}(\Delta L)^2 = \frac{1}{2}F\Delta L$. Dividing by volume $V = AL$ yields energy density $u = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{F}{A}\right)\left(\frac{\Delta L}{L}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\sigma\epsilon = \frac{1}{2}Y\epsilon^2$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Valid only within proportional limit; material property independent of geometric dimensions.

content_json.title: Solid State Formula Sheet

sections.title: Solid State Formula Sheet - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.title: Young's Modulus and Elastic Energy Density
formulas.derivation: Hooke's law states stress $\sigma$ is directly proportional to strain $\epsilon$, giving $Y = \sigma / \epsilon$. Work done in stretching is $W = \int_0^{\Delta L} F(x)dx = \int_0^{\Delta L} \frac{YA}{L}x dx = \frac{1}{2}\frac{YA}{L}(\Delta L)^2 = \frac{1}{2}F\Delta L$. Dividing by volume $V = AL$ yields energy density $u = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{F}{A}\right)\left(\frac{\Delta L}{L}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\sigma\epsilon = \frac{1}{2}Y\epsilon^2$.
formulas.description: Ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain within proportional limit, and energy stored per unit volume.
formulas.explanation: Valid only within proportional limit; material property independent of geometric dimensions.

formulas.latex: P(h) = P_0 + \rho g h, \quad F_B = \rho_{fluid} V_{sub} g
formulas.title: Hydrostatic Pressure and Archimedes' Principle
formulas.derivation: Consider cylindrical fluid column of height $dh$ and area $A$: vertical balance requires $(P+dP)A - PA = \rho (A\,dh) g \implies dP = \rho g dh$. Integrating yields $P = P_0 + \rho g h$. Buoyant force is the net upward pressure integral over surface: $F_B = \oint P(-d\vec{A}) = \int_V \vec{\nabla} P dV = \int_V \rho g dV = \rho g V_{sub}$, which equals the weight of displaced fluid.
formulas.description: Pressure depth variation in incompressible static fluid and buoyant upward force on submerged body.
formulas.explanation: Archimedes' law holds for bodies of any shape, floating or completely submerged.

formulas.title: Equation of Continuity
formulas.derivation: Mass passing section 1 in time $dt$ is $dm_1 = \rho_1 A_1 v_1 dt$. Mass passing section 2 is $dm_2 = \rho_2 A_2 v_2 dt$. By mass conservation, $dm_1 = dm_2$. For incompressible flow ($\rho_1 = \rho_2 = \rho$), dividing by $\rho dt$ gives $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$.
formulas.description: Conservation of mass for steady, incompressible fluid flow through conduits of varying cross-section.
formulas.explanation: Fluid accelerates through constrictions (venturi necks) and slows down in expansions.

formulas.title: Bernoulli's Equation
formulas.derivation: Work done on fluid element of volume $\Delta V$ moving along streamline: $W = (P_1 - P_2)\Delta V$. Change in kinetic energy is $\Delta K = \frac{1}{2}\rho\Delta V(v_2^2 - v_1^2)$. Change in potential energy is $\Delta U = \rho\Delta V g(h_2 - h_1)$. Work-energy theorem $W = \Delta K + \Delta U$ gives $(P_1 - P_2)\Delta V = \frac{1}{2}\rho\Delta V(v_2^2 - v_1^2) + \rho\Delta V g(h_2 - h_1)$. Rearranging yields $P_1 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 + \rho g h_1 = P_2 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2 + \rho g h_2$.
formulas.description: Conservation of mechanical energy per unit volume along a streamline for steady, inviscid, incompressible flow.
formulas.explanation: Explains dynamic lift on aerofoils, aspirator pumps, and Venturi meters.

formulas.title: Torricelli's Law of Efflux

variables.H: Total height of liquid in tank
variables.h: Depth of orifice below liquid surface
variables.R_{horizontal}: Range of liquid jet on floor

formulas.derivation: Apply Bernoulli between top surface (1) and orifice (2): $P_0 + 0 + \rho g h = P_0 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + 0$ (assuming tank area $A_1 \gg A_2$). Solving gives $v = \sqrt{2gh}$. Liquid falls distance $H - h$ to ground in time $t = \sqrt{2(H - h)/g}$. Range is $R = v t = \sqrt{2gh}\sqrt{2(H - h)/g} = 2\sqrt{h(H - h)}$.
formulas.description: Speed of fluid discharging from small orifice at depth h below open liquid surface of tank height H.
formulas.explanation: Range is maximized when orifice is drilled at mid-depth $h = H/2$, yielding $R_{max} = H$.

formulas.latex: \Delta P = \frac{2T}{R} \quad (\text{Drop / Bubble in liquid}), \quad \Delta P = \frac{4T}{R} \quad (\text{Soap Bubble in air})
formulas.title: Young-Laplace Equation for Excess Surface Tension Pressure
formulas.derivation: Consider hemispherical cap of bubble of radius $R$: separating line of circumference $2\pi R$ sustains surface tension force $F_T = T(2\pi R)$ for a single interface. Pressure force acting on cross-section is $F_P = \Delta P (\pi R^2)$. Equilibrium requires $\Delta P(\pi R^2) = 2\pi R T \implies \Delta P = \frac{2T}{R}$. A soap bubble in air possesses two surfaces (inner and outer), doubling force to $F_T = 2 \times T(2\pi R)$, yielding $\Delta P = \frac{4T}{R}$.
formulas.description: Overpressure inside a curved interface sustained by surface tension T.
formulas.explanation: Smaller bubbles have higher internal pressure, explaining why connecting two different sized bubbles causes smaller one to empty into larger one.

formulas.title: Jurin's Law for Capillary Rise
formulas.derivation: Meniscus radius of curvature is $R = r / \cos\theta$. Pressure just below meniscus is $P_0 - \frac{2T}{R} = P_0 - \frac{2T\cos\theta}{r}$. Hydrostatic balance at liquid reservoir surface gives $P_0 - \frac{2T\cos\theta}{r} + \rho g h = P_0 \implies \rho g h = \frac{2T\cos\theta}{r} \implies h = \frac{2T\cos\theta}{\rho g r}$.
formulas.description: Height of liquid column drawn up a narrow vertical tube of internal radius r due to wettability.
formulas.explanation: For wetting liquids ($\theta < 90^\circ$, e.g. water-glass), $h > 0$ (rises); for non-wetting liquids ($\theta > 90^\circ$, e.g. mercury), meniscus depresses ($h < 0$).

formulas.title: Stokes' Law and Terminal Velocity
formulas.derivation: Stokes derived laminar creeping drag $F_v = 6\pi\eta rv$ by solving Navier-Stokes equations for low Reynolds number ($Re \ll 1$). At terminal speed $v_t$, net acceleration vanishes: downward gravity equals buoyancy plus viscous drag: $m g = F_B + F_v \implies \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho_s g = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho_f g + 6\pi\eta r v_t$. Solving for $v_t$: $6\pi\eta r v_t = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 (\rho_s - \rho_f) g \implies v_t = \frac{2}{9}\frac{r^2(\rho_s - \rho_f)g}{\eta}$.
formulas.description: Viscous drag force on a creeping sphere of radius r and steady terminal settling speed.
formulas.explanation: Terminal speed scales with radius squared ($v_t \propto r^2$), explaining why tiny mist droplets stay suspended in air for hours.

formulas.title: Poiseuille's Law of Laminar Pipe Flow
formulas.derivation: Consider fluid cylinder of radius $y$ and length $L$: shear force balances pressure drop: $\Delta P (\pi y^2) = -\eta (2\pi y L) \frac{dv}{dy} \implies \frac{dv}{dy} = -\frac{\Delta P}{2\eta L} y$. Integrating with no-slip boundary $v(r) = 0$ gives parabolic velocity profile $v(y) = \frac{\Delta P}{4\eta L}(r^2 - y^2)$. Integrating flux across concentric rings: $Q = \int_0^r v(y) 2\pi y dy = 2\pi \frac{\Delta P}{4\eta L} \int_0^r (r^2 y - y^3) dy = \frac{\pi\Delta P}{2\eta L}\left(\frac{r^4}{2} - \frac{r^4}{4}\right) = \frac{\pi \Delta P r^4}{8\eta L}$.
formulas.description: Steady volumetric flow rate of viscous Newtonian fluid through a circular pipe of radius r and length L.
formulas.explanation: Extreme sensitivity to radius ($r^4$ dependence): halving artery diameter reduces blood flow rate by a factor of 16 for identical pressure.

formulas.title: Bulk Modulus and Compressibility
formulas.derivation: Bulk strain is $-\frac{\Delta V}{V}$ (negative because volume decreases with increasing pressure). Bulk stress is hydraulic pressure increment $\Delta P$. Bulk modulus is defined as ratio $B = \frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}} = \frac{\Delta P}{-\Delta V / V} = -V\frac{dP}{dV}$.
formulas.description: Resistance of substance to uniform volumetric compression and reciprocal isothermal compressibility.
formulas.explanation: For ideal gas: isothermal bulk modulus is $B_{iso} = P$; adiabatic bulk modulus is $B_{adi} = \gamma P$.

formulas.title: Reynolds Number and Turbulence Criterion
formulas.derivation: Inertial force per unit volume scales as $\rho(\vec{v}\cdot\vec{\nabla})\vec{v} \sim \rho \frac{v^2}{D}$. Viscous force per unit volume scales as $\eta \nabla^2 \vec{v} \sim \eta \frac{v}{D^2}$. Ratio of inertial to viscous force is $\frac{\rho v^2 / D}{\eta v / D^2} = \frac{\rho v D}{\eta} = N_R$.
formulas.description: Dimensionless ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces governing flow regime transition.
formulas.explanation: In pipe flow: $N_R < 2000$ indicates laminar streamline flow; $N_R > 3000$ indicates fully turbulent chaotic flow.

formulas.title: Thermal Expansion and Thermal Stress
formulas.derivation: Unconstrained rod expands by $\Delta L = L\alpha \Delta T$. If clamped between rigid immovable supports, supports exert compressive force $F$ to maintain zero net elongation: strain prevented is $\epsilon = \frac{\Delta L}{L} = \alpha \Delta T$. By definition of Young's modulus, stress generated is $\sigma = Y\epsilon = Y\alpha \Delta T$.
formulas.description: Fractional longitudinal thermal expansion and induced compressive/tensile stress when ends are rigidly clamped.
formulas.explanation: Explains why expansion gaps are engineered into railway tracks, bridges, and concrete highways.

content_json.derivation: Hooke's law states stress $\sigma$ is directly proportional to strain $\epsilon$, giving $Y = \sigma / \epsilon$. Work done in stretching is $W = \int_0^{\Delta L} F(x)dx = \int_0^{\Delta L} \frac{YA}{L}x dx = \frac{1}{2}\frac{YA}{L}(\Delta L)^2 = \frac{1}{2}F\Delta L$. Dividing by volume $V = AL$ yields energy density $u = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{F}{A}\right)\left(\frac{\Delta L}{L}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\sigma\epsilon = \frac{1}{2}Y\epsilon^2$.
content_json.explanation: Valid only within proportional limit; material property independent of geometric dimensions.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: Biomolecules Formula Sheet
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: Hans Bethe (1929) developed Crystal Field Theory: in octahedral ligand field, 6 ligands approach along Cartesian axes ($x, y, z$). Orbitals with lobes pointing directly along axes ($d_{x^2-y^2}, d_{z^2}$) experience strong electrostatic repulsion and are destabilized by $+0.6\Delta_o$ ($e_g$). Orbitals directed between axes ($d_{xy}, d_{yz}, d_{xz}$) experience less repulsion and are stabilized by $-0.4\Delta_o$ ($t_{2g}$). In tetrahedral geometry, 4 ligands approach corners of cube (between axes), inverting splitting pattern and reducing splitting magnitude by factor $\Delta_t = \frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$ because fewer ligands are present and none point directly at d-orbitals.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Because $\Delta_t < P$ (pairing energy) always, tetrahedral complexes are almost exclusively high-spin.

formulas.title: Crystal Field Splitting in Octahedral and Tetrahedral Fields
formulas.derivation: Hans Bethe (1929) developed Crystal Field Theory: in octahedral ligand field, 6 ligands approach along Cartesian axes ($x, y, z$). Orbitals with lobes pointing directly along axes ($d_{x^2-y^2}, d_{z^2}$) experience strong electrostatic repulsion and are destabilized by $+0.6\Delta_o$ ($e_g$). Orbitals directed between axes ($d_{xy}, d_{yz}, d_{xz}$) experience less repulsion and are stabilized by $-0.4\Delta_o$ ($t_{2g}$). In tetrahedral geometry, 4 ligands approach corners of cube (between axes), inverting splitting pattern and reducing splitting magnitude by factor $\Delta_t = \frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$ because fewer ligands are present and none point directly at d-orbitals.
formulas.description: Splitting of degenerate d-orbitals into $t_{2g}/e_g$ and $e/t_2$ manifolds in electrostatic ligand fields.
formulas.explanation: Because $\Delta_t < P$ (pairing energy) always, tetrahedral complexes are almost exclusively high-spin.

formulas.title: Crystal Field Stabilization Energy (CFSE) for Octahedral Complexes

variables.m: Number of extra electron pairs formed relative to free ion

formulas.derivation: Barycenter rule requires total energy shift of the 5 degenerate orbitals to sum to zero: $3(-0.4\Delta_o) + 2(+0.6\Delta_o) = -1.2\Delta_o + 1.2\Delta_o = 0$. Each electron occupying lower $t_{2g}$ level stabilizes complex by $-0.4\Delta_o$, while each electron occupying upper $e_g$ level destabilizes complex by $+0.6\Delta_o$. Summing contributions gives $CFSE = (-0.4 n_{t_{2g}} + 0.6 n_{e_g})\Delta_o$. When electrons pair in same orbital against Coulomb repulsion, pairing energy $+mP$ is added.
formulas.description: Net energetic stabilization of d-electron configuration relative to spherical barycenter.
formulas.explanation: If $\Delta_o > P$ (strong field ligands like $CN^-, CO$), pairing occurs producing low-spin complex. If $\Delta_o < P$ (weak field ligands like $F^-, Cl^-$), Hund's rule dominates producing high-spin complex.

formulas.latex: I^- < Br^- < S^{2-} < SCN^- < Cl^- < NO_3^- < N_3^- < F^- < OH^- < C_2O_4^{2-} < H_2O < NCS^- < CH_3CN < py < NH_3 < en < bipy < phen < NO_2^- < PPh_3 < CN^- < CO
formulas.title: Spectrochemical Series of Ligands
formulas.derivation: Derived from UV-visible absorption spectra ($d-d$ transition band wavenumbers $\Delta_o = h c \bar{\nu}$). Ligands fall into three classes based on metal-ligand bonding: (1) Halides and oxygen donors are $\pi$-donors: ligand filled p-orbitals donate electron density into metal $t_{2g}$, destabilizing $t_{2g}$ and shrinking $\Delta_o$ (weak field). (2) Ammonia and amines are pure $\sigma$-donors: intermediate $\Delta_o$. (3) $CN^-$ and $CO$ are strong $\pi$-acceptors (back-bonding): empty $\pi^*$ orbitals accept electron density from metal $t_{2g}$, dramatically stabilizing $t_{2g}$ and expanding $\Delta_o$ (strong field).
formulas.description: Empirical ranking of ligands according to increasing magnitude of crystal field splitting $\Delta_o$.
formulas.explanation: Enables predicting whether transition metal complex is high-spin or low-spin, and determines magnetic and color properties.

formulas.title: Magnetic Moments of Coordination Complexes

variables.\\mu_{eff}: Effective magnetic moment in Bohr Magnetons (BM)

formulas.derivation: In first-row ($3d$) transition metal complexes, non-spherical electrostatic crystal field of surrounding ligands quenches orbital angular momentum ($L \approx 0$) by breaking spatial rotational symmetry. Magnetic moment reduces to spin-only expression: $\mu_s = g\sqrt{S(S+1)}\mu_B$. With electron g-factor $g \approx 2.00$ and $S = n/2$: $\mu_s = 2\sqrt{\frac{n}{2}\left(\frac{n+2}{2}\right)} = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\mu_B$.
formulas.description: Spin-only magnetic moment and complete spin-plus-orbital magnetic moment for first-row transition ions.
formulas.explanation: Guouy balance magnetic measurement directly diagnoses high-spin vs low-spin states (e.g. $[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}$ has $n=1, \mu = 1.73\text{ BM}$ while $[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{3+}$ has $n=5, \mu = 5.92\text{ BM}$).

formulas.title: Sidgwick's Effective Atomic Number (EAN) Rule / 18-Electron Rule
formulas.derivation: Nevild Sidgwick (1927) proposed that coordinate covalent bonds donate 2 electrons per coordination bond. The total effective electrons surrounding metal core is $EAN = Z - (\text{oxidation state}) + 2 \times (\text{ligand pairs})$. If $EAN$ equals the atomic number of the next noble gas ($Kr=36, Xe=54, Rn=86$), the complex possesses a completely filled valence shell of 18 electrons ($ns^2 (n-1)d^{10} np^6$), conferring high kinetic and thermodynamic stability.
formulas.description: Predicts stability of coordination and organometallic complexes by mimicking next noble gas configuration.
formulas.explanation: Explains stoichiometry of metal carbonyls: $Ni(CO)_4$ ($28 - 0 + 8 = 36$, $18e^-$), $Fe(CO)_5$ ($26 - 0 + 10 = 36$), $Cr(CO)_6$ ($24 - 0 + 12 = 36$).

formulas.title: Stepwise and Overall Formation Constants of Complexes
formulas.derivation: Ligand complexation occurs in sequential stepwise equilibria: $M + L \rightleftharpoons ML$ ($k_1 = \frac{[ML]}{[M][L]}$); $ML + L \rightleftharpoons ML_2$ ($k_2 = \frac{[ML_2]}{[ML][L]}$); $\dots$ $ML_{n-1} + L \rightleftharpoons ML_n$ ($k_n = \frac{[ML_n]}{[ML_{n-1}][L]}$). Overall reaction is $M + n L \rightleftharpoons ML_n$ with equilibrium constant $\beta_n = \frac{[ML_n]}{[M][L]^n}$. Multiplying stepwise constants gives $k_1 \cdot k_2 \dots k_n = \frac{[ML]}{[M][L]} \frac{[ML_2]}{[ML][L]} \dots \frac{[ML_n]}{[ML_{n-1}][L]} = \frac{[ML_n]}{[M][L]^n} = \beta_n$.
formulas.description: Thermodynamic stability constants for stepwise ligand addition equilibrium $ML_{n-1} + L \rightleftharpoons ML_n$.
formulas.explanation: Typically $k_1 > k_2 > k_3 > \dots > k_n$ due to statistical factors and steric hindrance.

formulas.latex: \Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ \quad (\Delta S^\circ > 0 \implies \text{Chelate Effect})
formulas.title: The Chelate Effect
formulas.derivation: Consider substitution of 6 monodentate ligands by 3 bidentate ligands: $[Ni(NH_3)_6]^{2+} + 3 en \rightleftharpoons [Ni(en)_3]^{2+} + 6 NH_3$. Reactant count is $1 + 3 = 4$ species; product count is $1 + 6 = 7$ species. Net increase of 3 independent dissolved particles generates substantial positive entropy of reaction: $\Delta S^\circ \gg 0$. Since $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$, this large positive entropy makes $\Delta G^\circ$ significantly more negative, driving formation constant higher by several orders of magnitude.
formulas.description: Enhanced thermodynamic stability of polydentate chelate complexes over monodentate analogues driven by positive entropy.
formulas.explanation: EDTA ($hexadentate$) forms extremely stable complexes with almost all metal cations ($1 + 1 \to 1 + 6$ displacement release).

formulas.latex: t_{2g}^3 e_g^1, \quad t_{2g}^6 e_g^1, \quad t_{2g}^6 e_g^3 \implies \text{Jahn-Teller Distortion}
formulas.title: Jahn-Teller Theorem Distortion

variables.d^9, d^4, d^7: Electronic configurations exhibiting strong Jahn-Teller effect

formulas.derivation: Hermann Jahn and Edward Teller (1937) proved mathematically that any non-linear molecular system in an electronically degenerate ground state is inherently unstable and will undergo geometric distortion to lower its symmetry, remove orbital degeneracy, and lower overall energy. In octahedral $d^9$ complexes (e.g. $Cu^{2+}$: $t_{2g}^6 e_g^3$), the odd electron can reside in either $d_{z^2}$ or $d_{x^2-y^2}$. Elongating along z-axis lowers energy of $d_{z^2}$ and destabilizes $d_{x^2-y^2}$, yielding 4 short equatorial bonds and 2 elongated axial bonds (tetragonal distortion).
formulas.description: Geometric distortion of non-linear degenerate electronic states to remove orbital degeneracy and lower energy.
formulas.explanation: Explains why $Cu(II)$ octahedral complexes are never perfectly regular octahedra, displaying pronounced axial elongation.

formulas.latex: r_{tet} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a - r_{anion} \approx 0.225 r_A, \quad r_{oct} = \frac{a}{2} - r_{anion} \approx 0.414 r_A
formulas.title: Radius Ratio Rules for Coordination Polyhedra in Solid State
formulas.derivation: Geometric contact condition requires central cation to touch all surrounding anions without anions overlapping: Linear ($CN=2$): $r_+/r_- < 0.155$. Trigonal planar ($CN=3$): $0.155 \le r_+/r_- < 0.225$. Tetrahedral ($CN=4$): geometry gives $\cos(109.5^\circ/2) = \frac{r_-}{r_+ + r_-} \implies r_+/r_- = \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2} - 1 = 0.225$. Octahedral ($CN=6$): square in-plane diagonal gives $2(r_+ + r_-) = \sqrt{2}(2r_-) \implies r_+/r_- = \sqrt{2} - 1 = 0.414$. Cubic ($CN=8$): body diagonal gives $2(r_+ + r_-) = \sqrt{3}(2r_-) \implies r_+/r_- = \sqrt{3} - 1 = 0.732$.
formulas.description: Limiting radius ratios determining stable coordination numbers (tetrahedral, octahedral, cubic) in ionic crystals.
formulas.explanation: Example: $NaCl$ ($r_{Na+}/r_{Cl-} = 0.525$, in $0.414 - 0.732$ range $\implies CN=6$ octahedral); $CsCl$ ($0.93 > 0.732 \implies CN=8$ cubic).

formulas.title: Crystalline Unit Cell Density Formula

variables.Z: Number of formula units per unit cell

formulas.derivation: Density is mass divided by volume: $\rho = \frac{m_{cell}}{V_{cell}}$. Volume of cubic unit cell is $V = a^3$. Mass of unit cell is mass of $Z$ formula units: $m_{cell} = Z \times m_{atom} = Z \times \left(\frac{M}{N_A}\right)$. Substituting yields $\rho = \frac{Z \cdot M}{N_A \cdot a^3}$. Lattice parameters: Simple cubic ($Z=1, a=2R$); Body-centered cubic ($Z=2, \sqrt{3}a = 4R$); Face-centered cubic ($Z=4, \sqrt{2}a = 4R$).
formulas.description: Calculates macroscopic solid crystal density directly from unit cell edge length a and lattice particle count Z.
formulas.explanation: Fundamental crystallographic formula connecting atomic micro-structure to macroscopic laboratory density.

formulas.latex: 2 d \sin\theta = n \lambda \quad (\text{Bragg's Law of X-Ray Diffraction})
formulas.title: Bragg's Law of Crystal X-Ray Diffraction
formulas.derivation: William Henry Bragg and William Lawrence Bragg (1913) treated crystal planes as specular semi-reflecting mirrors. Path difference between rays reflected from two adjacent parallel planes separated by distance $d$ is $\Delta x = 2 d\sin\theta$. Constructive interference produces sharp diffraction peaks when path difference is an integer number of wavelengths: $2d\sin\theta = n\lambda$. For cubic crystal with Miller indices $(h, k, l)$: $d_{hkl} = \frac{a}{\sqrt{h^2 + k^2 + l^2}}$.
formulas.description: Constructive interference condition for X-rays reflected from parallel lattice planes separated by spacing d.
formulas.explanation: Primary experimental technique for solving 3D atomic structures of crystalline solids, proteins, and DNA.

formulas.title: Freundlich Adsorption Isotherm

variables.x/m: Mass of gas adsorbed per unit mass of solid adsorbent
variables.k, n: Freundlich empirical constants depending on adsorbent and gas

formulas.derivation: Herbert Freundlich (1909) deduced an empirical isotherm for multilayer/heterogeneous adsorption: $x/m = k P^{1/n}$. Taking base-10 logarithm: $\log(x/m) = \log k + \frac{1}{n}\log P$. Plotting $\log(x/m)$ versus $\log P$ yields straight line of slope $1/n$ ($0 \le 1/n \le 1$) and y-intercept $\log k$.
formulas.description: Empirical power-law relation for gas adsorption on solid heterogeneous surface at constant temperature.
formulas.explanation: At low pressure ($1/n = 1$): $x/m \propto P$. At high pressure ($1/n = 0$): $x/m = \text{constant}$ (adsorption saturation).

catalog_formula_sheets.name: Thermodynamics Formula Sheet
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: From universal energy conservation: change in internal state function $U$ equals energy entering system as heat ($q$) plus energy entering as mechanical boundary work ($w$). Under IUPAC sign convention, work done on the system by surroundings during compression is positive ($w > 0$), while work done by expanding system against external pressure $P_{ext}$ is negative: $w = -\int P_{ext}dV = -P_{ext}\Delta V$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: At constant volume (bomb calorimeter), $\Delta V = 0 \implies w = 0$, so $\Delta U = q_v$.

content_json.title: Thermodynamics Formula Sheet

sections.title: Thermodynamics Formula Sheet - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.latex: \Delta U = q + w = q - P_{ext}\Delta V
formulas.title: First Law of Chemical Thermodynamics (IUPAC Convention)
formulas.derivation: From universal energy conservation: change in internal state function $U$ equals energy entering system as heat ($q$) plus energy entering as mechanical boundary work ($w$). Under IUPAC sign convention, work done on the system by surroundings during compression is positive ($w > 0$), while work done by expanding system against external pressure $P_{ext}$ is negative: $w = -\int P_{ext}dV = -P_{ext}\Delta V$.
formulas.description: Conservation of energy for chemical system: heat absorbed plus mechanical work performed on the system.
formulas.explanation: At constant volume (bomb calorimeter), $\Delta V = 0 \implies w = 0$, so $\Delta U = q_v$.

formulas.title: Enthalpy and Internal Energy Relation for Chemical Reactions

variables.\\Delta n_g: Moles of gaseous products minus moles of gaseous reactants

formulas.derivation: By definition, enthalpy is $H = U + PV$. For finite change at constant pressure: $\Delta H = \Delta U + P\Delta V$. For ideal gas reaction where volume change is dominated by gases: $P V = n_g R T \implies P\Delta V = (\Delta n_g) R T$. Substituting yields $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g R T$.
formulas.description: Relates constant-pressure reaction heat $\Delta H$ to constant-volume reaction heat $\Delta U$ for ideal gas mixtures.
formulas.explanation: If $\Delta n_g = 0$ (e.g. $H_{2(g)} + I_{2(g)} \to 2HI_{(g)}$), $\Delta H = \Delta U$. If $\Delta n_g > 0$, expansion work means $\Delta H > \Delta U$.

formulas.title: Hess's Law and Standard Enthalpy of Reaction
formulas.derivation: Germain Hess (1840) established that because enthalpy $H$ is a thermodynamic state function, net heat evolved or absorbed in a chemical process depends solely on initial and final states, independent of pathway. By convention, standard enthalpies of formation of pure elements in reference standard states ($O_{2(g)}, C_{(graphite)}, H_{2(g)}$) are assigned zero: $\Delta_f H^\circ = 0$. Summing product enthalpies and subtracting reactant enthalpies gives the formula.
formulas.description: Reaction enthalpy calculated by summing standard enthalpies of formation of products minus reactants.
formulas.explanation: Allows indirect calculation of reaction heats that cannot be measured directly in a calorimeter.

formulas.title: Reaction Enthalpy from Bond Enthalpies
formulas.derivation: In a gas-phase reaction, chemical bonds in reactant molecules are first homolytically cleaved into isolated gaseous atoms (an endothermic process requiring energy input: $+ \sum BE_{reactants}$). The isolated atoms then recombine to synthesize product molecules (an exothermic process releasing energy: $- \sum BE_{products}$). By Hess's Law, the net reaction enthalpy is $\Delta_r H = \sum BE_{reactants} - \sum BE_{products}$.
formulas.description: Estimates gas-phase reaction enthalpy from homolytic covalent bond dissociation energies.
formulas.explanation: Applies strictly to gas-phase reactions with non-delocalized, localized covalent bonds.

formulas.latex: \frac{\Delta H_{T_2} - \Delta H_{T_1}}{T_2 - T_1} = \Delta C_p = \sum \nu_p C_{p, prod} - \sum \nu_r C_{p, react}
formulas.title: Kirchhoff's Law of Thermochemistry

variables.\\Delta C_p: Net change in molar heat capacity at constant pressure

formulas.derivation: At constant pressure, $\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial T}\right)_P = C_p$. Differentiating reaction enthalpy $\Delta_r H = H_{prod} - H_{react}$ with respect to temperature: $\frac{d(\Delta_r H)}{dT} = \left(\frac{\partial H_{prod}}{\partial T}\right) - \left(\frac{\partial H_{react}}{\partial T}\right) = C_{p, prod} - C_{p, react} = \Delta C_p$. Integrating from $T_1$ to $T_2$ assuming $\Delta C_p$ is approximately constant yields Kirchhoff's relation: $\Delta H_{T_2} = \Delta H_{T_1} + \Delta C_p (T_2 - T_1)$.
formulas.description: Temperature dependence of reaction enthalpy governed by reaction heat capacity change $\Delta C_p$.
formulas.explanation: If $\Delta C_p > 0$, reaction becomes more endothermic (or less exothermic) as temperature rises.

formulas.title: Second Law of Thermodynamics and Entropy Change
formulas.derivation: Rudolf Clausius (1865) proved that for any reversible cyclic process, $\oint \frac{dq_{rev}}{T} = 0$, establishing that $dS = \frac{dq_{rev}}{T}$ is an exact differential of a state function. For any spontaneous irreversible process, Clausius inequality gives $\oint \frac{dq}{T} < 0$, leading to $\Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr} = \Delta S_{univ} > 0$. At reversible equilibrium, $\Delta S_{univ} = 0$.
formulas.description: Definition of entropy as state function and universal condition for spontaneous irreversible processes.
formulas.explanation: All spontaneous real processes in the universe proceed with an overall increase in total entropy ($\Delta S_{univ} > 0$).

formulas.latex: \Delta S_{ideal\_gas} = n C_v \ln\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) + n R \ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right) = n C_p \ln\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) - n R \ln\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)
formulas.title: Entropy Change of an Ideal Gas
formulas.derivation: From First Law for reversible path: $dq_{rev} = dU - dw_{rev} = n C_v dT + P\,dV$. Dividing by $T$ using ideal gas law $P/T = nR/V$: $dS = \frac{dq_{rev}}{T} = n C_v \frac{dT}{T} + n R \frac{dV}{V}$. Integrating from initial state $(T_1, V_1)$ to final state $(T_2, V_2)$: $\Delta S = n C_v \ln(T_2 / T_1) + n R \ln(V_2 / V_1)$. Using $V_2 / V_1 = (T_2 P_1) / (T_1 P_2)$ and Mayer's relation $C_p = C_v + R$ gives the pressure form.
formulas.description: Entropy calculation for an ideal gas undergoing simultaneous temperature, volume, or pressure transitions.
formulas.explanation: For isothermal process ($T_1 = T_2$), $\Delta S = n R \ln(V_2/V_1) = -n R \ln(P_2/P_1)$.

formulas.latex: \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S, \quad \Delta G_{sys} = -T\Delta S_{univ} < 0 \text{ (Spontaneous)}
formulas.title: Gibbs Free Energy and Spontaneity Criterion
formulas.derivation: At constant $T$ and $P$, heat transferred to surroundings is $q_{surr} = -q_{sys} = -\Delta H_{sys}$. Surrounding entropy change is $\Delta S_{surr} = \frac{q_{surr}}{T} = -\frac{\Delta H_{sys}}{T}$. Universal entropy change is $\Delta S_{univ} = \Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr} = \Delta S_{sys} - \frac{\Delta H_{sys}}{T}$. Multiplying by $-T$: $-T\Delta S_{univ} = \Delta H_{sys} - T\Delta S_{sys}$. Defining Gibbs free energy $G = H - TS$ gives $\Delta G_{sys} = -T\Delta S_{univ}$. Since $\Delta S_{univ} > 0$ for spontaneity, $\Delta G_{sys} < 0$.
formulas.description: Thermodynamic potential determining spontaneity of chemical processes at constant temperature and pressure.
formulas.explanation: Criterion for spontaneity at constant $T, P$: $\Delta G < 0$ (spontaneous, exergonic); $\Delta G = 0$ (dynamic equilibrium); $\Delta G > 0$ (non-spontaneous, endergonic).

formulas.latex: \Delta G^\circ = -R T \ln K = -2.303 R T \log_{10} K
formulas.title: Standard Gibbs Free Energy and Equilibrium Constant Relation
formulas.derivation:
Chemical potential of species $i$ in mixture is $\mu_i = \mu_i^\circ + RT\ln a_i$. Reaction Gibbs free energy is $\Delta_r G = \sum 
u_i \mu_i = \sum 
u_i \mu_i^\circ + RT \sum 
u_i \ln a_i = \Delta_r G^\circ + RT\ln Q$ where $Q = \prod a_i^{
u_i}$ is the reaction quotient. At dynamic chemical equilibrium, net driving force vanishes: $\Delta_r G = 0$ and $Q = K_{eq}$. Substituting gives $0 = \Delta_r G^\circ + RT\ln K \implies \Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$.
formulas.description: Fundamental thermodynamic bridge connecting chemical equilibrium constant K to standard state free energy $\Delta G^\circ$.
formulas.explanation: If $\Delta G^\circ < 0$, then $K > 1$ (products favored at equilibrium); if $\Delta G^\circ > 0$, $K < 1$ (reactants favored).

formulas.title: van 't Hoff Equation
formulas.derivation: From $\ln K = -\frac{\Delta G^\circ}{RT} = -\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{RT} + \frac{\Delta S^\circ}{R}$. Differentiating with respect to temperature $T$ assuming $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ are independent of $T$: $\frac{d\ln K}{dT} = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{RT^2}$. Integrating from $T_1$ to $T_2$: $\int_{K_1}^{K_2} d\ln K = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\int_{T_1}^{T_2} T^{-2}dT \implies \ln(K_2/K_1) = -\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right) = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right)$.
formulas.description: Temperature sensitivity of chemical equilibrium constant governed by standard reaction enthalpy.
formulas.explanation: Thermodynamic proof of Le Chatelier's principle: for endothermic reactions ($\Delta H^\circ > 0$), increasing temperature increases $K$; for exothermic reactions ($\Delta H^\circ < 0$), increasing temperature decreases $K$.

formulas.latex: \Delta S_{fus} = \frac{\Delta H_{fus}}{T_m}, \quad \Delta S_{vap} = \frac{\Delta H_{vap}}{T_b} \approx 88 \text{ J/mol K (Trouton's Rule)}
formulas.title: Entropy of Phase Transitions and Trouton's Rule
formulas.derivation: At normal melting and boiling points, the two phases coexist in reversible dynamic equilibrium: $\Delta G = 0 \implies \Delta H - T\Delta S = 0 \implies \Delta S = \Delta H / T$. Trouton (1884) noted empirically that for non-associated liquids vaporizing to gas, the volume increase is roughly constant ($\sim 1000\times$), giving universal entropy of vaporization $\Delta S_{vap} = \frac{\Delta H_{vap}}{T_b} \approx 85 - 88\text{ J/mol K}$.
formulas.description: Entropy of fusion and vaporization at equilibrium phase transition temperatures.
formulas.explanation: Hydrogen-bonded liquids (water: $\Delta S_{vap} \approx 109\text{ J/mol K}$, ethanol) deviate positively from Trouton's rule due to high liquid-state order.

formulas.latex: S = k_B \ln \Omega, \quad S(T=0) = 0 \quad (\text{Third Law of Thermodynamics})
formulas.title: Boltzmann Entropy Formula and Third Law

variables.\\Omega: Number of accessible microstates corresponding to macroscopic state

formulas.derivation: Ludwig Boltzmann (1877) proved entropy is a logarithmic measure of microscopic multiplicity: $S = k_B \ln\Omega$. Nernst and Planck formulated the Third Law: as temperature approaches absolute zero ($T \to 0\text{ K}$), thermal motion ceases, and a perfectly ordered pure crystalline lattice settles into a unique non-degenerate quantum ground state ($\Omega = 1$). Therefore, $S_0 = k_B\ln(1) = 0$.
formulas.description: Microscopic statistical definition of entropy and absolute zero entropy of perfect crystalline substances.
formulas.explanation: Allows establishing absolute standard entropies $S^\circ$ for chemical substances, unlike internal energy or enthalpy which are only known relative to arbitrary references.

formulas.title: Maximum Non-Expansion Work and Cell EMF
formulas.derivation: From fundamental thermodynamic equation $dG = V dP - S dT + dw_{non-PV}$. At constant $T$ and $P$, $dG = dw_{non-PV}$. For reversible electrochemical cell, charge transferred is $Q = n F$, and electrical work done by cell is $w_{elec} = Q E_{cell} = n F E_{cell}$. Work done on system is $w = -n F E_{cell}$. Hence $\Delta G = -n F E_{cell}$.
formulas.description: Decrease in Gibbs free energy equals the maximum electrical reversible work extracted from an electrochemical cell.
formulas.explanation: For spontaneous galvanic cell, $E_{cell} > 0 \implies \Delta G < 0$.

formulas.latex: C_p - C_v = T \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = \frac{T V \beta^2}{\kappa_T}
formulas.title: General Thermodynamic Heat Capacity Difference
formulas.derivation: Internal energy differential is $dU = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_V dT + \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T dV$. Dividing by $dT$ at constant $P$ and noting $dH = dU + P\,dV + V\,dP$: $C_p - C_v = \left[P + \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T\right]\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P$. Using Maxwell relation $\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T = T\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V - P$, the $P$ terms cancel, yielding $C_p - C_v = T\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = \frac{TV\beta^2}{\kappa_T}$. For ideal gas ($PV = nRT$), $\beta = 1/T$ and $\kappa_T = 1/P$, recovering Mayer's relation $C_p - C_v = R$.
formulas.description: Universal relationship between isobaric and isochoric heat capacities for any substance (solid, liquid, or gas).
formulas.explanation: Because $T > 0, V > 0, \kappa_T > 0$, and $\beta^2 \ge 0$, $C_p$ is strictly greater than or equal to $C_v$ for all physical materials.

content_json.derivation: From universal energy conservation: change in internal state function $U$ equals energy entering system as heat ($q$) plus energy entering as mechanical boundary work ($w$). Under IUPAC sign convention, work done on the system by surroundings during compression is positive ($w > 0$), while work done by expanding system against external pressure $P_{ext}$ is negative: $w = -\int P_{ext}dV = -P_{ext}\Delta V$.
content_json.explanation: At constant volume (bomb calorimeter), $\Delta V = 0 \implies w = 0$, so $\Delta U = q_v$.

Setting $\omega^2 = k/m$ gives characteristic roots $r = \pm i\omega$. General real solution is $x(t) = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)$.

formulas.title: Differential Equation of Simple Harmonic Motion
formulas.derivation: Restoring force is Hooke's linear relation $F = -kx$. By Newton's second law: $m\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -kx \implies \frac{d^2x}{dt^2} + \frac{k}{m}x = 0$. Setting $\omega^2 = k/m$ gives characteristic roots $r = \pm i\omega$. General real solution is $x(t) = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)$.
formulas.description: Standard linear second-order differential equation describing simple harmonic oscillation.
formulas.explanation: Acceleration is always directed toward mean position and linearly proportional to displacement: $a(t) = -\omega^2 x(t)$.

formulas.title: Velocity as a Function of Position in SHM
formulas.derivation: From $a = v\frac{dv}{dx} = -\omega^2 x$. Separating variables: $v\,dv = -\omega^2 x\,dx$. Integrating from displacement $x$ (velocity $v$) to extreme $x=A$ (velocity $0$): $\int_v^0 v'dv' = -\omega^2 \int_x^A x'dx' \implies -\frac{v^2}{2} = -\frac{\omega^2}{2}(A^2 - x^2) \implies v = \pm\omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$.
formulas.description: Quadratic relationship between velocity and displacement from equilibrium in SHM.
formulas.explanation: Velocity reaches peak $v_{max} = \omega A$ at mean position ($x=0$) and vanishes at turning points ($x = \pm A$).

formulas.latex: E_{total} = K + U = \frac{1}{2}m v^2 + \frac{1}{2}k x^2 = \frac{1}{2}m \omega^2 A^2 = \frac{1}{2}k A^2
formulas.title: Total Mechanical Energy Conservation in SHM
formulas.derivation: Substitute $x(t) = A\sin(\omega t)$ and $v(t) = A\omega\cos(\omega t)$: $U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 \sin^2(\omega t)$, $K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}m(A\omega)^2 \cos^2(\omega t) = \frac{1}{2}kA^2\cos^2(\omega t)$. Summing: $E = K + U = \frac{1}{2}kA^2(\sin^2\omega t + \cos^2\omega t) = \frac{1}{2}kA^2$.
formulas.description: Sum of kinetic and potential energies remains constant at all points throughout oscillation.
formulas.explanation: Kinetic and potential energies oscillate at double frequency ($2\omega$). Time averages are equal: $\langle K \rangle = \langle U \rangle = \frac{1}{4}kA^2 = \frac{1}{2}E_{total}$.

formulas.title: Time Period of Simple Pendulum (Small and Large Lengths)
formulas.derivation: Restoring torque about suspension point is $\tau = -mgL\sin\theta \approx -mgL\theta$. Using $I = mL^2$: $mL^2\alpha = -mgL\theta \implies \alpha + \frac{g}{L}\theta = 0 \implies \omega = \sqrt{g/L} \implies T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$. If pendulum length $L$ is comparable to Earth radius $R$, accounting for non-parallel gravity vectors gives effective restoring force $F = -mg\left(\frac{x}{L} + \frac{x}{R}\right)$, leading to $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{1}{g(1/L + 1/R)}}$.
formulas.description: Period of small-amplitude pendulum, including finite Earth curvature correction for ultra-long pendulums.
formulas.explanation: As $L \to \infty$, period reaches asymptotic finite upper limit $T_{max} = 2\pi\sqrt{R/g} \approx 84.6\text{ minutes}$ (identical to near-Earth satellite orbital period).

formulas.latex: v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} \quad (\text{String}), \quad v = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma P}{\rho}} = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma R T}{M}} \quad (\text{Sound / Laplace})
formulas.title: Wave Speed on Stretched String and Laplace Formula for Sound
formulas.derivation: For string: consider small curved pulse arc $ds$ of radius $R$: net centripetal tension component is $2T\sin(\Delta\theta/2) \approx T\Delta\theta = T(ds/R)$. Mass of element is $dm = \mu\,ds$. Centripetal equation is $T\frac{ds}{R} = dm \frac{v^2}{R} = (\mu\,ds)\frac{v^2}{R} \implies v = \sqrt{T/\mu}$. For sound: Newton assumed isothermal compression ($v = \sqrt{P/\rho}$), which underpredicted speed by 15%. Laplace corrected this: sound vibrations are so rapid that no heat exchanges occur, making process adiabatic ($B = \gamma P$), giving $v = \sqrt{\gamma P / \rho} = \sqrt{\gamma RT / M}$.
formulas.description: Propagation velocity of transverse waves on a string and longitudinal acoustic waves in gas.
formulas.explanation: Sound speed in gas depends strictly on temperature ($v \propto \sqrt{T}$) and is completely independent of pressure at constant temperature.

formulas.title: Doppler Effect for Acoustic Waves
formulas.derivation: Let sound travel with speed $v$ through still air. When source moves toward observer with $v_s$, wavefronts compress to wavelength $\lambda' = \frac{v - v_s}{f_0}$. If observer moves toward source with $v_o$, relative speed of waves entering ear is $v_{rel} = v + v_o$. Apparent frequency detected is $f' = \frac{v_{rel}}{\lambda'} = \frac{v + v_o}{(v - v_s)/f_0} = f_0\left(\frac{v + v_o}{v - v_s}\right)$.
formulas.description: Apparent frequency shift detected by an observer when source and/or observer are in relative motion through medium.
formulas.explanation: Upper signs correspond to approach (frequency increases); lower signs correspond to recession (frequency decreases).

formulas.latex: f_n = n \frac{v}{2L} \quad (\text{String / Open Pipe}), \quad f_m = (2m - 1)\frac{v}{4L} \quad (\text{Closed Pipe})
formulas.title: Harmonics in Resonant Standing Waves
formulas.derivation: String fixed at both ends or pipe open at both ends: boundary condition requires node at both ends or antinode at both ends: length must accommodate integral half-wavelengths $L = n\frac{\lambda}{2} \implies \lambda_n = \frac{2L}{n} \implies f_n = \frac{v}{\lambda_n} = n\frac{v}{2L}$ (all harmonics $1, 2, 3...$ present). Pipe closed at one end: closed end has displacement node, open end has antinode: length must accommodate odd quarter-wavelengths $L = (2m - 1)\frac{\lambda}{4} \implies f_m = (2m - 1)\frac{v}{4L}$ (only odd harmonics $1, 3, 5...$ present).
formulas.description: Resonant eigenfrequencies for strings fixed at both ends, open organ pipes, and pipes closed at one end.
formulas.explanation: Open organ pipes produce richer acoustic tone quality because all even and odd harmonics are generated.

formulas.title: Beat Frequency
formulas.derivation: Superposition of two waves of equal amplitude: $y(t) = A\cos(2\pi f_1 t) + A\cos(2\pi f_2 t) = 2A\cos\left(2\pi\frac{f_1 - f_2}{2}t\right)\cos\left(2\pi\frac{f_1 + f_2}{2}t\right)$. Intensity is proportional to envelope amplitude squared: $I \propto 4A^2 \cos^2\left(\pi(f_1 - f_2)t\right) = 2A^2 [1 + \cos(2\pi(f_1 - f_2)t)]$. The frequency of intensity maxima is $|f_1 - f_2|$.
formulas.description: Periodic modulation of perceived sound intensity resulting from superposition of two waves of slightly differing frequencies.
formulas.explanation: Used for tuning musical instruments and acoustic resonance detection.

formulas.latex: I = 2\pi^2 \rho v f^2 A^2 = \frac{1}{2}\rho v \omega^2 A^2, \quad \beta = 10\log_{10}\left(\frac{I}{I_0}\right) \text{ dB}
formulas.title: Acoustic Wave Intensity and Decibel Sound Level
formulas.derivation: Energy density of harmonic wave is $u = \frac{1}{2}\rho \omega^2 A^2$. Energy passing through unit cross-sectional area per unit time is intensity $I = u v = \frac{1}{2}\rho v \omega^2 A^2$. Human perceived loudness scales logarithmically, defined as decibel level $\beta = 10\log_{10}(I/I_0)$.
formulas.description: Energy flux per unit area carried by wave and logarithmic decibel loudness scale.
formulas.explanation: A 10-fold increase in intensity corresponds to a $+10\text{ dB}$ increase; a 2-fold increase corresponds to $+3\text{ dB}$.

formulas.title: Damped Harmonic Oscillator
formulas.derivation: Newton's law: $m\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -kx - b\frac{dx}{dt} \implies \frac{d^2x}{dt^2} + 2\gamma \frac{dx}{dt} + \omega_0^2 x = 0$. Characteristic equation $r^2 + 2\gamma r + \omega_0^2 = 0$ has roots $r = -\gamma \pm i\sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \gamma^2}$. In underdamped regime ($\gamma < \omega_0$), solution is $x(t) = A_0 e^{-\gamma t}\cos(\omega' t + \phi)$.
formulas.description: Trajectory of underdamped harmonic motion experiencing linear viscous damping force $F_d = -b v$.
formulas.explanation: Mechanical energy decays exponentially with time constant $\tau = \frac{1}{2\gamma} = \frac{m}{b}$: $E(t) = E_0 e^{-2\gamma t}$.

formulas.title: Driven Harmonic Resonance Amplitude
formulas.derivation: Equation of motion is $\ddot{x} + 2\gamma\dot{x} + \omega_0^2 x = \frac{F_0}{m}\cos(\omega t)$. Using complex trial solution $x = X e^{i\omega t}$: $(-\omega^2 + 2i\gamma\omega + \omega_0^2)X = \frac{F_0}{m}$. Solving for magnitude $|X|$ gives $A(\omega) = \frac{F_0 / m}{\sqrt{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + (2\gamma\omega)^2}}$.
formulas.description: Steady-state oscillation amplitude when driven by periodic external force $F(t) = F_0\cos(\omega t)$.
formulas.explanation: Resonance peak occurs near $\omega_{res} = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - 2\gamma^2}$; quality factor $Q = \frac{\omega_0}{2\gamma}$ measures sharpness of resonance peak.

formulas.latex: e = 0.6 \, r \implies L_{eff} = L + e \quad (\text{One end open}), \quad L_{eff} = L + 2e \quad (\text{Both open})
formulas.title: Acoustic End Correction for Organ Pipes
formulas.derivation: Air molecules slightly outside the open end oscillate with the acoustic wave column, effectively extending acoustic boundary by distance $e \approx 0.6 r$ (derived analytically by Helmholtz and Rayleigh). Resonance conditions apply strictly to $L_{eff} = L + 0.6r$ for closed pipe, and $L_{eff} = L + 1.2r$ for pipe open at both ends.
formulas.description: Effective lengthening of acoustic pipe column due to vibrational antinode forming slightly beyond open tube boundary.
formulas.explanation: Allows determining sound speed with resonance tube apparatus by subtracting lengths of two successive resonances: $\lambda/2 = L_2 - L_1$, eliminating $e$ completely.

formulas.latex: F = G \frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}, \quad G = 6.674 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2/\text{kg}^2
formulas.title: Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
formulas.derivation: Kepler's third law $T^2 \propto r^3$ and circular orbit acceleration $a = \frac{v^2}{r} = \frac{4\pi^2 r}{T^2} \propto \frac{r}{r^3} = \frac{1}{r^2}$. By Newton's third law, mutual force must be symmetric in $m_1$ and $m_2$, yielding $F = G\frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$.
formulas.description: Inverse-square mutual attractive force between point masses.
formulas.explanation: Conservative central force field; operates between all matter in the universe.

formulas.title: Acceleration Due to Gravity at Altitude h
formulas.derivation: At surface $g_0 = \frac{GM}{R^2}$. At height $h$, $g(h) = \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2} = \frac{GM}{R^2(1 + h/R)^2} = g_0 (1 + h/R)^{-2}$. Expanding binomially for $h \ll R$: $(1 + h/R)^{-2} \approx 1 - \frac{2h}{R}$.
formulas.description: Variation of surface gravity with elevation above Earth's surface.
formulas.explanation: Gravity decreases twice as fast with altitude as it does with depth near Earth's surface.

formulas.title: Acceleration Due to Gravity at Depth d Inside Earth
formulas.derivation: At radius $r = R - d$, by Gauss's shell theorem, only the mass inside sphere of radius $r$ exerts net force: $M_{in} = M \frac{r^3}{R^3}$. Then $g(d) = \frac{G M_{in}}{r^2} = \frac{G (M r^3 / R^3)}{r^2} = \frac{GM}{R^3} r = g_0 \frac{R-d}{R} = g_0\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)$.
formulas.description: Linear decrease of gravitational acceleration within a uniform density spherical Earth.
formulas.explanation: At Earth's center ($d = R$), $g = 0$. Inside Earth, gravity acts as a linear restoring force leading to SHM.

formulas.title: Effect of Earth's Rotation on Gravity at Latitude $\phi$
formulas.derivation: Centrifugal acceleration on a body at latitude $\phi$ is $a_c = r\omega^2 = (R\cos\phi)\omega^2$ directed outwards perpendicular to rotation axis. The component opposing true gravity is $a_c \cos\phi = R\omega^2 \cos^2\phi$. Effective gravity is $g' = g_0 - R\omega^2\cos^2\phi$.
formulas.description: Apparent centrifugal reduction of gravity due to Earth's diurnal axial rotation.
formulas.explanation: Centrifugal reduction is maximum at the equator ($\phi = 0, \Delta g = R\omega^2 \approx 0.034\text{ m/s}^2$) and zero at the poles ($\phi = 90^\circ$).

formulas.title: Gravitational Potential and Potential Energy
formulas.derivation: $V(r) = -\int_\infty^r \vec{g}\cdot d\vec{r} = -\int_\infty^r \left(-\frac{GM}{r'^2}\right) dr' = -\left[\frac{GM}{r'}\right]_\infty^r = -\frac{GM}{r}$. Potential energy is $U(r) = m V(r) = -\frac{GMm}{r}$.
formulas.description: Gravitational potential and mutual binding potential energy of two masses separated by r with zero reference at infinity.
formulas.explanation: Negative sign signifies bound state; energy must be supplied from external agent to separate bodies to infinity.

formulas.title: Escape Velocity from Planetary Surface
formulas.derivation: Total mechanical energy at surface must be at least zero to reach infinity with zero kinetic energy: $E = K + U = \frac{1}{2}m v_e^2 - \frac{GMm}{R} = 0 \implies \frac{1}{2}m v_e^2 = \frac{GMm}{R} \implies v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}} = \sqrt{2gR}$.
formulas.description: Minimum ballistic launch speed required for an unpowered projectile to overcome planetary gravity.
formulas.explanation: Independent of launch mass $m$ and launch direction (neglecting atmospheric drag and planetary rotation).

formulas.title: Orbital Velocity of a Circular Satellite
formulas.derivation: Gravitational pull supplies exact centripetal force: $\frac{GMm}{r^2} = \frac{m v_o^2}{r} \implies v_o^2 = \frac{GM}{r} \implies v_o = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$.
formulas.description: Steady velocity required for stable circular orbit at radius $r = R + h$.
formulas.explanation: For near-Earth orbit ($h \ll R$), $v_o = \sqrt{gR} \approx 7.92\text{ km/s}$. Escape velocity is related by $v_e = \sqrt{2} v_o$.

formulas.title: Kepler's Third Law (Harmonic Law)
formulas.derivation: Period is circumference divided by speed: $T = \frac{2\pi r}{v_o} = \frac{2\pi r}{\sqrt{GM/r}} = \frac{2\pi r^{3/2}}{\sqrt{GM}}$. Squaring both sides: $T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM} r^3$.
formulas.description: Square of satellite orbital period is proportional to the cube of orbital semi-major axis.
formulas.explanation: For geostationary orbit, period $T = 24\text{ hours}$, yielding altitude $h \approx 35,786\text{ km}$ above the equator.

formulas.title: Total Mechanical Energy of Orbiting Satellite (Virial Theorem)
formulas.derivation: $K = \frac{1}{2}m v_o^2 = \frac{1}{2}m \left(\frac{GM}{r}\right) = \frac{GMm}{2r}$. $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$. Total energy is $E = K + U = \frac{GMm}{2r} - \frac{GMm}{r} = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$.
formulas.description: Binding energy relation demonstrating total orbital energy is negative and equals half the potential energy.
formulas.explanation: To transfer a satellite to a higher orbit, total energy must be increased (made less negative), although its orbital speed will decrease.

formulas.title: Kepler's Second Law (Areal Velocity Conservation)
formulas.derivation: Infinitesimal area swept in time $dt$ is triangle area $dA = \frac{1}{2} |\vec{r} \times d\vec{r}| = \frac{1}{2}|\vec{r} \times \vec{v} dt|$. Dividing by $dt$: $\frac{dA}{dt} = \frac{1}{2}|\vec{r} \times \vec{v}| = \frac{|\vec{r} \times m\vec{v}|}{2m} = \frac{L}{2m}$. Since gravitational force is strictly central ($\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F} = 0$), angular momentum $L$ is conserved, making areal velocity constant.
formulas.description: A line segment joining a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas during equal intervals of time.
formulas.explanation: Direct consequence of angular momentum conservation; implies planet moves fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion ($r_p v_p = r_a v_a$).

formulas.title: Hohmann Transfer Orbit Velocity Impulse

variables.r_1, r_2: Initial and target circular orbit radii

formulas.derivation: Semi-major axis of transfer ellipse is $a = \frac{r_1 + r_2}{2}$. Energy equation $v^2 = GM\left(\frac{2}{r} - \frac{1}{a}\right)$ gives periapsis speed $v_t = \sqrt{GM\left(\frac{2}{r_1} - \frac{2}{r_1 + r_2}\right)} = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r_1}}\sqrt{\frac{2r_2}{r_1 + r_2}}$. Subtracting initial circular speed $v_1 = \sqrt{GM/r_1}$ yields $\Delta v$.
formulas.description: Delta-v required to inject a satellite from circular orbit $r_1$ into an elliptical transfer orbit with apoapsis $r_2$.
formulas.explanation: Most fuel-efficient two-impulse orbital transfer trajectory between co-planar circular orbits.

formulas.title: Gravitational Potential Inside a Solid Uniform Sphere
formulas.derivation: $V_{in}(r) - V(R) = -\int_R^r g(r')dr' = -\int_R^r \left(-\frac{GM}{R^3}r'\right)dr' = \frac{GM}{R^3}\left[\frac{r'^2}{2}\right]_R^r = \frac{GM}{2R^3}(r^2 - R^2)$. Since surface potential is $V(R) = -\frac{GM}{R} = -\frac{2GMR^2}{2R^3}$, we get $V_{in}(r) = -\frac{GM}{2R^3}(3R^2 - r^2)$.
formulas.description: Potential profile inside a constant-density planetary core as a function of radial coordinate $r$.
formulas.explanation: At the exact center ($r = 0$), gravitational potential reaches its minimum $V(0) = -\frac{3}{2}\frac{GM}{R} = 1.5 V_{surface}$.

catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: Hans Bethe (1929) developed Crystal Field Theory: in octahedral ligand field, 6 ligands approach along Cartesian axes ($x, y, z$). Orbitals with lobes pointing directly along axes ($d_{x^2-y^2}, d_{z^2}$) experience strong electrostatic repulsion and are destabilized by $+0.6\Delta_o$ ($e_g$). Orbitals directed between axes ($d_{xy}, d_{yz}, d_{xz}$) experience less repulsion and are stabilized by $-0.4\Delta_o$ ($t_{2g}$). In tetrahedral geometry, 4 ligands approach corners of cube (between axes), inverting splitting pattern and reducing splitting magnitude by factor $\Delta_t = \frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$ because fewer ligands are present and none point directly at d-orbitals.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Because $\Delta_t < P$ (pairing energy) always, tetrahedral complexes are almost exclusively high-spin.
