catalog_formula_sheets.name: Wave Optics Formula Sheet
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: From paraxial ray geometry of reflection on spherical mirror: similar triangles formed by object, image, and center of curvature give $\frac{h_i}{h_o} = -\frac{v - R}{R - u} = -\frac{v}{u}$. Equating ratios and using $R = 2f$: $\frac{v - 2f}{2f - u} = \frac{v}{u} \implies u(v - 2f) = v(2f - u) \implies uv - 2uf = 2vf - uv \implies 2uv = 2f(u + v)$. Dividing both sides by $2uvf$ gives $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u}$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Concave mirror: $f < 0$; Convex mirror: $f > 0$. Real image: $m < 0$ (inverted); Virtual image: $m > 0$ (erect).

content_json.title: Wave Optics Formula Sheet

sections.title: Wave Optics Formula Sheet - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.title: Mirror Formula and Linear Magnification
formulas.derivation: From paraxial ray geometry of reflection on spherical mirror: similar triangles formed by object, image, and center of curvature give $\frac{h_i}{h_o} = -\frac{v - R}{R - u} = -\frac{v}{u}$. Equating ratios and using $R = 2f$: $\frac{v - 2f}{2f - u} = \frac{v}{u} \implies u(v - 2f) = v(2f - u) \implies uv - 2uf = 2vf - uv \implies 2uv = 2f(u + v)$. Dividing both sides by $2uvf$ gives $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u}$.
formulas.description: Relates object distance, image distance, and focal length for spherical mirrors using Cartesian sign convention.
formulas.explanation: Concave mirror: $f < 0$; Convex mirror: $f > 0$. Real image: $m < 0$ (inverted); Virtual image: $m > 0$ (erect).

formulas.title: Snell's Law of Refraction and Total Internal Reflection (TIR)
formulas.derivation: From Fermat's Principle of Least Time: travel time between points $A(0, a)$ and $B(d, -b)$ across boundary at $(x, 0)$ is $t(x) = \frac{\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}}{v_1} + \frac{\sqrt{b^2 + (d-x)^2}}{v_2}$. Setting $\frac{dt}{dx} = 0$: $\frac{x}{v_1\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}} - \frac{d-x}{v_2\sqrt{b^2 + (d-x)^2}} = 0 \implies \frac{\sin\theta_1}{v_1} = \frac{\sin\theta_2}{v_2}$. Multiplying by $c$ gives $n_1\sin\theta_1 = n_2\sin\theta_2$. At critical angle $\theta_c$, angle of refraction reaches $\theta_2 = 90^\circ \implies \sin\theta_c = n_2/n_1$.
formulas.description: Refraction at planar dielectric interface and critical angle threshold for total internal reflection.
formulas.explanation: Underlies optical fiber light guiding, mirage formation, and prism binocular design.

formulas.title: Refraction at a Single Spherical Curved Surface
formulas.derivation: From paraxial ray geometry: for small incident ray angles $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ with principal axis: $i = \alpha + \gamma$ and $\gamma = r + \beta \implies r = \gamma - \beta$. Snell's law in paraxial approximation is $\mu_1 i = \mu_2 r$. Substituting gives $\mu_1(\alpha + \gamma) = \mu_2(\gamma - \beta) \implies \mu_1 \alpha + \mu_2 \beta = (\mu_2 - \mu_1)\gamma$. For small angles, $\alpha \approx \frac{h}{-u}$, $\beta \approx \frac{h}{v}$, and $\gamma \approx \frac{h}{R}$. Canceling arc height $h$ yields $\frac{\mu_2}{v} - \frac{\mu_1}{u} = \frac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{R}$.
formulas.description: Fundamental Gaussian equation relating conjugate points for refraction across a spherical interface of radius R.
formulas.explanation: Direct precursor used twice in series to derive the Lens Maker's formula for thin lenses.

formulas.title: Lens Maker's Formula and Thin Lens Equation

variables.R_1, R_2: Radii of curvature of first and second faces

formulas.derivation: Apply spherical refraction formula to first surface of curvature $R_1$: $\frac{\mu}{v_1} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{\mu - 1}{R_1}$. For second surface of curvature $R_2$, $v_1$ acts as virtual object: $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{\mu}{v_1} = \frac{1 - \mu}{R_2} = -\frac{\mu - 1}{R_2}$. Adding both equations eliminates intermediate image $v_1$: $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)$. For object at infinity ($u = \infty$), image forms at focus ($v = f$), giving $\frac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)$.
formulas.description: Focal length of a thin lens computed from surface curvatures and lens material refractive index.
formulas.explanation: When immersed in a liquid medium of refractive index $\mu_l$, focal length alters to $f_{liq} = f_{air} \frac{\mu_g - 1}{\mu_g / \mu_l - 1}$.

formulas.latex: P = \frac{1}{f} \text{ (Diopters)}, \quad P_{eq} = P_1 + P_2 - d P_1 P_2
formulas.title: Optical Power and Combination of Lenses
formulas.derivation: Optical power measures deviation angle $\delta = h / f$ produced for a ray at unit height $h=1$, hence $P = 1/f$. For two lenses in close contact ($d=0$), net focal length is $\frac{1}{F} = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2} \implies P_{eq} = P_1 + P_2$. When separated by distance $d$, tracing ray deviation shows second lens receives incident ray at reduced height $h_2 = h_1 - d \delta_1 = h_1(1 - d/f_1)$, resulting in $P_{eq} = P_1 + P_2 - d P_1 P_2$.
formulas.description: Converging ability of optical lenses and equivalent power of two lenses separated by distance d.
formulas.explanation: Convex lens: $P > 0$; Concave lens: $P < 0$. Contact powers add algebraically.

formulas.title: Prism Formula at Minimum Deviation
formulas.derivation: Total deviation angle is $\delta = (i_1 + i_2) - A$ where $r_1 + r_2 = A$. At minimum deviation $\delta_m$, ray passes symmetrically through prism: $i_1 = i_2 = i$ and $r_1 = r_2 = r$. Then $r + r = A \implies r = A/2$. Deviation becomes $\delta_m = 2i - A \implies i = \frac{A + \delta_m}{2}$. Substituting into Snell's law $\mu = \frac{\sin i}{\sin r}$ gives $\mu = \frac{\sin((A + \delta_m)/2)}{\sin(A/2)}$.
formulas.description: Refractive index of a triangular prism of apex angle A determined from minimum deviation angle $\delta_m$.
formulas.explanation: Standard precision laboratory method for measuring refractive index using spectrometer.

formulas.title: Dispersive Power of an Optical Medium

variables.\\mu_v, \\mu_r, \\mu_y: Refractive indices for violet, red, and Fraunhofer yellow D-line

formulas.derivation: For small-angled prism, deviation is $\delta = (\mu - 1)A$. Angular dispersion is $\theta = \delta_v - \delta_r = (\mu_v - 1)A - (\mu_r - 1)A = (\mu_v - \mu_r)A$. Mean deviation is $\delta_y = (\mu_y - 1)A$. Dispersive power is defined as $\omega = \frac{\theta}{\delta_y} = \frac{(\mu_v - \mu_r)A}{(\mu_y - 1)A} = \frac{\mu_v - \mu_r}{\mu_y - 1}$.
formulas.description: Ratio of angular dispersion between violet and red light to mean yellow light deviation.
formulas.explanation: Flint glass has higher dispersive power than crown glass; combining crown and flint prisms creates achromatic doublets (dispersion without deviation or vice-versa).

formulas.title: Astronomical Refracting Telescope Magnification
formulas.derivation: Objective forms intermediate inverted real image of distant object at its focal plane ($h' = f_o \alpha$). Eyepiece acts as simple magnifier: in normal adjustment (image at infinity), visual angle is $\beta = h'/f_e$. Angular magnification is $M = \frac{\beta}{\alpha} = \frac{h'/f_e}{h'/f_o} = -\frac{f_o}{f_e}$. Separation between lenses is tube length $L = f_o + f_e$. If image forms at near point $D$, eyepiece magnification is $m_e = 1 + D/f_e$, yielding $M = -\frac{f_o}{f_e}\left(1 + \frac{f_e}{D}\right)$.
formulas.description: Angular magnification and barrel tube length of astronomical telescope under normal adjustment and near point.
formulas.explanation: High magnification requires large objective focal length $f_o$ and small eyepiece focal length $f_e$.

formulas.title: Compound Microscope Magnification
formulas.derivation: Total magnification is product of linear magnification of objective $m_o = -v_o / u_o$ and angular magnification of eyepiece $m_e = D / f_e$ (at infinity): $M = m_o \times m_e = -\left(\frac{v_o}{u_o}\right)\left(\frac{D}{f_e}\right)$. In standard microscope geometry, object is placed just outside $f_o$ ($u_o \approx f_o$) and image forms near eyepiece ($v_o \approx L$), giving $M \approx -\frac{L D}{f_o f_e}$.
formulas.description: Total magnifying power of objective lens and ocular eyepiece under normal adjustment.
formulas.explanation: Both $f_o$ and $f_e$ must be extremely small to achieve high microscopic magnification.

formulas.title: Young's Double Slit Experiment (YDSE) Fringe Width and Intensity
formulas.derivation: Path difference between rays from two slits is $\Delta x = d\sin\theta \approx d\frac{y}{D}$. Bright fringes occur at constructive interference: $\Delta x = n\lambda \implies y_n = n\frac{\lambda D}{d}$. Spacing between consecutive fringes is fringe width $\beta = y_{n+1} - y_n = \frac{\lambda D}{d}$. Phase difference is $\Delta\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x = \frac{2\pi y d}{\lambda D}$. Superposing two coherent waves $E = E_0 e^{i\omega t} + E_0 e^{i(\omega t + \Delta\phi)}$ gives resultant amplitude $E_R = 2E_0\cos(\Delta\phi/2)$, so intensity is $I = 4I_0\cos^2(\Delta\phi/2)$.
formulas.description: Equispaced interference fringe width and cosine-squared intensity distribution on screen.
formulas.explanation: If entire apparatus is immersed in liquid of index $\mu$, fringe width shrinks to $\beta' = \beta / \mu$.

formulas.title: Fringe Shift in YDSE Due to Thin Transparent Plate
formulas.derivation: Optical path length through sheet of thickness $t$ is $\mu t$ instead of geometric air path $t$. Extra optical path introduced in that beam is $\Delta_{opt} = \mu t - t = (\mu - 1)t$. Central fringe now occurs where net path difference vanishes: $d\frac{y_0}{D} - (\mu - 1)t = 0 \implies y_0 = \frac{(\mu - 1)t D}{d}$. Number of shifted fringes is $N = \frac{\Delta y}{\beta} = \frac{(\mu - 1)t}{\lambda}$.
formulas.description: Lateral shift of entire interference pattern when a dielectric sheet of thickness t and index $\mu$ covers one slit.
formulas.explanation: Fringe pattern shifts bodily toward the side where the transparent plate is introduced; fringe width $\beta$ remains unchanged.

formulas.latex: a \sin\theta = m\lambda \quad (\text{Minima}), \quad y_1 = \frac{\lambda D}{a}, \quad W_{central} = \frac{2\lambda D}{a}
formulas.title: Single-Slit Fraunhofer Diffraction

variables.W_{central}: Linear width of central maximum on screen

formulas.derivation: Divide slit of width $a$ into two equal halves of width $a/2$: path difference between corresponding wavelets from top and middle is $\frac{a}{2}\sin\theta$. Destructive interference occurs when this path difference is $\lambda/2 \implies \frac{a}{2}\sin\theta = \frac{\lambda}{2} \implies a\sin\theta = \lambda$. In general, dividing into $2m$ zones gives dark minima at $a\sin\theta = m\lambda$. Central maximum extends between first minima on either side ($m = \pm 1$): angular half-width $\theta_1 = \lambda/a$, so linear full width is $W_{central} = 2y_1 = 2\frac{\lambda D}{a}$.
formulas.description: Positions of intensity minima and linear angular width of central diffraction maximum.
formulas.explanation: Central diffraction peak is twice as wide as secondary subsidiary maxima and holds over 85% of total radiant energy.

formulas.title: Rayleigh's Criterion for Resolving Power
formulas.derivation: Diffraction of plane wave by circular aperture produces Airy disc pattern with first dark ring at angular radius $\theta = 1.22\frac{\lambda}{D}$ (derived from zeros of first-order Bessel function $J_1(x) = 0$). Lord Rayleigh postulated that two sources are barely resolved when the central maximum of one Airy disc falls exactly on the first minimum of the other: $\theta_R = 1.22\frac{\lambda}{D}$.
formulas.description: Minimum angular separation for two point sources to be barely resolved through circular aperture.
formulas.explanation: Explains why larger astronomical telescope mirrors provide both greater light-gathering power and finer angular resolution.

formulas.title: Polarization: Malus's Law and Brewster's Angle
formulas.derivation: Malus's Law: electric field vector $\vec{E}_0$ of polarized wave incident at angle $\theta$ to transmission axis has transmitted component $E = E_0\cos\theta$. Since intensity is proportional to amplitude squared: $I(\theta) \propto E^2 = E_0^2\cos^2\theta = I_0\cos^2\theta$. Brewster's Law: reflected ray is completely polarized perpendicular to plane of incidence when reflected and refracted rays are mutually perpendicular ($r + \theta_p = 90^\circ \implies r = 90^\circ - \theta_p$). Substituting into Snell's law: $\sin\theta_p = \mu \sin r = \mu \sin(90^\circ - \theta_p) = \mu \cos\theta_p \implies \tan\theta_p = \mu$.
formulas.description: Transmitted intensity through analyzer polarizer, and angle of incidence producing 100% linearly polarized reflected light.
formulas.explanation: At Brewster's angle, electrons oscillating along refracted beam direction cannot emit transverse waves in the direction of specular reflection.

content_json.derivation: From paraxial ray geometry of reflection on spherical mirror: similar triangles formed by object, image, and center of curvature give $\frac{h_i}{h_o} = -\frac{v - R}{R - u} = -\frac{v}{u}$. Equating ratios and using $R = 2f$: $\frac{v - 2f}{2f - u} = \frac{v}{u} \implies u(v - 2f) = v(2f - u) \implies uv - 2uf = 2vf - uv \implies 2uv = 2f(u + v)$. Dividing both sides by $2uvf$ gives $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u}$.
content_json.explanation: Concave mirror: $f < 0$; Convex mirror: $f > 0$. Real image: $m < 0$ (inverted); Virtual image: $m > 0$ (erect).

catalog_formula_sheets.name: Linear Inequalities Formula Sheet
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: Entry $(i, j)$ of $A \cdot \text{adj}(A)$ is $\sum_{k=1}^n A_{ik} [\text{adj}(A)]_{kj} = \sum_{k=1}^n A_{ik} C_{jk}$ where $C_{jk}$ is cofactor. By Laplace expansion: If $i = j$, $\sum A_{ik} C_{ik} = |A|$. If $i \ne j$, $\sum A_{ik} C_{jk} = 0$ (expansion of determinant with two identical rows). Thus $A \cdot \text{adj}(A) = |A| I_n$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: The core theorem of matrix algebra connecting matrix multiplication, adjoints, determinants, and inverses.

formulas.title: Fundamental Adjoint Theorem for Square Matrix
formulas.derivation: Entry $(i, j)$ of $A \cdot \text{adj}(A)$ is $\sum_{k=1}^n A_{ik} [\text{adj}(A)]_{kj} = \sum_{k=1}^n A_{ik} C_{jk}$ where $C_{jk}$ is cofactor. By Laplace expansion: If $i = j$, $\sum A_{ik} C_{ik} = |A|$. If $i \ne j$, $\sum A_{ik} C_{jk} = 0$ (expansion of determinant with two identical rows). Thus $A \cdot \text{adj}(A) = |A| I_n$.
formulas.description: Fundamental Adjoint Theorem for Square Matrix
formulas.explanation: The core theorem of matrix algebra connecting matrix multiplication, adjoints, determinants, and inverses.

formulas.title: Matrix Inversion Formula

variables.A^{-1}: multiplicative inverse satisfying A * A^{-1} = I

formulas.derivation: From $A \cdot \text{adj}(A) = |A| I_n$. For non-singular matrix $|A| \ne 0$, divide both sides by scalar $|A|$: $A \cdot \left(\frac{1}{|A|} \text{adj}(A)\right) = I_n$. By uniqueness of matrix inverse: $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|} \text{adj}(A)$.
formulas.description: Matrix Inversion Formula
formulas.explanation: Provides explicit analytical inverse for any non-singular square matrix.

formulas.title: Determinant of Adjoint Matrix
formulas.derivation: Take determinant of both sides of $A \cdot \text{adj}(A) = |A| I_n$: $|A \cdot \text{adj}(A)| = ||A| I_n|$. Using properties $|XY| = |X||Y|$ and $|k I_n| = k^n$: $|A| \cdot |\text{adj}(A)| = |A|^n$. For $|A| \ne 0$, divide by $|A|$: $|\text{adj}(A)| = |A|^{n-1}$. Holds by continuity for $|A| = 0$ as well.
formulas.description: Determinant of Adjoint Matrix
formulas.explanation: Direct power relation: for a 3x3 matrix ($n=3$), $|\text{adj}(A)| = |A|^2$.

formulas.title: Double Adjoint Matrix Identities
formulas.derivation: Replace $A$ with $B = \text{adj}(A)$ in adjoint formula: $B \cdot \text{adj}(B) = |B| I \implies \text{adj}(A) \cdot \text{adj}(\text{adj}(A)) = |\text{adj}(A)| I = |A|^{n-1} I$. Multiply on left by $A$: $A \cdot \text{adj}(A) \cdot \text{adj}(\text{adj}(A)) = A |A|^{n-1} I \implies |A| I \cdot \text{adj}(\text{adj}(A)) = |A|^{n-1} A \implies \text{adj}(\text{adj}(A)) = |A|^{n-2} A$. Taking determinant gives $|A|^{(n-1)^2}$.
formulas.description: Double Adjoint Matrix Identities
formulas.explanation: High-frequency JEE Advanced question evaluating compound adjoint operations.

formulas.title: Reversal Law for Inverses and Transposes
formulas.derivation: For transpose: $[(AB)^T]_{ij} = [AB]_{ji} = \sum A_{jk} B_{ki} = \sum B^T_{ik} A^T_{kj} = [B^T A^T]_{ij}$. For inverse: $(AB)(B^{-1} A^{-1}) = A(B B^{-1})A^{-1} = A I A^{-1} = A A^{-1} = I$. Thus by inverse uniqueness $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1} A^{-1}$.
formulas.description: Reversal Law for Inverses and Transposes
formulas.explanation: Multiplication order reverses whenever taking transposes, inverses, or adjoints of products.

formulas.title: Unique Decomposition into Symmetric and Skew-Symmetric Matrices
formulas.derivation: Direct algebra: $\frac{1}{2}(A + A^T) + \frac{1}{2}(A - A^T) = \frac{1}{2}A + \frac{1}{2}A^T + \frac{1}{2}A - \frac{1}{2}A^T = A$. Test symmetry of $P$: $P^T = [\frac{1}{2}(A+A^T)]^T = \frac{1}{2}(A^T+A) = P$. Test skew-symmetry of $Q$: $Q^T = [\frac{1}{2}(A-A^T)]^T = \frac{1}{2}(A^T-A) = -Q$. Diagonal elements of $Q$ must be zero.
formulas.description: Unique Decomposition into Symmetric and Skew-Symmetric Matrices
formulas.explanation: Any square matrix can be uniquely split into a symmetric part and a skew-symmetric part.

formulas.title: Cramer's Rule for System of 3 Linear Equations

variables.\\Delta_x, \\Delta_y, \\Delta_z: determinants with column replaced by constants vector

formulas.derivation: In matrix form $A X = B$. Multiply both sides by adjoint: $\text{adj}(A) A X = \text{adj}(A) B \implies |A| I X = \text{adj}(A) B \implies \Delta X = \text{adj}(A) B$. The first row of $\text{adj}(A) B$ is $C_{11}d_1 + C_{21}d_2 + C_{31}d_3$, which is the cofactor expansion of determinant $\Delta_x$. Thus $\Delta x = \Delta_x \implies x = \Delta_x / \Delta$.
formulas.description: Cramer's Rule for System of 3 Linear Equations
formulas.explanation: Explicit solution formula for non-singular linear systems using determinants.

formulas.latex: \Delta = 0 \text{ and at least one } \Delta_i \ne 0 \implies \text{No Solution (Inconsistent)}; \quad \Delta = \Delta_x = \Delta_y = \Delta_z = 0 \implies \text{Infinite Solutions or Inconsistent}
formulas.title: Consistency Criteria for Non-Homogeneous Linear Systems
formulas.derivation: If $\Delta = 0$, the planes are either parallel or intersect in a line or form a triangular prism. If at least one $\Delta_i \ne 0$, we have $0 \cdot x = \Delta_i \ne 0$, which is algebraically impossible $\implies$ no solution. If all $\Delta_i = 0$, equations may represent coincident or collinear planes (infinitely many solutions), or parallel distinct planes.
formulas.description: Consistency Criteria for Non-Homogeneous Linear Systems
formulas.explanation: Classifies whether a 3D linear system represents intersecting planes, parallel planes, or coincident planes.

formulas.title: Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
formulas.derivation: From matrix identity $(A - \lambda I) \cdot \text{adj}(A - \lambda I) = \det(A - \lambda I) I = p(\lambda) I$. The matrix $\text{adj}(A - \lambda I)$ is a polynomial in $\lambda$ of degree $n-1$: $B_{n-1} \lambda^{n-1} + \dots + B_1 \lambda + B_0$. Equating powers of $\lambda$ and summing matrix products eliminates intermediate matrices $B_k$, proving $p(A) = A^n + c_{n-1} A^{n-1} + \dots + c_0 I = 0$.
formulas.description: Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
formulas.explanation: Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial equation. Allows computing $A^{-1}$ and high powers $A^m$ linearly.

formulas.latex: A A^T = A^T A = I \implies A^{-1} = A^T, \quad |A| = \pm 1
formulas.title: Orthogonal Matrix Definition and Properties
formulas.derivation: By definition $A A^T = I$. Taking determinants: $|A A^T| = |I| \implies |A| |A^T| = 1$. Since $|A^T| = |A|$: $|A|^2 = 1 \implies |A| = \pm 1$. Multiplying $A A^T = I$ by $A^{-1}$ from left: $A^T = A^{-1}$. Columns and rows of orthogonal matrix form an orthonormal basis ($\vec{v}_i \cdot \vec{v}_j = \delta_{ij}$).
formulas.description: Orthogonal Matrix Definition and Properties
formulas.explanation: Represents rigid rotations ($|A| = +1$) and reflections ($|A| = -1$) that preserve lengths and angles in Euclidean space.

formulas.title: Scalar Multiplication Property of Determinants
formulas.derivation: Multiplying matrix $A$ by scalar $k$ multiplies every entry in every row by $k$. Determinant property: factoring $k$ out of a single row scales determinant by $k$. Since there are $n$ rows in an $n \times n$ matrix, factoring $k$ out of all $n$ rows gives $k \times k \times \dots \times k = k^n$. Thus $|kA| = k^n |A|$.
formulas.description: Scalar Multiplication Property of Determinants
formulas.explanation: Common trap in JEE: for 3x3 matrix, $|2A| = 2^3 |A| = 8|A|$, not $2|A|$.

formulas.latex: \begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \\ 1 & b & b^2 \\ 1 & c & c^2 \end{vmatrix} = (a - b)(b - c)(c - a)
formulas.title: Vandermonde Determinant Identity
formulas.derivation: Perform row operations $R_2 \rightarrow R_2 - R_1$ and $R_3 \rightarrow R_3 - R_1$: $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \\ 0 & b-a & b^2-a^2 \\ 0 & c-a & c^2-a^2 \end{vmatrix}$. Factor $(b-a)$ from row 2 and $(c-a)$ from row 3: $(b-a)(c-a) \begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \\ 0 & 1 & b+a \\ 0 & 1 & c+a \end{vmatrix}$. Expanding along first column: $(b-a)(c-a)[(c+a) - (b+a)] = (b-a)(c-a)(c-b) = (a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$.
formulas.description: Vandermonde Determinant Identity
formulas.explanation: Standard polynomial determinant; vanishes if and only if any two of a, b, c are identical.

By Laplace expansion: If $i = j$, $\sum A_{ik} C_{ik} = |A|$. If $i \ne j$, $\sum A_{ik} C_{jk} = 0$ (expansion of determinant with two identical rows). Thus $A \cdot \text{adj}(A) = |A| I_n$.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations Formula Sheet
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: Using Taylor series expansions: $e^{i\theta} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(i\theta)^k}{k!} = \left(1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2!} + \frac{\theta^4}{4!}...\right) + i\left(\theta - \frac{\theta^3}{3!} + \frac{\theta^5}{5!}...\right) = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$. Multiplying by modulus $r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ gives $z = r e^{i\theta}$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Connects Cartesian coordinates $(x, y)$ to magnitude $r$ and angle $\theta$, making multiplication and rotation geometric.

formulas.latex: z = x + i y = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta) = r e^{i\theta}
formulas.title: Euler Form and Polar Representation
formulas.derivation: Using Taylor series expansions: $e^{i\theta} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(i\theta)^k}{k!} = \left(1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2!} + \frac{\theta^4}{4!}...\right) + i\left(\theta - \frac{\theta^3}{3!} + \frac{\theta^5}{5!}...\right) = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$. Multiplying by modulus $r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ gives $z = r e^{i\theta}$.
formulas.description: Euler Form and Polar Representation
formulas.explanation: Connects Cartesian coordinates $(x, y)$ to magnitude $r$ and angle $\theta$, making multiplication and rotation geometric.

formulas.title: Triangle Inequalities for Complex Numbers
formulas.description: Triangle Inequalities for Complex Numbers
formulas.explanation: Geometrically states that any side of a triangle is bounded between the difference and sum of the other two sides.

formulas.title: De Moivre's Theorem for Integral and Rational Powers
formulas.derivation: Using Euler's identity: $(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n = (e^{i\theta})^n = e^{i n \theta}$. Re-expanding Euler's form gives $\cos(n\theta) + i\sin(n\theta)$. For integers, proven rigorously by induction.
formulas.description: De Moivre's Theorem for Integral and Rational Powers
formulas.explanation: Allows instantaneous computation of powers of complex numbers by multiplying the argument by n.

formulas.title: Cube Roots of Unity Fundamental Identities
formulas.derivation: Solve $z^3 - 1 = 0 \implies (z-1)(z^2+z+1) = 0$. Non-real roots satisfy $z^2+z+1=0$. Let $\omega = \frac{-1+i\sqrt{3}}{2} = e^{i 2\pi/3}$. Then $\omega^2 = e^{i 4\pi/3} = \frac{-1-i\sqrt{3}}{2}$. Sum: $1 + \omega + \omega^2 = 1 + \left(-\frac{1}{2}+i\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) + \left(-\frac{1}{2}-i\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 0$. Product: $\omega^3 = e^{i 2\pi} = 1$.
formulas.description: Cube Roots of Unity Fundamental Identities
formulas.explanation: Forms an equilateral triangle inscribed in the unit circle centered at origin. Powers reduce modulo 3: $\omega^{3k+r} = \omega^r$.

formulas.latex: z_k = e^{i \frac{2k\pi}{n}}, \quad k = 0, 1, \dots, n-1 \implies \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} z_k = 0, \quad \prod_{k=0}^{n-1} z_k = (-1)^{n-1}
formulas.title: n-th Roots of Unity and Geometric Properties
formulas.derivation: Roots of $z^n - 1 = 0$ are vertices of regular $n$-gon on unit circle: $z_k = \omega_n^k$ where $\omega_n = e^{i 2\pi/n}$. Sum is sum of finite GP: $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \omega_n^k = \frac{1 - \omega_n^n}{1 - \omega_n} = \frac{1 - 1}{1 - \omega_n} = 0$. Product from constant term in $z^n - 1 = \prod (z - z_k)$: $\prod z_k = (-1)^n (-1) = (-1)^{n-1}$.
formulas.description: n-th Roots of Unity and Geometric Properties
formulas.explanation: The n-th roots of unity form a regular n-sided polygon inscribed in the unit circle with center of mass at the origin.

formulas.title: Coni's Rotation Theorem in Complex Plane

variables.\\alpha: counter-clockwise angle between vector (z2 - z1) and (z3 - z1)

formulas.derivation: Let vector $z_2 - z_1 = r_1 e^{i\theta_1}$ and $z_3 - z_1 = r_2 e^{i\theta_2}$. The angle swept from segment $1-2$ to $1-3$ is $\alpha = \theta_2 - \theta_1$. Taking quotient: $\frac{z_3 - z_1}{z_2 - z_1} = \frac{r_2 e^{i\theta_2}}{r_1 e^{i\theta_1}} = \frac{r_2}{r_1} e^{i(\theta_2 - \theta_1)} = \left|\frac{z_3 - z_1}{z_2 - z_1}\right| e^{i\alpha}$.
formulas.description: Coni's Rotation Theorem in Complex Plane
formulas.explanation: Essential tool for geometry problems in IIT-JEE: rotates any line segment about a pivot point by angle $\alpha$.

formulas.title: Equation of Circle in Complex Plane
formulas.derivation: Distance between arbitrary point $z = x+iy$ and fixed point $z_0 = x_0+iy_0$ is $|z - z_0| = \sqrt{(x-x_0)^2 + (y-y_0)^2} = r$. Squaring both sides: $(z - z_0)(\bar{z} - \bar{z}_0) = r^2 \implies z\bar{z} - \bar{z}_0 z - z_0 \bar{z} + |z_0|^2 - r^2 = 0$, standard form $z\bar{z} + \bar{a}z + a\bar{z} + k = 0$.
formulas.description: Equation of Circle in Complex Plane
formulas.explanation: Locus of points maintaining constant distance r from fixed center z_0.

formulas.latex: |z - z_1| = |z - z_2| \implies \text{Perpendicular bisector of segment joining } z_1 \text{ and } z_2
formulas.title: Locus of Perpendicular Bisector
formulas.derivation: Square both sides: $(z - z_1)(\bar{z} - \bar{z}_1) = (z - z_2)(\bar{z} - \bar{z}_2) \implies |z|^2 - \bar{z}_1 z - z_1 \bar{z} + |z_1|^2 = |z|^2 - \bar{z}_2 z - z_2 \bar{z} + |z_2|^2 \implies (\bar{z}_2 - \bar{z}_1)z + (z_2 - z_1)\bar{z} + |z_1|^2 - |z_2|^2 = 0$, which is linear in $z, \bar{z}$ representing a straight line perpendicular to segment $z_1-z_2$ passing through midpoint $(z_1+z_2)/2$.
formulas.description: Locus of Perpendicular Bisector
formulas.explanation: Locus of points equidistant from two fixed points in the complex plane.

formulas.latex: \text{Arg}\left(\frac{z - z_1}{z - z_2}\right) = \pm \frac{\pi}{2} \implies \text{Circle with diameter } z_1 z_2
formulas.title: Angle in Semicircle Locus
formulas.derivation: Angle subtended by segment $z_1-z_2$ at point $z$ is $\theta = \text{Arg}\left(\frac{z - z_1}{z - z_2}\right)$. If $\theta = \pm \pi/2$, the real part of $\frac{z - z_1}{z - z_2}$ is zero: $\frac{z - z_1}{z - z_2} + \frac{\bar{z} - \bar{z}_1}{\bar{z} - \bar{z}_2} = 0 \implies (z - z_1)(\bar{z} - \bar{z}_2) + (\bar{z} - \bar{z}_1)(z - z_2) = 0$, which simplifies to equation of circle having $z_1, z_2$ as diameter endpoints.
formulas.description: Angle in Semicircle Locus
formulas.explanation: Direct complex realization of Thales' theorem: any triangle inscribed in a semicircle has a 90-degree angle.

formulas.latex: \text{Area}(\Delta z_1 z_2 z_3) = \frac{i}{4} \begin{vmatrix} z_1 & \bar{z}_1 & 1 \\ z_2 & \bar{z}_2 & 1 \\ z_3 & \bar{z}_3 & 1 \end{vmatrix}
formulas.title: Area of Triangle with Complex Vertices
formulas.derivation: Cartesian area $A = \frac{1}{2}|x_1(y_2-y_3) + x_2(y_3-y_1) + x_3(y_1-y_2)|$. Substitute $x = \frac{z+\bar{z}}{2}, y = \frac{z-\bar{z}}{2i}$. Determinant expansion: $\begin{vmatrix} x_i & y_i & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} \frac{z_i+\bar{z}_i}{2} & \frac{z_i-\bar{z}_i}{2i} & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \frac{1}{4i} \begin{vmatrix} z_i & \bar{z}_i & 1 \end{vmatrix} \implies A = \frac{i}{4} \begin{vmatrix} z_1 & \bar{z}_1 & 1 \\ z_2 & \\bar{z}_2 & 1 \\ z_3 & \\bar{z}_3 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$.
formulas.description: Area of Triangle with Complex Vertices
formulas.explanation: Calculates the area of triangle formed by complex vertices; value is zero if and only if points are collinear.

formulas.latex: z_1^2 + z_2^2 + z_3^2 = z_1 z_2 + z_2 z_3 + z_3 z_1 \implies \text{Equilateral Triangle}
formulas.title: Condition for Equilateral Triangle in Complex Plane
formulas.derivation: In equilateral triangle, side $z_3 - z_1$ is obtained by rotating $z_2 - z_1$ by $60^\circ$ ($e^{i\pi/3} = -\omega^2$): $\frac{z_3 - z_1}{z_2 - z_1} = e^{i\pi/3} = 1 + \omega$. Similarly $\frac{z_1 - z_2}{z_3 - z_2} = e^{i\pi/3}$. Eliminating angles and simplifying: $(z_1 - z_2)^2 + (z_2 - z_3)^2 + (z_3 - z_1)^2 = 0 \implies 2(z_1^2+z_2^2+z_3^2) - 2(z_1 z_2 + z_2 z_3 + z_3 z_1) = 0 \implies z_1^2 + z_2^2 + z_3^2 = z_1 z_2 + z_2 z_3 + z_3 z_1$.
formulas.description: Condition for Equilateral Triangle in Complex Plane
formulas.explanation: Famous IIT-JEE identity checking whether 3 given complex numbers form an equilateral triangle.

formulas.title: Conjugate Fundamental Identities
formulas.derivation: For $z = x+iy$, complex conjugate is $\bar{z} = x - iy$. Adding: $z + \bar{z} = 2x \implies x = \frac{z+\bar{z}}{2}$. Subtracting: $z - \bar{z} = 2iy \implies y = \frac{z-\bar{z}}{2i}$. Multiplying: $z\bar{z} = (x+iy)(x-iy) = x^2 - i^2 y^2 = x^2 + y^2 = |z|^2$.
formulas.description: Conjugate Fundamental Identities
formulas.explanation: Foundational relations connecting complex conjugate algebra to real and imaginary coordinates.

Multiplying by modulus $r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ gives $z = r e^{i\theta}$.
content_json.explanation: Connects Cartesian coordinates $(x, y)$ to magnitude $r$ and angle $\theta$, making multiplication and rotation geometric.

formulas.title: Crystal Field Splitting in Octahedral and Tetrahedral Fields
formulas.derivation: Hans Bethe (1929) developed Crystal Field Theory: in octahedral ligand field, 6 ligands approach along Cartesian axes ($x, y, z$). Orbitals with lobes pointing directly along axes ($d_{x^2-y^2}, d_{z^2}$) experience strong electrostatic repulsion and are destabilized by $+0.6\Delta_o$ ($e_g$). Orbitals directed between axes ($d_{xy}, d_{yz}, d_{xz}$) experience less repulsion and are stabilized by $-0.4\Delta_o$ ($t_{2g}$). In tetrahedral geometry, 4 ligands approach corners of cube (between axes), inverting splitting pattern and reducing splitting magnitude by factor $\Delta_t = \frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$ because fewer ligands are present and none point directly at d-orbitals.
formulas.description: Splitting of degenerate d-orbitals into $t_{2g}/e_g$ and $e/t_2$ manifolds in electrostatic ligand fields.
formulas.explanation: Because $\Delta_t < P$ (pairing energy) always, tetrahedral complexes are almost exclusively high-spin.

formulas.title: Crystal Field Stabilization Energy (CFSE) for Octahedral Complexes

variables.m: Number of extra electron pairs formed relative to free ion

formulas.derivation: Barycenter rule requires total energy shift of the 5 degenerate orbitals to sum to zero: $3(-0.4\Delta_o) + 2(+0.6\Delta_o) = -1.2\Delta_o + 1.2\Delta_o = 0$. Each electron occupying lower $t_{2g}$ level stabilizes complex by $-0.4\Delta_o$, while each electron occupying upper $e_g$ level destabilizes complex by $+0.6\Delta_o$. Summing contributions gives $CFSE = (-0.4 n_{t_{2g}} + 0.6 n_{e_g})\Delta_o$. When electrons pair in same orbital against Coulomb repulsion, pairing energy $+mP$ is added.
formulas.description: Net energetic stabilization of d-electron configuration relative to spherical barycenter.
formulas.explanation: If $\Delta_o > P$ (strong field ligands like $CN^-, CO$), pairing occurs producing low-spin complex. If $\Delta_o < P$ (weak field ligands like $F^-, Cl^-$), Hund's rule dominates producing high-spin complex.

formulas.latex: I^- < Br^- < S^{2-} < SCN^- < Cl^- < NO_3^- < N_3^- < F^- < OH^- < C_2O_4^{2-} < H_2O < NCS^- < CH_3CN < py < NH_3 < en < bipy < phen < NO_2^- < PPh_3 < CN^- < CO
formulas.title: Spectrochemical Series of Ligands
formulas.derivation: Derived from UV-visible absorption spectra ($d-d$ transition band wavenumbers $\Delta_o = h c \bar{\nu}$). Ligands fall into three classes based on metal-ligand bonding: (1) Halides and oxygen donors are $\pi$-donors: ligand filled p-orbitals donate electron density into metal $t_{2g}$, destabilizing $t_{2g}$ and shrinking $\Delta_o$ (weak field). (2) Ammonia and amines are pure $\sigma$-donors: intermediate $\Delta_o$. (3) $CN^-$ and $CO$ are strong $\pi$-acceptors (back-bonding): empty $\pi^*$ orbitals accept electron density from metal $t_{2g}$, dramatically stabilizing $t_{2g}$ and expanding $\Delta_o$ (strong field).
formulas.description: Empirical ranking of ligands according to increasing magnitude of crystal field splitting $\Delta_o$.
formulas.explanation: Enables predicting whether transition metal complex is high-spin or low-spin, and determines magnetic and color properties.

formulas.title: Magnetic Moments of Coordination Complexes

variables.\\mu_{eff}: Effective magnetic moment in Bohr Magnetons (BM)

formulas.derivation: In first-row ($3d$) transition metal complexes, non-spherical electrostatic crystal field of surrounding ligands quenches orbital angular momentum ($L \approx 0$) by breaking spatial rotational symmetry. Magnetic moment reduces to spin-only expression: $\mu_s = g\sqrt{S(S+1)}\mu_B$. With electron g-factor $g \approx 2.00$ and $S = n/2$: $\mu_s = 2\sqrt{\frac{n}{2}\left(\frac{n+2}{2}\right)} = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\mu_B$.
formulas.description: Spin-only magnetic moment and complete spin-plus-orbital magnetic moment for first-row transition ions.
formulas.explanation: Guouy balance magnetic measurement directly diagnoses high-spin vs low-spin states (e.g. $[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}$ has $n=1, \mu = 1.73\text{ BM}$ while $[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{3+}$ has $n=5, \mu = 5.92\text{ BM}$).

formulas.title: Sidgwick's Effective Atomic Number (EAN) Rule / 18-Electron Rule
formulas.derivation: Nevild Sidgwick (1927) proposed that coordinate covalent bonds donate 2 electrons per coordination bond. The total effective electrons surrounding metal core is $EAN = Z - (\text{oxidation state}) + 2 \times (\text{ligand pairs})$. If $EAN$ equals the atomic number of the next noble gas ($Kr=36, Xe=54, Rn=86$), the complex possesses a completely filled valence shell of 18 electrons ($ns^2 (n-1)d^{10} np^6$), conferring high kinetic and thermodynamic stability.
formulas.description: Predicts stability of coordination and organometallic complexes by mimicking next noble gas configuration.
formulas.explanation: Explains stoichiometry of metal carbonyls: $Ni(CO)_4$ ($28 - 0 + 8 = 36$, $18e^-$), $Fe(CO)_5$ ($26 - 0 + 10 = 36$), $Cr(CO)_6$ ($24 - 0 + 12 = 36$).

formulas.title: Stepwise and Overall Formation Constants of Complexes
formulas.derivation: Ligand complexation occurs in sequential stepwise equilibria: $M + L \rightleftharpoons ML$ ($k_1 = \frac{[ML]}{[M][L]}$); $ML + L \rightleftharpoons ML_2$ ($k_2 = \frac{[ML_2]}{[ML][L]}$); $\dots$ $ML_{n-1} + L \rightleftharpoons ML_n$ ($k_n = \frac{[ML_n]}{[ML_{n-1}][L]}$). Overall reaction is $M + n L \rightleftharpoons ML_n$ with equilibrium constant $\beta_n = \frac{[ML_n]}{[M][L]^n}$. Multiplying stepwise constants gives $k_1 \cdot k_2 \dots k_n = \frac{[ML]}{[M][L]} \frac{[ML_2]}{[ML][L]} \dots \frac{[ML_n]}{[ML_{n-1}][L]} = \frac{[ML_n]}{[M][L]^n} = \beta_n$.
formulas.description: Thermodynamic stability constants for stepwise ligand addition equilibrium $ML_{n-1} + L \rightleftharpoons ML_n$.
formulas.explanation: Typically $k_1 > k_2 > k_3 > \dots > k_n$ due to statistical factors and steric hindrance.

formulas.latex: \Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ \quad (\Delta S^\circ > 0 \implies \text{Chelate Effect})
formulas.title: The Chelate Effect
formulas.derivation: Consider substitution of 6 monodentate ligands by 3 bidentate ligands: $[Ni(NH_3)_6]^{2+} + 3 en \rightleftharpoons [Ni(en)_3]^{2+} + 6 NH_3$. Reactant count is $1 + 3 = 4$ species; product count is $1 + 6 = 7$ species. Net increase of 3 independent dissolved particles generates substantial positive entropy of reaction: $\Delta S^\circ \gg 0$. Since $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$, this large positive entropy makes $\Delta G^\circ$ significantly more negative, driving formation constant higher by several orders of magnitude.
formulas.description: Enhanced thermodynamic stability of polydentate chelate complexes over monodentate analogues driven by positive entropy.
formulas.explanation: EDTA ($hexadentate$) forms extremely stable complexes with almost all metal cations ($1 + 1 \to 1 + 6$ displacement release).

formulas.latex: t_{2g}^3 e_g^1, \quad t_{2g}^6 e_g^1, \quad t_{2g}^6 e_g^3 \implies \text{Jahn-Teller Distortion}
formulas.title: Jahn-Teller Theorem Distortion

variables.d^9, d^4, d^7: Electronic configurations exhibiting strong Jahn-Teller effect

formulas.derivation: Hermann Jahn and Edward Teller (1937) proved mathematically that any non-linear molecular system in an electronically degenerate ground state is inherently unstable and will undergo geometric distortion to lower its symmetry, remove orbital degeneracy, and lower overall energy. In octahedral $d^9$ complexes (e.g. $Cu^{2+}$: $t_{2g}^6 e_g^3$), the odd electron can reside in either $d_{z^2}$ or $d_{x^2-y^2}$. Elongating along z-axis lowers energy of $d_{z^2}$ and destabilizes $d_{x^2-y^2}$, yielding 4 short equatorial bonds and 2 elongated axial bonds (tetragonal distortion).
formulas.description: Geometric distortion of non-linear degenerate electronic states to remove orbital degeneracy and lower energy.
formulas.explanation: Explains why $Cu(II)$ octahedral complexes are never perfectly regular octahedra, displaying pronounced axial elongation.

formulas.latex: r_{tet} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a - r_{anion} \approx 0.225 r_A, \quad r_{oct} = \frac{a}{2} - r_{anion} \approx 0.414 r_A
formulas.title: Radius Ratio Rules for Coordination Polyhedra in Solid State
formulas.derivation: Geometric contact condition requires central cation to touch all surrounding anions without anions overlapping: Linear ($CN=2$): $r_+/r_- < 0.155$. Trigonal planar ($CN=3$): $0.155 \le r_+/r_- < 0.225$. Tetrahedral ($CN=4$): geometry gives $\cos(109.5^\circ/2) = \frac{r_-}{r_+ + r_-} \implies r_+/r_- = \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2} - 1 = 0.225$. Octahedral ($CN=6$): square in-plane diagonal gives $2(r_+ + r_-) = \sqrt{2}(2r_-) \implies r_+/r_- = \sqrt{2} - 1 = 0.414$. Cubic ($CN=8$): body diagonal gives $2(r_+ + r_-) = \sqrt{3}(2r_-) \implies r_+/r_- = \sqrt{3} - 1 = 0.732$.
formulas.description: Limiting radius ratios determining stable coordination numbers (tetrahedral, octahedral, cubic) in ionic crystals.
formulas.explanation: Example: $NaCl$ ($r_{Na+}/r_{Cl-} = 0.525$, in $0.414 - 0.732$ range $\implies CN=6$ octahedral); $CsCl$ ($0.93 > 0.732 \implies CN=8$ cubic).

formulas.title: Crystalline Unit Cell Density Formula

variables.Z: Number of formula units per unit cell

formulas.derivation: Density is mass divided by volume: $\rho = \frac{m_{cell}}{V_{cell}}$. Volume of cubic unit cell is $V = a^3$. Mass of unit cell is mass of $Z$ formula units: $m_{cell} = Z \times m_{atom} = Z \times \left(\frac{M}{N_A}\right)$. Substituting yields $\rho = \frac{Z \cdot M}{N_A \cdot a^3}$. Lattice parameters: Simple cubic ($Z=1, a=2R$); Body-centered cubic ($Z=2, \sqrt{3}a = 4R$); Face-centered cubic ($Z=4, \sqrt{2}a = 4R$).
formulas.description: Calculates macroscopic solid crystal density directly from unit cell edge length a and lattice particle count Z.
formulas.explanation: Fundamental crystallographic formula connecting atomic micro-structure to macroscopic laboratory density.

formulas.latex: 2 d \sin\theta = n \lambda \quad (\text{Bragg's Law of X-Ray Diffraction})
formulas.title: Bragg's Law of Crystal X-Ray Diffraction
formulas.derivation: William Henry Bragg and William Lawrence Bragg (1913) treated crystal planes as specular semi-reflecting mirrors. Path difference between rays reflected from two adjacent parallel planes separated by distance $d$ is $\Delta x = 2 d\sin\theta$. Constructive interference produces sharp diffraction peaks when path difference is an integer number of wavelengths: $2d\sin\theta = n\lambda$. For cubic crystal with Miller indices $(h, k, l)$: $d_{hkl} = \frac{a}{\sqrt{h^2 + k^2 + l^2}}$.
formulas.description: Constructive interference condition for X-rays reflected from parallel lattice planes separated by spacing d.
formulas.explanation: Primary experimental technique for solving 3D atomic structures of crystalline solids, proteins, and DNA.

formulas.title: Freundlich Adsorption Isotherm

variables.x/m: Mass of gas adsorbed per unit mass of solid adsorbent
variables.k, n: Freundlich empirical constants depending on adsorbent and gas

formulas.derivation: Herbert Freundlich (1909) deduced an empirical isotherm for multilayer/heterogeneous adsorption: $x/m = k P^{1/n}$. Taking base-10 logarithm: $\log(x/m) = \log k + \frac{1}{n}\log P$. Plotting $\log(x/m)$ versus $\log P$ yields straight line of slope $1/n$ ($0 \le 1/n \le 1$) and y-intercept $\log k$.
formulas.description: Empirical power-law relation for gas adsorption on solid heterogeneous surface at constant temperature.
formulas.explanation: At low pressure ($1/n = 1$): $x/m \propto P$. At high pressure ($1/n = 0$): $x/m = \text{constant}$ (adsorption saturation).

catalog_formula_sheets.name: Mechanical Properties of Solids Formula Sheet
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: Hooke's law states stress $\sigma$ is directly proportional to strain $\epsilon$, giving $Y = \sigma / \epsilon$. Work done in stretching is $W = \int_0^{\Delta L} F(x)dx = \int_0^{\Delta L} \frac{YA}{L}x dx = \frac{1}{2}\frac{YA}{L}(\Delta L)^2 = \frac{1}{2}F\Delta L$. Dividing by volume $V = AL$ yields energy density $u = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{F}{A}\right)\left(\frac{\Delta L}{L}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\sigma\epsilon = \frac{1}{2}Y\epsilon^2$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Valid only within proportional limit; material property independent of geometric dimensions.

formulas.title: Young's Modulus and Elastic Energy Density
formulas.derivation: Hooke's law states stress $\sigma$ is directly proportional to strain $\epsilon$, giving $Y = \sigma / \epsilon$. Work done in stretching is $W = \int_0^{\Delta L} F(x)dx = \int_0^{\Delta L} \frac{YA}{L}x dx = \frac{1}{2}\frac{YA}{L}(\Delta L)^2 = \frac{1}{2}F\Delta L$. formulas.description: Ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain within proportional limit, and energy stored per unit volume.

formulas.latex: P(h) = P_0 + \rho g h, \quad F_B = \rho_{fluid} V_{sub} g
formulas.title: Hydrostatic Pressure and Archimedes' Principle
formulas.derivation: Consider cylindrical fluid column of height $dh$ and area $A$: vertical balance requires $(P+dP)A - PA = \rho (A\,dh) g \implies dP = \rho g dh$. Integrating yields $P = P_0 + \rho g h$. Buoyant force is the net upward pressure integral over surface: $F_B = \oint P(-d\vec{A}) = \int_V \vec{\nabla} P dV = \int_V \rho g dV = \rho g V_{sub}$, which equals the weight of displaced fluid.
formulas.description: Pressure depth variation in incompressible static fluid and buoyant upward force on submerged body.
formulas.explanation: Archimedes' law holds for bodies of any shape, floating or completely submerged.

formulas.title: Equation of Continuity
formulas.derivation: Mass passing section 1 in time $dt$ is $dm_1 = \rho_1 A_1 v_1 dt$. Mass passing section 2 is $dm_2 = \rho_2 A_2 v_2 dt$. By mass conservation, $dm_1 = dm_2$. For incompressible flow ($\rho_1 = \rho_2 = \rho$), dividing by $\rho dt$ gives $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$.
formulas.description: Conservation of mass for steady, incompressible fluid flow through conduits of varying cross-section.
formulas.explanation: Fluid accelerates through constrictions (venturi necks) and slows down in expansions.

formulas.title: Bernoulli's Equation
formulas.derivation: Work done on fluid element of volume $\Delta V$ moving along streamline: $W = (P_1 - P_2)\Delta V$. Change in kinetic energy is $\Delta K = \frac{1}{2}\rho\Delta V(v_2^2 - v_1^2)$. Change in potential energy is $\Delta U = \rho\Delta V g(h_2 - h_1)$. Work-energy theorem $W = \Delta K + \Delta U$ gives $(P_1 - P_2)\Delta V = \frac{1}{2}\rho\Delta V(v_2^2 - v_1^2) + \rho\Delta V g(h_2 - h_1)$. Rearranging yields $P_1 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 + \rho g h_1 = P_2 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2 + \rho g h_2$.
formulas.description: Conservation of mechanical energy per unit volume along a streamline for steady, inviscid, incompressible flow.
formulas.explanation: Explains dynamic lift on aerofoils, aspirator pumps, and Venturi meters.

formulas.title: Torricelli's Law of Efflux

variables.H: Total height of liquid in tank
variables.h: Depth of orifice below liquid surface
variables.R_{horizontal}: Range of liquid jet on floor

formulas.derivation: Apply Bernoulli between top surface (1) and orifice (2): $P_0 + 0 + \rho g h = P_0 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + 0$ (assuming tank area $A_1 \gg A_2$). Solving gives $v = \sqrt{2gh}$. Liquid falls distance $H - h$ to ground in time $t = \sqrt{2(H - h)/g}$. Range is $R = v t = \sqrt{2gh}\sqrt{2(H - h)/g} = 2\sqrt{h(H - h)}$.
formulas.description: Speed of fluid discharging from small orifice at depth h below open liquid surface of tank height H.
formulas.explanation: Range is maximized when orifice is drilled at mid-depth $h = H/2$, yielding $R_{max} = H$.

formulas.latex: \Delta P = \frac{2T}{R} \quad (\text{Drop / Bubble in liquid}), \quad \Delta P = \frac{4T}{R} \quad (\text{Soap Bubble in air})
formulas.title: Young-Laplace Equation for Excess Surface Tension Pressure
formulas.derivation: Consider hemispherical cap of bubble of radius $R$: separating line of circumference $2\pi R$ sustains surface tension force $F_T = T(2\pi R)$ for a single interface. Pressure force acting on cross-section is $F_P = \Delta P (\pi R^2)$. Equilibrium requires $\Delta P(\pi R^2) = 2\pi R T \implies \Delta P = \frac{2T}{R}$. A soap bubble in air possesses two surfaces (inner and outer), doubling force to $F_T = 2 \times T(2\pi R)$, yielding $\Delta P = \frac{4T}{R}$.
formulas.description: Overpressure inside a curved interface sustained by surface tension T.
formulas.explanation: Smaller bubbles have higher internal pressure, explaining why connecting two different sized bubbles causes smaller one to empty into larger one.

formulas.title: Jurin's Law for Capillary Rise
formulas.derivation: Meniscus radius of curvature is $R = r / \cos\theta$. Pressure just below meniscus is $P_0 - \frac{2T}{R} = P_0 - \frac{2T\cos\theta}{r}$. Hydrostatic balance at liquid reservoir surface gives $P_0 - \frac{2T\cos\theta}{r} + \rho g h = P_0 \implies \rho g h = \frac{2T\cos\theta}{r} \implies h = \frac{2T\cos\theta}{\rho g r}$.
formulas.description: Height of liquid column drawn up a narrow vertical tube of internal radius r due to wettability.
formulas.explanation: For wetting liquids ($\theta < 90^\circ$, e.g. water-glass), $h > 0$ (rises); for non-wetting liquids ($\theta > 90^\circ$, e.g. mercury), meniscus depresses ($h < 0$).

formulas.title: Stokes' Law and Terminal Velocity
formulas.derivation: Stokes derived laminar creeping drag $F_v = 6\pi\eta rv$ by solving Navier-Stokes equations for low Reynolds number ($Re \ll 1$). At terminal speed $v_t$, net acceleration vanishes: downward gravity equals buoyancy plus viscous drag: $m g = F_B + F_v \implies \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho_s g = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho_f g + 6\pi\eta r v_t$. Solving for $v_t$: $6\pi\eta r v_t = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 (\rho_s - \rho_f) g \implies v_t = \frac{2}{9}\frac{r^2(\rho_s - \rho_f)g}{\eta}$.
formulas.description: Viscous drag force on a creeping sphere of radius r and steady terminal settling speed.
formulas.explanation: Terminal speed scales with radius squared ($v_t \propto r^2$), explaining why tiny mist droplets stay suspended in air for hours.

formulas.title: Poiseuille's Law of Laminar Pipe Flow
formulas.derivation: Consider fluid cylinder of radius $y$ and length $L$: shear force balances pressure drop: $\Delta P (\pi y^2) = -\eta (2\pi y L) \frac{dv}{dy} \implies \frac{dv}{dy} = -\frac{\Delta P}{2\eta L} y$. Integrating with no-slip boundary $v(r) = 0$ gives parabolic velocity profile $v(y) = \frac{\Delta P}{4\eta L}(r^2 - y^2)$. Integrating flux across concentric rings: $Q = \int_0^r v(y) 2\pi y dy = 2\pi \frac{\Delta P}{4\eta L} \int_0^r (r^2 y - y^3) dy = \frac{\pi\Delta P}{2\eta L}\left(\frac{r^4}{2} - \frac{r^4}{4}\right) = \frac{\pi \Delta P r^4}{8\eta L}$.
formulas.description: Steady volumetric flow rate of viscous Newtonian fluid through a circular pipe of radius r and length L.
formulas.explanation: Extreme sensitivity to radius ($r^4$ dependence): halving artery diameter reduces blood flow rate by a factor of 16 for identical pressure.

formulas.title: Bulk Modulus and Compressibility
formulas.derivation: Bulk strain is $-\frac{\Delta V}{V}$ (negative because volume decreases with increasing pressure). Bulk stress is hydraulic pressure increment $\Delta P$. Bulk modulus is defined as ratio $B = \frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}} = \frac{\Delta P}{-\Delta V / V} = -V\frac{dP}{dV}$.
formulas.description: Resistance of substance to uniform volumetric compression and reciprocal isothermal compressibility.
formulas.explanation: For ideal gas: isothermal bulk modulus is $B_{iso} = P$; adiabatic bulk modulus is $B_{adi} = \gamma P$.

formulas.title: Reynolds Number and Turbulence Criterion
formulas.derivation: Inertial force per unit volume scales as $\rho(\vec{v}\cdot\vec{\nabla})\vec{v} \sim \rho \frac{v^2}{D}$. Viscous force per unit volume scales as $\eta \nabla^2 \vec{v} \sim \eta \frac{v}{D^2}$. Ratio of inertial to viscous force is $\frac{\rho v^2 / D}{\eta v / D^2} = \frac{\rho v D}{\eta} = N_R$.
formulas.description: Dimensionless ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces governing flow regime transition.
formulas.explanation: In pipe flow: $N_R < 2000$ indicates laminar streamline flow; $N_R > 3000$ indicates fully turbulent chaotic flow.

formulas.title: Thermal Expansion and Thermal Stress
formulas.derivation: Unconstrained rod expands by $\Delta L = L\alpha \Delta T$. If clamped between rigid immovable supports, supports exert compressive force $F$ to maintain zero net elongation: strain prevented is $\epsilon = \frac{\Delta L}{L} = \alpha \Delta T$. By definition of Young's modulus, stress generated is $\sigma = Y\epsilon = Y\alpha \Delta T$.
formulas.description: Fractional longitudinal thermal expansion and induced compressive/tensile stress when ends are rigidly clamped.
formulas.explanation: Explains why expansion gaps are engineered into railway tracks, bridges, and concrete highways.

catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: From universal energy conservation: change in internal state function $U$ equals energy entering system as heat ($q$) plus energy entering as mechanical boundary work ($w$). Under IUPAC sign convention, work done on the system by surroundings during compression is positive ($w > 0$), while work done by expanding system against external pressure $P_{ext}$ is negative: $w = -\int P_{ext}dV = -P_{ext}\Delta V$.

formulas.latex: \Delta U = q + w = q - P_{ext}\Delta V

formulas.title: Enthalpy and Internal Energy Relation for Chemical Reactions

variables.\\Delta n_g: Moles of gaseous products minus moles of gaseous reactants

formulas.derivation: By definition, enthalpy is $H = U + PV$. For finite change at constant pressure: $\Delta H = \Delta U + P\Delta V$. For ideal gas reaction where volume change is dominated by gases: $P V = n_g R T \implies P\Delta V = (\Delta n_g) R T$. Substituting yields $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g R T$.
formulas.description: Relates constant-pressure reaction heat $\Delta H$ to constant-volume reaction heat $\Delta U$ for ideal gas mixtures.
formulas.explanation: If $\Delta n_g = 0$ (e.g. $H_{2(g)} + I_{2(g)} \to 2HI_{(g)}$), $\Delta H = \Delta U$. If $\Delta n_g > 0$, expansion work means $\Delta H > \Delta U$.

formulas.title: Hess's Law and Standard Enthalpy of Reaction
formulas.derivation: Germain Hess (1840) established that because enthalpy $H$ is a thermodynamic state function, net heat evolved or absorbed in a chemical process depends solely on initial and final states, independent of pathway. By convention, standard enthalpies of formation of pure elements in reference standard states ($O_{2(g)}, C_{(graphite)}, H_{2(g)}$) are assigned zero: $\Delta_f H^\circ = 0$. Summing product enthalpies and subtracting reactant enthalpies gives the formula.
formulas.description: Reaction enthalpy calculated by summing standard enthalpies of formation of products minus reactants.
formulas.explanation: Allows indirect calculation of reaction heats that cannot be measured directly in a calorimeter.

formulas.title: Reaction Enthalpy from Bond Enthalpies
formulas.derivation: In a gas-phase reaction, chemical bonds in reactant molecules are first homolytically cleaved into isolated gaseous atoms (an endothermic process requiring energy input: $+ \sum BE_{reactants}$). The isolated atoms then recombine to synthesize product molecules (an exothermic process releasing energy: $- \sum BE_{products}$). By Hess's Law, the net reaction enthalpy is $\Delta_r H = \sum BE_{reactants} - \sum BE_{products}$.
formulas.description: Estimates gas-phase reaction enthalpy from homolytic covalent bond dissociation energies.
formulas.explanation: Applies strictly to gas-phase reactions with non-delocalized, localized covalent bonds.

formulas.latex: \frac{\Delta H_{T_2} - \Delta H_{T_1}}{T_2 - T_1} = \Delta C_p = \sum \nu_p C_{p, prod} - \sum \nu_r C_{p, react}
formulas.title: Kirchhoff's Law of Thermochemistry

variables.\\Delta C_p: Net change in molar heat capacity at constant pressure

formulas.derivation: At constant pressure, $\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial T}\right)_P = C_p$. Differentiating reaction enthalpy $\Delta_r H = H_{prod} - H_{react}$ with respect to temperature: $\frac{d(\Delta_r H)}{dT} = \left(\frac{\partial H_{prod}}{\partial T}\right) - \left(\frac{\partial H_{react}}{\partial T}\right) = C_{p, prod} - C_{p, react} = \Delta C_p$. Integrating from $T_1$ to $T_2$ assuming $\Delta C_p$ is approximately constant yields Kirchhoff's relation: $\Delta H_{T_2} = \Delta H_{T_1} + \Delta C_p (T_2 - T_1)$.
formulas.description: Temperature dependence of reaction enthalpy governed by reaction heat capacity change $\Delta C_p$.
formulas.explanation: If $\Delta C_p > 0$, reaction becomes more endothermic (or less exothermic) as temperature rises.

formulas.title: Second Law of Thermodynamics and Entropy Change
formulas.derivation: Rudolf Clausius (1865) proved that for any reversible cyclic process, $\oint \frac{dq_{rev}}{T} = 0$, establishing that $dS = \frac{dq_{rev}}{T}$ is an exact differential of a state function. For any spontaneous irreversible process, Clausius inequality gives $\oint \frac{dq}{T} < 0$, leading to $\Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr} = \Delta S_{univ} > 0$. At reversible equilibrium, $\Delta S_{univ} = 0$.
formulas.description: Definition of entropy as state function and universal condition for spontaneous irreversible processes.
formulas.explanation: All spontaneous real processes in the universe proceed with an overall increase in total entropy ($\Delta S_{univ} > 0$).

formulas.latex: \Delta S_{ideal\_gas} = n C_v \ln\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) + n R \ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right) = n C_p \ln\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) - n R \ln\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)
formulas.title: Entropy Change of an Ideal Gas
formulas.derivation: From First Law for reversible path: $dq_{rev} = dU - dw_{rev} = n C_v dT + P\,dV$. Dividing by $T$ using ideal gas law $P/T = nR/V$: $dS = \frac{dq_{rev}}{T} = n C_v \frac{dT}{T} + n R \frac{dV}{V}$. Integrating from initial state $(T_1, V_1)$ to final state $(T_2, V_2)$: $\Delta S = n C_v \ln(T_2 / T_1) + n R \ln(V_2 / V_1)$. Using $V_2 / V_1 = (T_2 P_1) / (T_1 P_2)$ and Mayer's relation $C_p = C_v + R$ gives the pressure form.
formulas.description: Entropy calculation for an ideal gas undergoing simultaneous temperature, volume, or pressure transitions.
formulas.explanation: For isothermal process ($T_1 = T_2$), $\Delta S = n R \ln(V_2/V_1) = -n R \ln(P_2/P_1)$.

formulas.latex: \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S, \quad \Delta G_{sys} = -T\Delta S_{univ} < 0 \text{ (Spontaneous)}
formulas.title: Gibbs Free Energy and Spontaneity Criterion
formulas.derivation: At constant $T$ and $P$, heat transferred to surroundings is $q_{surr} = -q_{sys} = -\Delta H_{sys}$. Surrounding entropy change is $\Delta S_{surr} = \frac{q_{surr}}{T} = -\frac{\Delta H_{sys}}{T}$. Universal entropy change is $\Delta S_{univ} = \Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr} = \Delta S_{sys} - \frac{\Delta H_{sys}}{T}$. Multiplying by $-T$: $-T\Delta S_{univ} = \Delta H_{sys} - T\Delta S_{sys}$. Defining Gibbs free energy $G = H - TS$ gives $\Delta G_{sys} = -T\Delta S_{univ}$. Since $\Delta S_{univ} > 0$ for spontaneity, $\Delta G_{sys} < 0$.
formulas.description: Thermodynamic potential determining spontaneity of chemical processes at constant temperature and pressure.
formulas.explanation: Criterion for spontaneity at constant $T, P$: $\Delta G < 0$ (spontaneous, exergonic); $\Delta G = 0$ (dynamic equilibrium); $\Delta G > 0$ (non-spontaneous, endergonic).

formulas.latex: \Delta G^\circ = -R T \ln K = -2.303 R T \log_{10} K
formulas.title: Standard Gibbs Free Energy and Equilibrium Constant Relation
formulas.derivation:
Chemical potential of species $i$ in mixture is $\mu_i = \mu_i^\circ + RT\ln a_i$. Reaction Gibbs free energy is $\Delta_r G = \sum 
u_i \mu_i = \sum 
u_i \mu_i^\circ + RT \sum 
u_i \ln a_i = \Delta_r G^\circ + RT\ln Q$ where $Q = \prod a_i^{
u_i}$ is the reaction quotient. At dynamic chemical equilibrium, net driving force vanishes: $\Delta_r G = 0$ and $Q = K_{eq}$. Substituting gives $0 = \Delta_r G^\circ + RT\ln K \implies \Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$.
formulas.description: Fundamental thermodynamic bridge connecting chemical equilibrium constant K to standard state free energy $\Delta G^\circ$.
formulas.explanation: If $\Delta G^\circ < 0$, then $K > 1$ (products favored at equilibrium); if $\Delta G^\circ > 0$, $K < 1$ (reactants favored).

formulas.title: van 't Hoff Equation
formulas.derivation: From $\ln K = -\frac{\Delta G^\circ}{RT} = -\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{RT} + \frac{\Delta S^\circ}{R}$. Differentiating with respect to temperature $T$ assuming $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ are independent of $T$: $\frac{d\ln K}{dT} = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{RT^2}$. Integrating from $T_1$ to $T_2$: $\int_{K_1}^{K_2} d\ln K = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\int_{T_1}^{T_2} T^{-2}dT \implies \ln(K_2/K_1) = -\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right) = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right)$.
formulas.description: Temperature sensitivity of chemical equilibrium constant governed by standard reaction enthalpy.
formulas.explanation: Thermodynamic proof of Le Chatelier's principle: for endothermic reactions ($\Delta H^\circ > 0$), increasing temperature increases $K$; for exothermic reactions ($\Delta H^\circ < 0$), increasing temperature decreases $K$.

formulas.latex: \Delta S_{fus} = \frac{\Delta H_{fus}}{T_m}, \quad \Delta S_{vap} = \frac{\Delta H_{vap}}{T_b} \approx 88 \text{ J/mol K (Trouton's Rule)}
formulas.title: Entropy of Phase Transitions and Trouton's Rule
formulas.derivation: At normal melting and boiling points, the two phases coexist in reversible dynamic equilibrium: $\Delta G = 0 \implies \Delta H - T\Delta S = 0 \implies \Delta S = \Delta H / T$. Trouton (1884) noted empirically that for non-associated liquids vaporizing to gas, the volume increase is roughly constant ($\sim 1000\times$), giving universal entropy of vaporization $\Delta S_{vap} = \frac{\Delta H_{vap}}{T_b} \approx 85 - 88\text{ J/mol K}$.
formulas.description: Entropy of fusion and vaporization at equilibrium phase transition temperatures.
formulas.explanation: Hydrogen-bonded liquids (water: $\Delta S_{vap} \approx 109\text{ J/mol K}$, ethanol) deviate positively from Trouton's rule due to high liquid-state order.

formulas.latex: S = k_B \ln \Omega, \quad S(T=0) = 0 \quad (\text{Third Law of Thermodynamics})
formulas.title: Boltzmann Entropy Formula and Third Law

variables.\\Omega: Number of accessible microstates corresponding to macroscopic state

formulas.derivation: Ludwig Boltzmann (1877) proved entropy is a logarithmic measure of microscopic multiplicity: $S = k_B \ln\Omega$. Nernst and Planck formulated the Third Law: as temperature approaches absolute zero ($T \to 0\text{ K}$), thermal motion ceases, and a perfectly ordered pure crystalline lattice settles into a unique non-degenerate quantum ground state ($\Omega = 1$). Therefore, $S_0 = k_B\ln(1) = 0$.
formulas.description: Microscopic statistical definition of entropy and absolute zero entropy of perfect crystalline substances.
formulas.explanation: Allows establishing absolute standard entropies $S^\circ$ for chemical substances, unlike internal energy or enthalpy which are only known relative to arbitrary references.

formulas.title: Maximum Non-Expansion Work and Cell EMF
formulas.derivation: From fundamental thermodynamic equation $dG = V dP - S dT + dw_{non-PV}$. At constant $T$ and $P$, $dG = dw_{non-PV}$. For reversible electrochemical cell, charge transferred is $Q = n F$, and electrical work done by cell is $w_{elec} = Q E_{cell} = n F E_{cell}$. Work done on system is $w = -n F E_{cell}$. Hence $\Delta G = -n F E_{cell}$.
formulas.description: Decrease in Gibbs free energy equals the maximum electrical reversible work extracted from an electrochemical cell.
formulas.explanation: For spontaneous galvanic cell, $E_{cell} > 0 \implies \Delta G < 0$.

formulas.latex: C_p - C_v = T \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = \frac{T V \beta^2}{\kappa_T}
formulas.title: General Thermodynamic Heat Capacity Difference
formulas.derivation: Internal energy differential is $dU = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_V dT + \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T dV$. Dividing by $dT$ at constant $P$ and noting $dH = dU + P\,dV + V\,dP$: $C_p - C_v = \left[P + \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T\right]\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P$. Using Maxwell relation $\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T = T\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V - P$, the $P$ terms cancel, yielding $C_p - C_v = T\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = \frac{TV\beta^2}{\kappa_T}$. For ideal gas ($PV = nRT$), $\beta = 1/T$ and $\kappa_T = 1/P$, recovering Mayer's relation $C_p - C_v = R$.
formulas.description: Universal relationship between isobaric and isochoric heat capacities for any substance (solid, liquid, or gas).
formulas.explanation: Because $T > 0, V > 0, \kappa_T > 0$, and $\beta^2 \ge 0$, $C_p$ is strictly greater than or equal to $C_v$ for all physical materials.

content_json.derivation: From universal energy conservation: change in internal state function $U$ equals energy entering system as heat ($q$) plus energy entering as mechanical boundary work ($w$). Under IUPAC sign convention, work done on the system by surroundings during compression is positive ($w > 0$), while work done by expanding system against external pressure $P_{ext}$ is negative: $w = -\int P_{ext}dV = -P_{ext}\Delta V$.
content_json.explanation: At constant volume (bomb calorimeter), $\Delta V = 0 \implies w = 0$, so $\Delta U = q_v$.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: Three-Dimensional Geometry Formula Sheet
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: By Law of Cosines on triangle formed by $\vec{a}, \vec{b}$, and $\vec{c} = \vec{a} - \vec{b}$: $|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 - 2|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta$. Expanding in components: $\sum (a_i - b_i)^2 = \sum a_i^2 + \sum b_i^2 - 2\sum a_i b_i$. Equating: $|\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 - 2\sum a_i b_i = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 - 2|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta \implies \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta = \sum a_i b_i$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Fundamental vector operation measuring alignment. Two non-zero vectors are perpendicular if and only if their dot product is zero.

content_json.title: Three-Dimensional Geometry Formula Sheet

sections.title: Three-Dimensional Geometry Formula Sheet - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.latex: \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}| |\vec{b}| \cos\theta = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3
formulas.title: Scalar (Dot) Product of Vectors
formulas.derivation: By Law of Cosines on triangle formed by $\vec{a}, \vec{b}$, and $\vec{c} = \vec{a} - \vec{b}$: $|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 - 2|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta$. Expanding in components: $\sum (a_i - b_i)^2 = \sum a_i^2 + \sum b_i^2 - 2\sum a_i b_i$. Equating: $|\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 - 2\sum a_i b_i = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 - 2|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta \implies \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta = \sum a_i b_i$.
formulas.description: Scalar (Dot) Product of Vectors
formulas.explanation: Fundamental vector operation measuring alignment. Two non-zero vectors are perpendicular if and only if their dot product is zero.

formulas.latex: \vec{a} \times \vec{b} = |\vec{a}| |\vec{b}| \sin\theta \, \hat{n} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \end{vmatrix}
formulas.title: Vector (Cross) Product and Triangle Area

variables.\\hat{n}: unit vector normal to plane of a and b via right-hand rule

formulas.derivation: By geometric definition, $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ is vector perpendicular to both $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ with magnitude equal to the area of the parallelogram formed by them ($|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\sin\theta$). Expanding basis vectors: $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}$, $\hat{j} \times \hat{k} = \hat{i}$, $\hat{k} \times \hat{i} = \hat{j}$. Linearity gives the $3 \times 3$ determinant form.
formulas.description: Vector (Cross) Product and Triangle Area
formulas.explanation: Produces a vector mutually perpendicular to two vectors; magnitude equals the area of the spanned parallelogram.

formulas.latex: [\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}] = \vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \\ c_1 & c_2 & c_3 \end{vmatrix}
formulas.title: Scalar Triple Product (Box Product) and Parallelepiped Volume

variables.V = |[\\vec{a} \\vec{b} \\vec{c}]|: volume of parallelepiped spanned by vectors a, b, c

formulas.derivation: Volume of parallelepiped = $(\text{Base Area}) \times (\text{Height})$. Base is parallelogram spanned by $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$, so area vector is $\vec{A} = \vec{b} \times \vec{c}$. Height is projection of $\vec{a}$ onto normal $\hat{n} = \frac{\vec{b}\times\vec{c}}{|\vec{b}\times\vec{c}|}$: $h = |\vec{a}||\cos\phi|$. Volume $= |\vec{b}\times\vec{c}| |\vec{a}| |\cos\phi| = |\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b}\times\vec{c})|$. Substituting determinant components for cross and dot products yields the $3 \times 3$ determinant.
formulas.description: Scalar Triple Product (Box Product) and Parallelepiped Volume
formulas.explanation: Calculates the volume of a 3D parallelepiped; value is zero if and only if the three vectors are coplanar.

formulas.title: Vector Triple Product (BAC-CAB Rule)
formulas.derivation: The vector $\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})$ is perpendicular to $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}$, so it lies in the plane of $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$: $\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = x \vec{b} + y \vec{c}$. It is also perpendicular to $\vec{a}$, so $\vec{a} \cdot [x\vec{b} + y\vec{c}] = 0 \implies x(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}) + y(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}) = 0 \implies \frac{x}{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}} = -\frac{y}{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}} = \lambda$. Evaluating with standard basis vectors (e.g. $\vec{a}=\hat{i}, \vec{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}, \vec{c}=\hat{k}$) determines $\lambda = 1$. Thus $\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = (\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{b} - (\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})\vec{c}$.
formulas.description: Vector Triple Product (BAC-CAB Rule)
formulas.explanation: Famous 'BAC minus CAB' identity expressing double cross-products as a linear combination of the inner vectors.

formulas.title: Lagrange's Vector Identity
formulas.derivation: By definition: $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|^2 = (|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\sin\theta)^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 |\vec{b}|^2 \sin^2\theta$. Use Pythagorean trigonometric identity $\sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos^2\theta$: $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 |\vec{b}|^2 (1 - \cos^2\theta) = |\vec{a}|^2 |\vec{b}|^2 - (|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta)^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 |\vec{b}|^2 - (\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})^2$.
formulas.description: Lagrange's Vector Identity
formulas.explanation: Connects magnitude of cross product directly to dot product without calculating angles.

formulas.title: Direction Cosines of a Line in 3D Space

variables.\\alpha, \\beta, \\gamma: angles made by line with positive x, y, z coordinate axes

formulas.derivation: Let $\hat{u}$ be a unit vector along the line: $\hat{u} = l\hat{i} + m\hat{j} + n\hat{k}$. Since it is a unit vector: $|\hat{u}|^2 = l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$. Since $l = \cos\alpha, m = \cos\beta, n = \cos\gamma$: $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1$. Using $\sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos^2\theta$: $(1 - \sin^2\alpha) + (1 - \sin^2\beta) + (1 - \sin^2\gamma) = 1 \implies \sin^2\alpha + \sin^2\beta + \sin^2\gamma = 3 - 1 = 2$.
formulas.description: Direction Cosines of a Line in 3D Space
formulas.explanation: Fundamental identities governing direction angles of any directed line in 3-dimensional Euclidean space.

formulas.title: Symmetric Cartesian Equation of a Straight Line in 3D
formulas.derivation: Let $\vec{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$ be an arbitrary point on the line passing through point $A(\vec{a}) = x_1\hat{i} + y_1\hat{j} + z_1\hat{k}$ parallel to direction vector $\vec{b} = a\hat{i} + b\hat{j} + c\hat{k}$. Vector equation: $\vec{r} - \vec{a} = \lambda \vec{b} \implies (x - x_1)\hat{i} + (y - y_1)\hat{j} + (z - z_1)\hat{k} = \lambda(a\hat{i} + b\hat{j} + c\hat{k})$. Equating components: $x - x_1 = \lambda a, y - y_1 = \lambda b, z - z_1 = \lambda c \implies \lambda = \frac{x - x_1}{a} = \frac{y - y_1}{b} = \frac{z - z_1}{c}$.
formulas.description: Symmetric Cartesian Equation of a Straight Line in 3D
formulas.explanation: Standard equation of a straight line in 3D geometry defined by a point and direction ratios.

formulas.title: Shortest Distance Between Two Skew Lines
formulas.derivation: The common perpendicular line segment connecting the two skew lines is parallel to $\vec{n} = \vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2$. Unit normal is $\hat{n} = \frac{\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2}{|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2|}$. The shortest distance $d$ is the magnitude of the projection of the displacement vector $\vec{a}_2 - \\vec{a}_1$ joining points on the two lines onto this common normal: $d = |(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot \hat{n}| = \frac{|(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2)|}{|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2|}$.
formulas.description: Shortest Distance Between Two Skew Lines
formulas.explanation: Distance between two non-intersecting, non-parallel lines in 3D; lines intersect if and only if d = 0.

formulas.latex: (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) = 0 \iff \begin{vmatrix} x_2 - x_1 & y_2 - y_1 & z_2 - z_1 \\ a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \end{vmatrix} = 0
formulas.title: Condition for Two Lines in 3D to be Coplanar
formulas.derivation: Two lines are coplanar if and only if the shortest distance between them is zero. From the shortest distance formula, numerator vanishing gives $(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) = 0$. Writing displacement $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1$ and direction vectors $\vec{b}_1, \vec{b}_2$ in determinant form yields the coplanarity determinant equation.
formulas.description: Condition for Two Lines in 3D to be Coplanar
formulas.explanation: Tests whether two lines lie in the exact same plane in 3D space.

formulas.latex: A x + B y + C z + D = 0 \iff \vec{r} \cdot \vec{n} = d
formulas.title: General Equation of a Plane in 3D Space
formulas.derivation: Let plane pass through point $P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ with normal vector $\vec{n} = A\hat{i} + B\hat{j} + C\hat{k}$. For any point $P(x, y, z)$ on the plane, the vector $\vec{P_0 P} = (x-x_0)\hat{i} + (y-y_0)\hat{j} + (z-z_0)\hat{k}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{n}$: $\vec{P_0 P} \cdot \vec{n} = 0 \implies A(x - x_0) + B(y - y_0) + C(z - z_0) = 0 \implies Ax + By + Cz - (Ax_0 + By_0 + Cz_0) = 0$. Setting constant $D = -(Ax_0 + By_0 + Cz_0)$ gives $Ax + By + Cz + D = 0$.
formulas.description: General Equation of a Plane in 3D Space
formulas.explanation: Standard 3D linear equation describing a 2-dimensional flat plane with normal vector (A, B, C).

formulas.latex: d = \frac{|A x_0 + B y_0 + C z_0 + D|}{\sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + C^2}}
formulas.title: Perpendicular Distance from Point (x0, y0, z0) to Plane
formulas.derivation: Line through $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ along normal $\vec{n}$ has equation $\vec{r}(t) = (x_0 + At)\hat{i} + (y_0 + Bt)\hat{j} + (z_0 + Ct)\hat{k}$. Substitute into plane equation: $A(x_0 + At) + B(y_0 + Bt) + C(z_0 + Ct) + D = 0 \implies (A x_0 + B y_0 + C z_0 + D) + t(A^2 + B^2 + C^2) = 0 \implies t = -\\frac{A x_0 + B y_0 + C z_0 + D}{A^2 + B^2 + C^2}$. The distance is the displacement magnitude: $d = |t| |\vec{n}| = \\frac{|Ax_0 + By_0 + Cz_0 + D|}{A^2 + B^2 + C^2} \\sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + C^2} = \\frac{|Ax_0 + By_0 + Cz_0 + D|}{\\sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + C^2}}$.
formulas.description: Perpendicular Distance from Point (x0, y0, z0) to Plane
formulas.explanation: Measures the shortest Euclidean distance from any spatial point to a plane.

formulas.title: Angle Between Two Planes

variables.\\vec{n}_1, \\vec{n}_2: normal vectors to the two planes

formulas.derivation: The dihedral angle $\theta$ between two intersecting planes is identical to the angle between their respective normal vectors $\vec{n}_1 = A_1\hat{i} + B_1\hat{j} + C_1\hat{k}$ and $\vec{n}_2 = A_2\hat{i} + B_2\hat{j} + C_2\hat{k}$. By vector dot product: $\vec{n}_1 \cdot \vec{n}_2 = |\vec{n}_1| |\vec{n}_2| \cos\theta \implies \cos\theta = \frac{\vec{n}_1 \cdot \\vec{n}_2}{|\vec{n}_1| |\\vec{n}_2|}$. Planes are perpendicular if $A_1 A_2 + B_1 B_2 + C_1 C_2 = 0$.
formulas.description: Angle Between Two Planes
formulas.explanation: Calculates the angle between two flat planes by taking the dot product of their normal vectors.

formulas.latex: \sin\phi = \frac{|A a + B b + C c|}{\sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + C^2}\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}} = \frac{|\vec{n} \cdot \vec{b}|}{|\vec{n}| |\vec{b}|}
formulas.title: Angle Between a Line and a Plane
formulas.derivation: Let $\theta$ be the angle between the line's direction vector $\vec{b}$ and the plane's normal vector $\vec{n}$: $\cos\theta = \frac{\vec{n}\cdot\vec{b}}{|\vec{n}||\vec{b}|}$. The angle $\phi$ that the line makes with the plane is complementary to $\theta$: $\phi = 90^\circ - \theta$. Therefore $\sin\phi = \sin(90^\circ - \theta) = \cos\theta = \frac{|\vec{n}\cdot\vec{b}|}{|\vec{n}||\vec{b}|}$.
formulas.description: Angle Between a Line and a Plane
formulas.explanation: Notice the trigonometric function is sine (not cosine), because it measures the complementary angle to the plane normal.

formulas.latex: P_1 + \lambda P_2 = 0 \iff (A_1 x + B_1 y + C_1 z + D_1) + \lambda (A_2 x + B_2 y + C_2 z + D_2) = 0
formulas.title: Family of Planes Passing Through Line of Intersection

variables.\\lambda: real parameter determined by boundary condition

formulas.derivation: Let line of intersection of planes $P_1 = 0$ and $P_2 = 0$ be $L$. For any point $(x, y, z)$ on line $L$, both $P_1(x, y, z) = 0$ and $P_2(x, y, z) = 0$ are satisfied simultaneously. Thus $P_1 + \lambda P_2 = 0 + \lambda(0) = 0$ for any value of $\lambda$. Furthermore, $P_1 + \lambda P_2 = 0$ is linear in $x, y, z$, so it represents a plane. Hence it represents every plane passing through the intersection line $L$.
formulas.description: Family of Planes Passing Through Line of Intersection
formulas.explanation: Generates any plane containing the line of intersection of two known planes.

content_json.derivation: By Law of Cosines on triangle formed by $\vec{a}, \vec{b}$, and $\vec{c} = \vec{a} - \vec{b}$: $|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 - 2|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta$. Expanding in components: $\sum (a_i - b_i)^2 = \sum a_i^2 + \sum b_i^2 - 2\sum a_i b_i$. Equating: $|\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 - 2\sum a_i b_i = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 - 2|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta \implies \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta = \sum a_i b_i$.
content_json.explanation: Fundamental vector operation measuring alignment. Two non-zero vectors are perpendicular if and only if their dot product is zero.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: Inverse Trigonometric Functions Formula Sheet
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: In the unit circle, consider unit vectors $\vec{u} = \cos A \hat{i} + \sin A \hat{j}$ and $\vec{v} = \cos B \hat{i} + \sin B \hat{j}$. The angle between them is $A - B$. Scalar dot product: $\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v} = (1)(1)\cos(A - B)$. Component dot product: $\cos A \cos B + \sin A \sin B$. Equating gives $\cos(A - B) = \cos A \cos B + \sin A \sin B$. Replacing $B$ with $-B$ yields $\cos(A + B)$. Using co-function identities $\sin\theta = \cos(\pi/2 - \theta)$ gives the sine compound formulas.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Foundational compound angle identities used across all of geometry, trigonometry, and calculus.
