formulas.title: Crystal Field Splitting in Octahedral and Tetrahedral Fields
formulas.derivation: Hans Bethe (1929) developed Crystal Field Theory: in octahedral ligand field, 6 ligands approach along Cartesian axes ($x, y, z$). Orbitals with lobes pointing directly along axes ($d_{x^2-y^2}, d_{z^2}$) experience strong electrostatic repulsion and are destabilized by $+0.6\Delta_o$ ($e_g$). Orbitals directed between axes ($d_{xy}, d_{yz}, d_{xz}$) experience less repulsion and are stabilized by $-0.4\Delta_o$ ($t_{2g}$). In tetrahedral geometry, 4 ligands approach corners of cube (between axes), inverting splitting pattern and reducing splitting magnitude by factor $\Delta_t = \frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$ because fewer ligands are present and none point directly at d-orbitals.
formulas.description: Splitting of degenerate d-orbitals into $t_{2g}/e_g$ and $e/t_2$ manifolds in electrostatic ligand fields.
formulas.explanation: Because $\Delta_t < P$ (pairing energy) always, tetrahedral complexes are almost exclusively high-spin.

formulas.title: Crystal Field Stabilization Energy (CFSE) for Octahedral Complexes

variables.m: Number of extra electron pairs formed relative to free ion

formulas.derivation: Barycenter rule requires total energy shift of the 5 degenerate orbitals to sum to zero: $3(-0.4\Delta_o) + 2(+0.6\Delta_o) = -1.2\Delta_o + 1.2\Delta_o = 0$. Each electron occupying lower $t_{2g}$ level stabilizes complex by $-0.4\Delta_o$, while each electron occupying upper $e_g$ level destabilizes complex by $+0.6\Delta_o$. Summing contributions gives $CFSE = (-0.4 n_{t_{2g}} + 0.6 n_{e_g})\Delta_o$. When electrons pair in same orbital against Coulomb repulsion, pairing energy $+mP$ is added.
formulas.description: Net energetic stabilization of d-electron configuration relative to spherical barycenter.
formulas.explanation: If $\Delta_o > P$ (strong field ligands like $CN^-, CO$), pairing occurs producing low-spin complex. If $\Delta_o < P$ (weak field ligands like $F^-, Cl^-$), Hund's rule dominates producing high-spin complex.

formulas.latex: I^- < Br^- < S^{2-} < SCN^- < Cl^- < NO_3^- < N_3^- < F^- < OH^- < C_2O_4^{2-} < H_2O < NCS^- < CH_3CN < py < NH_3 < en < bipy < phen < NO_2^- < PPh_3 < CN^- < CO
formulas.title: Spectrochemical Series of Ligands
formulas.derivation: Derived from UV-visible absorption spectra ($d-d$ transition band wavenumbers $\Delta_o = h c \bar{\nu}$). Ligands fall into three classes based on metal-ligand bonding: (1) Halides and oxygen donors are $\pi$-donors: ligand filled p-orbitals donate electron density into metal $t_{2g}$, destabilizing $t_{2g}$ and shrinking $\Delta_o$ (weak field). (2) Ammonia and amines are pure $\sigma$-donors: intermediate $\Delta_o$. (3) $CN^-$ and $CO$ are strong $\pi$-acceptors (back-bonding): empty $\pi^*$ orbitals accept electron density from metal $t_{2g}$, dramatically stabilizing $t_{2g}$ and expanding $\Delta_o$ (strong field).
formulas.description: Empirical ranking of ligands according to increasing magnitude of crystal field splitting $\Delta_o$.
formulas.explanation: Enables predicting whether transition metal complex is high-spin or low-spin, and determines magnetic and color properties.

formulas.title: Magnetic Moments of Coordination Complexes

variables.\\mu_{eff}: Effective magnetic moment in Bohr Magnetons (BM)

formulas.derivation: In first-row ($3d$) transition metal complexes, non-spherical electrostatic crystal field of surrounding ligands quenches orbital angular momentum ($L \approx 0$) by breaking spatial rotational symmetry. Magnetic moment reduces to spin-only expression: $\mu_s = g\sqrt{S(S+1)}\mu_B$. With electron g-factor $g \approx 2.00$ and $S = n/2$: $\mu_s = 2\sqrt{\frac{n}{2}\left(\frac{n+2}{2}\right)} = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\mu_B$.
formulas.description: Spin-only magnetic moment and complete spin-plus-orbital magnetic moment for first-row transition ions.
formulas.explanation: Guouy balance magnetic measurement directly diagnoses high-spin vs low-spin states (e.g. $[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}$ has $n=1, \mu = 1.73\text{ BM}$ while $[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{3+}$ has $n=5, \mu = 5.92\text{ BM}$).

formulas.title: Sidgwick's Effective Atomic Number (EAN) Rule / 18-Electron Rule
formulas.derivation: Nevild Sidgwick (1927) proposed that coordinate covalent bonds donate 2 electrons per coordination bond. The total effective electrons surrounding metal core is $EAN = Z - (\text{oxidation state}) + 2 \times (\text{ligand pairs})$. If $EAN$ equals the atomic number of the next noble gas ($Kr=36, Xe=54, Rn=86$), the complex possesses a completely filled valence shell of 18 electrons ($ns^2 (n-1)d^{10} np^6$), conferring high kinetic and thermodynamic stability.
formulas.description: Predicts stability of coordination and organometallic complexes by mimicking next noble gas configuration.
formulas.explanation: Explains stoichiometry of metal carbonyls: $Ni(CO)_4$ ($28 - 0 + 8 = 36$, $18e^-$), $Fe(CO)_5$ ($26 - 0 + 10 = 36$), $Cr(CO)_6$ ($24 - 0 + 12 = 36$).

formulas.title: Stepwise and Overall Formation Constants of Complexes
formulas.derivation: Ligand complexation occurs in sequential stepwise equilibria: $M + L \rightleftharpoons ML$ ($k_1 = \frac{[ML]}{[M][L]}$); $ML + L \rightleftharpoons ML_2$ ($k_2 = \frac{[ML_2]}{[ML][L]}$); $\dots$ $ML_{n-1} + L \rightleftharpoons ML_n$ ($k_n = \frac{[ML_n]}{[ML_{n-1}][L]}$). Overall reaction is $M + n L \rightleftharpoons ML_n$ with equilibrium constant $\beta_n = \frac{[ML_n]}{[M][L]^n}$. Multiplying stepwise constants gives $k_1 \cdot k_2 \dots k_n = \frac{[ML]}{[M][L]} \frac{[ML_2]}{[ML][L]} \dots \frac{[ML_n]}{[ML_{n-1}][L]} = \frac{[ML_n]}{[M][L]^n} = \beta_n$.
formulas.description: Thermodynamic stability constants for stepwise ligand addition equilibrium $ML_{n-1} + L \rightleftharpoons ML_n$.
formulas.explanation: Typically $k_1 > k_2 > k_3 > \dots > k_n$ due to statistical factors and steric hindrance.

formulas.latex: \Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ \quad (\Delta S^\circ > 0 \implies \text{Chelate Effect})
formulas.title: The Chelate Effect
formulas.derivation: Consider substitution of 6 monodentate ligands by 3 bidentate ligands: $[Ni(NH_3)_6]^{2+} + 3 en \rightleftharpoons [Ni(en)_3]^{2+} + 6 NH_3$. Reactant count is $1 + 3 = 4$ species; product count is $1 + 6 = 7$ species. Net increase of 3 independent dissolved particles generates substantial positive entropy of reaction: $\Delta S^\circ \gg 0$. Since $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$, this large positive entropy makes $\Delta G^\circ$ significantly more negative, driving formation constant higher by several orders of magnitude.
formulas.description: Enhanced thermodynamic stability of polydentate chelate complexes over monodentate analogues driven by positive entropy.
formulas.explanation: EDTA ($hexadentate$) forms extremely stable complexes with almost all metal cations ($1 + 1 \to 1 + 6$ displacement release).

formulas.latex: t_{2g}^3 e_g^1, \quad t_{2g}^6 e_g^1, \quad t_{2g}^6 e_g^3 \implies \text{Jahn-Teller Distortion}
formulas.title: Jahn-Teller Theorem Distortion

variables.d^9, d^4, d^7: Electronic configurations exhibiting strong Jahn-Teller effect

formulas.derivation: Hermann Jahn and Edward Teller (1937) proved mathematically that any non-linear molecular system in an electronically degenerate ground state is inherently unstable and will undergo geometric distortion to lower its symmetry, remove orbital degeneracy, and lower overall energy. In octahedral $d^9$ complexes (e.g. $Cu^{2+}$: $t_{2g}^6 e_g^3$), the odd electron can reside in either $d_{z^2}$ or $d_{x^2-y^2}$. Elongating along z-axis lowers energy of $d_{z^2}$ and destabilizes $d_{x^2-y^2}$, yielding 4 short equatorial bonds and 2 elongated axial bonds (tetragonal distortion).
formulas.description: Geometric distortion of non-linear degenerate electronic states to remove orbital degeneracy and lower energy.
formulas.explanation: Explains why $Cu(II)$ octahedral complexes are never perfectly regular octahedra, displaying pronounced axial elongation.

formulas.latex: r_{tet} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a - r_{anion} \approx 0.225 r_A, \quad r_{oct} = \frac{a}{2} - r_{anion} \approx 0.414 r_A
formulas.title: Radius Ratio Rules for Coordination Polyhedra in Solid State
formulas.derivation: Geometric contact condition requires central cation to touch all surrounding anions without anions overlapping: Linear ($CN=2$): $r_+/r_- < 0.155$. Trigonal planar ($CN=3$): $0.155 \le r_+/r_- < 0.225$. Tetrahedral ($CN=4$): geometry gives $\cos(109.5^\circ/2) = \frac{r_-}{r_+ + r_-} \implies r_+/r_- = \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2} - 1 = 0.225$. Octahedral ($CN=6$): square in-plane diagonal gives $2(r_+ + r_-) = \sqrt{2}(2r_-) \implies r_+/r_- = \sqrt{2} - 1 = 0.414$. Cubic ($CN=8$): body diagonal gives $2(r_+ + r_-) = \sqrt{3}(2r_-) \implies r_+/r_- = \sqrt{3} - 1 = 0.732$.
formulas.description: Limiting radius ratios determining stable coordination numbers (tetrahedral, octahedral, cubic) in ionic crystals.
formulas.explanation: Example: $NaCl$ ($r_{Na+}/r_{Cl-} = 0.525$, in $0.414 - 0.732$ range $\implies CN=6$ octahedral); $CsCl$ ($0.93 > 0.732 \implies CN=8$ cubic).

formulas.title: Crystalline Unit Cell Density Formula

variables.Z: Number of formula units per unit cell

formulas.derivation: Density is mass divided by volume: $\rho = \frac{m_{cell}}{V_{cell}}$. Volume of cubic unit cell is $V = a^3$. Mass of unit cell is mass of $Z$ formula units: $m_{cell} = Z \times m_{atom} = Z \times \left(\frac{M}{N_A}\right)$. Substituting yields $\rho = \frac{Z \cdot M}{N_A \cdot a^3}$. Lattice parameters: Simple cubic ($Z=1, a=2R$); Body-centered cubic ($Z=2, \sqrt{3}a = 4R$); Face-centered cubic ($Z=4, \sqrt{2}a = 4R$).
formulas.description: Calculates macroscopic solid crystal density directly from unit cell edge length a and lattice particle count Z.
formulas.explanation: Fundamental crystallographic formula connecting atomic micro-structure to macroscopic laboratory density.

formulas.latex: 2 d \sin\theta = n \lambda \quad (\text{Bragg's Law of X-Ray Diffraction})
formulas.title: Bragg's Law of Crystal X-Ray Diffraction
formulas.derivation: William Henry Bragg and William Lawrence Bragg (1913) treated crystal planes as specular semi-reflecting mirrors. Path difference between rays reflected from two adjacent parallel planes separated by distance $d$ is $\Delta x = 2 d\sin\theta$. Constructive interference produces sharp diffraction peaks when path difference is an integer number of wavelengths: $2d\sin\theta = n\lambda$. For cubic crystal with Miller indices $(h, k, l)$: $d_{hkl} = \frac{a}{\sqrt{h^2 + k^2 + l^2}}$.
formulas.description: Constructive interference condition for X-rays reflected from parallel lattice planes separated by spacing d.
formulas.explanation: Primary experimental technique for solving 3D atomic structures of crystalline solids, proteins, and DNA.

formulas.title: Freundlich Adsorption Isotherm

variables.x/m: Mass of gas adsorbed per unit mass of solid adsorbent
variables.k, n: Freundlich empirical constants depending on adsorbent and gas

formulas.derivation: Herbert Freundlich (1909) deduced an empirical isotherm for multilayer/heterogeneous adsorption: $x/m = k P^{1/n}$. Taking base-10 logarithm: $\log(x/m) = \log k + \frac{1}{n}\log P$. Plotting $\log(x/m)$ versus $\log P$ yields straight line of slope $1/n$ ($0 \le 1/n \le 1$) and y-intercept $\log k$.
formulas.description: Empirical power-law relation for gas adsorption on solid heterogeneous surface at constant temperature.
formulas.explanation: At low pressure ($1/n = 1$): $x/m \propto P$. At high pressure ($1/n = 0$): $x/m = \text{constant}$ (adsorption saturation).

Lattice parameters: Simple cubic ($Z=1, a=2R$); Body-centered cubic ($Z=2, \sqrt{3}a = 4R$); Face-centered cubic ($Z=4, \sqrt{2}a = 4R$).
formulas.description: Calculates macroscopic solid crystal density directly from unit cell edge length a and lattice particle count Z.
formulas.explanation: Fundamental crystallographic formula connecting atomic micro-structure to macroscopic laboratory density.

formulas.latex: 2 d \sin\theta = n \lambda \quad (\text{Bragg's Law of X-Ray Diffraction})
formulas.title: Bragg's Law of Crystal X-Ray Diffraction
formulas.derivation: William Henry Bragg and William Lawrence Bragg (1913) treated crystal planes as specular semi-reflecting mirrors. Path difference between rays reflected from two adjacent parallel planes separated by distance $d$ is $\Delta x = 2 d\sin\theta$. Constructive interference produces sharp diffraction peaks when path difference is an integer number of wavelengths: $2d\sin\theta = n\lambda$. For cubic crystal with Miller indices $(h, k, l)$: $d_{hkl} = \frac{a}{\sqrt{h^2 + k^2 + l^2}}$.
formulas.description: Constructive interference condition for X-rays reflected from parallel lattice planes separated by spacing d.
formulas.explanation: Primary experimental technique for solving 3D atomic structures of crystalline solids, proteins, and DNA.

formulas.title: Freundlich Adsorption Isotherm

variables.x/m: Mass of gas adsorbed per unit mass of solid adsorbent
variables.k, n: Freundlich empirical constants depending on adsorbent and gas

formulas.derivation: Herbert Freundlich (1909) deduced an empirical isotherm for multilayer/heterogeneous adsorption: $x/m = k P^{1/n}$. Taking base-10 logarithm: $\log(x/m) = \log k + \frac{1}{n}\log P$. Plotting $\log(x/m)$ versus $\log P$ yields straight line of slope $1/n$ ($0 \le 1/n \le 1$) and y-intercept $\log k$.
formulas.description: Empirical power-law relation for gas adsorption on solid heterogeneous surface at constant temperature.
formulas.explanation: At low pressure ($1/n = 1$): $x/m \propto P$. At high pressure ($1/n = 0$): $x/m = \text{constant}$ (adsorption saturation).

content_json.derivation: Hans Bethe (1929) developed Crystal Field Theory: in octahedral ligand field, 6 ligands approach along Cartesian axes ($x, y, z$). Orbitals with lobes pointing directly along axes ($d_{x^2-y^2}, d_{z^2}$) experience strong electrostatic repulsion and are destabilized by $+0.6\Delta_o$ ($e_g$). Orbitals directed between axes ($d_{xy}, d_{yz}, d_{xz}$) experience less repulsion and are stabilized by $-0.4\Delta_o$ ($t_{2g}$). In tetrahedral geometry, 4 ligands approach corners of cube (between axes), inverting splitting pattern and reducing splitting magnitude by factor $\Delta_t = \frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$ because fewer ligands are present and none point directly at d-orbitals.
content_json.explanation: Because $\Delta_t < P$ (pairing energy) always, tetrahedral complexes are almost exclusively high-spin.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: Permutations and Combinations Formula Sheet
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: To arrange $r$ distinct items out of $n$: First position has $n$ choices, second has $n-1$, ..., $r$-th has $n-(r-1) = n-r+1$ choices. Total arrangements $= n(n-1)\dots(n-r+1) = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!} = ^n P_r$. Since each selection of $r$ items can be ordered in $r!$ ways, the number of unordered combinations is $\binom{n}{r} = \frac{^n P_r}{r!} = \frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Permutations count ordered sequences; Combinations count unordered subsets of size r from a set of size n.

formulas.title: Fundamental Permutations and Combinations Formulas
formulas.derivation: To arrange $r$ distinct items out of $n$: First position has $n$ choices, second has $n-1$, ..., $r$-th has $n-(r-1) = n-r+1$ choices. Total arrangements $= n(n-1)\dots(n-r+1) = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!} = ^n P_r$. Since each selection of $r$ items can be ordered in $r!$ ways, the number of unordered combinations is $\binom{n}{r} = \frac{^n P_r}{r!} = \frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}$.
formulas.description: Fundamental Permutations and Combinations Formulas
formulas.explanation: Permutations count ordered sequences; Combinations count unordered subsets of size r from a set of size n.

formulas.title: Pascal's Combinatorial Identity
formulas.derivation: Algebraic proof: $\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!} + \frac{n!}{(r-1)!(n-r+1)!} = \frac{n!}{(r-1)!(n-r)!}\left[\frac{1}{r} + \frac{1}{n-r+1}\right] = \frac{n!}{(r-1)!(n-r)!}\left[\frac{n+1}{r(n-r+1)}\right] = \frac{(n+1)!}{r!(n+1-r)!} = \binom{n+1}{r}$. Combinatorial proof: To pick $r$ elements from $n+1$ elements (including fixed element $X$), either include $X$ (choose remaining $r-1$ from $n$) or exclude $X$ (choose $r$ from $n$).
formulas.description: Pascal's Combinatorial Identity
formulas.explanation: Generates Pascal's Triangle row-by-row and proves recursive relations across combinations.

formulas.title: Circular Permutations of n Distinct Objects
formulas.derivation: Linear arrangements equal $n!$. In a circle, rotating an arrangement preserves relative circular order, so each distinct circular arrangement generates $n$ equivalent linear arrangements by shifting starting points. Hence distinct circular permutations $= n! / n = (n - 1)!$. If clockwise and counter-clockwise directions are indistinguishable (e.g. bead necklace flipped over), divide by 2: $(n - 1)! / 2$.
formulas.description: Circular Permutations of n Distinct Objects
formulas.explanation: Counts distinct circular seatings where shifting everyone by the same number of seats produces identical arrangements.

formulas.latex: N = \frac{n!}{p! \, q! \, r!} \quad (p + q + r = n)
formulas.title: Permutations of Multiset with Repeated Elements
formulas.derivation: If all $n$ items were distinct, total arrangements would be $n!$. However, swapping the $p$ identical items among themselves in any of their $p!$ internal positions leaves the overall sequence unchanged. Likewise for $q!$ and $r!$. By the multiplication principle of counting, total distinguishable permutations $= \frac{n!}{p! q! r!}$.
formulas.description: Permutations of Multiset with Repeated Elements
formulas.explanation: Calculates distinct anagrams of words containing repeated letters (e.g. MISSISSIPPI).

formulas.title: Stars and Bars: Non-negative integer solutions to x1 + x2 + ... + xr = n
formulas.derivation: Represent the sum $n$ as $n$ identical 'stars' ($*$). We must partition these stars into $r$ bins using $r - 1$ identical 'bars' ($|$). Total symbols to arrange in a line $= n + (r - 1) = n + r - 1$. Choosing the positions for the $r - 1$ bars from the $n + r - 1$ slots gives $\binom{n + r - 1}{r - 1}$.
formulas.description: Stars and Bars: Non-negative integer solutions to x1 + x2 + ... + xr = n
formulas.explanation: Standard method for distributing n identical items into r distinct boxes where empty boxes are allowed.

formulas.title: Stars and Bars: Strictly Positive integer solutions (x_i >= 1)

variables.x_i >= 1: each variable must receive at least 1

formulas.derivation: Place $n$ stars in a line. There are $n - 1$ spaces between adjacent stars. To partition into $r$ strictly non-empty groups, choose $r - 1$ spaces from the $n - 1$ available spaces to insert bars: $\binom{n - 1}{r - 1}$. Alternatively, substitute $y_i = x_i - 1 \ge 0$ into $\sum y_i = n - r$, yielding $\binom{(n-r) + r - 1}{r - 1} = \binom{n - 1}{r - 1}$.
formulas.description: Stars and Bars: Strictly Positive integer solutions (x_i >= 1)
formulas.explanation: Distributes n identical items into r distinct boxes such that no box is left empty.

formulas.title: Derangements Formula (No object in its original place)

variables.D_n: number of complete derangements of n items

formulas.derivation: By the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion (PIE): Let $A_i$ be property that item $i$ is in its original position. Number of derangements $= n! - |\bigcup A_i| = n! - \sum |A_i| + \sum |A_i \cap A_j| - \dots = n! - \binom{n}{1}(n-1)! + \binom{n}{2}(n-2)! - \dots = n! \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{(-1)^k}{k!}$. Recurrence: $D_n = (n - 1)(D_{n-1} + D_{n-2})$.
formulas.description: Derangements Formula (No object in its original place)
formulas.explanation: Calculates ways to put n letters into n envelopes such that every letter ends up in the wrong envelope ($D_1=0, D_2=1, D_3=2, D_4=9, D_5=44$).

formulas.title: Total Non-empty Selections from Multiset

variables.p, q, r: counts of identical items of type A, B, C

formulas.derivation: For items of type A (which are identical), we can select 0, 1, 2, ..., up to $p$ items, giving $p + 1$ choices. Similarly, $q + 1$ choices for type B, and $r + 1$ choices for type C. Total selections $= (p+1)(q+1)(r+1)$. Subtracting the 1 case where zero items are selected from all types gives $(p+1)(q+1)(r+1) - 1$.
formulas.description: Total Non-empty Selections from Multiset
formulas.explanation: Finds total distinct ways of picking at least one item from collections of identical objects.

formulas.title: Division of Objects into Groups
formulas.derivation: To divide $m+n$ distinct items into two specified distinct groups of size $m$ and $n$: choose $m$ items for first group in $\binom{m+n}{m} = \frac{(m+n)!}{m! n!}$ ways. If the two groups are of equal size $m$ and their names/identities do not matter (unlabeled groups), the 2! orderings of the groups are identical, dividing by $2!$: $\frac{(2m)!}{(m!)^2 2!}$.
formulas.description: Division of Objects into Groups
formulas.explanation: Calculates ways to partition a collection into groups of specified sizes with or without group labeling.

formulas.title: Grid Walking Paths on m x n Lattice Grid
formulas.derivation: To move from $(0, 0)$ to $(m, n)$ moving only right (R) and up (U): Total steps must be $m + n$. Any path is uniquely defined by choosing which $m$ of the $m+n$ total steps are rightward steps: $\binom{m+n}{m} = \frac{(m+n)!}{m! n!}$.
formulas.description: Grid Walking Paths on m x n Lattice Grid
formulas.explanation: Standard dynamic programming and combinatorics formula for counting shortest paths on rectangular grids.

formulas.title: Number of Divisors of Positive Integer N
formulas.derivation: Any divisor $d$ of $N$ has prime factorization $p_1^{b_1} p_2^{b_2}\dots p_k^{b_k}$ where each exponent satisfies $0 \le b_i \le a_i$. Thus there are $a_1 + 1$ independent choices for $b_1$, $a_2 + 1$ for $b_2$, ..., yielding $(a_1 + 1)(a_2 + 1)\dots(a_k + 1)$ total divisors.
formulas.description: Number of Divisors of Positive Integer N
formulas.explanation: Counts total positive factors of any integer from its canonical prime factorization.

formulas.title: Sum of Divisors of Positive Integer N
formulas.derivation: Expand the algebraic product $(1 + p_1 + p_1^2 + \dots + p_1^{a_1})(1 + p_2 + \dots + p_2^{a_2})\dots(1 + p_k + \dots + p_k^{a_k})$. Multiplying out produces every single divisor of $N$ exactly once. Each factor is a finite geometric series: $1 + p + \dots + p^a = \frac{p^{a+1} - 1}{p - 1}$. Multiplying these geometric sums gives $\prod \frac{p_i^{a_i+1}-1}{p_i-1}$.
formulas.description: Sum of Divisors of Positive Integer N
formulas.explanation: Calculates the exact sum of all divisors of an integer using finite geometric series summation.

catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: Empirical discovery by Michael Faraday (1831). The negative sign (Lenz's Law, Heinrich Lenz 1834) enforces energy conservation: the induced current flows in such a direction that its own magnetic field opposes the original flux change that produced it.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: If flux increases, induced magnetic field points opposite to applied field; if flux decreases, induced field reinforces it.

content_json.title: Alternating Current Formula Sheet

sections.title: Alternating Current Formula Sheet - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.title: Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction and Lenz's Law
formulas.derivation: Empirical discovery by Michael Faraday (1831). The negative sign (Lenz's Law, Heinrich Lenz 1834) enforces energy conservation: the induced current flows in such a direction that its own magnetic field opposes the original flux change that produced it.
formulas.description: Induced electromotive force in a circuit equals negative rate of change of magnetic flux through loop.
formulas.explanation: If flux increases, induced magnetic field points opposite to applied field; if flux decreases, induced field reinforces it.

formulas.title: Motional EMF in a Moving Conductor
formulas.derivation: Mobile conduction electrons inside rod experience magnetic Lorentz force $\vec{F}_B = -e(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$. Work done moving an electron through length $\vec{l}$ is $W = \int \vec{F}_B \cdot d\vec{l} = -e \int (\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot d\vec{l}$. Induced EMF is work done per unit positive charge: $\mathcal{E} = W/(-e) = (\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot\vec{l} = B v l\sin\theta$.
formulas.description: Electromotive force induced across ends of a conducting rod of length l translating with speed v through magnetic field B.
formulas.explanation: Forms the foundation of electrical power generation in alternators and dynamos.

formulas.title: Rotational Motional EMF of a Rotating Rod
formulas.derivation: Consider element $dr$ at distance $r$ from pivot: linear velocity is $v(r) = r\omega$. Motional EMF generated across element is $d\mathcal{E} = B v(r) dr = B(r\omega)dr$. Integrating from pivot $r=0$ to tip $r=l$: $\mathcal{E} = B\omega \int_0^l r dr = B\omega \left[\frac{r^2}{2}\right]_0^l = \frac{1}{2}B\omega l^2$.
formulas.description: EMF induced between pivot and tip of a conducting rod of length l rotating with angular speed $\omega$ in perpendicular field B.
formulas.explanation: Also equals $B\left(\frac{dA}{dt}\right) = B\left(\frac{1}{2}l^2\omega\right)$, matching rate of area swept.

formulas.latex: L = \frac{N \Phi_B}{I} = \mu_0 n^2 A l, \quad U_B = \frac{1}{2}L I^2, \quad u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}
formulas.title: Self-Inductance and Magnetic Energy Density
formulas.derivation: Inside solenoid, field is $B = \mu_0 n I$. Flux per turn is $\Phi = B A = \mu_0 n I A$. Total linkage is $\lambda = N\Phi = (nl)(\mu_0 n I A) = (\mu_0 n^2 A l)I$. By definition $L = \lambda / I = \mu_0 n^2 A l$. Work required to establish current $I$ against back-EMF $\mathcal{E}_L = -L\frac{di}{dt}$ is $U = \int P\,dt = \int (L\frac{di}{dt} i)dt = L \int_0^I i\,di = \frac{1}{2}LI^2$. Dividing by volume $V = Al$ and using $B = \mu_0 n I$ yields $u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$.
formulas.description: Self-inductance of solenoid, total energy stored in inductor magnetic field, and volume energy density.
formulas.explanation: Analogous to kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ and electrostatic energy density $\frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0 E^2$.

formulas.latex: M = \frac{N_2 \Phi_{21}}{I_1} = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l, \quad M \le \sqrt{L_1 L_2}
formulas.title: Mutual Inductance and Coupling Coefficient
formulas.derivation: Current $I_1$ in outer coil produces uniform field $B_1 = \mu_0 n_1 I_1$. Flux passing through each turn of inner coil of area $A$ is $\Phi_{21} = B_1 A = \mu_0 n_1 I_1 A$. Total linkage with coil 2 ($N_2 = n_2 l$ turns) is $\lambda_2 = N_2 \Phi_{21} = (n_2 l)(\mu_0 n_1 I_1 A) = (\mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l)I_1$. Mutual inductance is $M = \lambda_2 / I_1 = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l$. By reciprocity theorem, $M_{12} = M_{21} = M$.
formulas.description: Mutual inductance between two co-axial solenoids and coupling coefficient $k = M/\sqrt{L_1 L_2} \le 1$.
formulas.explanation: For perfectly coupled coils with zero flux leakage, $k = 1$ and $M = \sqrt{L_1 L_2}$.

formulas.latex: i(t) = I_0 (1 - e^{-t / \tau_L}) \quad (\text{Growth}), \quad i(t) = I_0 e^{-t / \tau_L} \quad (\text{Decay}), \quad \tau_L = \frac{L}{R}
formulas.title: Transient LR Circuit Growth and Decay
formulas.derivation: KVL during growth: $\mathcal{E} - L\frac{di}{dt} - iR = 0 \implies L\frac{di}{dt} = \mathcal{E} - iR$. Separating variables: $\frac{di}{\mathcal{E} - iR} = \frac{dt}{L}$. Integrating with $i(0) = 0$: $-\frac{1}{R}\ln\left(1 - \frac{iR}{\mathcal{E}}\right) = \frac{t}{L} \implies i(t) = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R}\left(1 - e^{-Rt/L}\right)$.
formulas.description: Time-dependent current build-up and decay in inductive RL circuit with inductive time constant $\tau_L = L/R$.
formulas.explanation: At $t = \tau_L = L/R$, current reaches $63.2\%$ of steady value $I_0$; inductor acts as open-circuit at $t=0^+$ and short-circuit as $t \to \infty$.

formulas.title: Root-Mean-Square (RMS) Values of Sinusoidal AC
formulas.derivation: For $i(t) = I_0 \sin(\omega t)$, Joule heat generated in resistor $R$ over one period $T = 2\pi/\omega$ is $H = \int_0^T i^2(t) R dt$. An equivalent DC current $I_{rms}$ dissipates identical heat: $I_{rms}^2 R T = R \int_0^T I_0^2 \sin^2(\omega t) dt$. Since the average of $\sin^2(\omega t)$ over full period is $\frac{1}{2}$: $I_{rms}^2 T = I_0^2 \left(\frac{T}{2}\right) \implies I_{rms} = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}$.
formulas.description: Effective heating value of alternating sinusoidal current and voltage over full periodic cycle.
formulas.explanation: Standard wall outlet voltages (e.g., $230\text{ V}$ or $120\text{ V}$) always quote RMS values; peak voltage is $V_0 = \sqrt{2}V_{rms}$ ($325\text{ V}$ for $230\text{ V}$).

formulas.latex: Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}, \quad X_L = \omega L, \quad X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C}
formulas.title: Impedance of Series LCR Circuit
formulas.derivation: Phasor analysis: current phasor $\tilde{I}$ is common in series loop. Resistor voltage $\tilde{V}_R = I R$ is in phase with current. Inductor voltage $\tilde{V}_L = I X_L$ leads current by $+90^\circ (+i)$. Capacitor voltage $\tilde{V}_C = I X_C$ lags current by $-90^\circ (-i)$. Total complex voltage is $\tilde{V} = \tilde{V}_R + \tilde{V}_L + \tilde{V}_C = I [R + i(X_L - X_C)]$. Impedance magnitude is $Z = |\tilde{V}|/I = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$.
formulas.description: Total opposition to sinusoidal alternating current flow combining resistance, inductive reactance, and capacitive reactance.
formulas.explanation: Phase angle between voltage and current is $\tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R}$.

formulas.title: Resonant Frequency and Quality Factor (Q) of Series LCR
formulas.derivation: Current amplitude is $I_0 = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{R^2 + (\omega L - 1/\omega C)^2}}$. Current is maximized when reactive term vanishes: $\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C} = 0 \implies \omega_0^2 = \frac{1}{LC} \implies \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$. At resonance, impedance is purely resistive ($Z_{min} = R$) and current is in phase with voltage ($\cos\phi = 1$). Quality factor is $Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} = \frac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega}$ where $\Delta\omega$ is bandwidth at half-power points.
formulas.description: Condition for minimum impedance, maximum current resonance, and sharpness factor of resonance curve.
formulas.explanation: High $Q$ produces extremely sharp tuning selectivity in radio receivers and RF filter circuits.

formulas.title: Average AC Power and Power Factor
formulas.derivation: Instantaneous power is $p(t) = v(t)i(t) = [V_0 \sin(\omega t)][I_0 \sin(\omega t - \phi)] = V_0 I_0 \sin(\omega t)[\sin\omega t\cos\phi - \cos\omega t\sin\phi] = V_0 I_0 [\sin^2\omega t\cos\phi - \sin\omega t\cos\omega t\sin\phi]$. Averaging over a full cycle: $\langle \sin^2\omega t \rangle = 1/2$ and $\langle \sin\omega t\cos\omega t \rangle = 0$. Hence $P_{avg} = \frac{1}{2}V_0 I_0 \cos\phi = \left(\frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\left(\frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\cos\phi = V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos\phi$. From impedance triangle, $\cos\phi = R/Z$.
formulas.description: Real active power dissipated in AC circuit over complete cycle governed by phase angle $\phi$.
formulas.explanation: For purely reactive circuits (pure $L$ or pure $C$), $\phi = \pm 90^\circ \implies \cos\phi = 0$, giving zero real power dissipation (wattless current).

formulas.title: Ideal Transformer Voltage, Current and Turns Ratio
formulas.derivation: Assuming ideal core with zero flux leakage: common flux $\Phi$ links both windings. Induced EMFs are $V_p = -N_p \frac{d\Phi}{dt}$ and $V_s = -N_s \frac{d\Phi}{dt}$. Dividing gives $\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$. For an ideal lossless transformer (100% efficiency), input power equals output power: $V_p I_p = V_s I_s \implies \frac{I_p}{I_s} = \frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$.
formulas.description: Transformation of AC voltage and current in magnetically coupled primary and secondary windings.
formulas.explanation: Step-up transformer ($N_s > N_p$): voltage increases and current decreases proportionately, minimizing $I^2 R$ transmission line losses.

formulas.latex: \omega_{LC} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}, \quad q(t) = Q_0 \cos(\omega_{LC} t), \quad i(t) = -\omega_{LC} Q_0 \sin(\omega_{LC} t)
formulas.title: LC Tank Circuit Oscillations
formulas.derivation: Total circuit energy is $E = U_E + U_B = \frac{q^2}{2C} + \frac{1}{2}Li^2$. In lossless circuit, $\frac{dE}{dt} = 0$: $\frac{q}{C}\frac{dq}{dt} + L i \frac{di}{dt} = 0$. Since $i = \frac{dq}{dt}$, dividing by $i$ gives $\frac{q}{C} + L\frac{d^2q}{dt^2} = 0 \implies \frac{d^2q}{dt^2} + \frac{1}{LC}q = 0$. This is standard SHM equation with $\omega_{LC} = 1/\sqrt{LC}$. Solution with initial charge $Q_0$ is $q(t) = Q_0\cos(\omega t)$.
formulas.description: Undamped harmonic exchange of energy between electric field of capacitor and magnetic field of inductor.
formulas.explanation: Energy sloshes sinusoidally between all-electric state ($U_E = Q_0^2/2C$) and all-magnetic state ($U_B = \frac{1}{2}L I_{max}^2$).

formulas.title: Maxwell's Displacement Current
formulas.derivation: Between capacitor plates during charging, no conduction electrons flow, yet magnetic field exists. Electric field is $E = \frac{Q}{\epsilon_0 A} \implies Q = \epsilon_0 E A = \epsilon_0 \Phi_E$. Differentiating charge with respect to time: $I_c = \frac{dQ}{dt} = \epsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$. Maxwell recognized this time-varying flux term acts as an effective displacement current $I_d = \epsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$, restoring Ampere's law to $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 (I_c + I_d)$.
formulas.description: Equivalent current arising from time-varying electric flux, completing Ampere-Maxwell law.
formulas.explanation: Displacement current between plates exactly equals conduction current in the connecting wires ($I_d = I_c$), ensuring continuity.

formulas.title: Speed of Electromagnetic Waves in Vacuum and Field Ratio
formulas.description: Propagation velocity of light from Maxwell's equations and relation between electric and magnetic field amplitudes.
formulas.explanation: Proved that light is an electromagnetic transverse wave propagating at universal speed $c$.

catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: From definition of instantaneous acceleration $a = \frac{dv}{dt}$. Separating variables yields $dv = a \, dt$. Integrating both sides from $t=0$ (where $v=u$) to $t$: $\int_{u}^{v} dv = a \int_{0}^{t} dt \implies v - u = at \implies v = u + at$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Applies strictly when acceleration is constant in magnitude and direction along a rectilinear path.

formulas.explanation: Applies strictly when acceleration is constant in magnitude and direction along a rectilinear path.

formulas.title: Displacement-Time Relation
formulas.derivation: Since instantaneous velocity $v = \frac{ds}{dt} = u + at$, we integrate $ds = (u + at)dt$: $\int_{0}^{s} ds = \int_{0}^{t} (u + at)dt = \left[ ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2 \right]_0^t = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$.
formulas.description: Calculates rectilinear displacement under constant acceleration over time t.
formulas.explanation: Yields net displacement, not total distance traversed if velocity reverses direction during interval $t$.

formulas.title: Velocity-Displacement Relation (Third Kinematic Equation)
formulas.derivation: Using chain rule for acceleration: $a = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{dv}{ds} \frac{ds}{dt} = v \frac{dv}{ds}$. Rearranging: $v \, dv = a \, ds$. Integrating from initial $(u, 0)$ to final $(v, s)$: $\int_{u}^{v} v \, dv = a \int_{0}^{s} ds \implies \frac{v^2 - u^2}{2} = as \implies v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.
formulas.description: Relates final speed to initial speed and displacement without requiring explicit time.
formulas.explanation: Directly links kinetic energy change per unit mass to mechanical work done by constant force.

formulas.title: Displacement in the n-th Second
formulas.description: Distance traveled strictly between time $t = n-1$ and $t = n$.
formulas.explanation: Dimensionally valid because the implicit factor multiplying $(2n-1)$ is $1\text{ s}$.

formulas.title: Maximum Height of 2D Projectile
formulas.derivation: At maximum height, vertical velocity component vanishes: $v_y = 0$. Using $v_y^2 = u_y^2 - 2gH$ with $u_y = u\sin\theta$: $0 = (u\sin\theta)^2 - 2gH \implies H = \frac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g}$.
formulas.description: Peak vertical elevation reached by a projectile launched at angle $\theta$ with initial speed $u$.
formulas.explanation: Depends only on vertical launch velocity component $u_y$.

formulas.title: Time of Flight for Projectile Motion
formulas.derivation: Set vertical displacement $y = 0$ in $y = (u\sin\theta)t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$: $t(u\sin\theta - \frac{1}{2}gt) = 0$. Since $t=0$ is launch, landing time is $t = T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$.
formulas.description: Total duration projectile remains airborne before landing on horizontal ground.
formulas.explanation: Time of ascent equals time of descent ($t_{up} = t_{down} = \frac{u\sin\theta}{g}$) under symmetric vacuum trajectory.

formulas.title: Horizontal Range of Projectile
formulas.derivation: $R = u_x \cdot T = (u\cos\theta) \cdot \left(\frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}\right) = \frac{u^2 (2\sin\theta\cos\theta)}{g} = \frac{u^2 \sin(2\theta)}{g}$.
formulas.description: Total horizontal displacement traveled by a projectile on flat ground.
formulas.explanation: Maximum range occurs at $\theta = 45^\circ$ where $\sin(2\theta) = 1$. Complementary launch angles $\theta$ and $90^\circ - \theta$ give identical ranges.

formulas.title: Equation of Projectile Trajectory
formulas.derivation: From horizontal motion: $x = (u\cos\theta)t \implies t = \frac{x}{u\cos\theta}$. Substituting into $y = (u\sin\theta)t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$: $y = u\sin\theta\left(\frac{x}{u\cos\theta}\right) - \frac{g}{2}\left(\frac{x^2}{u^2\cos^2\theta}\right) = x\tan\theta - \frac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$. Factoring out $x\tan\theta$ and noting $R = \frac{2u^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{g}$ gives $y = x\tan\theta(1 - x/R)$.
formulas.description: Parabolic path equation relating vertical coordinates $y$ and horizontal coordinates $x$.
formulas.explanation: Standard quadratic trajectory form; useful for collision, clearing hurdles, and angle-of-elevation problems.

formulas.title: Relative Velocity in 2D/3D

variables.\\vec{v}_A: Velocity of A in ground frame
variables.\\vec{v}_B: Velocity of B in ground frame
variables.\\vec{v}_{A/B}: Relative velocity of A w.r.t. B

formulas.derivation: Position vector of A relative to B is $\vec{r}_{A/B} = \vec{r}_A - \vec{r}_B$. Differentiating with respect to time: $\frac{d\vec{r}_{A/B}}{dt} = \frac{d\vec{r}_A}{dt} - \frac{d\vec{r}_B}{dt} \implies \vec{v}_{A/B} = \vec{v}_A - \vec{v}_B$.
formulas.description: Velocity of object A observed from the reference frame of moving observer B.
formulas.explanation: Crucial for river-swimmer problems, rain-umbrella problems, and minimum approach distance calculations.

formulas.title: River Crossing Time and Drift
formulas.derivation: Cross-river speed component is $v_y = v_{br}\cos\theta$, so $t = d / (v_{br}\cos\theta)$. Net downstream velocity along bank is $v_x = v_r - v_{br}\sin\theta$. Drift is $x = v_x \cdot t$.
formulas.description: Time taken by boat to cross river of width d and resultant downstream drift.
formulas.explanation: Shortest time occurs when heading straight across ($\theta = 0, t_{min} = d/v_{br}$). Zero drift requires $\sin\theta = v_r / v_{br}$ (valid if $v_{br} \ge v_r$).

formulas.title: Centripetal and Tangential Accelerations in Curvilinear Motion
formulas.derivation: In planar polar coordinates, position $\vec{r} = R\hat{r}$. Velocity is $\vec{v} = R\omega \hat{\theta}$. Differentiating velocity: $\vec{a} = R\alpha \hat{\theta} + R\omega \frac{d\hat{\theta}}{dt}$. Since $\frac{d\hat{\theta}}{dt} = -\omega\hat{r}$, $\vec{a} = -R\omega^2 \hat{r} + R\alpha \hat{\theta} = -\frac{v^2}{R}\hat{r} + a_t \hat{\theta}$. Total magnitude $a = \sqrt{a_n^2 + a_t^2}$.
formulas.description: Decomposition of total acceleration into normal (direction change) and tangential (speed change) components.
formulas.explanation: Centripetal acceleration always points toward center of curvature; tangential acceleration alters the magnitude of velocity.

formulas.title: Radius of Curvature of Trajectory
formulas.derivation: At any point, $a_n = \frac{v^2}{R_c} = g\cos\phi$. From differential geometry, curvature $\kappa = \frac{1}{R_c} = \frac{|y''|}{(1 + y'^2)^{3/2}}$, thus $R_c = \frac{(1 + y'^2)^{3/2}}{|y''|}$.
formulas.description: Local radius of osculating circle for any planar curve $y(x)$.
formulas.explanation: Enables computing normal contact force and centripetal load on curved tracks and projectile apogees.

content_json.derivation: From definition of instantaneous acceleration $a = \frac{dv}{dt}$. Separating variables yields $dv = a \, dt$. Integrating both sides from $t=0$ (where $v=u$) to $t$: $\int_{u}^{v} dv = a \int_{0}^{t} dt \implies v - u = at \implies v = u + at$.
content_json.explanation: Applies strictly when acceleration is constant in magnitude and direction along a rectilinear path.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: Laws of Motion Formula Sheet
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: Momentum is $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$. Differentiating using product rule: $\vec{F} = \frac{d(m\vec{v})}{dt} = m\frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} + \vec{v}\frac{dm}{dt}$. For constant mass systems ($dm/dt = 0$), this reduces to $\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a}$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Fundamental dynamical law; force causes acceleration, not velocity. In variable-mass systems (like rockets), the thrust term $\vec{v}_{rel}(dm/dt)$ must be included.

content_json.title: Laws of Motion Formula Sheet

sections.title: Laws of Motion Formula Sheet - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.title: Newton's Second Law of Motion
formulas.derivation: Momentum is $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$. Differentiating using product rule: $\vec{F} = \frac{d(m\vec{v})}{dt} = m\frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} + \vec{v}\frac{dm}{dt}$. For constant mass systems ($dm/dt = 0$), this reduces to $\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a}$.
formulas.description: Relates net external force to the rate of change of linear momentum, generalizing to variable-mass systems.
formulas.explanation: Fundamental dynamical law; force causes acceleration, not velocity. In variable-mass systems (like rockets), the thrust term $\vec{v}_{rel}(dm/dt)$ must be included.

formulas.title: Impulse-Momentum Theorem
formulas.derivation: From $\vec{F} = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$, multiply both sides by $dt$: $d\vec{p} = \vec{F}\,dt$. Integrating both sides from state 1 to state 2 gives $\Delta\vec{p} = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \vec{F}\,dt = \vec{J}$.
formulas.description: Integral of force over time equals the net change in linear momentum.
formulas.explanation: Useful in collision and impact problems where force varies dramatically over an extremely brief time interval.

formulas.title: Laws of Static and Kinetic Friction
formulas.derivation: Empirical Coulomb-Amontons laws: micro-welds between asperities generate shear resistance proportional to macroscopic normal contact force $N$. Before slippage, $f_s$ self-adjusts to balance tangential load up to $(f_s)_{max} = \mu_s N$. Once sliding occurs, asperity bonds continuously break and reform, giving $f_k = \mu_k N$ with $\mu_k \le \mu_s$.
formulas.description: Maximum limiting static friction and constant sliding kinetic friction proportional to normal reaction.
formulas.explanation: Static friction is an adjustable force directed to oppose impending relative motion; kinetic friction opposes actual relative sliding velocity.

formulas.title: Angle of Friction and Angle of Repose
formulas.derivation: Resultant contact force is $\vec{R} = \vec{N} + \vec{f}_s$. At limiting friction $f_s = \mu_s N$, the angle $\theta_s$ made with $\vec{N}$ satisfies $\tan\theta_s = \frac{f_s}{N} = \mu_s$. On an inclined plane of angle $\theta$, gravity down the incline is $mg\sin\theta$ and normal is $mg\cos\theta$. Limiting equilibrium requires $mg\sin\theta = \mu_s mg\cos\theta \implies \tan\theta = \mu_s$.
formulas.description: Angle between resultant contact force and normal, and minimum incline angle for sliding initiation.
formulas.explanation: A block placed on an incline stays at rest if incline angle $\theta \le \theta_r = \tan^{-1}(\mu_s)$.

formulas.latex: a = \frac{(m_2 - m_1)g}{m_1 + m_2}, \quad T = \frac{2 m_1 m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2}
formulas.title: Atwood Machine Acceleration and Tension
formulas.derivation: Equations of motion: for $m_2$ descending, $m_2 g - T = m_2 a$. For $m_1$ ascending, $T - m_1 g = m_1 a$. Adding equations eliminates $T$: $(m_2 - m_1)g = (m_1 + m_2)a \implies a = \frac{m_2 - m_1}{m_1 + m_2}g$. Substituting $a$ back into tension equation: $T = m_1(g + a) = m_1\left(g + \frac{m_2 - m_1}{m_1 + m_2}g\right) = \frac{2m_1 m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2}$.
formulas.description: Dynamics of two masses suspended over a frictionless, massless ideal pulley.
formulas.explanation: Tension is the harmonic mean of the two weights; common acceleration depends on net unbalance divided by total mass.

formulas.title: Maximum Safe Speed on a Banked Road
formulas.derivation: At impending outward slip, friction $f = \mu_s N$ acts downwards along the incline. Resolving vertically: $N\cos\theta - f\sin\theta = mg \implies N(\cos\theta - \mu_s\sin\theta) = mg$. Resolving horizontally for centripetal force: $N\sin\theta + f\cos\theta = \frac{m v^2}{R} \implies N(\sin\theta + \mu_s\cos\theta) = \frac{m v^2}{R}$. Dividing horizontal by vertical equation: $\frac{v_{max}^2}{Rg} = \frac{\sin\theta + \mu_s\cos\theta}{\cos\theta - \mu_s\sin\theta} = \frac{\tan\theta + \mu_s}{1 - \mu_s\tan\theta}$.
formulas.description: Maximum negotiated curve speed without skidding outwards on a banked circular turn.
formulas.explanation: If friction is absent ($\mu_s = 0$), optimum design speed is $v_0 = \sqrt{Rg\tan\theta}$, where tires exert no lateral friction.

formulas.title: Critical Speeds in Vertical Circular Motion
formulas.derivation: At highest point, string tension must satisfy $T_{top} \ge 0$. Equation of motion: $T_{top} + mg = \frac{m v_{top}^2}{R}$. Critical condition $T_{top} = 0 \implies v_{top} = \sqrt{gR}$. By conservation of mechanical energy between bottom and top: $\frac{1}{2}m v_{bottom}^2 = \frac{1}{2}m v_{top}^2 + mg(2R)$. Substituting $v_{top}^2 = gR$: $v_{bottom}^2 = gR + 4gR = 5gR \implies v_{bottom} = \sqrt{5gR}$.
formulas.description: Minimum bottom and top speeds required for a mass on a light string to complete vertical loop.
formulas.explanation: Tension at bottom under critical looping condition is $T_{bottom} = \frac{mv_{bottom}^2}{R} + mg = 5mg + mg = 6mg$.

formulas.title: Pseudo Force (D'Alembert Force)

variables.\\vec{a}_0: Acceleration of reference frame w.r.t. ground

formulas.derivation: In inertial frame, $\vec{F}_{real} = m\vec{a}_{in}$. If frame has acceleration $\vec{a}_0$, acceleration of particle relative to frame is $\vec{a}_{rel} = \vec{a}_{in} - \vec{a}_0$. Multiplying by mass $m$: $m\vec{a}_{rel} = m\vec{a}_{in} - m\vec{a}_0 = \vec{F}_{real} + (-m\vec{a}_0)$. Defining $\vec{F}_{pseudo} = -m\vec{a}_0$ restores $\sum \vec{F} = m\vec{a}_{rel}$.
formulas.description: Inertial fictitious force added when analyzing dynamics from an accelerating non-inertial reference frame.
formulas.explanation: Always acts in the direction opposite to the frame acceleration vector $\vec{a}_0$, passing through the center of mass.

formulas.title: Tsiolkovsky Rocket Equation with Gravity
formulas.derivation: Momentum balance for system at time $t$ and $t+dt$: $(m-dm)(v+dv) + dm(v - v_{rel}) - mv = -mg\,dt$. Neglecting second-order differential $dm\,dv$: $m\,dv - v_{rel}dm = -mg\,dt \implies dv = -v_{rel}\frac{dm}{m} - g\,dt$. Integrating from $m_0$ to $m(t)$: $v(t) - v_0 = v_{rel}\ln(m_0/m) - gt$.
formulas.description: Velocity acquired by a variable-mass rocket ejecting propellant exhaust at constant relative velocity.
formulas.explanation: Fundamental relation in astronautics; logarithmic scaling highlights why multi-stage staging is necessary to reach orbit.

formulas.title: Normal Contact Force Between Blocks
formulas.derivation: Common acceleration of combined system is $a = \frac{F}{m_1 + m_2}$. Isolating the forward block $m_2$, the only horizontal force acting on it is the contact normal force $N_{12}$. Applying Newton's second law: $N_{12} = m_2 a = m_2 \left(\frac{F}{m_1 + m_2}\right)$.
formulas.description: Internal normal contact force transmitted between two touching blocks pushed along a smooth surface.
formulas.explanation: The contact force equals the forward mass fraction multiplied by total applied force.

formulas.title: String Tension at Arbitrary Angle in Simple Pendulum
formulas.derivation: By energy conservation: $mgL(\cos\theta - \cos\theta_0) = \frac{1}{2}m v^2 \implies \frac{mv^2}{L} = 2mg(\cos\theta - \cos\theta_0)$. Radially, Newton's law gives $T - mg\cos\theta = \frac{mv^2}{L}$. Substituting $\frac{mv^2}{L}$: $T = mg\cos\theta + 2mg(\cos\theta - \cos\theta_0) = mg(3\cos\theta - 2\cos\theta_0)$.
formulas.description: Tension in pendulum string released from initial angular deflection $\theta_0$ as it passes through angle $\theta$.
formulas.explanation: At bottom ($\theta = 0$), $T = mg(3 - 2\cos\theta_0)$, which exceeds $mg$ substantially.

formulas.title: Acceleration of Movable Wedge on Smooth Floor
formulas.derivation: Let horizontal wedge acceleration be $A$ to the left. In wedge frame, block acceleration along incline is $a_r$. Normal force on block is $N = m(g\cos\alpha - A\sin\alpha)$. Horizontal force on wedge from block is $N\sin\alpha = MA$. Eliminating $N$ and using constraint equations yields $A = \frac{mg\sin\alpha\cos\alpha}{M + m\sin^2\alpha}$.
formulas.description: Horizontal acceleration of a smooth wedge of mass M supporting sliding block of mass m.
formulas.explanation: Classic constraint motion problem; conservation of horizontal momentum of the block-wedge system holds because horizontal external forces are zero.

content_json.derivation: Momentum is $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$. Differentiating using product rule: $\vec{F} = \frac{d(m\vec{v})}{dt} = m\frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} + \vec{v}\frac{dm}{dt}$. For constant mass systems ($dm/dt = 0$), this reduces to $\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a}$.
content_json.explanation: Fundamental dynamical law; force causes acceleration, not velocity. In variable-mass systems (like rockets), the thrust term $\vec{v}_{rel}(dm/dt)$ must be included.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: Trigonometric Functions Formula Sheet
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: In the unit circle, consider unit vectors $\vec{u} = \cos A \hat{i} + \sin A \hat{j}$ and $\vec{v} = \cos B \hat{i} + \sin B \hat{j}$. The angle between them is $A - B$. Scalar dot product: $\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v} = (1)(1)\cos(A - B)$. Component dot product: $\cos A \cos B + \sin A \sin B$. Equating gives $\cos(A - B) = \cos A \cos B + \sin A \sin B$. Replacing $B$ with $-B$ yields $\cos(A + B)$. Using co-function identities $\sin\theta = \cos(\pi/2 - \theta)$ gives the sine compound formulas.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Foundational compound angle identities used across all of geometry, trigonometry, and calculus.

content_json.title: Trigonometric Functions Formula Sheet

sections.title: Trigonometric Functions Formula Sheet - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.latex: \sin(A \pm B) = \sin A \cos B \pm \cos A \sin B, \quad \cos(A \pm B) = \cos A \cos B \mp \sin A \sin B
formulas.title: Compound Angle Addition and Subtraction Formulas
formulas.derivation: In the unit circle, consider unit vectors $\vec{u} = \cos A \hat{i} + \sin A \hat{j}$ and $\vec{v} = \cos B \hat{i} + \sin B \hat{j}$. The angle between them is $A - B$. Scalar dot product: $\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v} = (1)(1)\cos(A - B)$. Component dot product: $\cos A \cos B + \sin A \sin B$. Equating gives $\cos(A - B) = \cos A \cos B + \sin A \sin B$. Replacing $B$ with $-B$ yields $\cos(A + B)$. Using co-function identities $\sin\theta = \cos(\pi/2 - \theta)$ gives the sine compound formulas.
formulas.description: Compound Angle Addition and Subtraction Formulas
formulas.explanation: Foundational compound angle identities used across all of geometry, trigonometry, and calculus.

formulas.title: Tangent of Compound Angles
formulas.derivation: By definition: $\tan(A + B) = \frac{\sin(A + B)}{\cos(A + B)} = \frac{\sin A \cos B + \cos A \sin B}{\cos A \cos B - \sin A \sin B}$. Divide numerator and denominator by $\cos A \cos B$: $\tan(A + B) = \frac{\frac{\sin A \cos B}{\cos A \cos B} + \frac{\cos A \sin B}{\cos A \cos B}}{\frac{\cos A \cos B}{\cos A \cos B} - \frac{\sin A \sin B}{\cos A \cos B}} = \frac{\tan A + \\tan B}{1 - \\tan A \\tan B}$. Replacing $B$ with $-B$ and using $\tan(-B) = -\tan B$ yields the subtraction formula.
formulas.description: Tangent of Compound Angles
formulas.explanation: Used to evaluate slopes of composite directions and angles between intersecting lines.

formulas.latex: \sin C + \sin D = 2 \sin\left(\frac{C + D}{2}\right) \cos\left(\frac{C - D}{2}\right), \quad \cos C + \cos D = 2 \cos\left(\frac{C + D}{2}\right) \cos\left(\frac{C - D}{2}\right)
formulas.title: Sum-to-Product Trigonometric Identities
formulas.derivation: Let $A = \frac{C + D}{2}$ and $B = \frac{C - D}{2}$, so $A + B = C$ and $A - B = D$. Using compound angle identities: $\sin(A + B) = \sin A \cos B + \cos A \sin B$ and $\sin(A - B) = \sin A \cos B - \cos A \sin B$. Adding both equations: $\sin(A + B) + \sin(A - B) = 2 \sin A \cos B \implies \sin C + \sin D = 2 \sin\left(\frac{C+D}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{C-D}{2}\right)$. Similarly, adding cosine compound identities yields $\cos C + \cos D = 2\cos\left(\frac{C+D}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{C-D}{2}\right)$.
formulas.description: Sum-to-Product Trigonometric Identities
formulas.explanation: Transforms sums of trigonometric oscillations into products, crucial for beats in acoustics and integration.

formulas.latex: \cos C - \cos D = -2 \sin\left(\frac{C + D}{2}\right) \sin\left(\frac{C - D}{2}\right) = 2 \sin\left(\frac{C + D}{2}\right) \sin\left(\frac{D - C}{2}\right)
formulas.title: Difference of Cosines Identity
formulas.derivation: Subtracting $\cos(A + B) = \cos A \cos B - \sin A \sin B$ from $\cos(A - B) = \cos A \cos B + \sin A \sin B$: $\cos(A - B) - \cos(A + B) = 2 \sin A \sin B$. Substituting $C = A + B$ and $D = A - B$ gives $\cos D - \cos C = 2\sin\left(\frac{C+D}{2}\right)\sin\left(\frac{C-D}{2}\right) \implies \cos C - \cos D = -2\sin\left(\frac{C+D}{2}\right)\sin\left(\frac{C-D}{2}\right)$.
formulas.description: Difference of Cosines Identity
formulas.explanation: Notice the negative sign in front (or reversed argument D - C), a frequent trap in algebra.

formulas.latex: \sin(2A) = 2 \sin A \cos A = \frac{2 \tan A}{1 + \tan^2 A}, \quad \cos(2A) = \cos^2 A - \sin^2 A = 2\cos^2 A - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2 A = \frac{1 - \tan^2 A}{1 + \tan^2 A}
formulas.title: Double Angle Formulas for Sine and Cosine
formulas.derivation: Set $B = A$ in compound identities: $\sin(2A) = \sin(A + A) = \sin A \cos A + \cos A \sin A = 2\sin A\cos A$. For tangent form: divide by $1 = \cos^2 A + \sin^2 A$: $\sin(2A) = \frac{2\sin A\cos A}{\cos^2 A + \sin^2 A} = \frac{2\tan A}{1 + \tan^2 A}$. For cosine: $\cos(2A) = \cos(A + A) = \cos A \cos A - \sin A \sin A = \cos^2 A - \sin^2 A$. Using $\cos^2 A + \sin^2 A = 1$ yields $2\cos^2 A - 1$ and $1 - 2\sin^2 A$.
formulas.description: Double Angle Formulas for Sine and Cosine
formulas.explanation: Core formulas for reducing trigonometric powers ($\cos^2 A =  rac{1+\cos 2A}{2}$) in calculus integration.

formulas.latex: \tan(2A) = \frac{2 \tan A}{1 - \tan^2 A}, \quad \sin(3A) = 3\sin A - 4\sin^3 A, \quad \cos(3A) = 4\cos^3 A - 3\cos A
formulas.title: Double Angle Tangent and Triple Angle Formulas
formulas.derivation: Set $B = A$ in $\tan(A+B)$ gives $\tan(2A) = \frac{2\tan A}{1 - \tan^2 A}$. For triple angle: $\sin(3A) = \sin(2A + A) = \sin 2A \cos A + \cos 2A \sin A = (2\sin A\cos A)\cos A + (1 - 2\sin^2 A)\sin A = 2\sin A(1 - \sin^2 A) + \sin A - 2\sin^3 A = 3\sin A - 4\sin^3 A$. Similarly $\cos(3A) = \cos(2A + A) = \cos 2A \cos A - \sin 2A \sin A = 4\cos^3 A - 3\cos A$.
formulas.description: Double Angle Tangent and Triple Angle Formulas
formulas.explanation: Computes multiples of angles; indispensable for solving cubic trigonometric equations.

formulas.title: Sine Rule for Any Triangle

variables.a, b, c: side lengths opposite angles A, B, C

formulas.derivation: In circumscribed circle of $\Delta ABC$ with center $O$ and circumradius $R$: draw diameter $BD = 2R$. Since $\angle BCD$ is inscribed in semicircle, $\angle BCD = 90^\circ$. By inscribed angle theorem, $\angle BDC = \angle A$. In right $\Delta BCD$: $\sin(\angle BDC) = \frac{BC}{BD} \implies \sin A = \frac{a}{2R} \implies \frac{a}{\sin A} = 2R$. By symmetry, $\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C} = 2R$.
formulas.description: Sine Rule for Any Triangle
formulas.explanation: Relates the sides and angles of any general triangle to the radius of its circumscribed circle.

formulas.latex: \cos A = \frac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2 b c}, \quad a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2 b c \cos A
formulas.title: Cosine Rule for Any Triangle
formulas.derivation: Place vertex $A$ at origin $(0, 0)$ with side $c$ along positive x-axis so $B = (c, 0)$. Vertex $C$ has coordinates $(b\cos A, b\sin A)$. Length of side $a$ between $B$ and $C$ by distance formula: $a^2 = (b\cos A - c)^2 + (b\sin A - 0)^2 = b^2\cos^2 A - 2bc\cos A + c^2 + b^2\sin^2 A = b^2(\cos^2 A + \sin^2 A) + c^2 - 2bc\cos A = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A$. Solving for $\cos A$ yields $\cos A = \frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc}$.
formulas.description: Cosine Rule for Any Triangle
formulas.explanation: Generalization of Pythagorean theorem to any oblique triangle; solves for unknown side or angle.

formulas.latex: \Delta = \frac{1}{2} a b \sin C = \sqrt{s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)} \quad \left(s = \frac{a + b + c}{2}\right)
formulas.title: Triangle Area and Heron's Formula
formulas.derivation: Area is $\frac{1}{2}(\text{base})(\text{height}) = \frac{1}{2}a(b\sin C) = \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C$. To derive Heron's formula: $\sin^2 C = 1 - \cos^2 C = (1 - \cos C)(1 + \cos C)$. Substitute cosine rule $\cos C = \frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}$: $1 - \cos C = \frac{c^2 - (a-b)^2}{2ab} = \frac{(c - a + b)(c + a - b)}{2ab} = \frac{2(s-a)2(s-b)}{2ab}$. Similarly $1 + \cos C = \frac{2s 2(s-c)}{2ab}$. Multiplying: $\sin^2 C = \frac{16 s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}{4a^2 b^2}$. Thus $\Delta = \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C = \sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$.
formulas.description: Triangle Area and Heron's Formula
formulas.explanation: Calculates the area of any triangle directly from its three side lengths without computing any angles.

formulas.title: Inradius and Circumradius of Triangle
formulas.derivation: For inradius $r$: Incenter $I$ connected to vertices $A, B, C$ splits $\Delta ABC$ into 3 sub-triangles $\Delta IBC, \Delta ICA, \Delta IAB$. Their heights are all equal to inradius $r$. Total area $\Delta = \frac{1}{2}ar + \frac{1}{2}br + \frac{1}{2}cr = r\frac{a+b+c}{2} = r s \implies r = \Delta/s$. For circumradius $R$: From sine rule $\sin C = \frac{c}{2R}$. Substitute into area $\Delta = \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C = \frac{1}{2}ab\left(\frac{c}{2R}\right) = \frac{abc}{4R} \implies R = \frac{abc}{4\Delta}$.
formulas.description: Inradius and Circumradius of Triangle
formulas.explanation: Connects incircles and circumcircles to triangle area, side lengths, and semi-perimeter.

formulas.latex: \tan^{-1} x + \tan^{-1} y = \begin{cases} \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x + y}{1 - x y}\right) & \text{if } x y < 1 \\ \pi + \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x + y}{1 - x y}\right) & \text{if } x > 0, y > 0, x y > 1 \\ -\pi + \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x + y}{1 - x y}\right) & \text{if } x < 0, y < 0, x y > 1 \end{cases}
formulas.title: Addition Formula for Inverse Tangent
formulas.derivation: Let $\alpha = \tan^{-1} x$ and $\beta = \tan^{-1} y \implies \tan\alpha = x, \tan\beta = y$ with $\alpha, \beta \in (-\pi/2, \pi/2)$. Using compound angle: $\tan(\alpha + \beta) = \frac{\tan\alpha + \tan\beta}{1 - \tan\alpha\tan\beta} = \frac{x + y}{1 - xy}$. If $xy < 1$, then $\alpha + \beta \in (-\pi/2, \pi/2)$ lies inside the principal range of $\tan^{-1}$, so $\alpha + \beta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x+y}{1-xy}\right)$. If $x, y > 0$ and $xy > 1$, $\alpha + \beta \in (\pi/2, \pi)$, requiring subtraction of $\pi$: $\alpha + \beta = \pi + \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x+y}{1-xy}\right)$.
formulas.description: Addition Formula for Inverse Tangent
formulas.explanation: Combines two inverse tangents into a single angle; branch selection prevents 180-degree phase wrapping errors.

formulas.latex: \sin^{-1} x + \cos^{-1} x = \frac{\pi}{2}, \quad \tan^{-1} x + \cot^{-1} x = \frac{\pi}{2}, \quad \sec^{-1} x + \csc^{-1} x = \frac{\pi}{2}
formulas.title: Complementary Angles Property of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
formulas.derivation: Let $\theta = \sin^{-1} x \implies x = \sin\theta$. Using co-function identity: $x = \cos(\pi/2 - \theta)$. Taking principal $\cos^{-1}$ on both sides (since $\theta \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2] \implies \pi/2 - \theta \in [0, \pi]$, which is the principal branch of $\cos^{-1}$): $\cos^{-1} x = \pi/2 - \theta = \pi/2 - \sin^{-1} x \implies \sin^{-1} x + \\cos^{-1} x = \\pi/2$. Same logic applies to $\tan^{-1}$ and $\cot^{-1}$.
formulas.description: Complementary Angles Property of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
formulas.explanation: The sum of any inverse trigonometric function and its co-function at the same input equals pi/2 (90 degrees).

formulas.title: Double Angle Transformation for Inverse Tangent
formulas.derivation: Substitute $x = \tan\theta \implies \theta = \tan^{-1} x$. Then $\frac{2x}{1+x^2} = \frac{2\tan\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta} = \sin(2\theta) \implies \sin^{-1}(\frac{2x}{1+x^2}) = \sin^{-1}(\sin 2\theta) = 2\theta = 2\tan^{-1} x$. Similarly $\frac{1-x^2}{1+x^2} = \frac{1-\tan^2\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta} = \cos(2\theta)$, and $\frac{2x}{1-x^2} = \tan(2\theta)$.
formulas.description: Double Angle Transformation for Inverse Tangent
formulas.explanation: Vital substitution for converting algebraic rational expressions into pure trigonometric angles in calculus.

formulas.title: Negative Argument Properties of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
formulas.derivation: For $\sin^{-1}$: let $\theta = \sin^{-1}(-x) \implies \sin\theta = -x \implies -\sin\theta = x \implies \sin(-\theta) = x \implies -\theta = \sin^{-1} x \implies \theta = -\sin^{-1} x$. For $\cos^{-1}$: let $\theta = \cos^{-1}(-x) \implies \cos\theta = -x \implies -\cos\theta = x \implies \cos(\pi - \theta) = x$. Since $\theta \in [0, \pi] \implies \pi - \theta \in [0, \pi]$, we take $\cos^{-1}$: $\pi - \theta = \cos^{-1} x \implies \theta = \pi - \cos^{-1} x$.
formulas.description: Negative Argument Properties of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
formulas.explanation: Shows the difference between odd inverse functions (sine, tangent) and asymmetric inverse cosine.

content_json.derivation: In the unit circle, consider unit vectors $\vec{u} = \cos A \hat{i} + \sin A \hat{j}$ and $\vec{v} = \cos B \hat{i} + \sin B \hat{j}$. The angle between them is $A - B$. Scalar dot product: $\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v} = (1)(1)\cos(A - B)$. Component dot product: $\cos A \cos B + \sin A \sin B$. Equating gives $\cos(A - B) = \cos A \cos B + \sin A \sin B$. Replacing $B$ with $-B$ yields $\cos(A + B)$. Using co-function identities $\sin\theta = \cos(\pi/2 - \theta)$ gives the sine compound formulas.
content_json.explanation: Foundational compound angle identities used across all of geometry, trigonometry, and calculus.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: Thermodynamics Formulas
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: From universal energy conservation: change in internal state function $U$ equals energy entering system as heat ($q$) plus energy entering as mechanical boundary work ($w$). Under IUPAC sign convention, work done on the system by surroundings during compression is positive ($w > 0$), while work done by expanding system against external pressure $P_{ext}$ is negative: $w = -\int P_{ext}dV = -P_{ext}\Delta V$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: At constant volume (bomb calorimeter), $\Delta V = 0 \implies w = 0$, so $\Delta U = q_v$.

content_json.title: Thermodynamics Formulas

sections.title: Thermodynamics Formulas - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.latex: \Delta U = q + w = q - P_{ext}\Delta V
formulas.title: First Law of Chemical Thermodynamics (IUPAC Convention)
formulas.derivation: From universal energy conservation: change in internal state function $U$ equals energy entering system as heat ($q$) plus energy entering as mechanical boundary work ($w$). Under IUPAC sign convention, work done on the system by surroundings during compression is positive ($w > 0$), while work done by expanding system against external pressure $P_{ext}$ is negative: $w = -\int P_{ext}dV = -P_{ext}\Delta V$.
formulas.description: Conservation of energy for chemical system: heat absorbed plus mechanical work performed on the system.
formulas.explanation: At constant volume (bomb calorimeter), $\Delta V = 0 \implies w = 0$, so $\Delta U = q_v$.

formulas.title: Enthalpy and Internal Energy Relation for Chemical Reactions

variables.\\Delta n_g: Moles of gaseous products minus moles of gaseous reactants

formulas.derivation: By definition, enthalpy is $H = U + PV$. For finite change at constant pressure: $\Delta H = \Delta U + P\Delta V$. For ideal gas reaction where volume change is dominated by gases: $P V = n_g R T \implies P\Delta V = (\Delta n_g) R T$. Substituting yields $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g R T$.
formulas.description: Relates constant-pressure reaction heat $\Delta H$ to constant-volume reaction heat $\Delta U$ for ideal gas mixtures.
formulas.explanation: If $\Delta n_g = 0$ (e.g. $H_{2(g)} + I_{2(g)} \to 2HI_{(g)}$), $\Delta H = \Delta U$. If $\Delta n_g > 0$, expansion work means $\Delta H > \Delta U$.

formulas.title: Hess's Law and Standard Enthalpy of Reaction
formulas.derivation: Germain Hess (1840) established that because enthalpy $H$ is a thermodynamic state function, net heat evolved or absorbed in a chemical process depends solely on initial and final states, independent of pathway. By convention, standard enthalpies of formation of pure elements in reference standard states ($O_{2(g)}, C_{(graphite)}, H_{2(g)}$) are assigned zero: $\Delta_f H^\circ = 0$. Summing product enthalpies and subtracting reactant enthalpies gives the formula.
formulas.description: Reaction enthalpy calculated by summing standard enthalpies of formation of products minus reactants.
formulas.explanation: Allows indirect calculation of reaction heats that cannot be measured directly in a calorimeter.

formulas.title: Reaction Enthalpy from Bond Enthalpies
formulas.derivation: In a gas-phase reaction, chemical bonds in reactant molecules are first homolytically cleaved into isolated gaseous atoms (an endothermic process requiring energy input: $+ \sum BE_{reactants}$). The isolated atoms then recombine to synthesize product molecules (an exothermic process releasing energy: $- \sum BE_{products}$). By Hess's Law, the net reaction enthalpy is $\Delta_r H = \sum BE_{reactants} - \sum BE_{products}$.
formulas.description: Estimates gas-phase reaction enthalpy from homolytic covalent bond dissociation energies.
formulas.explanation: Applies strictly to gas-phase reactions with non-delocalized, localized covalent bonds.

formulas.latex: \frac{\Delta H_{T_2} - \Delta H_{T_1}}{T_2 - T_1} = \Delta C_p = \sum \nu_p C_{p, prod} - \sum \nu_r C_{p, react}
formulas.title: Kirchhoff's Law of Thermochemistry

variables.\\Delta C_p: Net change in molar heat capacity at constant pressure

formulas.derivation: At constant pressure, $\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial T}\right)_P = C_p$. Differentiating reaction enthalpy $\Delta_r H = H_{prod} - H_{react}$ with respect to temperature: $\frac{d(\Delta_r H)}{dT} = \left(\frac{\partial H_{prod}}{\partial T}\right) - \left(\frac{\partial H_{react}}{\partial T}\right) = C_{p, prod} - C_{p, react} = \Delta C_p$. Integrating from $T_1$ to $T_2$ assuming $\Delta C_p$ is approximately constant yields Kirchhoff's relation: $\Delta H_{T_2} = \Delta H_{T_1} + \Delta C_p (T_2 - T_1)$.
formulas.description: Temperature dependence of reaction enthalpy governed by reaction heat capacity change $\Delta C_p$.
formulas.explanation: If $\Delta C_p > 0$, reaction becomes more endothermic (or less exothermic) as temperature rises.

formulas.title: Second Law of Thermodynamics and Entropy Change
formulas.derivation: Rudolf Clausius (1865) proved that for any reversible cyclic process, $\oint \frac{dq_{rev}}{T} = 0$, establishing that $dS = \frac{dq_{rev}}{T}$ is an exact differential of a state function. For any spontaneous irreversible process, Clausius inequality gives $\oint \frac{dq}{T} < 0$, leading to $\Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr} = \Delta S_{univ} > 0$. At reversible equilibrium, $\Delta S_{univ} = 0$.
formulas.description: Definition of entropy as state function and universal condition for spontaneous irreversible processes.
formulas.explanation: All spontaneous real processes in the universe proceed with an overall increase in total entropy ($\Delta S_{univ} > 0$).

formulas.latex: \Delta S_{ideal\_gas} = n C_v \ln\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) + n R \ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right) = n C_p \ln\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) - n R \ln\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)
formulas.title: Entropy Change of an Ideal Gas
formulas.derivation: From First Law for reversible path: $dq_{rev} = dU - dw_{rev} = n C_v dT + P\,dV$. Dividing by $T$ using ideal gas law $P/T = nR/V$: $dS = \frac{dq_{rev}}{T} = n C_v \frac{dT}{T} + n R \frac{dV}{V}$. Integrating from initial state $(T_1, V_1)$ to final state $(T_2, V_2)$: $\Delta S = n C_v \ln(T_2 / T_1) + n R \ln(V_2 / V_1)$. Using $V_2 / V_1 = (T_2 P_1) / (T_1 P_2)$ and Mayer's relation $C_p = C_v + R$ gives the pressure form.
formulas.description: Entropy calculation for an ideal gas undergoing simultaneous temperature, volume, or pressure transitions.
formulas.explanation: For isothermal process ($T_1 = T_2$), $\Delta S = n R \ln(V_2/V_1) = -n R \ln(P_2/P_1)$.

formulas.latex: \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S, \quad \Delta G_{sys} = -T\Delta S_{univ} < 0 \text{ (Spontaneous)}
formulas.title: Gibbs Free Energy and Spontaneity Criterion
formulas.derivation: At constant $T$ and $P$, heat transferred to surroundings is $q_{surr} = -q_{sys} = -\Delta H_{sys}$. Surrounding entropy change is $\Delta S_{surr} = \frac{q_{surr}}{T} = -\frac{\Delta H_{sys}}{T}$. Universal entropy change is $\Delta S_{univ} = \Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr} = \Delta S_{sys} - \frac{\Delta H_{sys}}{T}$. Multiplying by $-T$: $-T\Delta S_{univ} = \Delta H_{sys} - T\Delta S_{sys}$. Defining Gibbs free energy $G = H - TS$ gives $\Delta G_{sys} = -T\Delta S_{univ}$. Since $\Delta S_{univ} > 0$ for spontaneity, $\Delta G_{sys} < 0$.
formulas.description: Thermodynamic potential determining spontaneity of chemical processes at constant temperature and pressure.
formulas.explanation: Criterion for spontaneity at constant $T, P$: $\Delta G < 0$ (spontaneous, exergonic); $\Delta G = 0$ (dynamic equilibrium); $\Delta G > 0$ (non-spontaneous, endergonic).

formulas.latex: \Delta G^\circ = -R T \ln K = -2.303 R T \log_{10} K
formulas.title: Standard Gibbs Free Energy and Equilibrium Constant Relation
formulas.derivation:
Chemical potential of species $i$ in mixture is $\mu_i = \mu_i^\circ + RT\ln a_i$. Reaction Gibbs free energy is $\Delta_r G = \sum 
u_i \mu_i = \sum 
u_i \mu_i^\circ + RT \sum 
u_i \ln a_i = \Delta_r G^\circ + RT\ln Q$ where $Q = \prod a_i^{
u_i}$ is the reaction quotient. At dynamic chemical equilibrium, net driving force vanishes: $\Delta_r G = 0$ and $Q = K_{eq}$. Substituting gives $0 = \Delta_r G^\circ + RT\ln K \implies \Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$.
formulas.description: Fundamental thermodynamic bridge connecting chemical equilibrium constant K to standard state free energy $\Delta G^\circ$.
formulas.explanation: If $\Delta G^\circ < 0$, then $K > 1$ (products favored at equilibrium); if $\Delta G^\circ > 0$, $K < 1$ (reactants favored).

formulas.title: van 't Hoff Equation
formulas.derivation: From $\ln K = -\frac{\Delta G^\circ}{RT} = -\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{RT} + \frac{\Delta S^\circ}{R}$. Differentiating with respect to temperature $T$ assuming $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ are independent of $T$: $\frac{d\ln K}{dT} = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{RT^2}$. Integrating from $T_1$ to $T_2$: $\int_{K_1}^{K_2} d\ln K = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\int_{T_1}^{T_2} T^{-2}dT \implies \ln(K_2/K_1) = -\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right) = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right)$.
formulas.description: Temperature sensitivity of chemical equilibrium constant governed by standard reaction enthalpy.
formulas.explanation: Thermodynamic proof of Le Chatelier's principle: for endothermic reactions ($\Delta H^\circ > 0$), increasing temperature increases $K$; for exothermic reactions ($\Delta H^\circ < 0$), increasing temperature decreases $K$.

formulas.latex: \Delta S_{fus} = \frac{\Delta H_{fus}}{T_m}, \quad \Delta S_{vap} = \frac{\Delta H_{vap}}{T_b} \approx 88 \text{ J/mol K (Trouton's Rule)}
formulas.title: Entropy of Phase Transitions and Trouton's Rule
formulas.derivation: At normal melting and boiling points, the two phases coexist in reversible dynamic equilibrium: $\Delta G = 0 \implies \Delta H - T\Delta S = 0 \implies \Delta S = \Delta H / T$. Trouton (1884) noted empirically that for non-associated liquids vaporizing to gas, the volume increase is roughly constant ($\sim 1000\times$), giving universal entropy of vaporization $\Delta S_{vap} = \frac{\Delta H_{vap}}{T_b} \approx 85 - 88\text{ J/mol K}$.
formulas.description: Entropy of fusion and vaporization at equilibrium phase transition temperatures.
formulas.explanation: Hydrogen-bonded liquids (water: $\Delta S_{vap} \approx 109\text{ J/mol K}$, ethanol) deviate positively from Trouton's rule due to high liquid-state order.

formulas.latex: S = k_B \ln \Omega, \quad S(T=0) = 0 \quad (\text{Third Law of Thermodynamics})
formulas.title: Boltzmann Entropy Formula and Third Law

variables.\\Omega: Number of accessible microstates corresponding to macroscopic state

formulas.derivation: Ludwig Boltzmann (1877) proved entropy is a logarithmic measure of microscopic multiplicity: $S = k_B \ln\Omega$. Nernst and Planck formulated the Third Law: as temperature approaches absolute zero ($T \to 0\text{ K}$), thermal motion ceases, and a perfectly ordered pure crystalline lattice settles into a unique non-degenerate quantum ground state ($\Omega = 1$). Therefore, $S_0 = k_B\ln(1) = 0$.
formulas.description: Microscopic statistical definition of entropy and absolute zero entropy of perfect crystalline substances.
formulas.explanation: Allows establishing absolute standard entropies $S^\circ$ for chemical substances, unlike internal energy or enthalpy which are only known relative to arbitrary references.

formulas.title: Maximum Non-Expansion Work and Cell EMF
formulas.derivation: From fundamental thermodynamic equation $dG = V dP - S dT + dw_{non-PV}$. At constant $T$ and $P$, $dG = dw_{non-PV}$. For reversible electrochemical cell, charge transferred is $Q = n F$, and electrical work done by cell is $w_{elec} = Q E_{cell} = n F E_{cell}$. Work done on system is $w = -n F E_{cell}$. Hence $\Delta G = -n F E_{cell}$.
formulas.description: Decrease in Gibbs free energy equals the maximum electrical reversible work extracted from an electrochemical cell.
formulas.explanation: For spontaneous galvanic cell, $E_{cell} > 0 \implies \Delta G < 0$.

formulas.latex: C_p - C_v = T \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = \frac{T V \beta^2}{\kappa_T}
formulas.title: General Thermodynamic Heat Capacity Difference
formulas.derivation: Internal energy differential is $dU = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_V dT + \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T dV$. Dividing by $dT$ at constant $P$ and noting $dH = dU + P\,dV + V\,dP$: $C_p - C_v = \left[P + \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T\right]\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P$. Using Maxwell relation $\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T = T\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V - P$, the $P$ terms cancel, yielding $C_p - C_v = T\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = \frac{TV\beta^2}{\kappa_T}$. For ideal gas ($PV = nRT$), $\beta = 1/T$ and $\kappa_T = 1/P$, recovering Mayer's relation $C_p - C_v = R$.
formulas.description: Universal relationship between isobaric and isochoric heat capacities for any substance (solid, liquid, or gas).
formulas.explanation: Because $T > 0, V > 0, \kappa_T > 0$, and $\beta^2 \ge 0$, $C_p$ is strictly greater than or equal to $C_v$ for all physical materials.

content_json.derivation: From universal energy conservation: change in internal state function $U$ equals energy entering system as heat ($q$) plus energy entering as mechanical boundary work ($w$). Under IUPAC sign convention, work done on the system by surroundings during compression is positive ($w > 0$), while work done by expanding system against external pressure $P_{ext}$ is negative: $w = -\int P_{ext}dV = -P_{ext}\Delta V$.
content_json.explanation: At constant volume (bomb calorimeter), $\Delta V = 0 \implies w = 0$, so $\Delta U = q_v$.
