sections.title: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits Formula Sheet - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.title: Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction and Lenz's Law
formulas.derivation: Empirical discovery by Michael Faraday (1831). The negative sign (Lenz's Law, Heinrich Lenz 1834) enforces energy conservation: the induced current flows in such a direction that its own magnetic field opposes the original flux change that produced it.
formulas.description: Induced electromotive force in a circuit equals negative rate of change of magnetic flux through loop.
formulas.explanation: If flux increases, induced magnetic field points opposite to applied field; if flux decreases, induced field reinforces it.

formulas.title: Motional EMF in a Moving Conductor
formulas.derivation: Mobile conduction electrons inside rod experience magnetic Lorentz force $\vec{F}_B = -e(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$. Work done moving an electron through length $\vec{l}$ is $W = \int \vec{F}_B \cdot d\vec{l} = -e \int (\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot d\vec{l}$. Induced EMF is work done per unit positive charge: $\mathcal{E} = W/(-e) = (\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot\vec{l} = B v l\sin\theta$.
formulas.description: Electromotive force induced across ends of a conducting rod of length l translating with speed v through magnetic field B.
formulas.explanation: Forms the foundation of electrical power generation in alternators and dynamos.

formulas.title: Rotational Motional EMF of a Rotating Rod
formulas.derivation: Consider element $dr$ at distance $r$ from pivot: linear velocity is $v(r) = r\omega$. Motional EMF generated across element is $d\mathcal{E} = B v(r) dr = B(r\omega)dr$. Integrating from pivot $r=0$ to tip $r=l$: $\mathcal{E} = B\omega \int_0^l r dr = B\omega \left[\frac{r^2}{2}\right]_0^l = \frac{1}{2}B\omega l^2$.
formulas.description: EMF induced between pivot and tip of a conducting rod of length l rotating with angular speed $\omega$ in perpendicular field B.
formulas.explanation: Also equals $B\left(\frac{dA}{dt}\right) = B\left(\frac{1}{2}l^2\omega\right)$, matching rate of area swept.

formulas.latex: L = \frac{N \Phi_B}{I} = \mu_0 n^2 A l, \quad U_B = \frac{1}{2}L I^2, \quad u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}
formulas.title: Self-Inductance and Magnetic Energy Density
formulas.derivation: Inside solenoid, field is $B = \mu_0 n I$. Flux per turn is $\Phi = B A = \mu_0 n I A$. Total linkage is $\lambda = N\Phi = (nl)(\mu_0 n I A) = (\mu_0 n^2 A l)I$. By definition $L = \lambda / I = \mu_0 n^2 A l$. Work required to establish current $I$ against back-EMF $\mathcal{E}_L = -L\frac{di}{dt}$ is $U = \int P\,dt = \int (L\frac{di}{dt} i)dt = L \int_0^I i\,di = \frac{1}{2}LI^2$. Dividing by volume $V = Al$ and using $B = \mu_0 n I$ yields $u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$.
formulas.description: Self-inductance of solenoid, total energy stored in inductor magnetic field, and volume energy density.
formulas.explanation: Analogous to kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ and electrostatic energy density $\frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0 E^2$.

formulas.latex: M = \frac{N_2 \Phi_{21}}{I_1} = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l, \quad M \le \sqrt{L_1 L_2}
formulas.title: Mutual Inductance and Coupling Coefficient
formulas.derivation: Current $I_1$ in outer coil produces uniform field $B_1 = \mu_0 n_1 I_1$. Flux passing through each turn of inner coil of area $A$ is $\Phi_{21} = B_1 A = \mu_0 n_1 I_1 A$. Total linkage with coil 2 ($N_2 = n_2 l$ turns) is $\lambda_2 = N_2 \Phi_{21} = (n_2 l)(\mu_0 n_1 I_1 A) = (\mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l)I_1$. Mutual inductance is $M = \lambda_2 / I_1 = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l$. By reciprocity theorem, $M_{12} = M_{21} = M$.
formulas.description: Mutual inductance between two co-axial solenoids and coupling coefficient $k = M/\sqrt{L_1 L_2} \le 1$.
formulas.explanation: For perfectly coupled coils with zero flux leakage, $k = 1$ and $M = \sqrt{L_1 L_2}$.

formulas.latex: i(t) = I_0 (1 - e^{-t / \tau_L}) \quad (\text{Growth}), \quad i(t) = I_0 e^{-t / \tau_L} \quad (\text{Decay}), \quad \tau_L = \frac{L}{R}
formulas.title: Transient LR Circuit Growth and Decay
formulas.derivation: KVL during growth: $\mathcal{E} - L\frac{di}{dt} - iR = 0 \implies L\frac{di}{dt} = \mathcal{E} - iR$. Separating variables: $\frac{di}{\mathcal{E} - iR} = \frac{dt}{L}$. Integrating with $i(0) = 0$: $-\frac{1}{R}\ln\left(1 - \frac{iR}{\mathcal{E}}\right) = \frac{t}{L} \implies i(t) = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R}\left(1 - e^{-Rt/L}\right)$.
formulas.description: Time-dependent current build-up and decay in inductive RL circuit with inductive time constant $\tau_L = L/R$.
formulas.explanation: At $t = \tau_L = L/R$, current reaches $63.2\%$ of steady value $I_0$; inductor acts as open-circuit at $t=0^+$ and short-circuit as $t \to \infty$.

formulas.title: Root-Mean-Square (RMS) Values of Sinusoidal AC
formulas.derivation: For $i(t) = I_0 \sin(\omega t)$, Joule heat generated in resistor $R$ over one period $T = 2\pi/\omega$ is $H = \int_0^T i^2(t) R dt$. An equivalent DC current $I_{rms}$ dissipates identical heat: $I_{rms}^2 R T = R \int_0^T I_0^2 \sin^2(\omega t) dt$. Since the average of $\sin^2(\omega t)$ over full period is $\frac{1}{2}$: $I_{rms}^2 T = I_0^2 \left(\frac{T}{2}\right) \implies I_{rms} = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}$.
formulas.description: Effective heating value of alternating sinusoidal current and voltage over full periodic cycle.
formulas.explanation: Standard wall outlet voltages (e.g., $230\text{ V}$ or $120\text{ V}$) always quote RMS values; peak voltage is $V_0 = \sqrt{2}V_{rms}$ ($325\text{ V}$ for $230\text{ V}$).

formulas.latex: Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}, \quad X_L = \omega L, \quad X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C}
formulas.title: Impedance of Series LCR Circuit
formulas.derivation: Phasor analysis: current phasor $\tilde{I}$ is common in series loop. Resistor voltage $\tilde{V}_R = I R$ is in phase with current. Inductor voltage $\tilde{V}_L = I X_L$ leads current by $+90^\circ (+i)$. Capacitor voltage $\tilde{V}_C = I X_C$ lags current by $-90^\circ (-i)$. Total complex voltage is $\tilde{V} = \tilde{V}_R + \tilde{V}_L + \tilde{V}_C = I [R + i(X_L - X_C)]$. Impedance magnitude is $Z = |\tilde{V}|/I = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$.
formulas.description: Total opposition to sinusoidal alternating current flow combining resistance, inductive reactance, and capacitive reactance.
formulas.explanation: Phase angle between voltage and current is $\tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R}$.

formulas.title: Resonant Frequency and Quality Factor (Q) of Series LCR
formulas.derivation: Current amplitude is $I_0 = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{R^2 + (\omega L - 1/\omega C)^2}}$. Current is maximized when reactive term vanishes: $\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C} = 0 \implies \omega_0^2 = \frac{1}{LC} \implies \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$. At resonance, impedance is purely resistive ($Z_{min} = R$) and current is in phase with voltage ($\cos\phi = 1$). Quality factor is $Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} = \frac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega}$ where $\Delta\omega$ is bandwidth at half-power points.
formulas.description: Condition for minimum impedance, maximum current resonance, and sharpness factor of resonance curve.
formulas.explanation: High $Q$ produces extremely sharp tuning selectivity in radio receivers and RF filter circuits.

formulas.title: Average AC Power and Power Factor
formulas.derivation: Instantaneous power is $p(t) = v(t)i(t) = [V_0 \sin(\omega t)][I_0 \sin(\omega t - \phi)] = V_0 I_0 \sin(\omega t)[\sin\omega t\cos\phi - \cos\omega t\sin\phi] = V_0 I_0 [\sin^2\omega t\cos\phi - \sin\omega t\cos\omega t\sin\phi]$. Averaging over a full cycle: $\langle \sin^2\omega t \rangle = 1/2$ and $\langle \sin\omega t\cos\omega t \rangle = 0$. Hence $P_{avg} = \frac{1}{2}V_0 I_0 \cos\phi = \left(\frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\left(\frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\cos\phi = V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos\phi$. From impedance triangle, $\cos\phi = R/Z$.
formulas.description: Real active power dissipated in AC circuit over complete cycle governed by phase angle $\phi$.
formulas.explanation: For purely reactive circuits (pure $L$ or pure $C$), $\phi = \pm 90^\circ \implies \cos\phi = 0$, giving zero real power dissipation (wattless current).

formulas.title: Ideal Transformer Voltage, Current and Turns Ratio
formulas.derivation: Assuming ideal core with zero flux leakage: common flux $\Phi$ links both windings. Induced EMFs are $V_p = -N_p \frac{d\Phi}{dt}$ and $V_s = -N_s \frac{d\Phi}{dt}$. Dividing gives $\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$. For an ideal lossless transformer (100% efficiency), input power equals output power: $V_p I_p = V_s I_s \implies \frac{I_p}{I_s} = \frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$.
formulas.description: Transformation of AC voltage and current in magnetically coupled primary and secondary windings.
formulas.explanation: Step-up transformer ($N_s > N_p$): voltage increases and current decreases proportionately, minimizing $I^2 R$ transmission line losses.

formulas.latex: \omega_{LC} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}, \quad q(t) = Q_0 \cos(\omega_{LC} t), \quad i(t) = -\omega_{LC} Q_0 \sin(\omega_{LC} t)
formulas.title: LC Tank Circuit Oscillations
formulas.derivation: Total circuit energy is $E = U_E + U_B = \frac{q^2}{2C} + \frac{1}{2}Li^2$. In lossless circuit, $\frac{dE}{dt} = 0$: $\frac{q}{C}\frac{dq}{dt} + L i \frac{di}{dt} = 0$. Since $i = \frac{dq}{dt}$, dividing by $i$ gives $\frac{q}{C} + L\frac{d^2q}{dt^2} = 0 \implies \frac{d^2q}{dt^2} + \frac{1}{LC}q = 0$. This is standard SHM equation with $\omega_{LC} = 1/\sqrt{LC}$. Solution with initial charge $Q_0$ is $q(t) = Q_0\cos(\omega t)$.
formulas.description: Undamped harmonic exchange of energy between electric field of capacitor and magnetic field of inductor.
formulas.explanation: Energy sloshes sinusoidally between all-electric state ($U_E = Q_0^2/2C$) and all-magnetic state ($U_B = \frac{1}{2}L I_{max}^2$).

formulas.title: Maxwell's Displacement Current
formulas.derivation: Between capacitor plates during charging, no conduction electrons flow, yet magnetic field exists. Electric field is $E = \frac{Q}{\epsilon_0 A} \implies Q = \epsilon_0 E A = \epsilon_0 \Phi_E$. Differentiating charge with respect to time: $I_c = \frac{dQ}{dt} = \epsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$. Maxwell recognized this time-varying flux term acts as an effective displacement current $I_d = \epsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$, restoring Ampere's law to $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 (I_c + I_d)$.
formulas.description: Equivalent current arising from time-varying electric flux, completing Ampere-Maxwell law.
formulas.explanation: Displacement current between plates exactly equals conduction current in the connecting wires ($I_d = I_c$), ensuring continuity.

formulas.title: Speed of Electromagnetic Waves in Vacuum and Field Ratio
formulas.description: Propagation velocity of light from Maxwell's equations and relation between electric and magnetic field amplitudes.
formulas.explanation: Proved that light is an electromagnetic transverse wave propagating at universal speed $c$.

content_json.derivation: Empirical discovery by Michael Faraday (1831). The negative sign (Lenz's Law, Heinrich Lenz 1834) enforces energy conservation: the induced current flows in such a direction that its own magnetic field opposes the original flux change that produced it.
content_json.explanation: If flux increases, induced magnetic field points opposite to applied field; if flux decreases, induced field reinforces it.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: Introduction to Three-dimensional Geometry Formula Sheet
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: By Law of Cosines on triangle formed by $\vec{a}, \vec{b}$, and $\vec{c} = \vec{a} - \vec{b}$: $|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 - 2|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta$. Expanding in components: $\sum (a_i - b_i)^2 = \sum a_i^2 + \sum b_i^2 - 2\sum a_i b_i$. Equating: $|\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 - 2\sum a_i b_i = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 - 2|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta \implies \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta = \sum a_i b_i$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Fundamental vector operation measuring alignment. Two non-zero vectors are perpendicular if and only if their dot product is zero.

content_json.title: Introduction to Three-dimensional Geometry Formula Sheet

sections.title: Introduction to Three-dimensional Geometry Formula Sheet - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.latex: \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}| |\vec{b}| \cos\theta = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3
formulas.title: Scalar (Dot) Product of Vectors
formulas.derivation: By Law of Cosines on triangle formed by $\vec{a}, \vec{b}$, and $\vec{c} = \vec{a} - \vec{b}$: $|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 - 2|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta$. Expanding in components: $\sum (a_i - b_i)^2 = \sum a_i^2 + \sum b_i^2 - 2\sum a_i b_i$. Equating: $|\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 - 2\sum a_i b_i = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 - 2|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta \implies \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta = \sum a_i b_i$.
formulas.description: Scalar (Dot) Product of Vectors
formulas.explanation: Fundamental vector operation measuring alignment. Two non-zero vectors are perpendicular if and only if their dot product is zero.

formulas.latex: \vec{a} \times \vec{b} = |\vec{a}| |\vec{b}| \sin\theta \, \hat{n} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \end{vmatrix}
formulas.title: Vector (Cross) Product and Triangle Area

variables.\\hat{n}: unit vector normal to plane of a and b via right-hand rule

formulas.derivation: By geometric definition, $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ is vector perpendicular to both $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ with magnitude equal to the area of the parallelogram formed by them ($|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\sin\theta$). Expanding basis vectors: $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}$, $\hat{j} \times \hat{k} = \hat{i}$, $\hat{k} \times \hat{i} = \hat{j}$. Linearity gives the $3 \times 3$ determinant form.
formulas.description: Vector (Cross) Product and Triangle Area
formulas.explanation: Produces a vector mutually perpendicular to two vectors; magnitude equals the area of the spanned parallelogram.

formulas.latex: [\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}] = \vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \\ c_1 & c_2 & c_3 \end{vmatrix}
formulas.title: Scalar Triple Product (Box Product) and Parallelepiped Volume

variables.V = |[\\vec{a} \\vec{b} \\vec{c}]|: volume of parallelepiped spanned by vectors a, b, c

formulas.derivation: Volume of parallelepiped = $(\text{Base Area}) \times (\text{Height})$. Base is parallelogram spanned by $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$, so area vector is $\vec{A} = \vec{b} \times \vec{c}$. Height is projection of $\vec{a}$ onto normal $\hat{n} = \frac{\vec{b}\times\vec{c}}{|\vec{b}\times\vec{c}|}$: $h = |\vec{a}||\cos\phi|$. Volume $= |\vec{b}\times\vec{c}| |\vec{a}| |\cos\phi| = |\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b}\times\vec{c})|$. Substituting determinant components for cross and dot products yields the $3 \times 3$ determinant.
formulas.description: Scalar Triple Product (Box Product) and Parallelepiped Volume
formulas.explanation: Calculates the volume of a 3D parallelepiped; value is zero if and only if the three vectors are coplanar.

formulas.title: Vector Triple Product (BAC-CAB Rule)
formulas.derivation: The vector $\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})$ is perpendicular to $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}$, so it lies in the plane of $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$: $\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = x \vec{b} + y \vec{c}$. It is also perpendicular to $\vec{a}$, so $\vec{a} \cdot [x\vec{b} + y\vec{c}] = 0 \implies x(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}) + y(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}) = 0 \implies \frac{x}{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}} = -\frac{y}{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}} = \lambda$. Evaluating with standard basis vectors (e.g. $\vec{a}=\hat{i}, \vec{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}, \vec{c}=\hat{k}$) determines $\lambda = 1$. Thus $\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = (\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{b} - (\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})\vec{c}$.
formulas.description: Vector Triple Product (BAC-CAB Rule)
formulas.explanation: Famous 'BAC minus CAB' identity expressing double cross-products as a linear combination of the inner vectors.

formulas.title: Lagrange's Vector Identity
formulas.derivation: By definition: $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|^2 = (|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\sin\theta)^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 |\vec{b}|^2 \sin^2\theta$. Use Pythagorean trigonometric identity $\sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos^2\theta$: $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 |\vec{b}|^2 (1 - \cos^2\theta) = |\vec{a}|^2 |\vec{b}|^2 - (|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta)^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 |\vec{b}|^2 - (\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})^2$.
formulas.description: Lagrange's Vector Identity
formulas.explanation: Connects magnitude of cross product directly to dot product without calculating angles.

formulas.title: Direction Cosines of a Line in 3D Space

variables.\\alpha, \\beta, \\gamma: angles made by line with positive x, y, z coordinate axes

formulas.derivation: Let $\hat{u}$ be a unit vector along the line: $\hat{u} = l\hat{i} + m\hat{j} + n\hat{k}$. Since it is a unit vector: $|\hat{u}|^2 = l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$. Since $l = \cos\alpha, m = \cos\beta, n = \cos\gamma$: $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1$. Using $\sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos^2\theta$: $(1 - \sin^2\alpha) + (1 - \sin^2\beta) + (1 - \sin^2\gamma) = 1 \implies \sin^2\alpha + \sin^2\beta + \sin^2\gamma = 3 - 1 = 2$.
formulas.description: Direction Cosines of a Line in 3D Space
formulas.explanation: Fundamental identities governing direction angles of any directed line in 3-dimensional Euclidean space.

formulas.title: Symmetric Cartesian Equation of a Straight Line in 3D
formulas.derivation: Let $\vec{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$ be an arbitrary point on the line passing through point $A(\vec{a}) = x_1\hat{i} + y_1\hat{j} + z_1\hat{k}$ parallel to direction vector $\vec{b} = a\hat{i} + b\hat{j} + c\hat{k}$. Vector equation: $\vec{r} - \vec{a} = \lambda \vec{b} \implies (x - x_1)\hat{i} + (y - y_1)\hat{j} + (z - z_1)\hat{k} = \lambda(a\hat{i} + b\hat{j} + c\hat{k})$. Equating components: $x - x_1 = \lambda a, y - y_1 = \lambda b, z - z_1 = \lambda c \implies \lambda = \frac{x - x_1}{a} = \frac{y - y_1}{b} = \frac{z - z_1}{c}$.
formulas.description: Symmetric Cartesian Equation of a Straight Line in 3D
formulas.explanation: Standard equation of a straight line in 3D geometry defined by a point and direction ratios.

formulas.title: Shortest Distance Between Two Skew Lines
formulas.derivation: The common perpendicular line segment connecting the two skew lines is parallel to $\vec{n} = \vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2$. Unit normal is $\hat{n} = \frac{\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2}{|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2|}$. The shortest distance $d$ is the magnitude of the projection of the displacement vector $\vec{a}_2 - \\vec{a}_1$ joining points on the two lines onto this common normal: $d = |(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot \hat{n}| = \frac{|(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2)|}{|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2|}$.
formulas.description: Shortest Distance Between Two Skew Lines
formulas.explanation: Distance between two non-intersecting, non-parallel lines in 3D; lines intersect if and only if d = 0.

formulas.latex: (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) = 0 \iff \begin{vmatrix} x_2 - x_1 & y_2 - y_1 & z_2 - z_1 \\ a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \end{vmatrix} = 0
formulas.title: Condition for Two Lines in 3D to be Coplanar
formulas.derivation: Two lines are coplanar if and only if the shortest distance between them is zero. From the shortest distance formula, numerator vanishing gives $(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) = 0$. Writing displacement $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1$ and direction vectors $\vec{b}_1, \vec{b}_2$ in determinant form yields the coplanarity determinant equation.
formulas.description: Condition for Two Lines in 3D to be Coplanar
formulas.explanation: Tests whether two lines lie in the exact same plane in 3D space.

formulas.latex: A x + B y + C z + D = 0 \iff \vec{r} \cdot \vec{n} = d
formulas.title: General Equation of a Plane in 3D Space
formulas.derivation: Let plane pass through point $P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ with normal vector $\vec{n} = A\hat{i} + B\hat{j} + C\hat{k}$. For any point $P(x, y, z)$ on the plane, the vector $\vec{P_0 P} = (x-x_0)\hat{i} + (y-y_0)\hat{j} + (z-z_0)\hat{k}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{n}$: $\vec{P_0 P} \cdot \vec{n} = 0 \implies A(x - x_0) + B(y - y_0) + C(z - z_0) = 0 \implies Ax + By + Cz - (Ax_0 + By_0 + Cz_0) = 0$. Setting constant $D = -(Ax_0 + By_0 + Cz_0)$ gives $Ax + By + Cz + D = 0$.
formulas.description: General Equation of a Plane in 3D Space
formulas.explanation: Standard 3D linear equation describing a 2-dimensional flat plane with normal vector (A, B, C).

formulas.latex: d = \frac{|A x_0 + B y_0 + C z_0 + D|}{\sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + C^2}}
formulas.title: Perpendicular Distance from Point (x0, y0, z0) to Plane
formulas.derivation: Line through $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ along normal $\vec{n}$ has equation $\vec{r}(t) = (x_0 + At)\hat{i} + (y_0 + Bt)\hat{j} + (z_0 + Ct)\hat{k}$. Substitute into plane equation: $A(x_0 + At) + B(y_0 + Bt) + C(z_0 + Ct) + D = 0 \implies (A x_0 + B y_0 + C z_0 + D) + t(A^2 + B^2 + C^2) = 0 \implies t = -\\frac{A x_0 + B y_0 + C z_0 + D}{A^2 + B^2 + C^2}$. The distance is the displacement magnitude: $d = |t| |\vec{n}| = \\frac{|Ax_0 + By_0 + Cz_0 + D|}{A^2 + B^2 + C^2} \\sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + C^2} = \\frac{|Ax_0 + By_0 + Cz_0 + D|}{\\sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + C^2}}$.
formulas.description: Perpendicular Distance from Point (x0, y0, z0) to Plane
formulas.explanation: Measures the shortest Euclidean distance from any spatial point to a plane.

formulas.title: Angle Between Two Planes

variables.\\vec{n}_1, \\vec{n}_2: normal vectors to the two planes

formulas.derivation: The dihedral angle $\theta$ between two intersecting planes is identical to the angle between their respective normal vectors $\vec{n}_1 = A_1\hat{i} + B_1\hat{j} + C_1\hat{k}$ and $\vec{n}_2 = A_2\hat{i} + B_2\hat{j} + C_2\hat{k}$. By vector dot product: $\vec{n}_1 \cdot \vec{n}_2 = |\vec{n}_1| |\vec{n}_2| \cos\theta \implies \cos\theta = \frac{\vec{n}_1 \cdot \\vec{n}_2}{|\vec{n}_1| |\\vec{n}_2|}$. Planes are perpendicular if $A_1 A_2 + B_1 B_2 + C_1 C_2 = 0$.
formulas.description: Angle Between Two Planes
formulas.explanation: Calculates the angle between two flat planes by taking the dot product of their normal vectors.

formulas.latex: \sin\phi = \frac{|A a + B b + C c|}{\sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + C^2}\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}} = \frac{|\vec{n} \cdot \vec{b}|}{|\vec{n}| |\vec{b}|}
formulas.title: Angle Between a Line and a Plane
formulas.derivation: Let $\theta$ be the angle between the line's direction vector $\vec{b}$ and the plane's normal vector $\vec{n}$: $\cos\theta = \frac{\vec{n}\cdot\vec{b}}{|\vec{n}||\vec{b}|}$. The angle $\phi$ that the line makes with the plane is complementary to $\theta$: $\phi = 90^\circ - \theta$. Therefore $\sin\phi = \sin(90^\circ - \theta) = \cos\theta = \frac{|\vec{n}\cdot\vec{b}|}{|\vec{n}||\vec{b}|}$.
formulas.description: Angle Between a Line and a Plane
formulas.explanation: Notice the trigonometric function is sine (not cosine), because it measures the complementary angle to the plane normal.

formulas.latex: P_1 + \lambda P_2 = 0 \iff (A_1 x + B_1 y + C_1 z + D_1) + \lambda (A_2 x + B_2 y + C_2 z + D_2) = 0
formulas.title: Family of Planes Passing Through Line of Intersection

variables.\\lambda: real parameter determined by boundary condition

formulas.derivation: Let line of intersection of planes $P_1 = 0$ and $P_2 = 0$ be $L$. For any point $(x, y, z)$ on line $L$, both $P_1(x, y, z) = 0$ and $P_2(x, y, z) = 0$ are satisfied simultaneously. Thus $P_1 + \lambda P_2 = 0 + \lambda(0) = 0$ for any value of $\lambda$. Furthermore, $P_1 + \lambda P_2 = 0$ is linear in $x, y, z$, so it represents a plane. Hence it represents every plane passing through the intersection line $L$.
formulas.description: Family of Planes Passing Through Line of Intersection
formulas.explanation: Generates any plane containing the line of intersection of two known planes.

content_json.derivation: By Law of Cosines on triangle formed by $\vec{a}, \vec{b}$, and $\vec{c} = \vec{a} - \vec{b}$: $|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 - 2|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta$. Expanding in components: $\sum (a_i - b_i)^2 = \sum a_i^2 + \sum b_i^2 - 2\sum a_i b_i$. Equating: $|\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 - 2\sum a_i b_i = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 - 2|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta \implies \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta = \sum a_i b_i$.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: Magnetism and Matter Formula Sheet
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: Electric force $\vec{F}_E = q\vec{E}$ is independent of velocity. Magnetic force $\vec{F}_B = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$ acts perpendicularly to both velocity and magnetic field (established by Hendrik Lorentz). Superposition yields total force $\vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v}\times\vec{B})$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Magnetic force does zero mechanical work on a charged particle ($dW = \vec{F}_B \cdot d\vec{r} = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot \vec{v}dt = 0$), altering direction of motion without changing kinetic energy or speed.

content_json.title: Magnetism and Matter Formula Sheet

sections.title: Magnetism and Matter Formula Sheet - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.title: Lorentz Force Equation
formulas.derivation: Electric force $\vec{F}_E = q\vec{E}$ is independent of velocity. Magnetic force $\vec{F}_B = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$ acts perpendicularly to both velocity and magnetic field (established by Hendrik Lorentz). Superposition yields total force $\vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v}\times\vec{B})$.
formulas.description: Total electromagnetic force experienced by a particle carrying charge q moving with velocity v.
formulas.explanation: Magnetic force does zero mechanical work on a charged particle ($dW = \vec{F}_B \cdot d\vec{r} = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot \vec{v}dt = 0$), altering direction of motion without changing kinetic energy or speed.

formulas.title: Cyclotron Motion and Gyrofrequency
formulas.derivation: Magnetic force provides centripetal acceleration: $q v_\perp B = \frac{m v_\perp^2}{r} \implies r = \frac{mv_\perp}{qB}$. Period is circumference divided by speed: $T = \frac{2\pi r}{v_\perp} = \frac{2\pi (mv_\perp / qB)}{v_\perp} = \frac{2\pi m}{qB}$. Frequency is $f_c = 1/T = \frac{qB}{2\pi m}$.
formulas.description: Radius, time period, and cyclotron frequency of a charged particle orbiting in a uniform magnetic field.
formulas.explanation: Orbital period and cyclotron frequency are completely independent of particle speed and radius (isochronous resonance).

formulas.title: Biot-Savart Law

variables.\\hat{r}: Unit vector from element to field point

formulas.derivation: Deduced experimentally by Jean-Baptiste Biot and Félix Savart: field magnitude scales as $dB \propto \frac{I dl \sin\theta}{r^2}$ with direction governed by right-hand thumb rule. In vector notation: $d\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I d\vec{l}\times\hat{r}}{r^2}$.
formulas.description: Fundamental law yielding differential magnetic field produced by an infinitesimal current element.
formulas.explanation: Magnetic counterpart to Coulomb's electrostatic law; integrates over complete current circuits to evaluate net magnetic field.

formulas.latex: B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d} \quad (\text{Infinite Wire}), \quad B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}(\sin\alpha + \sin\beta) \quad (\text{Finite Wire})
formulas.title: Magnetic Field of Straight Current-Carrying Conductor

variables.\\alpha, \\beta: Angles subtended by wire endpoints at the point

formulas.derivation: From Biot-Savart law: $dl = d\sec^2\theta d\theta$, $r = d\sec\theta$. Then $dB = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi} \frac{\cos\theta dl}{r^2} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}\cos\theta d\theta$. Integrating from $-\beta$ to $\alpha$: $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}[\sin\alpha - \sin(-\beta)] = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}(\sin\alpha + \sin\beta)$. For infinite wire, $\alpha = \beta = 90^\circ \implies B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}$.
formulas.description: Field at perpendicular distance d from straight current wire subtending boundary angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
formulas.explanation: Field lines form concentric circles centered on the wire following the right-hand grip rule.

formulas.latex: B_{axial} = \frac{\mu_0 N I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}, \quad B_{center} = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}
formulas.title: Magnetic Field on Axis and Center of Circular Current Loop
formulas.derivation: Element $I d\vec{l}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{r}$ where $r = \sqrt{R^2 + x^2}$. Differential field is $dB = \frac{\mu_0 I dl}{4\pi r^2}$. Components perpendicular to the axis cancel by symmetry around the ring. The axial component is $dB_x = dB\sin\theta = dB\left(\frac{R}{r}\right) = \frac{\mu_0 I R dl}{4\pi (R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$. Integrating over loop circumference $\oint dl = 2\pi R$ and multiplying by $N$ turns gives $B = \frac{\mu_0 N I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$. Setting $x=0$ yields center field $B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}$.
formulas.description: Field produced by circular coil of N turns and radius R at axial distance x from its center.
formulas.explanation: At large distances ($x \gg R$), field reduces to dipole form $B = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2M}{x^3}$ where magnetic dipole moment is $M = N I (\pi R^2)$.

formulas.title: Ampere's Circuital Law

variables.I_{enclosed}: Net current passing through area bounded by loop

formulas.derivation: Integrate around concentric circular path of radius $r$ centered on infinite wire: by axial symmetry, $\vec{B}$ has constant tangential magnitude $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$. Line integral is $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = B \oint dl = \left(\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\right)(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I$. By linear superposition, this holds for any closed loop enclosing total current $I_{enclosed}$.
formulas.description: Line integral of magnetic field around closed loop equals permeability multiplied by net enclosed current.
formulas.explanation: Used to analytically calculate fields in solenoids, toroids, and coaxial conductors with high geometric symmetry.

formulas.latex: B_{solenoid} = \mu_0 n I, \quad B_{toroid} = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2\pi r}
formulas.title: Magnetic Fields of Ideal Solenoid and Toroid
formulas.derivation: Solenoid: take rectangular Amperian loop of length $L$ with one side inside solenoid and opposite side far outside where field is negligible ($B_{out} \approx 0$). Transverse sides have $\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = 0$. Net line integral is $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = B L$. Enclosed current is $I_{enc} = (n L)I$. By Ampere's law: $B L = \mu_0 (n L I) \implies B = \mu_0 n I$. Toroid: Amperian circle of radius $r$ encloses $N$ turns: $B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 N I \implies B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2\pi r}$.
formulas.description: Uniform internal field of tightly wound solenoid ($n$ turns/length) and circular toroid.
formulas.explanation: Field inside a long solenoid is remarkably uniform and zero outside.

formulas.title: Force Between Parallel Current-Carrying Conductors
formulas.derivation: Wire 1 produces magnetic field at location of wire 2: $B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi d}$ directed perpendicular to plane containing wires. Segment of wire 2 of length $L$ carrying current $I_2$ experiences magnetic force $F = I_2 L B_1 = I_2 L \left(\frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi d}\right)$. Dividing by length: $\frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$.
formulas.description: Mutual magnetic force per unit length between two infinite parallel wires separated by distance d.
formulas.explanation: Parallel currents attract; anti-parallel currents repel. Serves as the historical SI definition of the Ampere.

formulas.title: Torque and Potential Energy of Magnetic Dipole
formulas.derivation: For rectangular loop of sides $a$ and $b$ in field $B$: forces on sides of length $a$ are $F = I a B$ forming a couple of lever arm $b\sin\theta$. Net torque is $\tau = F(b\sin\theta) = I(ab)B\sin\theta = I A B\sin\theta = |\vec{M}\times\vec{B}|$. Potential energy is work required to rotate dipole: $U = -\int \tau d\theta = -M B\cos\theta = -\vec{M}\cdot\vec{B}$.
formulas.description: Torque on a current loop or magnetic dipole in external magnetic field, and magnetic orientation potential energy.
formulas.explanation: Forms the operating principle of moving-coil galvanometers and DC electric motors.

formulas.title: Magnetic Susceptibility and Temperature Dependence
formulas.derivation: Paramagnetism arises from alignment of permanent atomic dipoles against randomizing thermal agitation ($k_B T$). Boltzmann statistics gives magnetization $M = N m L(x) \approx \frac{N m^2 B}{3k_B T}$ for weak fields ($x \ll 1$). Susceptibility is $\chi_m = \frac{M}{H} = \frac{\mu_0 M}{B} = \frac{\mu_0 N m^2}{3k_B T} = \frac{C}{T}$. In ferromagnets, internal exchange coupling field $B_{int} = \lambda M$ modifies alignment to give $\chi_m = \frac{C}{T - T_c}$ above $T_c$.
formulas.description: Paramagnetic susceptibility inverse temperature dependence and ferromagnetic transition above Curie temperature $T_c$.
formulas.explanation: Diamagnets have small negative susceptibility ($\chi < 0$) independent of temperature. Ferromagnets become paramagnetic above $T_c$.

formulas.title: Bohr Magneton
formulas.derivation: Orbital current of electron in circular orbit of radius $r$ and period $T = 2\pi r/v$ is $I = e/T = \frac{ev}{2\pi r}$. Orbital magnetic moment is $\mu_L = I A = \left(\frac{ev}{2\pi r}\right)(\pi r^2) = \frac{1}{2}e v r = \frac{e}{2m_e}(m_e v r) = \frac{e}{2m_e}L$. In Bohr model, orbital angular momentum is quantized as $L = n\hbar$. For ground state $n=1$, the fundamental magnetic moment is $\mu_B = \frac{e\hbar}{2m_e}$.
formulas.description: Fundamental quantum unit of orbital and spin magnetic dipole moment of an electron.
formulas.explanation: Gyromagnetic ratio for electron orbital motion is $\gamma = \frac{\mu_L}{L} = \frac{e}{2m_e}$.

formulas.latex: V_H = \frac{I B}{n q d} = \frac{R_H I B}{d}, \quad R_H = \frac{1}{n q}
formulas.title: Hall Effect Voltage and Hall Coefficient
formulas.derivation: Magnetic Lorentz force deflects drifting carriers sideways, accumulating charge on lateral faces until transverse Hall electric field $E_H$ balances magnetic deflection: $q E_H = q v_d B \implies E_H = v_d B$. Transverse voltage across width $w$ is $V_H = E_H w = v_d B w$. Using $I = n q (w d) v_d \implies v_d = \frac{I}{n q w d}$: $V_H = \left(\frac{I}{n q w d}\right) B w = \frac{I B}{n q d}$.
formulas.description: Transverse electric voltage generated across current-carrying conductor in transverse magnetic field.
formulas.explanation: Sign of Hall voltage directly determines whether majority charge carriers are negative electrons ($R_H < 0$) or positive holes ($R_H > 0$).

formulas.latex: B(r) = \frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi R^2} \quad (r \le R), \quad B(r) = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} \quad (r \ge R)
formulas.title: Magnetic Field Inside and Outside Solid Cylindrical Wire
formulas.derivation: Uniform current density $J = I / (\pi R^2)$. For $r \le R$, circular Amperian loop of radius $r$ encloses current $I_{enc} = J(\pi r^2) = I\frac{r^2}{R^2}$. By Ampere's circuital law: $B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I_{enc} = \mu_0 I \frac{r^2}{R^2} \implies B(r) = \frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi R^2}$. Outside ($r \ge R$), loop encloses full current $I$, giving $B(r) = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$.
formulas.description: Field profile inside uniform current carrying cylinder of radius R.
formulas.explanation: Magnetic field rises linearly from zero at center to maximum at surface ($r=R$), then falls off as $1/r$.

formulas.title: Helical Path Pitch of Charged Particle in Magnetic Field
formulas.derivation: Magnetic force has zero component along $\vec{B}$: $\vec{F}_\parallel = 0$, so parallel velocity $v_\parallel = v\cos\theta$ remains constant. Transverse component $v_\perp = v\sin\theta$ generates uniform circular orbit of period $T = \frac{2\pi m}{qB}$. Axial distance traveled during one complete period is pitch $p = v_\parallel T = (v\cos\theta)\left(\frac{2\pi m}{qB}\right)$.
formulas.description: Distance traveled along magnetic field direction per complete circular revolution when velocity makes angle $\theta$ with field.
formulas.explanation: Underlies magnetic confinement in tokamaks and planetary auroral particle precipitation along geomagnetic field lines.

content_json.derivation: Electric force $\vec{F}_E = q\vec{E}$ is independent of velocity. Magnetic force $\vec{F}_B = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$ acts perpendicularly to both velocity and magnetic field (established by Hendrik Lorentz). Superposition yields total force $\vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v}\times\vec{B})$.
content_json.explanation: Magnetic force does zero mechanical work on a charged particle ($dW = \vec{F}_B \cdot d\vec{r} = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot \vec{v}dt = 0$), altering direction of motion without changing kinetic energy or speed.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: Redox Reactions Formula Sheet
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: For ideal gas, partial pressure of component $i$ is $P_i = \frac{n_i R T}{V} = [C_i] R T$. For reaction $a A + b B \rightleftharpoons c C + d D$: $K_p = \frac{P_C^c P_D^d}{P_A^a P_B^b} = \frac{([C]RT)^c ([D]RT)^d}{([A]RT)^a ([B]RT)^b} = \frac{[C]^c [D]^d}{[A]^a [B]^b} (RT)^{(c+d) - (a+b)} = K_c (RT)^{\Delta n_g}$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: If $\Delta n_g = 0$, $K_p = K_c$ (dimensionless and pressure-independent). If $\Delta n_g \ne 0$, changing total pressure shifts equilibrium according to Le Chatelier's principle.

content_json.title: Redox Reactions Formula Sheet

sections.title: Redox Reactions Formula Sheet - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.latex: K_p = K_c (R T)^{\Delta n_g}, \quad \Delta n_g = \sum \nu_{g, prod} - \sum \nu_{g, react}
formulas.title: Relation Between Partial Pressure and Molar Concentration Equilibrium Constants

variables.K_p: Equilibrium constant in partial pressures (atm or bar)

formulas.derivation: For ideal gas, partial pressure of component $i$ is $P_i = \frac{n_i R T}{V} = [C_i] R T$. For reaction $a A + b B \rightleftharpoons c C + d D$: $K_p = \frac{P_C^c P_D^d}{P_A^a P_B^b} = \frac{([C]RT)^c ([D]RT)^d}{([A]RT)^a ([B]RT)^b} = \frac{[C]^c [D]^d}{[A]^a [B]^b} (RT)^{(c+d) - (a+b)} = K_c (RT)^{\Delta n_g}$.
formulas.description: Connects pressure-based equilibrium constant $K_p$ to concentration-based $K_c$ for gaseous equilibria.
formulas.explanation: If $\Delta n_g = 0$, $K_p = K_c$ (dimensionless and pressure-independent). If $\Delta n_g \ne 0$, changing total pressure shifts equilibrium according to Le Chatelier's principle.

formulas.latex: Q < K \implies \text{Forward Shift}, \quad Q = K \implies \text{Equilibrium}, \quad Q > K \implies \text{Reverse Shift}
formulas.title: Reaction Quotient (Q) Spontaneity Direction Criterion
formulas.derivation: From $\Delta_r G = \Delta_r G^\circ + RT\ln Q$ and $\Delta_r G^\circ = -RT\ln K$: $\Delta_r G = -RT\ln K + RT\ln Q = RT\ln(Q/K)$. If $Q < K$, then $\ln(Q/K) < 0 \implies \Delta_r G < 0$, so reaction proceeds spontaneously in the forward direction. If $Q > K$, $\Delta_r G > 0$, so reaction proceeds in the reverse direction. If $Q = K$, $\Delta_r G = 0$, system is in dynamic equilibrium.
formulas.description: Predicts spontaneous direction of chemical reaction toward equilibrium by comparing quotient Q to K.
formulas.explanation: Essential diagnostic tool for reaction mixtures far from equilibrium.

formulas.title: Ostwald's Dilution Law for Weak Monoprotic Acids
formulas.derivation: Equilibrium: $HA \rightleftharpoons H^+ + A^-$. Equilibrium concentrations: $[HA] = C(1-\alpha)$, $[H^+] = C\alpha$, $[A^-] = C\alpha$. Acid constant is $K_a = \frac{[H^+][A^-]}{[HA]} = \frac{(C\alpha)(C\alpha)}{C(1-\alpha)} = \frac{C\alpha^2}{1-\alpha}$. For weak electrolytes where $\alpha \ll 1$ (typically $\alpha \le 0.05$), approximation $1 - \alpha \approx 1$ gives $K_a \approx C\alpha^2 \implies \alpha = \sqrt{K_a / C}$. Hydronium is $[H^+] = C\alpha = C\sqrt{K_a/C} = \sqrt{K_a C}$. Taking negative logarithm: $pH = -\log\sqrt{K_a C} = \frac{1}{2}(pK_a - \log C)$.
formulas.description: Degree of ionization $\alpha$ and hydronium concentration for weak acid $HA$ of concentration C.
formulas.explanation: As dilution increases ($C \to 0$), degree of dissociation approaches unity ($\alpha \to 1$), as stated by Wilhelm Ostwald.

formulas.title: Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation for Acidic Buffers
formulas.derivation: From acid ionization equilibrium: $K_a = \frac{[H^+][A^-]}{[HA]}$. Rearranging for hydrogen ion concentration: $[H^+] = K_a \frac{[HA]}{[A^-]}$. Taking negative logarithm of both sides: $-\log[H^+] = -\log K_a - \log\left(\frac{[HA]}{[A^-]}\right) \implies pH = pK_a + \log\left(\frac{[A^-]}{[HA]}\right)$.
formulas.description: Calculates buffer pH of a weak acid and its conjugate salt mixture.
formulas.explanation: Buffer capacity is maximized when $[\text{Salt}] = [\text{Acid}]$, at which point $pH = pK_a$ (buffer range is $pK_a \pm 1$).

formulas.latex: pOH = pK_b + \log_{10}\left(\frac{[\text{Conjugate Acid}]}{[\text{Weak Base}]}\right), \quad pH + pOH = pK_w = 14 \quad (25^\circ\text{C})
formulas.title: Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation for Basic Buffers
formulas.derivation: Equilibrium: $B + H_2O \rightleftharpoons BH^+ + OH^-$. Base constant: $K_b = \frac{[BH^+][OH^-]}{[B]} \implies [OH^-] = K_b \frac{[B]}{[BH^+]}$. Taking negative logarithm: $pOH = pK_b + \log\left(\frac{[BH^+]}{[B]}\right)$. Since water auto-ionization $K_w = [H^+][OH^-] = 10^{-14}$ at $298\text{ K}$, $pH + pOH = 14$.
formulas.description: Calculates buffer pOH of a weak base ($NH_3$) and its conjugate cation ($NH_4^+$) mixture.
formulas.explanation: Standard formulation for ammoniacal buffers ($NH_4OH + NH_4Cl$).

formulas.latex: pH = 7 + \frac{1}{2}pK_a + \frac{1}{2}\log C \quad (\text{Salt of Weak Acid & Strong Base, e.g. } CH_3COONa)
formulas.title: Hydrolysis of Salt of Weak Acid and Strong Base
formulas.derivation: Anion hydrolysis: $A^- + H_2O \rightleftharpoons HA + OH^-$. Equilibrium: $K_h = \frac{[HA][OH^-]}{[A^-]} = \frac{K_w}{K_a}$. Degree of hydrolysis is $h = \sqrt{K_h / C} = \sqrt{\frac{K_w}{K_a C}}$. Hydroxide concentration is $[OH^-] = Ch = \sqrt{\frac{K_w C}{K_a}}$. Then $[H^+] = \frac{K_w}{[OH^-]} = \sqrt{\frac{K_w K_a}{C}}$. Taking negative logarithm: $pH = -\frac{1}{2}\log K_w - \frac{1}{2}\log K_a + \frac{1}{2}\log C = 7 + \frac{1}{2}pK_a + \frac{1}{2}\log C$.
formulas.description: Anionic hydrolysis producing alkaline solution ($pH > 7$) and hydrodynamic hydrolysis constant $K_h = K_w / K_a$.
formulas.explanation: Solution is distinctly basic because conjugate base of weak acid hydrolyzes to generate excess $OH^-$.

formulas.latex: pH = 7 - \frac{1}{2}pK_b - \frac{1}{2}\log C \quad (\text{Salt of Strong Acid & Weak Base, e.g. } NH_4Cl)
formulas.title: Hydrolysis of Salt of Strong Acid and Weak Base
formulas.derivation: Cation hydrolysis: $B^+ + H_2O \rightleftharpoons BOH + H^+$. Hydrolysis constant: $K_h = \frac{[BOH][H^+]}{[B^+]} = \frac{K_w}{K_b}$. Degree of hydrolysis is $h = \sqrt{K_h / C} = \sqrt{\frac{K_w}{K_b C}}$. Hydronium concentration is $[H^+] = Ch = \sqrt{\frac{K_w C}{K_b}}$. Taking negative logarithm: $pH = \frac{1}{2}pK_w - \frac{1}{2}pK_b - \frac{1}{2}\log C = 7 - \frac{1}{2}pK_b - \frac{1}{2}\log C$.
formulas.description: Cationic hydrolysis producing acidic solution ($pH < 7$) and hydrolysis constant $K_h = K_w / K_b$.
formulas.explanation: Solution is distinctly acidic due to hydronium generation by ammonium-type cations.

formulas.latex: pH = 7 + \frac{1}{2}(pK_a - pK_b) \quad (\text{Salt of Weak Acid & Weak Base, e.g. } CH_3COONH_4)
formulas.title: Hydrolysis of Salt of Weak Acid and Weak Base

variables.pK_a: Negative log of weak acid constant
variables.pK_b: Negative log of weak base constant

formulas.derivation: Both ions hydrolyze: $A^- + B^+ + H_2O \rightleftharpoons HA + BOH$. Hydrolysis constant is $K_h = \frac{[HA][BOH]}{[A^-][B^+]} = \frac{K_w}{K_a K_b}$. Degree of hydrolysis: $h = \sqrt{K_h} = \sqrt{\frac{K_w}{K_a K_b}}$ (independent of $C$). From acid equilibrium $[H^+] = K_a \frac{[HA]}{[A^-]} = K_a \frac{h}{1-h} \approx K_a \sqrt{K_h} = K_a \sqrt{\frac{K_w}{K_a K_b}} = \sqrt{\frac{K_w K_a}{K_b}}$. Taking negative log: $pH = \frac{1}{2}(pK_w + pK_a - pK_b) = 7 + \frac{1}{2}(pK_a - pK_b)$.
formulas.description: Simultaneous cationic and anionic hydrolysis where solution pH is completely independent of salt concentration C.
formulas.explanation: If $pK_a < pK_b$, solution is slightly acidic ($pH < 7$); if $pK_a > pK_b$, solution is slightly basic ($pH > 7$); completely independent of dilution.

formulas.latex: K_{sp} = x^x y^y S^{x+y} \implies S = \left(\frac{K_{sp}}{x^x y^y}\right)^{\frac{1}{x+y}}
formulas.title: Solubility Product Constant ($K_{sp}$) and Molar Solubility (S)
formulas.derivation: Dissolution equilibrium: $A_x B_{y(s)} \rightleftharpoons x A^{y+}_{(aq)} + y B^{x-}_{(aq)}$. If molar solubility is $S$, then ion concentrations at saturation are $[A^{y+}] = x S$ and $[B^{x-}] = y S$. The solubility product is $K_{sp} = [A^{y+}]^x [B^{x-}]^y = (x S)^x (y S)^y = x^x y^y S^{x+y}$. Solving for $S$ gives $S = \left(\frac{K_{sp}}{x^x y^y}\right)^{1/(x+y)}$.
formulas.description: Relates equilibrium solubility S of sparingly soluble salt $A_x B_y$ to solubility product $K_{sp}$.
formulas.explanation: Examples: $AB$ salt ($AgCl$): $K_{sp} = S^2 \implies S = \sqrt{K_{sp}}$. $AB_2$ salt ($PbCl_2, CaF_2$): $K_{sp} = 1^1 2^2 S^3 = 4S^3 \implies S = (K_{sp}/4)^{1/3}$. $A_2 B_3$ ($As_2S_3$): $K_{sp} = 108 S^5$.

formulas.latex: Q_{sp} > K_{sp} \implies \text{Precipitation}, \quad Q_{sp} = K_{sp} \implies \text{Saturated}, \quad Q_{sp} < K_{sp} \implies \text{Unsaturated}
formulas.title: Ionic Product ($Q_{sp}$) and Precipitation Condition
formulas.derivation: Analogous to chemical reaction quotient: ionic product $Q_{sp} = [A^{y+}]_{initial}^x [B^{x-}]_{initial}^y$ evaluates current ion concentrations. If $Q_{sp} < K_{sp}$, solution can dissolve more solid (unsaturated). If $Q_{sp} = K_{sp}$, solution is at exact dynamic saturation. If $Q_{sp} > K_{sp}$, solution is supersaturated; excess ions spontaneously precipitate out of solution until remaining ion product equals $K_{sp}$.
formulas.description: Criterion for onset of precipitation by comparing experimental ionic activity product to $K_{sp}$.
formulas.explanation: Explains qualitative inorganic salt analysis group separations (e.g. precipitating Group II sulfides in dilute acidic medium using common ion effect).

formulas.latex: S' = \frac{K_{sp}}{C} \quad (\text{for } AB \text{ salt in } C \text{ M common ion})
formulas.title: Common Ion Effect on Solubility

variables.S': Depressed solubility in common ion presence

formulas.derivation: Consider $AgCl_{(s)} \rightleftharpoons Ag^+ + Cl^-$ in solution containing $C\text{ M } NaCl$. Total chloride is $[Cl^-] = C + S' \approx C$ since $S' \ll C$. By solubility product: $K_{sp} = [Ag^+][Cl^-] = S' \times C \implies S' = \frac{K_{sp}}{C}$.
formulas.description: Suppression of molar solubility of sparingly soluble salt in presence of a common dissolved ion.
formulas.explanation: Solubility of $AgCl$ in $0.1\text{ M } NaCl$ ($K_{sp} = 10^{-10}$) is $S' = 10^{-10} / 0.1 = 10^{-9}\text{ M}$, a 100-fold decrease compared to pure water ($10^{-5}\text{ M}$).

formulas.latex: S' = S \sqrt{1 + \frac{[H^+]}{K_a}} \quad (\text{Solubility of Basic Anion in Acid})
formulas.title: Effect of pH on Solubility of Sparingly Soluble Salts

variables.K_a: Dissociation constant of conjugate weak acid

formulas.derivation: For salt $MA \rightleftharpoons M^+ + A^-$, anion reacts with acid: $A^- + H^+ \rightleftharpoons HA$ with $K = 1/K_a$. Total dissolved salt is $S' = [M^+] = [A^-] + [HA] = [A^-]\left(1 + \frac{[H^+]}{K_a}\right)$. Then $K_{sp} = [M^+][A^-] = S' \frac{S'}{1 + [H^+]/K_a} = \frac{(S')^2}{1 + [H^+]/K_a}$. Solving gives $S' = \sqrt{K_{sp}\left(1 + \frac{[H^+]}{K_a}\right)} = S\sqrt{1 + \frac{[H^+]}{K_a}}$.
formulas.description: Enhanced solubility of salts containing basic conjugate anions ($F^-, CO_3^{2-}, S^{2-}, C_2O_4^{2-}$) in acidic media.
formulas.explanation: Explains why carbonates, oxalates, and fluorides dissolve readily in dilute mineral acids.

formulas.latex: [H^+] = \sqrt{K_{a1} K_{a2}} \implies pH = \frac{pK_{a1} + pK_{a2}}{2} \quad (\text{Amphiprotic Ion, e.g. } HCO_3^-, H_2PO_4^-)
formulas.title: pH of Amphiprotic Species (Polyprotic Intermediate Ions)

variables.K_{a1}, K_{a2}: Consecutive acid dissociation constants of polyprotic acid

formulas.derivation: Intermediate ion $HA^-$ undergoes acid dissociation $HA^- \rightleftharpoons H^+ + A^{2-}$ ($K_{a2}$) and base hydrolysis $HA^- + H_2O \rightleftharpoons H_2A + OH^-$ ($K_b = K_w / K_{a1}$). Charge balance and mass balance equations combine to give $[H^+] = \sqrt{\frac{K_{a1} K_{a2} C + K_{a1} K_w}{C + K_{a1}}}$. When concentration $C \gg K_{a1}$ and $K_{a2} C \gg K_w$: $[H^+] \approx \sqrt{K_{a1} K_{a2}}$. Taking negative logarithm: $pH = \frac{pK_{a1} + pK_{a2}}{2}$.
formulas.description: Calculates solution pH of an amphoteric intermediate ion capable of both donating and accepting a proton.
formulas.explanation: Solution pH is independent of salt concentration; e.g. for sodium bicarbonate ($NaHCO_3$), $pH = \frac{6.35 + 10.33}{2} = 8.34$.

formulas.title: Isoelectric Point (pI) of Amino Acids
formulas.derivation: At isoelectric point, concentration of cationic form ($H_2A^+$) strictly equals concentration of anionic form ($A^-$): $[H_2A^+] = [A^-]$. From first dissociation: $[H_2A^+] = \frac{[H^+][HA]}{K_{a1}}$. From second dissociation: $[A^-] = \frac{K_{a2}[HA]}{[H^+]}$. Equating concentrations: $\frac{[H^+][HA]}{K_{a1}} = \frac{K_{a2}[HA]}{[H^+]} \implies [H^+]^2 = K_{a1} K_{a2} \implies [H^+] = \sqrt{K_{a1} K_{a2}}$. Taking negative log gives $pI = \frac{pK_{a1} + pK_{a2}}{2}$.
formulas.description: pH at which an amino acid carries net zero electrical charge and exists predominantly as neutral zwitterion.
formulas.explanation: At $pH = pI$, amino acid does not migrate in an electric field (electrophoresis) and exhibits minimum water solubility.

content_json.derivation: For ideal gas, partial pressure of component $i$ is $P_i = \frac{n_i R T}{V} = [C_i] R T$. For reaction $a A + b B \rightleftharpoons c C + d D$: $K_p = \frac{P_C^c P_D^d}{P_A^a P_B^b} = \frac{([C]RT)^c ([D]RT)^d}{([A]RT)^a ([B]RT)^b} = \frac{[C]^c [D]^d}{[A]^a [B]^b} (RT)^{(c+d) - (a+b)} = K_c (RT)^{\Delta n_g}$.
content_json.explanation: If $\Delta n_g = 0$, $K_p = K_c$ (dimensionless and pressure-independent). If $\Delta n_g \ne 0$, changing total pressure shifts equilibrium according to Le Chatelier's principle.

sections.title: JEE Master: Kinematics 1D & 2D Projectile Motion - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.title: First Equation of Uniformly Accelerated Motion
formulas.derivation: From definition of instantaneous acceleration $a = \frac{dv}{dt}$. Separating variables yields $dv = a \, dt$. Integrating both sides from $t=0$ (where $v=u$) to $t$: $\int_{u}^{v} dv = a \int_{0}^{t} dt \implies v - u = at \implies v = u + at$.
formulas.description: Relates final velocity, initial velocity, constant acceleration, and elapsed time.
formulas.explanation: Applies strictly when acceleration is constant in magnitude and direction along a rectilinear path.

formulas.title: Displacement-Time Relation
formulas.derivation: Since instantaneous velocity $v = \frac{ds}{dt} = u + at$, we integrate $ds = (u + at)dt$: $\int_{0}^{s} ds = \int_{0}^{t} (u + at)dt = \left[ ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2 \right]_0^t = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$.
formulas.description: Calculates rectilinear displacement under constant acceleration over time t.
formulas.explanation: Yields net displacement, not total distance traversed if velocity reverses direction during interval $t$.

formulas.title: Velocity-Displacement Relation (Third Kinematic Equation)
formulas.derivation: Using chain rule for acceleration: $a = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{dv}{ds} \frac{ds}{dt} = v \frac{dv}{ds}$. Rearranging: $v \, dv = a \, ds$. Integrating from initial $(u, 0)$ to final $(v, s)$: $\int_{u}^{v} v \, dv = a \int_{0}^{s} ds \implies \frac{v^2 - u^2}{2} = as \implies v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.
formulas.description: Relates final speed to initial speed and displacement without requiring explicit time.
formulas.explanation: Directly links kinetic energy change per unit mass to mechanical work done by constant force.

formulas.title: Displacement in the n-th Second
formulas.description: Distance traveled strictly between time $t = n-1$ and $t = n$.
formulas.explanation: Dimensionally valid because the implicit factor multiplying $(2n-1)$ is $1\text{ s}$.

formulas.title: Maximum Height of 2D Projectile
formulas.derivation: At maximum height, vertical velocity component vanishes: $v_y = 0$. Using $v_y^2 = u_y^2 - 2gH$ with $u_y = u\sin\theta$: $0 = (u\sin\theta)^2 - 2gH \implies H = \frac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g}$.
formulas.description: Peak vertical elevation reached by a projectile launched at angle $\theta$ with initial speed $u$.
formulas.explanation: Depends only on vertical launch velocity component $u_y$.

formulas.title: Time of Flight for Projectile Motion
formulas.derivation: Set vertical displacement $y = 0$ in $y = (u\sin\theta)t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$: $t(u\sin\theta - \frac{1}{2}gt) = 0$. Since $t=0$ is launch, landing time is $t = T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$.
formulas.description: Total duration projectile remains airborne before landing on horizontal ground.
formulas.explanation: Time of ascent equals time of descent ($t_{up} = t_{down} = \frac{u\sin\theta}{g}$) under symmetric vacuum trajectory.

formulas.title: Horizontal Range of Projectile
formulas.derivation: $R = u_x \cdot T = (u\cos\theta) \cdot \left(\frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}\right) = \frac{u^2 (2\sin\theta\cos\theta)}{g} = \frac{u^2 \sin(2\theta)}{g}$.
formulas.description: Total horizontal displacement traveled by a projectile on flat ground.
formulas.explanation: Maximum range occurs at $\theta = 45^\circ$ where $\sin(2\theta) = 1$. Complementary launch angles $\theta$ and $90^\circ - \theta$ give identical ranges.

formulas.title: Equation of Projectile Trajectory
formulas.derivation: From horizontal motion: $x = (u\cos\theta)t \implies t = \frac{x}{u\cos\theta}$. Substituting into $y = (u\sin\theta)t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$: $y = u\sin\theta\left(\frac{x}{u\cos\theta}\right) - \frac{g}{2}\left(\frac{x^2}{u^2\cos^2\theta}\right) = x\tan\theta - \frac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$. Factoring out $x\tan\theta$ and noting $R = \frac{2u^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{g}$ gives $y = x\tan\theta(1 - x/R)$.
formulas.description: Parabolic path equation relating vertical coordinates $y$ and horizontal coordinates $x$.
formulas.explanation: Standard quadratic trajectory form; useful for collision, clearing hurdles, and angle-of-elevation problems.

formulas.title: Relative Velocity in 2D/3D

variables.\\vec{v}_A: Velocity of A in ground frame
variables.\\vec{v}_B: Velocity of B in ground frame
variables.\\vec{v}_{A/B}: Relative velocity of A w.r.t. B

formulas.derivation: Position vector of A relative to B is $\vec{r}_{A/B} = \vec{r}_A - \vec{r}_B$. Differentiating with respect to time: $\frac{d\vec{r}_{A/B}}{dt} = \frac{d\vec{r}_A}{dt} - \frac{d\vec{r}_B}{dt} \implies \vec{v}_{A/B} = \vec{v}_A - \vec{v}_B$.
formulas.description: Velocity of object A observed from the reference frame of moving observer B.
formulas.explanation: Crucial for river-swimmer problems, rain-umbrella problems, and minimum approach distance calculations.

formulas.title: River Crossing Time and Drift
formulas.derivation: Cross-river speed component is $v_y = v_{br}\cos\theta$, so $t = d / (v_{br}\cos\theta)$. Net downstream velocity along bank is $v_x = v_r - v_{br}\sin\theta$. Drift is $x = v_x \cdot t$.
formulas.description: Time taken by boat to cross river of width d and resultant downstream drift.
formulas.explanation: Shortest time occurs when heading straight across ($\theta = 0, t_{min} = d/v_{br}$). Zero drift requires $\sin\theta = v_r / v_{br}$ (valid if $v_{br} \ge v_r$).

formulas.title: Centripetal and Tangential Accelerations in Curvilinear Motion
formulas.derivation: In planar polar coordinates, position $\vec{r} = R\hat{r}$. Velocity is $\vec{v} = R\omega \hat{\theta}$. Differentiating velocity: $\vec{a} = R\alpha \hat{\theta} + R\omega \frac{d\hat{\theta}}{dt}$. Since $\frac{d\hat{\theta}}{dt} = -\omega\hat{r}$, $\vec{a} = -R\omega^2 \hat{r} + R\alpha \hat{\theta} = -\frac{v^2}{R}\hat{r} + a_t \hat{\theta}$. Total magnitude $a = \sqrt{a_n^2 + a_t^2}$.
formulas.description: Decomposition of total acceleration into normal (direction change) and tangential (speed change) components.
formulas.explanation: Centripetal acceleration always points toward center of curvature; tangential acceleration alters the magnitude of velocity.

formulas.title: Radius of Curvature of Trajectory
formulas.derivation: At any point, $a_n = \frac{v^2}{R_c} = g\cos\phi$. From differential geometry, curvature $\kappa = \frac{1}{R_c} = \frac{|y''|}{(1 + y'^2)^{3/2}}$, thus $R_c = \frac{(1 + y'^2)^{3/2}}{|y''|}$.
formulas.description: Local radius of osculating circle for any planar curve $y(x)$.
formulas.explanation: Enables computing normal contact force and centripetal load on curved tracks and projectile apogees.

content_json.explanation: Applies strictly when acceleration is constant in magnitude and direction along a rectilinear path.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: JEE Master: Laws of Motion, Friction & Circular Dynamics
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: Momentum is $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$. Differentiating using product rule: $\vec{F} = \frac{d(m\vec{v})}{dt} = m\frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} + \vec{v}\frac{dm}{dt}$. For constant mass systems ($dm/dt = 0$), this reduces to $\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a}$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Fundamental dynamical law; force causes acceleration, not velocity. In variable-mass systems (like rockets), the thrust term $\vec{v}_{rel}(dm/dt)$ must be included.

sections.title: JEE Master: Laws of Motion, Friction & Circular Dynamics - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.title: Newton's Second Law of Motion
formulas.derivation: Momentum is $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$. Differentiating using product rule: $\vec{F} = \frac{d(m\vec{v})}{dt} = m\frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} + \vec{v}\frac{dm}{dt}$. For constant mass systems ($dm/dt = 0$), this reduces to $\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a}$.
formulas.description: Relates net external force to the rate of change of linear momentum, generalizing to variable-mass systems.
formulas.explanation: Fundamental dynamical law; force causes acceleration, not velocity. In variable-mass systems (like rockets), the thrust term $\vec{v}_{rel}(dm/dt)$ must be included.

formulas.title: Impulse-Momentum Theorem
formulas.derivation: From $\vec{F} = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$, multiply both sides by $dt$: $d\vec{p} = \vec{F}\,dt$. Integrating both sides from state 1 to state 2 gives $\Delta\vec{p} = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \vec{F}\,dt = \vec{J}$.
formulas.description: Integral of force over time equals the net change in linear momentum.
formulas.explanation: Useful in collision and impact problems where force varies dramatically over an extremely brief time interval.

formulas.title: Laws of Static and Kinetic Friction
formulas.derivation: Empirical Coulomb-Amontons laws: micro-welds between asperities generate shear resistance proportional to macroscopic normal contact force $N$. Before slippage, $f_s$ self-adjusts to balance tangential load up to $(f_s)_{max} = \mu_s N$. Once sliding occurs, asperity bonds continuously break and reform, giving $f_k = \mu_k N$ with $\mu_k \le \mu_s$.
formulas.description: Maximum limiting static friction and constant sliding kinetic friction proportional to normal reaction.
formulas.explanation: Static friction is an adjustable force directed to oppose impending relative motion; kinetic friction opposes actual relative sliding velocity.

formulas.title: Angle of Friction and Angle of Repose
formulas.derivation: Resultant contact force is $\vec{R} = \vec{N} + \vec{f}_s$. At limiting friction $f_s = \mu_s N$, the angle $\theta_s$ made with $\vec{N}$ satisfies $\tan\theta_s = \frac{f_s}{N} = \mu_s$. On an inclined plane of angle $\theta$, gravity down the incline is $mg\sin\theta$ and normal is $mg\cos\theta$. Limiting equilibrium requires $mg\sin\theta = \mu_s mg\cos\theta \implies \tan\theta = \mu_s$.
formulas.description: Angle between resultant contact force and normal, and minimum incline angle for sliding initiation.
formulas.explanation: A block placed on an incline stays at rest if incline angle $\theta \le \theta_r = \tan^{-1}(\mu_s)$.

formulas.latex: a = \frac{(m_2 - m_1)g}{m_1 + m_2}, \quad T = \frac{2 m_1 m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2}
formulas.title: Atwood Machine Acceleration and Tension
formulas.derivation: Equations of motion: for $m_2$ descending, $m_2 g - T = m_2 a$. For $m_1$ ascending, $T - m_1 g = m_1 a$. Adding equations eliminates $T$: $(m_2 - m_1)g = (m_1 + m_2)a \implies a = \frac{m_2 - m_1}{m_1 + m_2}g$. Substituting $a$ back into tension equation: $T = m_1(g + a) = m_1\left(g + \frac{m_2 - m_1}{m_1 + m_2}g\right) = \frac{2m_1 m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2}$.
formulas.description: Dynamics of two masses suspended over a frictionless, massless ideal pulley.
formulas.explanation: Tension is the harmonic mean of the two weights; common acceleration depends on net unbalance divided by total mass.

formulas.title: Maximum Safe Speed on a Banked Road
formulas.derivation: At impending outward slip, friction $f = \mu_s N$ acts downwards along the incline. Resolving vertically: $N\cos\theta - f\sin\theta = mg \implies N(\cos\theta - \mu_s\sin\theta) = mg$. Resolving horizontally for centripetal force: $N\sin\theta + f\cos\theta = \frac{m v^2}{R} \implies N(\sin\theta + \mu_s\cos\theta) = \frac{m v^2}{R}$. Dividing horizontal by vertical equation: $\frac{v_{max}^2}{Rg} = \frac{\sin\theta + \mu_s\cos\theta}{\cos\theta - \mu_s\sin\theta} = \frac{\tan\theta + \mu_s}{1 - \mu_s\tan\theta}$.
formulas.description: Maximum negotiated curve speed without skidding outwards on a banked circular turn.
formulas.explanation: If friction is absent ($\mu_s = 0$), optimum design speed is $v_0 = \sqrt{Rg\tan\theta}$, where tires exert no lateral friction.

formulas.title: Critical Speeds in Vertical Circular Motion
formulas.derivation: At highest point, string tension must satisfy $T_{top} \ge 0$. Equation of motion: $T_{top} + mg = \frac{m v_{top}^2}{R}$. Critical condition $T_{top} = 0 \implies v_{top} = \sqrt{gR}$. By conservation of mechanical energy between bottom and top: $\frac{1}{2}m v_{bottom}^2 = \frac{1}{2}m v_{top}^2 + mg(2R)$. Substituting $v_{top}^2 = gR$: $v_{bottom}^2 = gR + 4gR = 5gR \implies v_{bottom} = \sqrt{5gR}$.
formulas.description: Minimum bottom and top speeds required for a mass on a light string to complete vertical loop.
formulas.explanation: Tension at bottom under critical looping condition is $T_{bottom} = \frac{mv_{bottom}^2}{R} + mg = 5mg + mg = 6mg$.

formulas.title: Pseudo Force (D'Alembert Force)

variables.\\vec{a}_0: Acceleration of reference frame w.r.t. ground

formulas.derivation: In inertial frame, $\vec{F}_{real} = m\vec{a}_{in}$. If frame has acceleration $\vec{a}_0$, acceleration of particle relative to frame is $\vec{a}_{rel} = \vec{a}_{in} - \vec{a}_0$. Multiplying by mass $m$: $m\vec{a}_{rel} = m\vec{a}_{in} - m\vec{a}_0 = \vec{F}_{real} + (-m\vec{a}_0)$. Defining $\vec{F}_{pseudo} = -m\vec{a}_0$ restores $\sum \vec{F} = m\vec{a}_{rel}$.
formulas.description: Inertial fictitious force added when analyzing dynamics from an accelerating non-inertial reference frame.
formulas.explanation: Always acts in the direction opposite to the frame acceleration vector $\vec{a}_0$, passing through the center of mass.

formulas.title: Tsiolkovsky Rocket Equation with Gravity
formulas.derivation: Momentum balance for system at time $t$ and $t+dt$: $(m-dm)(v+dv) + dm(v - v_{rel}) - mv = -mg\,dt$. Neglecting second-order differential $dm\,dv$: $m\,dv - v_{rel}dm = -mg\,dt \implies dv = -v_{rel}\frac{dm}{m} - g\,dt$. Integrating from $m_0$ to $m(t)$: $v(t) - v_0 = v_{rel}\ln(m_0/m) - gt$.
formulas.description: Velocity acquired by a variable-mass rocket ejecting propellant exhaust at constant relative velocity.
formulas.explanation: Fundamental relation in astronautics; logarithmic scaling highlights why multi-stage staging is necessary to reach orbit.

formulas.title: Normal Contact Force Between Blocks
formulas.derivation: Common acceleration of combined system is $a = \frac{F}{m_1 + m_2}$. Isolating the forward block $m_2$, the only horizontal force acting on it is the contact normal force $N_{12}$. Applying Newton's second law: $N_{12} = m_2 a = m_2 \left(\frac{F}{m_1 + m_2}\right)$.
formulas.description: Internal normal contact force transmitted between two touching blocks pushed along a smooth surface.
formulas.explanation: The contact force equals the forward mass fraction multiplied by total applied force.

formulas.title: String Tension at Arbitrary Angle in Simple Pendulum
formulas.derivation: By energy conservation: $mgL(\cos\theta - \cos\theta_0) = \frac{1}{2}m v^2 \implies \frac{mv^2}{L} = 2mg(\cos\theta - \cos\theta_0)$. Radially, Newton's law gives $T - mg\cos\theta = \frac{mv^2}{L}$. Substituting $\frac{mv^2}{L}$: $T = mg\cos\theta + 2mg(\cos\theta - \cos\theta_0) = mg(3\cos\theta - 2\cos\theta_0)$.
formulas.description: Tension in pendulum string released from initial angular deflection $\theta_0$ as it passes through angle $\theta$.
formulas.explanation: At bottom ($\theta = 0$), $T = mg(3 - 2\cos\theta_0)$, which exceeds $mg$ substantially.

formulas.title: Acceleration of Movable Wedge on Smooth Floor
formulas.derivation: Let horizontal wedge acceleration be $A$ to the left. In wedge frame, block acceleration along incline is $a_r$. Normal force on block is $N = m(g\cos\alpha - A\sin\alpha)$. Horizontal force on wedge from block is $N\sin\alpha = MA$. Eliminating $N$ and using constraint equations yields $A = \frac{mg\sin\alpha\cos\alpha}{M + m\sin^2\alpha}$.
formulas.description: Horizontal acceleration of a smooth wedge of mass M supporting sliding block of mass m.
formulas.explanation: Classic constraint motion problem; conservation of horizontal momentum of the block-wedge system holds because horizontal external forces are zero.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: JEE Master: Work, Energy, Power & Collisions
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: Work for infinitesimal step $d\vec{r}$ is $dW = \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} = |\vec{F}||d\vec{r}|\cos\theta$. Total work along path from initial point $\vec{r}_1$ to final point $\vec{r}_2$ is obtained by Riemann line integration: $W = \int_{\vec{r}_1}^{\vec{r}_2} \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Work is positive when force component aligns with motion ($\theta < 90^\circ$), negative when opposing motion ($\theta > 90^\circ$), and zero when perpendicular (e.g. magnetic Lorentz force or normal force on fixed tracks).

formulas.latex: W = \int_{\vec{r}_1}^{\vec{r}_2} \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = \int (F_x dx + F_y dy + F_z dz)
formulas.title: Work Done by a General Variable Force
formulas.derivation: Work for infinitesimal step $d\vec{r}$ is $dW = \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} = |\vec{F}||d\vec{r}|\cos\theta$. Total work along path from initial point $\vec{r}_1$ to final point $\vec{r}_2$ is obtained by Riemann line integration: $W = \int_{\vec{r}_1}^{\vec{r}_2} \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}$.
formulas.description: Line integral of force vector along particle displacement trajectory.
formulas.explanation: Work is positive when force component aligns with motion ($\theta < 90^\circ$), negative when opposing motion ($\theta > 90^\circ$), and zero when perpendicular (e.g. magnetic Lorentz force or normal force on fixed tracks).

formulas.title: Work-Energy Theorem
formulas.derivation: From Newton's second law: $F_{net} = m\frac{dv}{dt}$. Net work is $W_{net} = \int F_{net}ds = \int m\frac{dv}{dt}ds = \int m\,v\,dv = \left[\frac{1}{2}mv^2\right]_{v_i}^{v_f} = \frac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \frac{1}{2}mv_i^2$.
formulas.description: Net work done by all acting forces (conservative, non-conservative, and pseudo) equals the change in kinetic energy.
formulas.explanation: Holds universally in all inertial frames, and in non-inertial frames provided pseudo-force work is included.

formulas.latex: \vec{F} = -\vec{\nabla} U = -\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial x}\hat{i} + \frac{\partial U}{\partial y}\hat{j} + \frac{\partial U}{\partial z}\hat{k}\right)
formulas.title: Conservative Force as Potential Energy Gradient
formulas.derivation: By definition, work done by conservative force in differential displacement is $dW = -dU = \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} = F_x dx + F_y dy + F_z dz$. From multivariable calculus, $dU = \frac{\partial U}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial U}{\partial y}dy + \frac{\partial U}{\partial z}dz$. Equating coefficients yields $F_x = -\frac{\partial U}{\partial x}$, $F_y = -\frac{\partial U}{\partial y}$, $F_z = -\frac{\partial U}{\partial z}$, or $\vec{F} = -\vec{\nabla}U$.
formulas.description: Spatial negative gradient of potential energy scalar field yields conservative vector force.
formulas.explanation: Equilibrium occurs where $\vec{F} = 0 \implies \vec{\nabla}U = 0$. Stable equilibrium corresponds to a local minimum ($\frac{\partial^2 U}{\partial x^2} > 0$); unstable to a maximum.

formulas.title: Elastic Potential Energy of an Ideal Spring
formulas.derivation: Restoring force is Hooke's law $F = -kx$. Work done by external agent against spring is $W = \int_0^x (-F)dx' = \int_0^x kx' dx' = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$. This work is stored as elastic potential energy $U_s$.
formulas.description: Potential energy stored when an ideal spring of stiffness k is stretched or compressed by x.
formulas.explanation: Always non-negative whether compressed ($x < 0$) or extended ($x > 0$).

formulas.title: Instantaneous Mechanical Power
formulas.derivation: Instantaneous work done over time $dt$ during displacement $d\vec{r}$ is $dW = \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}$. Dividing by $dt$: $P = \frac{dW}{dt} = \vec{F}\cdot \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt} = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$.
formulas.description: Rate at which mechanical work is performed by a force acting on a particle moving with velocity v.
formulas.explanation: If vehicle moves at steady speed against resistance $F_{drag}$, engine output power required is $P = F_{drag} \cdot v$.

formulas.latex: e = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{u_1 - u_2} = \frac{\text{Velocity of Separation}}{\text{Velocity of Approach}}
formulas.title: Newton's Coefficient of Restitution
formulas.derivation: Defined through impulse phases of collision: ratio of restitution impulse to deformation impulse $e = \frac{\int_{max}^{end} F\,dt}{\int_0^{max} F\,dt} = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{u_1 - u_2}$.
formulas.description: Ratio of relative velocity after collision to relative velocity before collision along line of impact.
formulas.explanation: For perfectly elastic collisions, $e = 1$ (kinetic energy conserved). For perfectly inelastic collisions, $e = 0$ (bodies coalesce). For realistic inelastic collisions, $0 < e < 1$.

formulas.title: Post-Collision Velocities in 1D Inelastic Collision
formulas.derivation: Solving system of two equations: (1) Conservation of linear momentum $m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2$, (2) Restitution definition $v_2 - v_1 = e(u_1 - u_2)$. Substituting $v_2 = v_1 + e(u_1 - u_2)$ into momentum equation yields $v_1$; symmetric substitution gives $v_2$.
formulas.description: General 1D collision velocities incorporating masses, initial velocities, and coefficient of restitution.
formulas.explanation: When $e=1$ and $m_1 = m_2$, velocities are completely exchanged ($v_1 = u_2, v_2 = u_1$).

formulas.title: Loss of Kinetic Energy in 1D Collision
formulas.derivation: In center-of-mass frame, total kinetic energy before collision is $K_{initial} = \frac{1}{2}\mu (u_1 - u_2)^2$. Relative velocity after collision is $v_{rel} = e(u_1 - u_2)$, so final kinetic energy in CM frame is $K_{final} = \frac{1}{2}\mu [e(u_1 - u_2)]^2 = \frac{1}{2}\mu e^2 (u_1 - u_2)^2$. The difference is $\Delta K_{loss} = K_{initial} - K_{final} = \frac{1}{2}\mu (1 - e^2)(u_1 - u_2)^2$.
formulas.description: Mechanical kinetic energy converted into heat, sound, and internal plastic deformation.
formulas.explanation: Loss is zero if and only if $e = 1$. Maximum energy loss occurs when $e = 0$ (completely inelastic).

formulas.latex: h_n = e^{2n} h_0, \quad H_{total} = h_0 \left(\frac{1 + e^2}{1 - e^2}\right)
formulas.title: Bouncing Ball Height and Total Traveled Distance
formulas.derivation: Speed just before first impact is $v_0 = \sqrt{2gh_0}$. Speed right after first bounce is $v_1 = e v_0 = e\sqrt{2gh_0}$. Height reached is $h_1 = \frac{v_1^2}{2g} = e^2 h_0$. Inductively, $h_n = e^{2n}h_0$. Total distance is $H = h_0 + 2h_1 + 2h_2 + \dots = h_0 + 2h_0\sum_{n=1}^\infty e^{2n} = h_0 + 2h_0\frac{e^2}{1 - e^2} = h_0\left(\frac{1 + e^2}{1 - e^2}\right)$.
formulas.description: Successive bounce heights and infinite geometric series sum of total vertical distance for a dropped ball.
formulas.explanation: Total time until motion ceases is finite: $T = t_0 + 2t_1 + \dots = \sqrt{\frac{2h_0}{g}}\left(\frac{1+e}{1-e}\right)$ despite infinitely many bounces.

formulas.title: Kinetic Energy-Momentum Relation
formulas.derivation: $K = \frac{1}{2}m v^2 = \frac{1}{2}m \left(\frac{p}{m}\right)^2 = \frac{p^2}{2m}$. Taking natural logarithm: $\ln K = 2\ln p - \ln(2m)$. Differentiating: $\frac{dK}{K} = 2\frac{dp}{p}$. For small percentage changes, $\%\Delta K \approx 2(\%\Delta p)$.
formulas.description: Quadratic dependence between kinetic energy and linear momentum magnitude.
formulas.explanation: If momentum increases by 100%, kinetic energy increases by a factor of $2^2 = 4$ (a 300% increase).

formulas.title: Combination of Springs
formulas.derivation: Parallel: common elongation $x$; total restoring force $F = F_1 + F_2 = k_1 x + k_2 x = (k_1 + k_2)x \implies k_{eff} = k_1 + k_2$. Series: common tension force $F$; total elongation $x = x_1 + x_2 = \frac{F}{k_1} + \frac{F}{k_2} = F\left(\frac{1}{k_1} + \frac{1}{k_2}\right) \implies \frac{1}{k_{eff}} = \frac{1}{k_1} + \frac{1}{k_2}$.
formulas.description: Equivalent stiffness for parallel and series spring networks.
formulas.explanation: Cutting a spring of stiffness $k$ into two halves doubles the stiffness of each half ($k' = 2k$).

formulas.title: Work Done by Kinetic Friction and Thermal Dissipation
formulas.derivation: Let surface 1 move by $s_1$ and surface 2 move by $s_2$. Work on 1 is $-f_k s_1$; work on 2 is $+f_k s_2$. Net mechanical work is $W_{net} = -f_k(s_1 - s_2) = -f_k s_{rel}$. This negative work precisely matches heat generated at the contact interface.
formulas.description: Net mechanical energy loss equals kinetic friction multiplied by relative interface sliding distance.
formulas.explanation: Total work done by static friction on an entire system is always zero, but kinetic friction always dissipates mechanical energy into thermal internal energy.

content_json.derivation: Work for infinitesimal step $d\vec{r}$ is $dW = \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} = |\vec{F}||d\vec{r}|\cos\theta$. Total work along path from initial point $\vec{r}_1$ to final point $\vec{r}_2$ is obtained by Riemann line integration: $W = \int_{\vec{r}_1}^{\vec{r}_2} \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}$.
content_json.explanation: Work is positive when force component aligns with motion ($\theta < 90^\circ$), negative when opposing motion ($\theta > 90^\circ$), and zero when perpendicular (e.g. magnetic Lorentz force or normal force on fixed tracks).

catalog_formula_sheets.name: JEE Master: Rotational Motion & Rigid Body Dynamics
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: Angular momentum is $\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$. Differentiating: $\frac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt} \times \vec{p} + \vec{r} \times \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \vec{v} \times (m\vec{v}) + \vec{r} \times \vec{F}_{net} = 0 + \vec{\tau}_{net}$. For rigid bodies rotating about fixed axis, $\vec{L} = I\vec{\omega}$, so $\vec{\tau} = I\frac{d\vec{\omega}}{dt} = I\vec{\alpha}$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: If net external torque about an origin is zero, angular momentum $\vec{L}$ about that origin is conserved.
