formulas.title: Torque and Angular Momentum Equation
formulas.derivation: Angular momentum is $\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$. Differentiating: $\frac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt} \times \vec{p} + \vec{r} \times \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \vec{v} \times (m\vec{v}) + \vec{r} \times \vec{F}_{net} = 0 + \vec{\tau}_{net}$. For rigid bodies rotating about fixed axis, $\vec{L} = I\vec{\omega}$, so $\vec{\tau} = I\frac{d\vec{\omega}}{dt} = I\vec{\alpha}$.
formulas.description: Rotational analog of Newton's second law relating net torque to moment of inertia and angular acceleration.
formulas.explanation: If net external torque about an origin is zero, angular momentum $\vec{L}$ about that origin is conserved.

formulas.title: Parallel Axis Theorem (Steiner's Theorem)

variables.I_{cm}: Moment of inertia about parallel axis through center of mass
variables.I_{parallel}: Moment of inertia about arbitrary parallel axis

formulas.derivation: Let origin be CM. Coordinate along new axis is $(x + d, y)$. Then $I = \int [(x+d)^2 + y^2] dm = \int (x^2 + y^2) dm + 2d \int x dm + d^2 \int dm$. Since origin is CM, first moment $\int x dm = 0$. Hence $I = I_{cm} + Md^2$.
formulas.description: Moment of inertia about any axis parallel to a centroidal axis at perpendicular distance d.
formulas.explanation: Applies to rigid bodies of arbitrary 3D geometry; must always start from the center-of-mass axis.

formulas.title: Perpendicular Axis Theorem

variables.I_z: Moment of inertia about axis perpendicular to lamina plane
variables.I_x, I_y: Moments of inertia about in-plane orthogonal axes

formulas.derivation: For a planar lamina in xy-plane ($z=0$), distance of mass element $dm$ to z-axis is $r_z^2 = x^2 + y^2$. Integrating: $I_z = \int (x^2 + y^2) dm = \int y^2 dm + \int x^2 dm = I_x + I_y$.
formulas.description: Relates moments of inertia of a planar laminar body about three mutually perpendicular intersecting axes.
formulas.explanation: Valid strictly for flat 2D planar laminas, never for 3D volumetric bodies like spheres or cylinders.

formulas.title: Kinetic Energy of Pure Rolling Body
formulas.derivation: In rolling without slipping, $v_{cm} = R\omega$. Substituting $I_{cm} = Mk^2$: $K = \frac{1}{2}M v_{cm}^2 + \frac{1}{2}(Mk^2)\left(\frac{v_{cm}}{R}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2}M v_{cm}^2\left(1 + \frac{k^2}{R^2}\right)$.
formulas.description: Total kinetic energy decomposed into translational motion of CM and rotation about CM.
formulas.explanation: Fraction of kinetic energy in rotation is $\frac{K_{rot}}{K_{total}} = \frac{k^2/R^2}{1 + k^2/R^2}$ (e.g., $2/7$ for solid sphere, $1/3$ for solid cylinder).

formulas.title: Acceleration of Body Rolling Down an Incline
formulas.derivation: Equations of motion: along incline $Mg\sin\theta - f = Ma$; torque about CM $f R = I_{cm}\alpha = I_{cm}\frac{a}{R} \implies f = \frac{I_{cm}a}{R^2}$. Substituting friction into force equation: $Mg\sin\theta - \frac{I_{cm}a}{R^2} = Ma \implies a\left(M + \frac{I_{cm}}{R^2}\right) = Mg\sin\theta \implies a = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1 + \frac{I_{cm}}{MR^2}}$.
formulas.description: Linear acceleration of a circular symmetric body rolling without slipping down an angle $\theta$.
formulas.explanation: A solid sphere ($k^2/R^2 = 2/5$) reaches the bottom fastest, followed by spherical shell ($2/3$), disc ($1/2$), and hoop/ring ($1$).

formulas.title: Minimum Friction Coefficient for Pure Rolling
formulas.derivation: Friction force is $f = \frac{I_{cm}a}{R^2} = \frac{Mg\sin\theta}{1 + MR^2/I_{cm}}$. Normal force is $N = Mg\cos\theta$. Pure rolling requires $f \le \mu_s N \implies \frac{Mg\sin\theta}{1 + MR^2/I_{cm}} \le \mu_s Mg\cos\theta \implies \mu_s \ge \frac{\tan\theta}{1 + MR^2/I_{cm}}$.
formulas.description: Threshold static friction coefficient required to prevent slipping on an incline.
formulas.explanation: If surface friction $\mu < \mu_{min}$, the body rolls with forward slipping ($v_{cm} \ne R\omega$).

formulas.title: Standard Moments of Inertia of Common Geometries
formulas.derivation: For disc: divide into concentric thin rings of radius $r$, width $dr$, mass $dm = \frac{M}{\pi R^2} 2\pi r dr = \frac{2M}{R^2} r dr$. Ring inertia is $dI = r^2 dm = \frac{2M}{R^2} r^3 dr$. Integrating: $I = \frac{2M}{R^2}\int_0^R r^3 dr = \frac{2M}{R^2}\frac{R^4}{4} = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$. Solid sphere: integrate spherical shells of $dm = 4\pi r^2 \rho dr$ with $I = \frac{2}{5}MR^2$.
formulas.description: Centroidal moments of inertia for standard rigid bodies rotating about symmetry axis.
formulas.explanation: Essential reference constants for rigid body rotational dynamics.

formulas.title: Moment of Inertia of Thin Uniform Rod
formulas.derivation: Linear mass density $\lambda = M/L$. For CM axis: $I_{cm} = \int_{-L/2}^{L/2} x^2 (\lambda dx) = \lambda \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-L/2}^{L/2} = \frac{M}{L}\left(\frac{L^3}{24} - \left(-\frac{L^3}{24}\right)\right) = \frac{1}{12}ML^2$. For end axis, parallel axis theorem gives $I_{end} = I_{cm} + M(L/2)^2 = \frac{1}{12}ML^2 + \frac{1}{4}ML^2 = \frac{1}{3}ML^2$.
formulas.description: Inertia about transverse axes passing through center of mass and one end.
formulas.explanation: Rotating about the end takes 4 times more torque for same angular acceleration as rotating about the center.

formulas.latex: v_c = \frac{m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2}{m_1 + m_2}, \quad L_O = \vec{r}_{cm} \times M\vec{v}_{cm} + \vec{L}_{cm}
formulas.title: Center of Mass Velocity and Koenig's Theorem for Angular Momentum
formulas.derivation: Let $\vec{r}_i = \vec{r}_{cm} + \vec{r}'_i$ and $\vec{v}_i = \vec{v}_{cm} + \vec{v}'_i$. Total angular momentum $\vec{L}_O = \sum m_i (\vec{r}_{cm} + \vec{r}'_i) \times (\vec{v}_{cm} + \vec{v}'_i) = \vec{r}_{cm} \times M\vec{v}_{cm} + \sum m_i \vec{r}'_i \times \vec{v}'_i + \vec{r}_{cm} \times \sum m_i \vec{v}'_i + (\sum m_i \vec{r}'_i) \times \vec{v}_{cm}$. By definition of CM, cross terms vanish, giving $\vec{L}_O = \vec{r}_{cm} \times M\vec{v}_{cm} + I_{cm}\vec{\omega}$.
formulas.description: Decomposition of total angular momentum about origin O into CM orbital part and intrinsic spin part.
formulas.explanation: Allows decoupling orbital angular momentum of planetary motion from planetary axial spin.

formulas.title: Condition for Toppling Before Sliding

variables.\\mu: Coefficient of friction between block and floor

formulas.derivation: Let horizontal force $F$ be applied at top height $h$. Sliding occurs when $F = \mu mg$. Toppling occurs about front edge when overturning torque exceeds stabilizing torque: $F h > mg (b/2) \implies F > mg \frac{b}{2h}$. Toppling occurs prior to sliding if $F_{topple} < F_{slide} \implies mg \frac{b}{2h} < \mu mg \implies \mu > \frac{b}{2h}$.
formulas.description: Threshold coefficient of friction determining whether a rectangular block of width b and height h topples or slips.
formulas.explanation: Tall, narrow blocks (large $h$, small $b$) topple easily on rough floors; squat blocks slide first.

formulas.title: Time Period of Physical (Compound) Pendulum
formulas.derivation: Restoring torque about pivot for deflection $\theta$ is $\tau = -mgd\sin\theta \approx -mgd\theta$. Equation of motion: $I\alpha = -mgd\theta \implies \frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} + \frac{mgd}{I}\theta = 0$. Angular frequency is $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{mgd}{I}}$. Period $T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{mgd}}$. Using parallel axis theorem $I = m(k^2 + d^2)$ gives $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{k^2 + d^2}{gd}}$.
formulas.description: Small-angle oscillation period of a rigid body pivoted at distance d from its center of mass.
formulas.explanation: Equivalent simple pendulum length is $L_{eq} = \frac{k^2 + d^2}{d}$. Minimum period occurs when $d = k$.

formulas.latex: x_{cm} = \frac{\int x \, dm}{\int dm}, \quad x_{cm, hem} = \frac{3}{8}R, \quad y_{cm, cone} = \frac{h}{4}
formulas.title: Center of Mass of Continuous Bodies
formulas.derivation: Solid hemisphere of radius $R$: slice into thin circular discs of thickness $dy$ at distance $y$ from base. Disc radius is $r = \sqrt{R^2 - y^2}$, mass $dm = \rho \pi (R^2 - y^2) dy$. Centroid is $y_{cm} = \frac{\int_0^R y \rho \pi (R^2 - y^2) dy}{\frac{2}{3}\pi R^3 \rho} = \frac{\pi [\frac{R^2 y^2}{2} - \frac{y^4}{4}]_0^R}{\frac{2}{3}\pi R^3} = \frac{R^4 / 4}{\frac{2}{3}R^3} = \frac{3}{8}R$.
formulas.description: Centroid coordinates for hemisphere, solid cone, and semicircular disc.
formulas.explanation: For hollow hemisphere, $y_{cm} = R/2$. For semicircular wire loop, $y_{cm} = 2R/\pi$.

formulas.title: Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
formulas.derivation: Kepler's third law $T^2 \propto r^3$ and circular orbit acceleration $a = \frac{v^2}{r} = \frac{4\pi^2 r}{T^2} \propto \frac{r}{r^3} = \frac{1}{r^2}$. By Newton's third law, mutual force must be symmetric in $m_1$ and $m_2$, yielding $F = G\frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$.
formulas.description: Inverse-square mutual attractive force between point masses.
formulas.explanation: Conservative central force field; operates between all matter in the universe.

formulas.title: Acceleration Due to Gravity at Altitude h
formulas.derivation: At surface $g_0 = \frac{GM}{R^2}$. At height $h$, $g(h) = \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2} = \frac{GM}{R^2(1 + h/R)^2} = g_0 (1 + h/R)^{-2}$. Expanding binomially for $h \ll R$: $(1 + h/R)^{-2} \approx 1 - \frac{2h}{R}$.
formulas.description: Variation of surface gravity with elevation above Earth's surface.
formulas.explanation: Gravity decreases twice as fast with altitude as it does with depth near Earth's surface.

formulas.title: Acceleration Due to Gravity at Depth d Inside Earth
formulas.derivation: At radius $r = R - d$, by Gauss's shell theorem, only the mass inside sphere of radius $r$ exerts net force: $M_{in} = M \frac{r^3}{R^3}$. Then $g(d) = \frac{G M_{in}}{r^2} = \frac{G (M r^3 / R^3)}{r^2} = \frac{GM}{R^3} r = g_0 \frac{R-d}{R} = g_0\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)$.
formulas.description: Linear decrease of gravitational acceleration within a uniform density spherical Earth.
formulas.explanation: At Earth's center ($d = R$), $g = 0$. Inside Earth, gravity acts as a linear restoring force leading to SHM.

formulas.title: Effect of Earth's Rotation on Gravity at Latitude $\phi$
formulas.derivation: Centrifugal acceleration on a body at latitude $\phi$ is $a_c = r\omega^2 = (R\cos\phi)\omega^2$ directed outwards perpendicular to rotation axis. The component opposing true gravity is $a_c \cos\phi = R\omega^2 \cos^2\phi$. Effective gravity is $g' = g_0 - R\omega^2\cos^2\phi$.
formulas.description: Apparent centrifugal reduction of gravity due to Earth's diurnal axial rotation.
formulas.explanation: Centrifugal reduction is maximum at the equator ($\phi = 0, \Delta g = R\omega^2 \approx 0.034\text{ m/s}^2$) and zero at the poles ($\phi = 90^\circ$).

formulas.title: Gravitational Potential and Potential Energy
formulas.derivation: $V(r) = -\int_\infty^r \vec{g}\cdot d\vec{r} = -\int_\infty^r \left(-\frac{GM}{r'^2}\right) dr' = -\left[\frac{GM}{r'}\right]_\infty^r = -\frac{GM}{r}$. Potential energy is $U(r) = m V(r) = -\frac{GMm}{r}$.
formulas.description: Gravitational potential and mutual binding potential energy of two masses separated by r with zero reference at infinity.
formulas.explanation: Negative sign signifies bound state; energy must be supplied from external agent to separate bodies to infinity.

formulas.title: Escape Velocity from Planetary Surface
formulas.derivation: Total mechanical energy at surface must be at least zero to reach infinity with zero kinetic energy: $E = K + U = \frac{1}{2}m v_e^2 - \frac{GMm}{R} = 0 \implies \frac{1}{2}m v_e^2 = \frac{GMm}{R} \implies v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}} = \sqrt{2gR}$.
formulas.description: Minimum ballistic launch speed required for an unpowered projectile to overcome planetary gravity.
formulas.explanation: Independent of launch mass $m$ and launch direction (neglecting atmospheric drag and planetary rotation).

formulas.title: Orbital Velocity of a Circular Satellite
formulas.derivation: Gravitational pull supplies exact centripetal force: $\frac{GMm}{r^2} = \frac{m v_o^2}{r} \implies v_o^2 = \frac{GM}{r} \implies v_o = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$.
formulas.description: Steady velocity required for stable circular orbit at radius $r = R + h$.
formulas.explanation: For near-Earth orbit ($h \ll R$), $v_o = \sqrt{gR} \approx 7.92\text{ km/s}$. Escape velocity is related by $v_e = \sqrt{2} v_o$.

formulas.title: Kepler's Third Law (Harmonic Law)
formulas.derivation: Period is circumference divided by speed: $T = \frac{2\pi r}{v_o} = \frac{2\pi r}{\sqrt{GM/r}} = \frac{2\pi r^{3/2}}{\sqrt{GM}}$. Squaring both sides: $T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM} r^3$.
formulas.description: Square of satellite orbital period is proportional to the cube of orbital semi-major axis.
formulas.explanation: For geostationary orbit, period $T = 24\text{ hours}$, yielding altitude $h \approx 35,786\text{ km}$ above the equator.

formulas.title: Total Mechanical Energy of Orbiting Satellite (Virial Theorem)
formulas.derivation: $K = \frac{1}{2}m v_o^2 = \frac{1}{2}m \left(\frac{GM}{r}\right) = \frac{GMm}{2r}$. $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$. Total energy is $E = K + U = \frac{GMm}{2r} - \frac{GMm}{r} = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$.
formulas.description: Binding energy relation demonstrating total orbital energy is negative and equals half the potential energy.
formulas.explanation: To transfer a satellite to a higher orbit, total energy must be increased (made less negative), although its orbital speed will decrease.

formulas.title: Kepler's Second Law (Areal Velocity Conservation)
formulas.derivation: Infinitesimal area swept in time $dt$ is triangle area $dA = \frac{1}{2} |\vec{r} \times d\vec{r}| = \frac{1}{2}|\vec{r} \times \vec{v} dt|$. Dividing by $dt$: $\frac{dA}{dt} = \frac{1}{2}|\vec{r} \times \vec{v}| = \frac{|\vec{r} \times m\vec{v}|}{2m} = \frac{L}{2m}$. Since gravitational force is strictly central ($\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F} = 0$), angular momentum $L$ is conserved, making areal velocity constant.
formulas.description: A line segment joining a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas during equal intervals of time.
formulas.explanation: Direct consequence of angular momentum conservation; implies planet moves fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion ($r_p v_p = r_a v_a$).

formulas.title: Hohmann Transfer Orbit Velocity Impulse

variables.r_1, r_2: Initial and target circular orbit radii

formulas.derivation: Semi-major axis of transfer ellipse is $a = \frac{r_1 + r_2}{2}$. Energy equation $v^2 = GM\left(\frac{2}{r} - \frac{1}{a}\right)$ gives periapsis speed $v_t = \sqrt{GM\left(\frac{2}{r_1} - \frac{2}{r_1 + r_2}\right)} = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r_1}}\sqrt{\frac{2r_2}{r_1 + r_2}}$. Subtracting initial circular speed $v_1 = \sqrt{GM/r_1}$ yields $\Delta v$.

formulas.explanation: Most fuel-efficient two-impulse orbital transfer trajectory between co-planar circular orbits.

Since surface potential is $V(R) = -\frac{GM}{R} = -\frac{2GMR^2}{2R^3}$, we get $V_{in}(r) = -\frac{GM}{2R^3}(3R^2 - r^2)$.

Under IUPAC sign convention, work done on the system by surroundings during compression is positive ($w > 0$), while work done by expanding system against external pressure $P_{ext}$ is negative: $w = -\int P_{ext}dV = -P_{ext}\Delta V$.

formulas.latex: \Delta U = q + w = q - P_{ext}\Delta V
formulas.title: First Law of Chemical Thermodynamics (IUPAC Convention)
formulas.derivation: From universal energy conservation: change in internal state function $U$ equals energy entering system as heat ($q$) plus energy entering as mechanical boundary work ($w$). Under IUPAC sign convention, work done on the system by surroundings during compression is positive ($w > 0$), while work done by expanding system against external pressure $P_{ext}$ is negative: $w = -\int P_{ext}dV = -P_{ext}\Delta V$.
formulas.description: Conservation of energy for chemical system: heat absorbed plus mechanical work performed on the system.
formulas.explanation: At constant volume (bomb calorimeter), $\Delta V = 0 \implies w = 0$, so $\Delta U = q_v$.

formulas.title: Enthalpy and Internal Energy Relation for Chemical Reactions

variables.\\Delta n_g: Moles of gaseous products minus moles of gaseous reactants

formulas.derivation: By definition, enthalpy is $H = U + PV$. For finite change at constant pressure: $\Delta H = \Delta U + P\Delta V$. For ideal gas reaction where volume change is dominated by gases: $P V = n_g R T \implies P\Delta V = (\Delta n_g) R T$. Substituting yields $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g R T$.
formulas.description: Relates constant-pressure reaction heat $\Delta H$ to constant-volume reaction heat $\Delta U$ for ideal gas mixtures.
formulas.explanation: If $\Delta n_g = 0$ (e.g. $H_{2(g)} + I_{2(g)} \to 2HI_{(g)}$), $\Delta H = \Delta U$. If $\Delta n_g > 0$, expansion work means $\Delta H > \Delta U$.

formulas.title: Hess's Law and Standard Enthalpy of Reaction
formulas.derivation: Germain Hess (1840) established that because enthalpy $H$ is a thermodynamic state function, net heat evolved or absorbed in a chemical process depends solely on initial and final states, independent of pathway. By convention, standard enthalpies of formation of pure elements in reference standard states ($O_{2(g)}, C_{(graphite)}, H_{2(g)}$) are assigned zero: $\Delta_f H^\circ = 0$. Summing product enthalpies and subtracting reactant enthalpies gives the formula.
formulas.description: Reaction enthalpy calculated by summing standard enthalpies of formation of products minus reactants.
formulas.explanation: Allows indirect calculation of reaction heats that cannot be measured directly in a calorimeter.

formulas.title: Reaction Enthalpy from Bond Enthalpies
formulas.derivation: In a gas-phase reaction, chemical bonds in reactant molecules are first homolytically cleaved into isolated gaseous atoms (an endothermic process requiring energy input: $+ \sum BE_{reactants}$). The isolated atoms then recombine to synthesize product molecules (an exothermic process releasing energy: $- \sum BE_{products}$). By Hess's Law, the net reaction enthalpy is $\Delta_r H = \sum BE_{reactants} - \sum BE_{products}$.
formulas.description: Estimates gas-phase reaction enthalpy from homolytic covalent bond dissociation energies.
formulas.explanation: Applies strictly to gas-phase reactions with non-delocalized, localized covalent bonds.

formulas.latex: \frac{\Delta H_{T_2} - \Delta H_{T_1}}{T_2 - T_1} = \Delta C_p = \sum \nu_p C_{p, prod} - \sum \nu_r C_{p, react}
formulas.title: Kirchhoff's Law of Thermochemistry

variables.\\Delta C_p: Net change in molar heat capacity at constant pressure

formulas.derivation: At constant pressure, $\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial T}\right)_P = C_p$. Differentiating reaction enthalpy $\Delta_r H = H_{prod} - H_{react}$ with respect to temperature: $\frac{d(\Delta_r H)}{dT} = \left(\frac{\partial H_{prod}}{\partial T}\right) - \left(\frac{\partial H_{react}}{\partial T}\right) = C_{p, prod} - C_{p, react} = \Delta C_p$. Integrating from $T_1$ to $T_2$ assuming $\Delta C_p$ is approximately constant yields Kirchhoff's relation: $\Delta H_{T_2} = \Delta H_{T_1} + \Delta C_p (T_2 - T_1)$.
formulas.description: Temperature dependence of reaction enthalpy governed by reaction heat capacity change $\Delta C_p$.
formulas.explanation: If $\Delta C_p > 0$, reaction becomes more endothermic (or less exothermic) as temperature rises.

formulas.title: Second Law of Thermodynamics and Entropy Change
formulas.derivation: Rudolf Clausius (1865) proved that for any reversible cyclic process, $\oint \frac{dq_{rev}}{T} = 0$, establishing that $dS = \frac{dq_{rev}}{T}$ is an exact differential of a state function. For any spontaneous irreversible process, Clausius inequality gives $\oint \frac{dq}{T} < 0$, leading to $\Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr} = \Delta S_{univ} > 0$. At reversible equilibrium, $\Delta S_{univ} = 0$.
formulas.description: Definition of entropy as state function and universal condition for spontaneous irreversible processes.
formulas.explanation: All spontaneous real processes in the universe proceed with an overall increase in total entropy ($\Delta S_{univ} > 0$).

formulas.latex: \Delta S_{ideal\_gas} = n C_v \ln\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) + n R \ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right) = n C_p \ln\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) - n R \ln\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)
formulas.title: Entropy Change of an Ideal Gas
formulas.derivation: From First Law for reversible path: $dq_{rev} = dU - dw_{rev} = n C_v dT + P\,dV$. Dividing by $T$ using ideal gas law $P/T = nR/V$: $dS = \frac{dq_{rev}}{T} = n C_v \frac{dT}{T} + n R \frac{dV}{V}$. Integrating from initial state $(T_1, V_1)$ to final state $(T_2, V_2)$: $\Delta S = n C_v \ln(T_2 / T_1) + n R \ln(V_2 / V_1)$. Using $V_2 / V_1 = (T_2 P_1) / (T_1 P_2)$ and Mayer's relation $C_p = C_v + R$ gives the pressure form.
formulas.description: Entropy calculation for an ideal gas undergoing simultaneous temperature, volume, or pressure transitions.
formulas.explanation: For isothermal process ($T_1 = T_2$), $\Delta S = n R \ln(V_2/V_1) = -n R \ln(P_2/P_1)$.

formulas.latex: \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S, \quad \Delta G_{sys} = -T\Delta S_{univ} < 0 \text{ (Spontaneous)}
formulas.title: Gibbs Free Energy and Spontaneity Criterion
formulas.derivation: At constant $T$ and $P$, heat transferred to surroundings is $q_{surr} = -q_{sys} = -\Delta H_{sys}$. Surrounding entropy change is $\Delta S_{surr} = \frac{q_{surr}}{T} = -\frac{\Delta H_{sys}}{T}$. Universal entropy change is $\Delta S_{univ} = \Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr} = \Delta S_{sys} - \frac{\Delta H_{sys}}{T}$. Multiplying by $-T$: $-T\Delta S_{univ} = \Delta H_{sys} - T\Delta S_{sys}$. Defining Gibbs free energy $G = H - TS$ gives $\Delta G_{sys} = -T\Delta S_{univ}$. Since $\Delta S_{univ} > 0$ for spontaneity, $\Delta G_{sys} < 0$.
formulas.description: Thermodynamic potential determining spontaneity of chemical processes at constant temperature and pressure.
formulas.explanation: Criterion for spontaneity at constant $T, P$: $\Delta G < 0$ (spontaneous, exergonic); $\Delta G = 0$ (dynamic equilibrium); $\Delta G > 0$ (non-spontaneous, endergonic).

formulas.latex: \Delta G^\circ = -R T \ln K = -2.303 R T \log_{10} K
formulas.title: Standard Gibbs Free Energy and Equilibrium Constant Relation
formulas.derivation:
Chemical potential of species $i$ in mixture is $\mu_i = \mu_i^\circ + RT\ln a_i$. Reaction Gibbs free energy is $\Delta_r G = \sum 
u_i \mu_i = \sum 
u_i \mu_i^\circ + RT \sum 
u_i \ln a_i = \Delta_r G^\circ + RT\ln Q$ where $Q = \prod a_i^{
u_i}$ is the reaction quotient. At dynamic chemical equilibrium, net driving force vanishes: $\Delta_r G = 0$ and $Q = K_{eq}$. Substituting gives $0 = \Delta_r G^\circ + RT\ln K \implies \Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$.
formulas.description: Fundamental thermodynamic bridge connecting chemical equilibrium constant K to standard state free energy $\Delta G^\circ$.
formulas.explanation: If $\Delta G^\circ < 0$, then $K > 1$ (products favored at equilibrium); if $\Delta G^\circ > 0$, $K < 1$ (reactants favored).

formulas.title: van 't Hoff Equation
formulas.derivation: From $\ln K = -\frac{\Delta G^\circ}{RT} = -\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{RT} + \frac{\Delta S^\circ}{R}$. Differentiating with respect to temperature $T$ assuming $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ are independent of $T$: $\frac{d\ln K}{dT} = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{RT^2}$. Integrating from $T_1$ to $T_2$: $\int_{K_1}^{K_2} d\ln K = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\int_{T_1}^{T_2} T^{-2}dT \implies \ln(K_2/K_1) = -\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right) = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right)$.
formulas.description: Temperature sensitivity of chemical equilibrium constant governed by standard reaction enthalpy.
formulas.explanation: Thermodynamic proof of Le Chatelier's principle: for endothermic reactions ($\Delta H^\circ > 0$), increasing temperature increases $K$; for exothermic reactions ($\Delta H^\circ < 0$), increasing temperature decreases $K$.

formulas.latex: \Delta S_{fus} = \frac{\Delta H_{fus}}{T_m}, \quad \Delta S_{vap} = \frac{\Delta H_{vap}}{T_b} \approx 88 \text{ J/mol K (Trouton's Rule)}
formulas.title: Entropy of Phase Transitions and Trouton's Rule
formulas.derivation: At normal melting and boiling points, the two phases coexist in reversible dynamic equilibrium: $\Delta G = 0 \implies \Delta H - T\Delta S = 0 \implies \Delta S = \Delta H / T$. Trouton (1884) noted empirically that for non-associated liquids vaporizing to gas, the volume increase is roughly constant ($\sim 1000\times$), giving universal entropy of vaporization $\Delta S_{vap} = \frac{\Delta H_{vap}}{T_b} \approx 85 - 88\text{ J/mol K}$.
formulas.description: Entropy of fusion and vaporization at equilibrium phase transition temperatures.
formulas.explanation: Hydrogen-bonded liquids (water: $\Delta S_{vap} \approx 109\text{ J/mol K}$, ethanol) deviate positively from Trouton's rule due to high liquid-state order.

formulas.latex: S = k_B \ln \Omega, \quad S(T=0) = 0 \quad (\text{Third Law of Thermodynamics})
formulas.title: Boltzmann Entropy Formula and Third Law

variables.\\Omega: Number of accessible microstates corresponding to macroscopic state

formulas.derivation: Ludwig Boltzmann (1877) proved entropy is a logarithmic measure of microscopic multiplicity: $S = k_B \ln\Omega$. Nernst and Planck formulated the Third Law: as temperature approaches absolute zero ($T \to 0\text{ K}$), thermal motion ceases, and a perfectly ordered pure crystalline lattice settles into a unique non-degenerate quantum ground state ($\Omega = 1$). Therefore, $S_0 = k_B\ln(1) = 0$.
formulas.description: Microscopic statistical definition of entropy and absolute zero entropy of perfect crystalline substances.
formulas.explanation: Allows establishing absolute standard entropies $S^\circ$ for chemical substances, unlike internal energy or enthalpy which are only known relative to arbitrary references.

formulas.title: Maximum Non-Expansion Work and Cell EMF
formulas.derivation: From fundamental thermodynamic equation $dG = V dP - S dT + dw_{non-PV}$. At constant $T$ and $P$, $dG = dw_{non-PV}$. For reversible electrochemical cell, charge transferred is $Q = n F$, and electrical work done by cell is $w_{elec} = Q E_{cell} = n F E_{cell}$. Work done on system is $w = -n F E_{cell}$. Hence $\Delta G = -n F E_{cell}$.
formulas.description: Decrease in Gibbs free energy equals the maximum electrical reversible work extracted from an electrochemical cell.
formulas.explanation: For spontaneous galvanic cell, $E_{cell} > 0 \implies \Delta G < 0$.

formulas.latex: C_p - C_v = T \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = \frac{T V \beta^2}{\kappa_T}
formulas.title: General Thermodynamic Heat Capacity Difference
formulas.derivation: Internal energy differential is $dU = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_V dT + \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T dV$. Dividing by $dT$ at constant $P$ and noting $dH = dU + P\,dV + V\,dP$: $C_p - C_v = \left[P + \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T\right]\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P$. Using Maxwell relation $\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T = T\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V - P$, the $P$ terms cancel, yielding $C_p - C_v = T\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = \frac{TV\beta^2}{\kappa_T}$. For ideal gas ($PV = nRT$), $\beta = 1/T$ and $\kappa_T = 1/P$, recovering Mayer's relation $C_p - C_v = R$.
formulas.description: Universal relationship between isobaric and isochoric heat capacities for any substance (solid, liquid, or gas).
formulas.explanation: Because $T > 0, V > 0, \kappa_T > 0$, and $\beta^2 \ge 0$, $C_p$ is strictly greater than or equal to $C_v$ for all physical materials.

content_json.derivation: From universal energy conservation: change in internal state function $U$ equals energy entering system as heat ($q$) plus energy entering as mechanical boundary work ($w$). Under IUPAC sign convention, work done on the system by surroundings during compression is positive ($w > 0$), while work done by expanding system against external pressure $P_{ext}$ is negative: $w = -\int P_{ext}dV = -P_{ext}\Delta V$.
content_json.explanation: At constant volume (bomb calorimeter), $\Delta V = 0 \implies w = 0$, so $\Delta U = q_v$.

variables.\\hat{r}: Unit vector along line joining charges

formulas.derivation: Empirical inverse-square relation established by Charles-Augustin de Coulomb via torsion balance measurements, following gauge invariance and conservation laws for static central electromagnetic field.
formulas.description: Electrostatic mutual interaction force between two stationary point charges in vacuum.
formulas.explanation: Like charges repel; opposite charges attract. In a dielectric medium of relative permittivity $\epsilon_r$, force reduces by factor $K = \epsilon_r$ ($F_{med} = F_{vac} / K$).

formulas.title: Gauss's Law of Electrostatics

variables.d\\vec{A}: Outward normal differential surface area element

formulas.derivation: For a point charge $q$ at origin, electric field through sphere of radius $r$ is $\vec{E} = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2}\hat{r}$. Total flux is $\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2} \oint dA = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2}(4\pi r^2) = \frac{q}{\epsilon_0}$. By superposition, this holds for any arbitrary distribution of charges and any closed surface containing them.
formulas.description: Total electric flux through any closed Gaussian surface equals net enclosed charge divided by permittivity.
formulas.explanation: Powerful technique for calculating electric fields with spherical, cylindrical, or planar symmetries.

formulas.title: Electric Fields from Symmetric Charge Distributions
formulas.derivation: Infinite wire: Gaussian cylinder of radius $r$ and length $L$: flux through ends is zero; flux through curved wall is $E(2\pi r L) = \frac{\lambda L}{\epsilon_0} \implies E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 r}$. Infinite sheet: Gaussian pillbox of cross-sectional area $A$ piercing sheet: flux through both flat faces is $2EA = \frac{\sigma A}{\epsilon_0} \implies E = \frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$. Conductor: inside conductor $E_{in} = 0$; pillbox face inside has zero flux, giving $EA = \frac{\sigma A}{\epsilon_0} \implies E = \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}$.
formulas.description: Electric fields generated by an infinite linear charge, non-conducting infinite sheet, and conducting surface.
formulas.explanation: Field of an infinite sheet is uniform and independent of distance $r$ from the sheet.

formulas.latex: V(r) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{r}, \quad \vec{E} = -\vec{\nabla}V = -\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial x}\hat{i} + \frac{\partial V}{\partial y}\hat{j} + \frac{\partial V}{\partial z}\hat{k}\right)
formulas.title: Electric Potential and Potential Gradient
formulas.derivation: Potential is work done per unit positive charge bringing test charge from infinity to $r$: $V(r) = -\int_\infty^r \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r}' = -\int_\infty^r \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r'^2}dr' = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r}$. Since $dV = -\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r} = -(E_x dx + E_y dy + E_z dz)$, equating differentials gives $E_x = -\frac{\partial V}{\partial x}$, etc., or $\vec{E} = -\vec{\nabla}V$.
formulas.description: Electrostatic scalar potential and its negative gradient producing electric field vector.
formulas.explanation: Electric field lines always point down the steepest descent of electric potential. Equipotential surfaces are everywhere perpendicular to field lines.

formulas.title: Electric Dipole Potential and Field
formulas.derivation: Potential at $(r, \theta)$ is $V = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left(\frac{1}{r_+} - \frac{1}{r_-}\right)$. Binomial approximation for $r \gg a$ yields $V = \frac{p\cos\theta}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2}$. Axial field ($\theta = 0$): $E = -\frac{dV}{dr} = \frac{2p}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^3}$. Equatorial field ($\theta = 90^\circ$): component parallel to dipole gives $E = \frac{p}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^3}$ directed antiparallel to $\vec{p}$.
formulas.description: Potential and electric fields at axial and equatorial positions for an electric dipole $\vec{p} = q(2\vec{a})$.
formulas.explanation: Axial field is twice the equatorial field at the same distance; dipole field decays as $1/r^3$ (faster than monopole $1/r^2$).

formulas.title: Torque and Potential Energy of Dipole in External Field
formulas.derivation: Forces on $+q$ and $-q$ form a couple: $\vec{F}_+ = q\vec{E}$, $\vec{F}_- = -q\vec{E}$. Torque is $\vec{\tau} = (2\vec{a}) \times (q\vec{E}) = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}$. Work done in rotating dipole from $\theta_1$ to $\theta_2$ is $W = \int \tau d\theta = \int pE\sin\theta d\theta = -pE[\cos\theta]_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2}$. Taking reference zero at $\theta = 90^\circ$ gives $U = -pE\cos\theta = -\vec{p}\cdot\vec{E}$.
formulas.description: Mechanical torque aligning dipole with electric field and electrostatic orientation energy.
formulas.explanation: Stable equilibrium occurs at $\theta = 0^\circ$ ($U = -pE$, torque is zero); unstable equilibrium at $\theta = 180^\circ$ ($U = +pE$).

formulas.title: Capacitance of Parallel Plate Capacitor
formulas.derivation: Plates carry charges $+Q$ and $-Q$. Electric field between plates is uniform: $E = \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0} = \frac{Q}{\epsilon_0 A}$. Potential difference is $V = E d = \frac{Q d}{\epsilon_0 A}$. Capacitance is defined as $C = \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{Q}{Q d / (\epsilon_0 A)} = \frac{\epsilon_0 A}{d}$. With dielectric slab filling space, electric field weakens to $E/K$, boosting capacitance by factor $K$: $C' = K C$.
formulas.description: Capacitance of two parallel conducting plates of area A separated by distance d in vacuum and with dielectric K.
formulas.explanation: Capacitance depends solely on geometric dimensions and dielectric medium, completely independent of applied voltage or charge.

formulas.title: Electrostatic Energy Stored in Capacitor and Energy Density
formulas.derivation: Work to transfer charge $dq$ at instantaneous voltage $v = q/C$ is $dW = v\,dq = \frac{q}{C}dq$. Total work to charge from $0$ to $Q$ is $U = \int_0^Q \frac{q}{C}dq = \frac{Q^2}{2C} = \frac{1}{2}CV^2$. Dividing by volume $V_{vol} = A d$: $u_E = \frac{\frac{1}{2}C V^2}{A d} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}(\epsilon_0 A / d)(E d)^2}{A d} = \frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0 E^2$.
formulas.description: Total energy stored in capacitor electric field and energy density per unit volume.
formulas.explanation: Energy resides physically distributed throughout the volume of the electrostatic field.

formulas.title: Capacitor Networks (Series and Parallel)
formulas.derivation: Series: equal charge $Q$ on each capacitor. Total voltage is $V = V_1 + V_2 = \frac{Q}{C_1} + \frac{Q}{C_2} = Q\left(\frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2}\right) = \frac{Q}{C_{eq}} \implies \frac{1}{C_{eq}} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2}$. Parallel: common voltage $V$ across each capacitor. Total charge is $Q = Q_1 + Q_2 = C_1 V + C_2 V = (C_1 + C_2)V = C_{eq}V \implies C_{eq} = C_1 + C_2$.
formulas.description: Equivalent capacitance for capacitors connected in series (equal charge) and parallel (equal voltage).
formulas.explanation: Series combination is always smaller than the smallest capacitor; parallel combination is always larger than the largest capacitor.

formulas.latex: V_{common} = \frac{C_1 V_1 + C_2 V_2}{C_1 + C_2}, \quad \Delta U_{loss} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{C_1 C_2}{C_1 + C_2}(V_1 - V_2)^2
formulas.title: Charge Sharing and Energy Loss Between Capacitors
formulas.derivation: By conservation of total charge: $Q_{total} = C_1 V_1 + C_2 V_2 = (C_1 + C_2)V_{common} \implies V_{common} = \frac{C_1 V_1 + C_2 V_2}{C_1 + C_2}$. Initial stored energy is $U_i = \frac{1}{2}C_1 V_1^2 + \frac{1}{2}C_2 V_2^2$. Final stored energy is $U_f = \frac{1}{2}(C_1 + C_2)V_{common}^2$. Subtracting yields $\Delta U = U_i - U_f = \frac{1}{2}\frac{C_1 C_2}{C_1 + C_2}(V_1 - V_2)^2$.
formulas.description: Common steady potential and unavoidable Joule heating energy loss when connecting two charged capacitors.
formulas.explanation: Energy loss is independent of connecting wire resistance, dissipating through Joule heating and transient electromagnetic radiation.

formulas.title: Electrostatic Attractive Force Between Capacitor Plates
formulas.derivation: Field created by one plate alone is $E_1 = \frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0} = \frac{Q}{2\epsilon_0 A}$. The other plate carrying charge $Q$ experiences force from this field: $F = Q E_1 = Q \left(\frac{Q}{2\epsilon_0 A}\right) = \frac{Q^2}{2\epsilon_0 A} = \frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0 E^2 A$. Alternatively, virtual work $F = -\frac{dU}{dx} = -\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{Q^2 x}{2\epsilon_0 A}\right) = -\frac{Q^2}{2\epsilon_0 A}$.
formulas.description: Mechanical attractive tension force exerted between oppositely charged parallel plates.
formulas.explanation: The factor of $1/2$ arises because a plate does not exert force on itself; it experiences only the field of the opposite plate.

formulas.latex: q(t) = Q_0 (1 - e^{-t / RC}) \quad (\text{Charging}), \quad q(t) = Q_0 e^{-t / RC} \quad (\text{Discharging})
formulas.title: Transient Response of RC Circuit
formulas.derivation: Kirchhoff loop during charging: $\mathcal{E} - iR - \frac{q}{C} = 0$. Using $i = \frac{dq}{dt}$: $R\frac{dq}{dt} = \mathcal{E} - \frac{q}{C} = \frac{C\mathcal{E} - q}{C}$. Separating variables: $\frac{dq}{C\mathcal{E} - q} = \frac{dt}{RC}$. Integrating with initial condition $q(0) = 0$: $-\ln(1 - q/C\mathcal{E}) = t/RC \implies q(t) = C\mathcal{E}(1 - e^{-t/RC})$.
formulas.description: Time-dependent charge accumulation and discharge on a capacitor through series resistor R.
formulas.explanation: At time $t = \tau = RC$, charge reaches $63.2\%$ of maximum capacity; at $t = 5\tau$, circuit is $99.3\%$ charged.

formulas.title: Capacitance of Spherical Capacitors
formulas.derivation: Concentric shells with charges $+Q$ and $-Q$: field between shells is $E(r) = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2}$. Potential difference is $V = \int_a^b E(r)dr = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left(\frac{1}{a} - \frac{1}{b}\right) = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left(\frac{b-a}{ab}\right)$. Capacitance $C = \frac{Q}{V} = 4\pi\epsilon_0 \frac{ab}{b-a}$. For isolated single sphere, set outer radius $b \to \infty$: $C = 4\pi\epsilon_0 a$.
formulas.description: Capacitance of concentric spherical shells of radii a and b, and isolated conducting sphere of radius R.
formulas.explanation: For Earth ($R \approx 6.4 \times 10^6\text{ m}$), isolated capacitance is $C = 4\pi\epsilon_0 R \approx 711\text{ }\mu\text{F}$.

formulas.latex: U_{self} = \frac{3}{5}\frac{G M^2}{R} \quad (\text{Gravitational}), \quad U_{self} = \frac{3}{5}\frac{Q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R} \quad (\text{Electrostatic Solid Sphere})
formulas.title: Self-Energy of Uniformly Charged / Mass Solid Sphere
formulas.derivation: Assemble sphere layer by layer: bringing shell of thickness $dr$ with charge $dq = \rho 4\pi r^2 dr$ from infinity to sphere of radius $r$ and charge $q(r) = Q\frac{r^3}{R^3}$: work is $dW = \frac{q(r)dq}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r} = \frac{(Q r^3 / R^3)(3Q r^2 dr / R^3)}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r} = \frac{3Q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R^6} r^4 dr$. Integrating from $r=0$ to $R$: $U = \frac{3Q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R^6} \left[\frac{r^5}{5}\right]_0^R = \frac{3}{5}\frac{Q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R}$.
formulas.description: Total electrostatic assembly work of a uniformly charged ball of radius R and charge Q.
formulas.explanation: For hollow spherical shell of radius $R$, self-energy is $U_{shell} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{Q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R}$.

formulas.title: Drift Velocity and Current Density Relation
formulas.derivation: Between collisions, electrons accelerate under electric field: $a = \frac{eE}{m}$. Average drift speed acquired between collisions is $v_d = a\tau = \frac{eE}{m}\tau$. Volume of charge passing cross-section $A$ in time $\Delta t$ is $\Delta V = A v_d \Delta t$. Total charge is $\Delta Q = n(A v_d \Delta t)e$. Dividing by $\Delta t$: $I = \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} = n e A v_d$.
formulas.description: Relates macroscopic current to microscopic electron drift velocity and mean relaxation time.
formulas.explanation: Current density is $J = I/A = n e v_d = \left(\frac{n e^2 \tau}{m}\right)E = \sigma E$ (microscopic Ohm's law).

formulas.title: Resistance, Resistivity and Temperature Coefficient
formulas.derivation: From microscopic Ohm's law $J = \sigma E$, we have $E = \rho J = \rho \frac{I}{A}$. Voltage across length $L$ is $V = E L = \left(\rho \frac{L}{A}\right)I = R I \implies R = \rho \frac{L}{A}$. For metals, increased lattice thermal vibrations decrease relaxation time $\tau$, causing resistivity to rise linearly near room temperature: $\rho(T) = \rho_0(1 + \alpha \Delta T)$.
formulas.description: Macroscopic resistance based on material resistivity, geometry, and linear temperature dependence.
formulas.explanation: For metals $\alpha > 0$ (resistance increases with heating); for semiconductors and electrolytes $\alpha < 0$ (resistance decreases due to thermal carrier generation).

formulas.title: Kirchhoff's Current and Voltage Laws
formulas.derivation: KCL follows from charge conservation: $\frac{dQ}{dt} = 0$ in steady state at any junction node. KVL follows from energy conservation: line integral of conservative electrostatic field around any closed loop is zero: $\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{l} = 0$, meaning the net sum of potential rises and drops around any closed loop is identically zero.
formulas.description: Conservation of charge at circuit junctions and conservation of energy around closed loops.
formulas.explanation: Cornerstone laws for analyzing complex multi-loop DC and AC electrical circuits.

formulas.title: Balanced Wheatstone Bridge Condition
formulas.derivation: For $I_G = 0$, potential at junction $B$ equals potential at junction $D$ ($V_B = V_D$). Hence voltage drop across $P$ equals drop across $R$: $I_1 P = I_2 R$. Similarly, voltage drop across $Q$ equals drop across $S$: $I_1 Q = I_2 S$. Dividing equations gives $\frac{I_1 P}{I_1 Q} = \frac{I_2 R}{I_2 S} \implies \frac{P}{Q} = \frac{R}{S}$.
formulas.description: Condition for zero galvanometer current in a four-resistor bridge network.
formulas.explanation: Enables null-deflection precision resistance measurement independent of supply EMF and internal resistance.

formulas.title: Maximum Power Transfer Theorem
formulas.derivation: Circuit current is $I = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R_L + r}$. Power dissipated in load is $P(R_L) = I^2 R_L = \frac{\mathcal{E}^2 R_L}{(R_L + r)^2}$. Differentiating with respect to $R_L$ and setting to zero: $\frac{dP}{dR_L} = \mathcal{E}^2 \frac{(R_L + r)^2 - 2R_L(R_L + r)}{(R_L + r)^4} = \mathcal{E}^2 \frac{r - R_L}{(R_L + r)^3} = 0 \implies R_L = r$. Substituting $R_L = r$ yields $P_{max} = \frac{\mathcal{E}^2}{4r}$.
formulas.description: Maximum power is delivered to a load resistance when load equals internal resistance of power source.
formulas.explanation: At maximum power transfer, circuit efficiency is exactly 50%; the remaining 50% is dissipated internally as heat within the source.

formulas.title: Millman's Theorem / Cells in Parallel

variables.\\mathcal{E}_i, r_i: EMF and internal resistance of i-th branch

formulas.derivation: Let terminal voltage be $V$. Current from branch $i$ is $I_i = \frac{\mathcal{E}_i - V}{r_i}$. By KCL, total output current is $I = \sum I_i = \sum \frac{\mathcal{E}_i}{r_i} - V \sum \frac{1}{r_i}$. Rearranging gives $V = \frac{\sum \mathcal{E}_i / r_i}{\sum 1 / r_i} - I \left(\frac{1}{\sum 1 / r_i}\right) = \mathcal{E}_{eq} - I r_{eq}$.
formulas.description: Equivalent EMF and internal resistance of multiple parallel battery branches.
formulas.explanation: Essential for resolving complex active networks with unequal non-ideal voltage sources.

formulas.latex: S = \frac{I_g R_g}{I - I_g} \quad (\text{Ammeter Shunt}), \quad R_{se} = \frac{V}{I_g} - R_g \quad (\text{Voltmeter Multiplier})
formulas.title: Conversion of Galvanometer to Ammeter and Voltmeter
formulas.derivation: Ammeter: Shunt $S$ placed in parallel with galvanometer must divert excess current $I - I_g$. Equal voltage drop: $I_g R_g = (I - I_g)S \implies S = \frac{I_g R_g}{I - I_g}$. Voltmeter: Resistor $R_{se}$ placed in series with galvanometer: total voltage drop is $V = I_g(R_g + R_{se}) \implies R_{se} = \frac{V}{I_g} - R_g$.
formulas.description: Low-resistance parallel shunt for current range extension, and high-resistance series multiplier for voltage measurement.
formulas.explanation: An ideal ammeter has zero internal resistance; an ideal voltmeter has infinite internal resistance.

formulas.title: Potentiometer Principles (EMF Comparison and Internal Resistance)

variables.l_2: Balancing length with shunt resistor R

formulas.derivation: Potential gradient along uniform wire is $k = V/L$. On open circuit, null point at $l_1$ satisfies $\mathcal{E} = k l_1$. When shunted by external resistance $R$, terminal voltage is $V' = \frac{\mathcal{E} R}{R + r} = k l_2$. Dividing equations: $\frac{\mathcal{E}}{V'} = \frac{R + r}{R} = 1 + \frac{r}{R} = \frac{l_1}{l_2} \implies r = R\left(\frac{l_1}{l_2} - 1\right)$.
formulas.description: Null-method determination of cell EMF ratio and cell internal resistance using potentiometer wire.
formulas.explanation: Because no current is drawn from test cell at null balance point, potentiometer measures true EMF without loading error.

formulas.latex: H = I^2 R t = \frac{V^2}{R}t = V I t
formulas.title: Joule's Law of Electrical Heating
formulas.derivation: Electric field accelerates mobile charge carriers; collisions with lattice ions transfer kinetic energy into lattice vibrations (phonons). Work done moving charge $\Delta q = I\Delta t$ across potential difference $V$ is $\Delta W = V\Delta q = V I \Delta t$. Using Ohm's law $V = IR$ gives $H = I^2 R t = \frac{V^2}{R}t$.
formulas.description: Thermal energy generated by electrical current flowing through a dissipative resistive element.
formulas.explanation: Rate of heat dissipation is electric power $P = I^2 R$.

formulas.title: Power Ratings of Bulbs in Series and Parallel
formulas.derivation: Bulb resistance is $R_i = \frac{V_0^2}{P_i}$. In series, total resistance is $R_{eq} = \sum R_i = V_0^2 \sum \frac{1}{P_i}$, so total power at rated voltage is $P_{series} = \frac{V_0^2}{R_{eq}} = \left(\sum \frac{1}{P_i}\right)^{-1}$. In parallel, equivalent resistance is $\frac{1}{R_{eq}} = \sum \frac{1}{R_i} = \frac{1}{V_0^2}\sum P_i$, giving $P_{parallel} = \frac{V_0^2}{R_{eq}} = \sum P_i$.
formulas.description: Effective power consumption of incandescent bulbs rated at standard supply voltage $V_0$.
formulas.explanation: In series, the lowest-wattage bulb has the highest resistance and therefore glows the brightest.

formulas.title: Resistance of Concentric Spherical Shell Conductor
formulas.derivation: Radial shell element of thickness $dr$ at radius $r$ has area $A(r) = 4\pi r^2$. Elementary resistance is $dR = \rho \frac{dr}{4\pi r^2}$. Integrating from $r=r_1$ to $r_2$: $R = \frac{\rho}{4\pi} \int_{r_1}^{r_2} \frac{dr}{r^2} = \frac{\rho}{4\pi}\left(\frac{1}{r_1} - \frac{1}{r_2}\right)$.
formulas.description: Radial resistance of a conducting shell of resistivity $\rho$ between radii $r_1$ and $r_2$.
formulas.explanation: For coaxial cylindrical cable of length $L$, radial resistance is $R = \frac{\rho}{2\pi L}\ln(r_2 / r_1)$.

formulas.latex: m = Z I t = \frac{M}{n F} I t
formulas.title: Faraday's Laws of Electrolysis
formulas.derivation: Faraday's first law: $m \propto Q = It \implies m = ZIt$. Faraday's second law: mass deposited by 1 Faraday of charge ($F = N_A e \approx 96485\text{ C}$) is 1 gram-equivalent $= M/n$. Thus electrochemical equivalent is $Z = \frac{M}{nF}$, giving $m = \frac{M}{nF}It$.
formulas.description: Mass of chemical substance deposited at electrode proportional to total electrical charge passed.
formulas.explanation: Directly links stoichiometry and electrochemistry to fundamental electronic charge.

formulas.latex: R_T = \frac{R_1 R_2 + R_2 R_3 + R_3 R_1}{R_3} \quad (\Delta \leftrightarrow Y \text{ Transformation})
formulas.title: Delta-Wye (Star-Delta) Resistance Transformation
formulas.derivation: Equating terminal resistances between corresponding pairs of terminals in Delta and Wye networks yields $R_1 = \frac{R_B R_C}{R_A + R_B + R_C}$, $R_2 = \frac{R_A R_C}{R_A + R_B + R_C}$, $R_3 = \frac{R_A R_B}{R_A + R_B + R_C}$. Inverting gives the Delta resistor $R_A = \frac{R_1 R_2 + R_2 R_3 + R_3 R_1}{R_1}$.
formulas.description: Network equivalence formula converting three-terminal Delta (mesh) to Wye (star) configuration.
formulas.explanation: Resolves complex non-bridge bridge circuits that cannot be solved by simple series-parallel reductions.

formulas.latex: V_{drift} = \mu E, \quad \sigma = n_e e \mu_e + n_h e \mu_h
formulas.title: Carrier Mobility and Semiconductor Electrical Conductivity
formulas.derivation: Mobility is drift speed per unit electric field: $\mu = v_d / E = \frac{e\tau}{m}$. Total current density is sum of electron and hole currents: $J = J_e + J_h = n_e e v_{de} + n_h e v_{dh} = (n_e e \mu_e + n_h e \mu_h)E$. Since $J = \sigma E$, electrical conductivity is $\sigma = e(n_e \mu_e + n_h \mu_h)$.
formulas.description: Conductivity of intrinsic/extrinsic semiconductor with both electrons and holes.
formulas.explanation: Electron mobility is systematically higher than hole mobility ($\mu_e > \mu_h$) because conduction band effective mass is lower.

content_json.derivation: Between collisions, electrons accelerate under electric field: $a = \frac{eE}{m}$. Average drift speed acquired between collisions is $v_d = a\tau = \frac{eE}{m}\tau$. Volume of charge passing cross-section $A$ in time $\Delta t$ is $\Delta V = A v_d \Delta t$. Total charge is $\Delta Q = n(A v_d \Delta t)e$. Dividing by $\Delta t$: $I = \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} = n e A v_d$.
content_json.explanation: Current density is $J = I/A = n e v_d = \left(\frac{n e^2 \tau}{m}\right)E = \sigma E$ (microscopic Ohm's law).

catalog_formula_sheets.name: JEE Master: Magnetic Effects of Current & Ampere's Law
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: Electric force $\vec{F}_E = q\vec{E}$ is independent of velocity. Magnetic force $\vec{F}_B = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$ acts perpendicularly to both velocity and magnetic field (established by Hendrik Lorentz). Superposition yields total force $\vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v}\times\vec{B})$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Magnetic force does zero mechanical work on a charged particle ($dW = \vec{F}_B \cdot d\vec{r} = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot \vec{v}dt = 0$), altering direction of motion without changing kinetic energy or speed.

sections.title: JEE Master: Magnetic Effects of Current & Ampere's Law - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.title: Lorentz Force Equation
formulas.derivation: Electric force $\vec{F}_E = q\vec{E}$ is independent of velocity. Magnetic force $\vec{F}_B = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$ acts perpendicularly to both velocity and magnetic field (established by Hendrik Lorentz). Superposition yields total force $\vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v}\times\vec{B})$.
formulas.description: Total electromagnetic force experienced by a particle carrying charge q moving with velocity v.
formulas.explanation: Magnetic force does zero mechanical work on a charged particle ($dW = \vec{F}_B \cdot d\vec{r} = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot \vec{v}dt = 0$), altering direction of motion without changing kinetic energy or speed.

formulas.title: Cyclotron Motion and Gyrofrequency
formulas.derivation: Magnetic force provides centripetal acceleration: $q v_\perp B = \frac{m v_\perp^2}{r} \implies r = \frac{mv_\perp}{qB}$. Period is circumference divided by speed: $T = \frac{2\pi r}{v_\perp} = \frac{2\pi (mv_\perp / qB)}{v_\perp} = \frac{2\pi m}{qB}$. Frequency is $f_c = 1/T = \frac{qB}{2\pi m}$.
formulas.description: Radius, time period, and cyclotron frequency of a charged particle orbiting in a uniform magnetic field.
formulas.explanation: Orbital period and cyclotron frequency are completely independent of particle speed and radius (isochronous resonance).

formulas.title: Biot-Savart Law

variables.\\hat{r}: Unit vector from element to field point

formulas.derivation: Deduced experimentally by Jean-Baptiste Biot and Félix Savart: field magnitude scales as $dB \propto \frac{I dl \sin\theta}{r^2}$ with direction governed by right-hand thumb rule. In vector notation: $d\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I d\vec{l}\times\hat{r}}{r^2}$.
formulas.description: Fundamental law yielding differential magnetic field produced by an infinitesimal current element.
formulas.explanation: Magnetic counterpart to Coulomb's electrostatic law; integrates over complete current circuits to evaluate net magnetic field.

formulas.latex: B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d} \quad (\text{Infinite Wire}), \quad B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}(\sin\alpha + \sin\beta) \quad (\text{Finite Wire})
formulas.title: Magnetic Field of Straight Current-Carrying Conductor

variables.\\alpha, \\beta: Angles subtended by wire endpoints at the point

formulas.derivation: From Biot-Savart law: $dl = d\sec^2\theta d\theta$, $r = d\sec\theta$. Then $dB = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi} \frac{\cos\theta dl}{r^2} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}\cos\theta d\theta$. Integrating from $-\beta$ to $\alpha$: $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}[\sin\alpha - \sin(-\beta)] = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}(\sin\alpha + \sin\beta)$. For infinite wire, $\alpha = \beta = 90^\circ \implies B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}$.
formulas.description: Field at perpendicular distance d from straight current wire subtending boundary angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
formulas.explanation: Field lines form concentric circles centered on the wire following the right-hand grip rule.

formulas.latex: B_{axial} = \frac{\mu_0 N I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}, \quad B_{center} = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}
formulas.title: Magnetic Field on Axis and Center of Circular Current Loop
formulas.derivation: Element $I d\vec{l}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{r}$ where $r = \sqrt{R^2 + x^2}$. Differential field is $dB = \frac{\mu_0 I dl}{4\pi r^2}$. Components perpendicular to the axis cancel by symmetry around the ring. The axial component is $dB_x = dB\sin\theta = dB\left(\frac{R}{r}\right) = \frac{\mu_0 I R dl}{4\pi (R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$. Integrating over loop circumference $\oint dl = 2\pi R$ and multiplying by $N$ turns gives $B = \frac{\mu_0 N I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$. Setting $x=0$ yields center field $B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}$.
formulas.description: Field produced by circular coil of N turns and radius R at axial distance x from its center.
formulas.explanation: At large distances ($x \gg R$), field reduces to dipole form $B = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2M}{x^3}$ where magnetic dipole moment is $M = N I (\pi R^2)$.

formulas.title: Ampere's Circuital Law

variables.I_{enclosed}: Net current passing through area bounded by loop

formulas.derivation: Integrate around concentric circular path of radius $r$ centered on infinite wire: by axial symmetry, $\vec{B}$ has constant tangential magnitude $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$. Line integral is $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = B \oint dl = \left(\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\right)(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I$. By linear superposition, this holds for any closed loop enclosing total current $I_{enclosed}$.
formulas.description: Line integral of magnetic field around closed loop equals permeability multiplied by net enclosed current.
formulas.explanation: Used to analytically calculate fields in solenoids, toroids, and coaxial conductors with high geometric symmetry.

formulas.latex: B_{solenoid} = \mu_0 n I, \quad B_{toroid} = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2\pi r}
formulas.title: Magnetic Fields of Ideal Solenoid and Toroid
formulas.derivation: Solenoid: take rectangular Amperian loop of length $L$ with one side inside solenoid and opposite side far outside where field is negligible ($B_{out} \approx 0$). Transverse sides have $\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = 0$. Net line integral is $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = B L$. Enclosed current is $I_{enc} = (n L)I$. By Ampere's law: $B L = \mu_0 (n L I) \implies B = \mu_0 n I$. Toroid: Amperian circle of radius $r$ encloses $N$ turns: $B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 N I \implies B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2\pi r}$.
formulas.description: Uniform internal field of tightly wound solenoid ($n$ turns/length) and circular toroid.
formulas.explanation: Field inside a long solenoid is remarkably uniform and zero outside.

formulas.title: Force Between Parallel Current-Carrying Conductors
formulas.derivation: Wire 1 produces magnetic field at location of wire 2: $B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi d}$ directed perpendicular to plane containing wires. Segment of wire 2 of length $L$ carrying current $I_2$ experiences magnetic force $F = I_2 L B_1 = I_2 L \left(\frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi d}\right)$. Dividing by length: $\frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$.
formulas.description: Mutual magnetic force per unit length between two infinite parallel wires separated by distance d.
formulas.explanation: Parallel currents attract; anti-parallel currents repel. Serves as the historical SI definition of the Ampere.

formulas.title: Torque and Potential Energy of Magnetic Dipole
formulas.derivation: For rectangular loop of sides $a$ and $b$ in field $B$: forces on sides of length $a$ are $F = I a B$ forming a couple of lever arm $b\sin\theta$. Net torque is $\tau = F(b\sin\theta) = I(ab)B\sin\theta = I A B\sin\theta = |\vec{M}\times\vec{B}|$. Potential energy is work required to rotate dipole: $U = -\int \tau d\theta = -M B\cos\theta = -\vec{M}\cdot\vec{B}$.
formulas.description: Torque on a current loop or magnetic dipole in external magnetic field, and magnetic orientation potential energy.
formulas.explanation: Forms the operating principle of moving-coil galvanometers and DC electric motors.

formulas.title: Magnetic Susceptibility and Temperature Dependence
formulas.derivation: Paramagnetism arises from alignment of permanent atomic dipoles against randomizing thermal agitation ($k_B T$). Boltzmann statistics gives magnetization $M = N m L(x) \approx \frac{N m^2 B}{3k_B T}$ for weak fields ($x \ll 1$). Susceptibility is $\chi_m = \frac{M}{H} = \frac{\mu_0 M}{B} = \frac{\mu_0 N m^2}{3k_B T} = \frac{C}{T}$. In ferromagnets, internal exchange coupling field $B_{int} = \lambda M$ modifies alignment to give $\chi_m = \frac{C}{T - T_c}$ above $T_c$.
formulas.description: Paramagnetic susceptibility inverse temperature dependence and ferromagnetic transition above Curie temperature $T_c$.
formulas.explanation: Diamagnets have small negative susceptibility ($\chi < 0$) independent of temperature. Ferromagnets become paramagnetic above $T_c$.

formulas.title: Bohr Magneton
formulas.derivation: Orbital current of electron in circular orbit of radius $r$ and period $T = 2\pi r/v$ is $I = e/T = \frac{ev}{2\pi r}$. Orbital magnetic moment is $\mu_L = I A = \left(\frac{ev}{2\pi r}\right)(\pi r^2) = \frac{1}{2}e v r = \frac{e}{2m_e}(m_e v r) = \frac{e}{2m_e}L$. In Bohr model, orbital angular momentum is quantized as $L = n\hbar$. For ground state $n=1$, the fundamental magnetic moment is $\mu_B = \frac{e\hbar}{2m_e}$.
formulas.description: Fundamental quantum unit of orbital and spin magnetic dipole moment of an electron.
formulas.explanation: Gyromagnetic ratio for electron orbital motion is $\gamma = \frac{\mu_L}{L} = \frac{e}{2m_e}$.

formulas.latex: V_H = \frac{I B}{n q d} = \frac{R_H I B}{d}, \quad R_H = \frac{1}{n q}
formulas.title: Hall Effect Voltage and Hall Coefficient
formulas.derivation: Magnetic Lorentz force deflects drifting carriers sideways, accumulating charge on lateral faces until transverse Hall electric field $E_H$ balances magnetic deflection: $q E_H = q v_d B \implies E_H = v_d B$. Transverse voltage across width $w$ is $V_H = E_H w = v_d B w$. Using $I = n q (w d) v_d \implies v_d = \frac{I}{n q w d}$: $V_H = \left(\frac{I}{n q w d}\right) B w = \frac{I B}{n q d}$.
formulas.description: Transverse electric voltage generated across current-carrying conductor in transverse magnetic field.
formulas.explanation: Sign of Hall voltage directly determines whether majority charge carriers are negative electrons ($R_H < 0$) or positive holes ($R_H > 0$).

formulas.latex: B(r) = \frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi R^2} \quad (r \le R), \quad B(r) = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} \quad (r \ge R)
formulas.title: Magnetic Field Inside and Outside Solid Cylindrical Wire
formulas.derivation: Uniform current density $J = I / (\pi R^2)$. For $r \le R$, circular Amperian loop of radius $r$ encloses current $I_{enc} = J(\pi r^2) = I\frac{r^2}{R^2}$. By Ampere's circuital law: $B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I_{enc} = \mu_0 I \frac{r^2}{R^2} \implies B(r) = \frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi R^2}$. Outside ($r \ge R$), loop encloses full current $I$, giving $B(r) = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$.
formulas.description: Field profile inside uniform current carrying cylinder of radius R.
formulas.explanation: Magnetic field rises linearly from zero at center to maximum at surface ($r=R$), then falls off as $1/r$.

formulas.title: Helical Path Pitch of Charged Particle in Magnetic Field
formulas.derivation: Magnetic force has zero component along $\vec{B}$: $\vec{F}_\parallel = 0$, so parallel velocity $v_\parallel = v\cos\theta$ remains constant. Transverse component $v_\perp = v\sin\theta$ generates uniform circular orbit of period $T = \frac{2\pi m}{qB}$. Axial distance traveled during one complete period is pitch $p = v_\parallel T = (v\cos\theta)\left(\frac{2\pi m}{qB}\right)$.
formulas.description: Distance traveled along magnetic field direction per complete circular revolution when velocity makes angle $\theta$ with field.
formulas.explanation: Underlies magnetic confinement in tokamaks and planetary auroral particle precipitation along geomagnetic field lines.

formulas.title: Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction and Lenz's Law
formulas.derivation: Empirical discovery by Michael Faraday (1831). The negative sign (Lenz's Law, Heinrich Lenz 1834) enforces energy conservation: the induced current flows in such a direction that its own magnetic field opposes the original flux change that produced it.
formulas.description: Induced electromotive force in a circuit equals negative rate of change of magnetic flux through loop.
formulas.explanation: If flux increases, induced magnetic field points opposite to applied field; if flux decreases, induced field reinforces it.

formulas.title: Motional EMF in a Moving Conductor
formulas.derivation: Mobile conduction electrons inside rod experience magnetic Lorentz force $\vec{F}_B = -e(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$. Work done moving an electron through length $\vec{l}$ is $W = \int \vec{F}_B \cdot d\vec{l} = -e \int (\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot d\vec{l}$. Induced EMF is work done per unit positive charge: $\mathcal{E} = W/(-e) = (\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot\vec{l} = B v l\sin\theta$.
formulas.description: Electromotive force induced across ends of a conducting rod of length l translating with speed v through magnetic field B.
formulas.explanation: Forms the foundation of electrical power generation in alternators and dynamos.

formulas.title: Rotational Motional EMF of a Rotating Rod
formulas.derivation: Consider element $dr$ at distance $r$ from pivot: linear velocity is $v(r) = r\omega$. Motional EMF generated across element is $d\mathcal{E} = B v(r) dr = B(r\omega)dr$. Integrating from pivot $r=0$ to tip $r=l$: $\mathcal{E} = B\omega \int_0^l r dr = B\omega \left[\frac{r^2}{2}\right]_0^l = \frac{1}{2}B\omega l^2$.
formulas.description: EMF induced between pivot and tip of a conducting rod of length l rotating with angular speed $\omega$ in perpendicular field B.
formulas.explanation: Also equals $B\left(\frac{dA}{dt}\right) = B\left(\frac{1}{2}l^2\omega\right)$, matching rate of area swept.

formulas.latex: L = \frac{N \Phi_B}{I} = \mu_0 n^2 A l, \quad U_B = \frac{1}{2}L I^2, \quad u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}
formulas.title: Self-Inductance and Magnetic Energy Density
formulas.derivation: Inside solenoid, field is $B = \mu_0 n I$. Flux per turn is $\Phi = B A = \mu_0 n I A$. Total linkage is $\lambda = N\Phi = (nl)(\mu_0 n I A) = (\mu_0 n^2 A l)I$. By definition $L = \lambda / I = \mu_0 n^2 A l$. Work required to establish current $I$ against back-EMF $\mathcal{E}_L = -L\frac{di}{dt}$ is $U = \int P\,dt = \int (L\frac{di}{dt} i)dt = L \int_0^I i\,di = \frac{1}{2}LI^2$. Dividing by volume $V = Al$ and using $B = \mu_0 n I$ yields $u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$.
formulas.description: Self-inductance of solenoid, total energy stored in inductor magnetic field, and volume energy density.
formulas.explanation: Analogous to kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ and electrostatic energy density $\frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0 E^2$.

formulas.latex: M = \frac{N_2 \Phi_{21}}{I_1} = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l, \quad M \le \sqrt{L_1 L_2}
formulas.title: Mutual Inductance and Coupling Coefficient
formulas.derivation: Current $I_1$ in outer coil produces uniform field $B_1 = \mu_0 n_1 I_1$. Flux passing through each turn of inner coil of area $A$ is $\Phi_{21} = B_1 A = \mu_0 n_1 I_1 A$. Total linkage with coil 2 ($N_2 = n_2 l$ turns) is $\lambda_2 = N_2 \Phi_{21} = (n_2 l)(\mu_0 n_1 I_1 A) = (\mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l)I_1$. Mutual inductance is $M = \lambda_2 / I_1 = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l$. By reciprocity theorem, $M_{12} = M_{21} = M$.
formulas.description: Mutual inductance between two co-axial solenoids and coupling coefficient $k = M/\sqrt{L_1 L_2} \le 1$.
formulas.explanation: For perfectly coupled coils with zero flux leakage, $k = 1$ and $M = \sqrt{L_1 L_2}$.

formulas.latex: i(t) = I_0 (1 - e^{-t / \tau_L}) \quad (\text{Growth}), \quad i(t) = I_0 e^{-t / \tau_L} \quad (\text{Decay}), \quad \tau_L = \frac{L}{R}
formulas.title: Transient LR Circuit Growth and Decay
formulas.derivation: KVL during growth: $\mathcal{E} - L\frac{di}{dt} - iR = 0 \implies L\frac{di}{dt} = \mathcal{E} - iR$. Separating variables: $\frac{di}{\mathcal{E} - iR} = \frac{dt}{L}$. Integrating with $i(0) = 0$: $-\frac{1}{R}\ln\left(1 - \frac{iR}{\mathcal{E}}\right) = \frac{t}{L} \implies i(t) = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R}\left(1 - e^{-Rt/L}\right)$.
formulas.description: Time-dependent current build-up and decay in inductive RL circuit with inductive time constant $\tau_L = L/R$.
formulas.explanation: At $t = \tau_L = L/R$, current reaches $63.2\%$ of steady value $I_0$; inductor acts as open-circuit at $t=0^+$ and short-circuit as $t \to \infty$.

formulas.title: Root-Mean-Square (RMS) Values of Sinusoidal AC
formulas.derivation: For $i(t) = I_0 \sin(\omega t)$, Joule heat generated in resistor $R$ over one period $T = 2\pi/\omega$ is $H = \int_0^T i^2(t) R dt$. An equivalent DC current $I_{rms}$ dissipates identical heat: $I_{rms}^2 R T = R \int_0^T I_0^2 \sin^2(\omega t) dt$. Since the average of $\sin^2(\omega t)$ over full period is $\frac{1}{2}$: $I_{rms}^2 T = I_0^2 \left(\frac{T}{2}\right) \implies I_{rms} = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}$.
formulas.description: Effective heating value of alternating sinusoidal current and voltage over full periodic cycle.
formulas.explanation: Standard wall outlet voltages (e.g., $230\text{ V}$ or $120\text{ V}$) always quote RMS values; peak voltage is $V_0 = \sqrt{2}V_{rms}$ ($325\text{ V}$ for $230\text{ V}$).

formulas.latex: Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}, \quad X_L = \omega L, \quad X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C}
formulas.title: Impedance of Series LCR Circuit
formulas.derivation: Phasor analysis: current phasor $\tilde{I}$ is common in series loop. Resistor voltage $\tilde{V}_R = I R$ is in phase with current. Inductor voltage $\tilde{V}_L = I X_L$ leads current by $+90^\circ (+i)$. Capacitor voltage $\tilde{V}_C = I X_C$ lags current by $-90^\circ (-i)$. Total complex voltage is $\tilde{V} = \tilde{V}_R + \tilde{V}_L + \tilde{V}_C = I [R + i(X_L - X_C)]$. Impedance magnitude is $Z = |\tilde{V}|/I = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$.
formulas.description: Total opposition to sinusoidal alternating current flow combining resistance, inductive reactance, and capacitive reactance.
formulas.explanation: Phase angle between voltage and current is $\tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R}$.

formulas.title: Resonant Frequency and Quality Factor (Q) of Series LCR
formulas.derivation: Current amplitude is $I_0 = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{R^2 + (\omega L - 1/\omega C)^2}}$. Current is maximized when reactive term vanishes: $\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C} = 0 \implies \omega_0^2 = \frac{1}{LC} \implies \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$. At resonance, impedance is purely resistive ($Z_{min} = R$) and current is in phase with voltage ($\cos\phi = 1$). Quality factor is $Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} = \frac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega}$ where $\Delta\omega$ is bandwidth at half-power points.
formulas.description: Condition for minimum impedance, maximum current resonance, and sharpness factor of resonance curve.
formulas.explanation: High $Q$ produces extremely sharp tuning selectivity in radio receivers and RF filter circuits.

formulas.title: Average AC Power and Power Factor
formulas.derivation: Instantaneous power is $p(t) = v(t)i(t) = [V_0 \sin(\omega t)][I_0 \sin(\omega t - \phi)] = V_0 I_0 \sin(\omega t)[\sin\omega t\cos\phi - \cos\omega t\sin\phi] = V_0 I_0 [\sin^2\omega t\cos\phi - \sin\omega t\cos\omega t\sin\phi]$. Averaging over a full cycle: $\langle \sin^2\omega t \rangle = 1/2$ and $\langle \sin\omega t\cos\omega t \rangle = 0$. Hence $P_{avg} = \frac{1}{2}V_0 I_0 \cos\phi = \left(\frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\left(\frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\cos\phi = V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos\phi$. From impedance triangle, $\cos\phi = R/Z$.
formulas.description: Real active power dissipated in AC circuit over complete cycle governed by phase angle $\phi$.
formulas.explanation: For purely reactive circuits (pure $L$ or pure $C$), $\phi = \pm 90^\circ \implies \cos\phi = 0$, giving zero real power dissipation (wattless current).

formulas.title: Ideal Transformer Voltage, Current and Turns Ratio
formulas.derivation: Assuming ideal core with zero flux leakage: common flux $\Phi$ links both windings. Induced EMFs are $V_p = -N_p \frac{d\Phi}{dt}$ and $V_s = -N_s \frac{d\Phi}{dt}$. Dividing gives $\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$. For an ideal lossless transformer (100% efficiency), input power equals output power: $V_p I_p = V_s I_s \implies \frac{I_p}{I_s} = \frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$.
formulas.description: Transformation of AC voltage and current in magnetically coupled primary and secondary windings.
formulas.explanation: Step-up transformer ($N_s > N_p$): voltage increases and current decreases proportionately, minimizing $I^2 R$ transmission line losses.

formulas.latex: \omega_{LC} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}, \quad q(t) = Q_0 \cos(\omega_{LC} t), \quad i(t) = -\omega_{LC} Q_0 \sin(\omega_{LC} t)
formulas.title: LC Tank Circuit Oscillations
formulas.derivation: Total circuit energy is $E = U_E + U_B = \frac{q^2}{2C} + \frac{1}{2}Li^2$. In lossless circuit, $\frac{dE}{dt} = 0$: $\frac{q}{C}\frac{dq}{dt} + L i \frac{di}{dt} = 0$. Since $i = \frac{dq}{dt}$, dividing by $i$ gives $\frac{q}{C} + L\frac{d^2q}{dt^2} = 0 \implies \frac{d^2q}{dt^2} + \frac{1}{LC}q = 0$. This is standard SHM equation with $\omega_{LC} = 1/\sqrt{LC}$. Solution with initial charge $Q_0$ is $q(t) = Q_0\cos(\omega t)$.
formulas.description: Undamped harmonic exchange of energy between electric field of capacitor and magnetic field of inductor.
formulas.explanation: Energy sloshes sinusoidally between all-electric state ($U_E = Q_0^2/2C$) and all-magnetic state ($U_B = \frac{1}{2}L I_{max}^2$).

formulas.title: Maxwell's Displacement Current
formulas.derivation: Between capacitor plates during charging, no conduction electrons flow, yet magnetic field exists. Electric field is $E = \frac{Q}{\epsilon_0 A} \implies Q = \epsilon_0 E A = \epsilon_0 \Phi_E$. Differentiating charge with respect to time: $I_c = \frac{dQ}{dt} = \epsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$. Maxwell recognized this time-varying flux term acts as an effective displacement current $I_d = \epsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$, restoring Ampere's law to $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 (I_c + I_d)$.
formulas.description: Equivalent current arising from time-varying electric flux, completing Ampere-Maxwell law.
formulas.explanation: Displacement current between plates exactly equals conduction current in the connecting wires ($I_d = I_c$), ensuring continuity.

formulas.title: Speed of Electromagnetic Waves in Vacuum and Field Ratio
formulas.description: Propagation velocity of light from Maxwell's equations and relation between electric and magnetic field amplitudes.
formulas.explanation: Proved that light is an electromagnetic transverse wave propagating at universal speed $c$.

content_json.derivation: Empirical discovery by Michael Faraday (1831). The negative sign (Lenz's Law, Heinrich Lenz 1834) enforces energy conservation: the induced current flows in such a direction that its own magnetic field opposes the original flux change that produced it.
content_json.explanation: If flux increases, induced magnetic field points opposite to applied field; if flux decreases, induced field reinforces it.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: JEE Master: Ray Optics, Optical Instruments & Wave Optics
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: From paraxial ray geometry of reflection on spherical mirror: similar triangles formed by object, image, and center of curvature give $\frac{h_i}{h_o} = -\frac{v - R}{R - u} = -\frac{v}{u}$. Equating ratios and using $R = 2f$: $\frac{v - 2f}{2f - u} = \frac{v}{u} \implies u(v - 2f) = v(2f - u) \implies uv - 2uf = 2vf - uv \implies 2uv = 2f(u + v)$. Dividing both sides by $2uvf$ gives $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u}$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Concave mirror: $f < 0$; Convex mirror: $f > 0$. Real image: $m < 0$ (inverted); Virtual image: $m > 0$ (erect).
