formulas.title: Mirror Formula and Linear Magnification
formulas.derivation: From paraxial ray geometry of reflection on spherical mirror: similar triangles formed by object, image, and center of curvature give $\frac{h_i}{h_o} = -\frac{v - R}{R - u} = -\frac{v}{u}$. Equating ratios and using $R = 2f$: $\frac{v - 2f}{2f - u} = \frac{v}{u} \implies u(v - 2f) = v(2f - u) \implies uv - 2uf = 2vf - uv \implies 2uv = 2f(u + v)$. Dividing both sides by $2uvf$ gives $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u}$.
formulas.description: Relates object distance, image distance, and focal length for spherical mirrors using Cartesian sign convention.
formulas.explanation: Concave mirror: $f < 0$; Convex mirror: $f > 0$. Real image: $m < 0$ (inverted); Virtual image: $m > 0$ (erect).

formulas.title: Snell's Law of Refraction and Total Internal Reflection (TIR)
formulas.derivation: From Fermat's Principle of Least Time: travel time between points $A(0, a)$ and $B(d, -b)$ across boundary at $(x, 0)$ is $t(x) = \frac{\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}}{v_1} + \frac{\sqrt{b^2 + (d-x)^2}}{v_2}$. Setting $\frac{dt}{dx} = 0$: $\frac{x}{v_1\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}} - \frac{d-x}{v_2\sqrt{b^2 + (d-x)^2}} = 0 \implies \frac{\sin\theta_1}{v_1} = \frac{\sin\theta_2}{v_2}$. Multiplying by $c$ gives $n_1\sin\theta_1 = n_2\sin\theta_2$. At critical angle $\theta_c$, angle of refraction reaches $\theta_2 = 90^\circ \implies \sin\theta_c = n_2/n_1$.
formulas.description: Refraction at planar dielectric interface and critical angle threshold for total internal reflection.
formulas.explanation: Underlies optical fiber light guiding, mirage formation, and prism binocular design.

formulas.title: Refraction at a Single Spherical Curved Surface
formulas.derivation: From paraxial ray geometry: for small incident ray angles $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ with principal axis: $i = \alpha + \gamma$ and $\gamma = r + \beta \implies r = \gamma - \beta$. Snell's law in paraxial approximation is $\mu_1 i = \mu_2 r$. Substituting gives $\mu_1(\alpha + \gamma) = \mu_2(\gamma - \beta) \implies \mu_1 \alpha + \mu_2 \beta = (\mu_2 - \mu_1)\gamma$. For small angles, $\alpha \approx \frac{h}{-u}$, $\beta \approx \frac{h}{v}$, and $\gamma \approx \frac{h}{R}$. Canceling arc height $h$ yields $\frac{\mu_2}{v} - \frac{\mu_1}{u} = \frac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{R}$.
formulas.description: Fundamental Gaussian equation relating conjugate points for refraction across a spherical interface of radius R.
formulas.explanation: Direct precursor used twice in series to derive the Lens Maker's formula for thin lenses.

formulas.title: Lens Maker's Formula and Thin Lens Equation

variables.R_1, R_2: Radii of curvature of first and second faces

formulas.derivation: Apply spherical refraction formula to first surface of curvature $R_1$: $\frac{\mu}{v_1} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{\mu - 1}{R_1}$. For second surface of curvature $R_2$, $v_1$ acts as virtual object: $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{\mu}{v_1} = \frac{1 - \mu}{R_2} = -\frac{\mu - 1}{R_2}$. Adding both equations eliminates intermediate image $v_1$: $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)$. For object at infinity ($u = \infty$), image forms at focus ($v = f$), giving $\frac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)$.
formulas.description: Focal length of a thin lens computed from surface curvatures and lens material refractive index.
formulas.explanation: When immersed in a liquid medium of refractive index $\mu_l$, focal length alters to $f_{liq} = f_{air} \frac{\mu_g - 1}{\mu_g / \mu_l - 1}$.

formulas.latex: P = \frac{1}{f} \text{ (Diopters)}, \quad P_{eq} = P_1 + P_2 - d P_1 P_2
formulas.title: Optical Power and Combination of Lenses
formulas.derivation: Optical power measures deviation angle $\delta = h / f$ produced for a ray at unit height $h=1$, hence $P = 1/f$. For two lenses in close contact ($d=0$), net focal length is $\frac{1}{F} = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2} \implies P_{eq} = P_1 + P_2$. When separated by distance $d$, tracing ray deviation shows second lens receives incident ray at reduced height $h_2 = h_1 - d \delta_1 = h_1(1 - d/f_1)$, resulting in $P_{eq} = P_1 + P_2 - d P_1 P_2$.
formulas.description: Converging ability of optical lenses and equivalent power of two lenses separated by distance d.
formulas.explanation: Convex lens: $P > 0$; Concave lens: $P < 0$. Contact powers add algebraically.

formulas.title: Prism Formula at Minimum Deviation
formulas.derivation: Total deviation angle is $\delta = (i_1 + i_2) - A$ where $r_1 + r_2 = A$. At minimum deviation $\delta_m$, ray passes symmetrically through prism: $i_1 = i_2 = i$ and $r_1 = r_2 = r$. Then $r + r = A \implies r = A/2$. Deviation becomes $\delta_m = 2i - A \implies i = \frac{A + \delta_m}{2}$. Substituting into Snell's law $\mu = \frac{\sin i}{\sin r}$ gives $\mu = \frac{\sin((A + \delta_m)/2)}{\sin(A/2)}$.
formulas.description: Refractive index of a triangular prism of apex angle A determined from minimum deviation angle $\delta_m$.
formulas.explanation: Standard precision laboratory method for measuring refractive index using spectrometer.

formulas.title: Dispersive Power of an Optical Medium

variables.\\mu_v, \\mu_r, \\mu_y: Refractive indices for violet, red, and Fraunhofer yellow D-line

formulas.derivation: For small-angled prism, deviation is $\delta = (\mu - 1)A$. Angular dispersion is $\theta = \delta_v - \delta_r = (\mu_v - 1)A - (\mu_r - 1)A = (\mu_v - \mu_r)A$. Mean deviation is $\delta_y = (\mu_y - 1)A$. Dispersive power is defined as $\omega = \frac{\theta}{\delta_y} = \frac{(\mu_v - \mu_r)A}{(\mu_y - 1)A} = \frac{\mu_v - \mu_r}{\mu_y - 1}$.
formulas.description: Ratio of angular dispersion between violet and red light to mean yellow light deviation.
formulas.explanation: Flint glass has higher dispersive power than crown glass; combining crown and flint prisms creates achromatic doublets (dispersion without deviation or vice-versa).

formulas.title: Astronomical Refracting Telescope Magnification
formulas.derivation: Objective forms intermediate inverted real image of distant object at its focal plane ($h' = f_o \alpha$). Eyepiece acts as simple magnifier: in normal adjustment (image at infinity), visual angle is $\beta = h'/f_e$. Angular magnification is $M = \frac{\beta}{\alpha} = \frac{h'/f_e}{h'/f_o} = -\frac{f_o}{f_e}$. Separation between lenses is tube length $L = f_o + f_e$. If image forms at near point $D$, eyepiece magnification is $m_e = 1 + D/f_e$, yielding $M = -\frac{f_o}{f_e}\left(1 + \frac{f_e}{D}\right)$.
formulas.description: Angular magnification and barrel tube length of astronomical telescope under normal adjustment and near point.
formulas.explanation: High magnification requires large objective focal length $f_o$ and small eyepiece focal length $f_e$.

formulas.title: Compound Microscope Magnification
formulas.derivation: Total magnification is product of linear magnification of objective $m_o = -v_o / u_o$ and angular magnification of eyepiece $m_e = D / f_e$ (at infinity): $M = m_o \times m_e = -\left(\frac{v_o}{u_o}\right)\left(\frac{D}{f_e}\right)$. In standard microscope geometry, object is placed just outside $f_o$ ($u_o \approx f_o$) and image forms near eyepiece ($v_o \approx L$), giving $M \approx -\frac{L D}{f_o f_e}$.
formulas.description: Total magnifying power of objective lens and ocular eyepiece under normal adjustment.
formulas.explanation: Both $f_o$ and $f_e$ must be extremely small to achieve high microscopic magnification.

formulas.title: Young's Double Slit Experiment (YDSE) Fringe Width and Intensity
formulas.derivation: Path difference between rays from two slits is $\Delta x = d\sin\theta \approx d\frac{y}{D}$. Bright fringes occur at constructive interference: $\Delta x = n\lambda \implies y_n = n\frac{\lambda D}{d}$. Spacing between consecutive fringes is fringe width $\beta = y_{n+1} - y_n = \frac{\lambda D}{d}$. Phase difference is $\Delta\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x = \frac{2\pi y d}{\lambda D}$. Superposing two coherent waves $E = E_0 e^{i\omega t} + E_0 e^{i(\omega t + \Delta\phi)}$ gives resultant amplitude $E_R = 2E_0\cos(\Delta\phi/2)$, so intensity is $I = 4I_0\cos^2(\Delta\phi/2)$.
formulas.description: Equispaced interference fringe width and cosine-squared intensity distribution on screen.
formulas.explanation: If entire apparatus is immersed in liquid of index $\mu$, fringe width shrinks to $\beta' = \beta / \mu$.

formulas.title: Fringe Shift in YDSE Due to Thin Transparent Plate
formulas.derivation: Optical path length through sheet of thickness $t$ is $\mu t$ instead of geometric air path $t$. Extra optical path introduced in that beam is $\Delta_{opt} = \mu t - t = (\mu - 1)t$. Central fringe now occurs where net path difference vanishes: $d\frac{y_0}{D} - (\mu - 1)t = 0 \implies y_0 = \frac{(\mu - 1)t D}{d}$. Number of shifted fringes is $N = \frac{\Delta y}{\beta} = \frac{(\mu - 1)t}{\lambda}$.
formulas.description: Lateral shift of entire interference pattern when a dielectric sheet of thickness t and index $\mu$ covers one slit.
formulas.explanation: Fringe pattern shifts bodily toward the side where the transparent plate is introduced; fringe width $\beta$ remains unchanged.

formulas.latex: a \sin\theta = m\lambda \quad (\text{Minima}), \quad y_1 = \frac{\lambda D}{a}, \quad W_{central} = \frac{2\lambda D}{a}
formulas.title: Single-Slit Fraunhofer Diffraction

variables.W_{central}: Linear width of central maximum on screen

formulas.derivation: Divide slit of width $a$ into two equal halves of width $a/2$: path difference between corresponding wavelets from top and middle is $\frac{a}{2}\sin\theta$. Destructive interference occurs when this path difference is $\lambda/2 \implies \frac{a}{2}\sin\theta = \frac{\lambda}{2} \implies a\sin\theta = \lambda$. In general, dividing into $2m$ zones gives dark minima at $a\sin\theta = m\lambda$. Central maximum extends between first minima on either side ($m = \pm 1$): angular half-width $\theta_1 = \lambda/a$, so linear full width is $W_{central} = 2y_1 = 2\frac{\lambda D}{a}$.
formulas.description: Positions of intensity minima and linear angular width of central diffraction maximum.
formulas.explanation: Central diffraction peak is twice as wide as secondary subsidiary maxima and holds over 85% of total radiant energy.

formulas.title: Rayleigh's Criterion for Resolving Power
formulas.derivation: Diffraction of plane wave by circular aperture produces Airy disc pattern with first dark ring at angular radius $\theta = 1.22\frac{\lambda}{D}$ (derived from zeros of first-order Bessel function $J_1(x) = 0$). Lord Rayleigh postulated that two sources are barely resolved when the central maximum of one Airy disc falls exactly on the first minimum of the other: $\theta_R = 1.22\frac{\lambda}{D}$.
formulas.description: Minimum angular separation for two point sources to be barely resolved through circular aperture.
formulas.explanation: Explains why larger astronomical telescope mirrors provide both greater light-gathering power and finer angular resolution.

formulas.title: Polarization: Malus's Law and Brewster's Angle
formulas.derivation: Malus's Law: electric field vector $\vec{E}_0$ of polarized wave incident at angle $\theta$ to transmission axis has transmitted component $E = E_0\cos\theta$. Since intensity is proportional to amplitude squared: $I(\theta) \propto E^2 = E_0^2\cos^2\theta = I_0\cos^2\theta$. Brewster's Law: reflected ray is completely polarized perpendicular to plane of incidence when reflected and refracted rays are mutually perpendicular ($r + \theta_p = 90^\circ \implies r = 90^\circ - \theta_p$). Substituting into Snell's law: $\sin\theta_p = \mu \sin r = \mu \sin(90^\circ - \theta_p) = \mu \cos\theta_p \implies \tan\theta_p = \mu$.
formulas.description: Transmitted intensity through analyzer polarizer, and angle of incidence producing 100% linearly polarized reflected light.
formulas.explanation: At Brewster's angle, electrons oscillating along refracted beam direction cannot emit transverse waves in the direction of specular reflection.

formulas.title: Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction and Lenz's Law
formulas.derivation: Empirical discovery by Michael Faraday (1831). The negative sign (Lenz's Law, Heinrich Lenz 1834) enforces energy conservation: the induced current flows in such a direction that its own magnetic field opposes the original flux change that produced it.
formulas.description: Induced electromotive force in a circuit equals negative rate of change of magnetic flux through loop.
formulas.explanation: If flux increases, induced magnetic field points opposite to applied field; if flux decreases, induced field reinforces it.

formulas.title: Motional EMF in a Moving Conductor
formulas.derivation: Mobile conduction electrons inside rod experience magnetic Lorentz force $\vec{F}_B = -e(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$. Work done moving an electron through length $\vec{l}$ is $W = \int \vec{F}_B \cdot d\vec{l} = -e \int (\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot d\vec{l}$. Induced EMF is work done per unit positive charge: $\mathcal{E} = W/(-e) = (\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot\vec{l} = B v l\sin\theta$.
formulas.description: Electromotive force induced across ends of a conducting rod of length l translating with speed v through magnetic field B.
formulas.explanation: Forms the foundation of electrical power generation in alternators and dynamos.

formulas.title: Rotational Motional EMF of a Rotating Rod
formulas.derivation: Consider element $dr$ at distance $r$ from pivot: linear velocity is $v(r) = r\omega$. Motional EMF generated across element is $d\mathcal{E} = B v(r) dr = B(r\omega)dr$. Integrating from pivot $r=0$ to tip $r=l$: $\mathcal{E} = B\omega \int_0^l r dr = B\omega \left[\frac{r^2}{2}\right]_0^l = \frac{1}{2}B\omega l^2$.
formulas.description: EMF induced between pivot and tip of a conducting rod of length l rotating with angular speed $\omega$ in perpendicular field B.
formulas.explanation: Also equals $B\left(\frac{dA}{dt}\right) = B\left(\frac{1}{2}l^2\omega\right)$, matching rate of area swept.

formulas.latex: L = \frac{N \Phi_B}{I} = \mu_0 n^2 A l, \quad U_B = \frac{1}{2}L I^2, \quad u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}
formulas.title: Self-Inductance and Magnetic Energy Density
formulas.derivation: Inside solenoid, field is $B = \mu_0 n I$. Flux per turn is $\Phi = B A = \mu_0 n I A$. Total linkage is $\lambda = N\Phi = (nl)(\mu_0 n I A) = (\mu_0 n^2 A l)I$. By definition $L = \lambda / I = \mu_0 n^2 A l$. Work required to establish current $I$ against back-EMF $\mathcal{E}_L = -L\frac{di}{dt}$ is $U = \int P\,dt = \int (L\frac{di}{dt} i)dt = L \int_0^I i\,di = \frac{1}{2}LI^2$. Dividing by volume $V = Al$ and using $B = \mu_0 n I$ yields $u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$.
formulas.description: Self-inductance of solenoid, total energy stored in inductor magnetic field, and volume energy density.
formulas.explanation: Analogous to kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ and electrostatic energy density $\frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0 E^2$.

formulas.latex: M = \frac{N_2 \Phi_{21}}{I_1} = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l, \quad M \le \sqrt{L_1 L_2}
formulas.title: Mutual Inductance and Coupling Coefficient
formulas.derivation: Current $I_1$ in outer coil produces uniform field $B_1 = \mu_0 n_1 I_1$. Flux passing through each turn of inner coil of area $A$ is $\Phi_{21} = B_1 A = \mu_0 n_1 I_1 A$. Total linkage with coil 2 ($N_2 = n_2 l$ turns) is $\lambda_2 = N_2 \Phi_{21} = (n_2 l)(\mu_0 n_1 I_1 A) = (\mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l)I_1$. Mutual inductance is $M = \lambda_2 / I_1 = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l$. By reciprocity theorem, $M_{12} = M_{21} = M$.
formulas.description: Mutual inductance between two co-axial solenoids and coupling coefficient $k = M/\sqrt{L_1 L_2} \le 1$.
formulas.explanation: For perfectly coupled coils with zero flux leakage, $k = 1$ and $M = \sqrt{L_1 L_2}$.

formulas.latex: i(t) = I_0 (1 - e^{-t / \tau_L}) \quad (\text{Growth}), \quad i(t) = I_0 e^{-t / \tau_L} \quad (\text{Decay}), \quad \tau_L = \frac{L}{R}
formulas.title: Transient LR Circuit Growth and Decay
formulas.derivation: KVL during growth: $\mathcal{E} - L\frac{di}{dt} - iR = 0 \implies L\frac{di}{dt} = \mathcal{E} - iR$. Separating variables: $\frac{di}{\mathcal{E} - iR} = \frac{dt}{L}$. Integrating with $i(0) = 0$: $-\frac{1}{R}\ln\left(1 - \frac{iR}{\mathcal{E}}\right) = \frac{t}{L} \implies i(t) = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R}\left(1 - e^{-Rt/L}\right)$.
formulas.description: Time-dependent current build-up and decay in inductive RL circuit with inductive time constant $\tau_L = L/R$.
formulas.explanation: At $t = \tau_L = L/R$, current reaches $63.2\%$ of steady value $I_0$; inductor acts as open-circuit at $t=0^+$ and short-circuit as $t \to \infty$.

formulas.title: Root-Mean-Square (RMS) Values of Sinusoidal AC
formulas.derivation: For $i(t) = I_0 \sin(\omega t)$, Joule heat generated in resistor $R$ over one period $T = 2\pi/\omega$ is $H = \int_0^T i^2(t) R dt$. An equivalent DC current $I_{rms}$ dissipates identical heat: $I_{rms}^2 R T = R \int_0^T I_0^2 \sin^2(\omega t) dt$. Since the average of $\sin^2(\omega t)$ over full period is $\frac{1}{2}$: $I_{rms}^2 T = I_0^2 \left(\frac{T}{2}\right) \implies I_{rms} = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}$.
formulas.description: Effective heating value of alternating sinusoidal current and voltage over full periodic cycle.
formulas.explanation: Standard wall outlet voltages (e.g., $230\text{ V}$ or $120\text{ V}$) always quote RMS values; peak voltage is $V_0 = \sqrt{2}V_{rms}$ ($325\text{ V}$ for $230\text{ V}$).

formulas.latex: Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}, \quad X_L = \omega L, \quad X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C}
formulas.title: Impedance of Series LCR Circuit
formulas.derivation: Phasor analysis: current phasor $\tilde{I}$ is common in series loop. Resistor voltage $\tilde{V}_R = I R$ is in phase with current. Inductor voltage $\tilde{V}_L = I X_L$ leads current by $+90^\circ (+i)$. Capacitor voltage $\tilde{V}_C = I X_C$ lags current by $-90^\circ (-i)$. Total complex voltage is $\tilde{V} = \tilde{V}_R + \tilde{V}_L + \tilde{V}_C = I [R + i(X_L - X_C)]$. Impedance magnitude is $Z = |\tilde{V}|/I = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$.
formulas.description: Total opposition to sinusoidal alternating current flow combining resistance, inductive reactance, and capacitive reactance.
formulas.explanation: Phase angle between voltage and current is $\tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R}$.

formulas.title: Resonant Frequency and Quality Factor (Q) of Series LCR
formulas.derivation: Current amplitude is $I_0 = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{R^2 + (\omega L - 1/\omega C)^2}}$. Current is maximized when reactive term vanishes: $\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C} = 0 \implies \omega_0^2 = \frac{1}{LC} \implies \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$. At resonance, impedance is purely resistive ($Z_{min} = R$) and current is in phase with voltage ($\cos\phi = 1$). Quality factor is $Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} = \frac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega}$ where $\Delta\omega$ is bandwidth at half-power points.
formulas.description: Condition for minimum impedance, maximum current resonance, and sharpness factor of resonance curve.
formulas.explanation: High $Q$ produces extremely sharp tuning selectivity in radio receivers and RF filter circuits.

formulas.title: Average AC Power and Power Factor
formulas.derivation: Instantaneous power is $p(t) = v(t)i(t) = [V_0 \sin(\omega t)][I_0 \sin(\omega t - \phi)] = V_0 I_0 \sin(\omega t)[\sin\omega t\cos\phi - \cos\omega t\sin\phi] = V_0 I_0 [\sin^2\omega t\cos\phi - \sin\omega t\cos\omega t\sin\phi]$. Averaging over a full cycle: $\langle \sin^2\omega t \rangle = 1/2$ and $\langle \sin\omega t\cos\omega t \rangle = 0$. Hence $P_{avg} = \frac{1}{2}V_0 I_0 \cos\phi = \left(\frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\left(\frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\cos\phi = V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos\phi$. From impedance triangle, $\cos\phi = R/Z$.
formulas.description: Real active power dissipated in AC circuit over complete cycle governed by phase angle $\phi$.
formulas.explanation: For purely reactive circuits (pure $L$ or pure $C$), $\phi = \pm 90^\circ \implies \cos\phi = 0$, giving zero real power dissipation (wattless current).

formulas.title: Ideal Transformer Voltage, Current and Turns Ratio
formulas.derivation: Assuming ideal core with zero flux leakage: common flux $\Phi$ links both windings. Induced EMFs are $V_p = -N_p \frac{d\Phi}{dt}$ and $V_s = -N_s \frac{d\Phi}{dt}$. Dividing gives $\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$. For an ideal lossless transformer (100% efficiency), input power equals output power: $V_p I_p = V_s I_s \implies \frac{I_p}{I_s} = \frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$.
formulas.description: Transformation of AC voltage and current in magnetically coupled primary and secondary windings.
formulas.explanation: Step-up transformer ($N_s > N_p$): voltage increases and current decreases proportionately, minimizing $I^2 R$ transmission line losses.

formulas.latex: \omega_{LC} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}, \quad q(t) = Q_0 \cos(\omega_{LC} t), \quad i(t) = -\omega_{LC} Q_0 \sin(\omega_{LC} t)
formulas.title: LC Tank Circuit Oscillations
formulas.derivation: Total circuit energy is $E = U_E + U_B = \frac{q^2}{2C} + \frac{1}{2}Li^2$. In lossless circuit, $\frac{dE}{dt} = 0$: $\frac{q}{C}\frac{dq}{dt} + L i \frac{di}{dt} = 0$. Since $i = \frac{dq}{dt}$, dividing by $i$ gives $\frac{q}{C} + L\frac{d^2q}{dt^2} = 0 \implies \frac{d^2q}{dt^2} + \frac{1}{LC}q = 0$. This is standard SHM equation with $\omega_{LC} = 1/\sqrt{LC}$. Solution with initial charge $Q_0$ is $q(t) = Q_0\cos(\omega t)$.
formulas.description: Undamped harmonic exchange of energy between electric field of capacitor and magnetic field of inductor.
formulas.explanation: Energy sloshes sinusoidally between all-electric state ($U_E = Q_0^2/2C$) and all-magnetic state ($U_B = \frac{1}{2}L I_{max}^2$).

formulas.title: Maxwell's Displacement Current
formulas.derivation: Between capacitor plates during charging, no conduction electrons flow, yet magnetic field exists. Electric field is $E = \frac{Q}{\epsilon_0 A} \implies Q = \epsilon_0 E A = \epsilon_0 \Phi_E$. Differentiating charge with respect to time: $I_c = \frac{dQ}{dt} = \epsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$. Maxwell recognized this time-varying flux term acts as an effective displacement current $I_d = \epsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$, restoring Ampere's law to $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 (I_c + I_d)$.
formulas.description: Equivalent current arising from time-varying electric flux, completing Ampere-Maxwell law.
formulas.explanation: Displacement current between plates exactly equals conduction current in the connecting wires ($I_d = I_c$), ensuring continuity.

formulas.title: Speed of Electromagnetic Waves in Vacuum and Field Ratio
formulas.description: Propagation velocity of light from Maxwell's equations and relation between electric and magnetic field amplitudes.
formulas.explanation: Proved that light is an electromagnetic transverse wave propagating at universal speed $c$.

content_json.derivation: Empirical discovery by Michael Faraday (1831). The negative sign (Lenz's Law, Heinrich Lenz 1834) enforces energy conservation: the induced current flows in such a direction that its own magnetic field opposes the original flux change that produced it.
content_json.explanation: If flux increases, induced magnetic field points opposite to applied field; if flux decreases, induced field reinforces it.

formulas.explanation: Explains why photoelectron emission occurs with zero detectable time lag ($< 10^{-9}\text{ s}$) and why emission stops entirely below threshold frequency $\nu_0$ regardless of light intensity.

formulas.title: de Broglie Wavelength of Matter Waves
formulas.derivation: Louis de Broglie hypothesized nature is symmetric: if photons have momentum $p = E/c = h\nu/c = h/\lambda$, matter particles must carry wavelength $\lambda = h/p$. For non-relativistic particle accelerated through voltage $V$: $K = qV = \frac{p^2}{2m} \implies p = \sqrt{2mqV}$. Hence $\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$. For electron ($m = 9.109 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}, q = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$), this evaluates to $\lambda = \frac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}\text{ nm}$.
formulas.description: Wave-particle duality wavelength associated with any material particle of momentum p.
formulas.explanation: Confirmed experimentally by Davisson-Germer electron diffraction on nickel crystals; forms the basis of electron microscopy.

formulas.title: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle
formulas.derivation: Follows from Fourier transform properties of wavepackets: spatial width $\Delta x$ and wavenumber spread $\Delta k$ obey $\Delta x \Delta k \ge 1/2$. Using de Broglie relation $p = \hbar k \implies \Delta p = \hbar \Delta k$, multiplying by $\hbar$ yields $\Delta x \Delta p_x \ge \hbar / 2$.
formulas.description: Fundamental quantum limit on simultaneous measurement precision of conjugate variables.
formulas.explanation: Strict quantum mechanical property; proves why electrons cannot exist inside atomic nuclei.

formulas.latex: r_n = \frac{n^2 h^2 \epsilon_0}{\pi m e^2 Z} = \frac{n^2}{Z} a_0, \quad a_0 \approx 0.529 \text{ \AA}
formulas.title: Bohr Atomic Model: Orbital Radii
formulas.derivation: Bohr's quantization postulate: $m v r = \frac{n h}{2\pi} \implies v = \frac{n h}{2\pi m r}$. Coulomb force supplies centripetal force: $\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Z e^2}{r^2} = \frac{m v^2}{r} = \frac{m}{r}\left(\frac{n h}{2\pi m r}\right)^2 = \frac{n^2 h^2}{4\pi^2 m r^3}$. Solving for $r$: $r_n = \frac{\epsilon_0 n^2 h^2}{\pi m Z e^2} = \frac{n^2}{Z} a_0$.
formulas.description: Quantized orbital radii of hydrogen-like single-electron atoms.
formulas.explanation: Orbital radius scales as $n^2 / Z$.

formulas.latex: E_n = -\frac{m Z^2 e^4}{8 \epsilon_0^2 h^2 n^2} = -13.6 \frac{Z^2}{n^2} \text{ eV}
formulas.title: Bohr Atomic Model: Quantized Energy Levels
formulas.derivation: Kinetic energy: $K = \frac{1}{2}m v^2 = \frac{1}{8\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Z e^2}{r}$. Potential energy: $U = -\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Z e^2}{r}$. Total energy: $E = K + U = -\frac{1}{8\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Z e^2}{r} = -K = \frac{1}{2}U$. Substituting orbital radius $r_n$: $E_n = -\frac{m Z^2 e^4}{8\epsilon_0^2 h^2 n^2} = -13.6 \frac{Z^2}{n^2}\text{ eV}$.
formulas.description: Total discrete energy levels of bound electron in hydrogenic atom.
formulas.explanation: Negative sign signifies bound state. Ground state of hydrogen ($n=1, Z=1$) has ionization energy $13.6\text{ eV}$.

formulas.title: Rydberg Formula for Hydrogen Spectral Series

formulas.derivation: Conservation of energy: $E_{photon} = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = E_{n_2} - E_{n_1} = \frac{m Z^2 e^4}{8\epsilon_0^2 h^2}\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$. Dividing by $hc$: $\frac{1}{\lambda} = \left(\frac{m e^4}{8\epsilon_0^2 h^3 c}\right) Z^2 \left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right) = R_H Z^2 \left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$.
formulas.description: Wavenumber of photon emitted or absorbed during electron transition between quantum states $n_2 \to n_1$.
formulas.explanation: Lyman series ($n_1=1$, Ultraviolet); Balmer series ($n_1=2$, Visible); Paschen series ($n_1=3$, Infrared); Brackett ($n_1=4$); Pfund ($n_1=5$).

formulas.latex: N(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda t} = N_0 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t / T_{1/2}}, \quad T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda} \approx \frac{0.693}{\lambda}, \quad \tau = \frac{1}{\lambda}
formulas.title: Law of Radioactive Decay
formulas.derivation: Rate of disintegration is directly proportional to present population: $-\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N \implies \frac{dN}{N} = -\lambda dt$. Integrating from $t=0$ ($N=N_0$) to $t$: $\ln(N/N_0) = -\lambda t \implies N(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$. At half-life $t = T_{1/2}$, $N = N_0 / 2$: $e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}} = 1/2 \implies \lambda T_{1/2} = \ln 2 \implies T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda} \approx \frac{0.693}{\lambda}$. Mean life is $\tau = \frac{1}{N_0}\int_0^\infty N(t)dt = \frac{1}{\lambda}$.
formulas.description: Exponential disintegration of unstable radionuclides, half-life $T_{1/2}$, and mean lifetime $\tau$.
formulas.explanation: Activity is $A(t) = -dN/dt = \lambda N(t) = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$; 1 Becquerel (Bq) $= 1\text{ decay/sec}$, 1 Curie (Ci) $= 3.7 \times 10^{10}\text{ Bq}$.

formulas.latex: \Delta m = [Z m_p + (A - Z)m_n] - M_{nucleus}, \quad E_b = \Delta m \cdot c^2 = \Delta m (931.5 \text{ MeV/u})
formulas.title: Nuclear Mass Defect and Binding Energy
formulas.derivation: Free nucleons have greater combined rest mass than the bound composite nucleus. The missing mass $\Delta m = Z m_p + (A-Z)m_n - M$ was liberated as binding energy during nucleosynthesis following Einstein's mass-energy equivalence $E = \Delta m \cdot c^2$. Using $1\text{ u} = 1.6605 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$ and $c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$ yields $1\text{ u} \equiv 931.5\text{ MeV}$.
formulas.description: Mass converted into binding energy holding nucleons together within the nucleus.
formulas.explanation: Binding energy per nucleon curve peaks near Iron-56 ($E_b/A \approx 8.8\text{ MeV/nucleon}$), explaining why light nuclei undergo nuclear fusion and heavy nuclei undergo nuclear fission.

formulas.latex: R = R_0 A^{1/3}, \quad R_0 \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \text{ m} = 1.2 \text{ fm}, \quad \rho_{nuclear} \approx 2.3 \times 10^{17} \text{ kg/m}^3
formulas.title: Nuclear Radius and Constant Nuclear Density
formulas.derivation: High-energy electron scattering experiments demonstrate nuclear volume is directly proportional to number of nucleons $A$: $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \propto A \implies R = R_0 A^{1/3}$. Nuclear mass is $M \approx A m_N$. Density is $\rho = \frac{M}{V} = \frac{A m_N}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \frac{3 m_N}{4\pi R_0^3} = \text{constant} \approx 2.3 \times 10^{17}\text{ kg/m}^3$.
formulas.description: Nuclear size scaling with mass number A and universal nuclear matter density.
formulas.explanation: Nuclear density is invariant across the entire periodic table, independent of atomic number.

formulas.latex: n_i^2 = n_e n_h \quad (\text{Mass Action Law}), \quad I = I_0 (e^{e V / \eta k_B T} - 1) \quad (\text{Diode Equation})
formulas.title: Semiconductor Mass Action Law and Shockley Diode Equation
formulas.derivation: Law of Mass Action: thermal generation rate of electron-hole pairs equals recombination rate $R = r n_e n_h$. In thermal equilibrium, generation equals recombination, yielding $n_e n_h = n_i^2$, valid for both intrinsic and doped extrinsic semiconductors. Shockley diode equation follows from Boltzmann diffusion of majority carriers across depletion barrier: $I = I_0(e^{eV / \eta k_B T} - 1)$.
formulas.description: Carrier concentration product in thermal equilibrium and I-V characteristic of p-n junction diode.
formulas.explanation: For n-type semiconductor ($n_e \approx N_D$), minority hole density drops to $n_h = n_i^2 / N_D$.

formulas.title: Bipolar Junction Transistor (BJT) Current Gains
formulas.derivation: By Kirchhoff's law on transistor: $I_E = I_B + I_C$. Dividing by $I_C$: $\frac{I_E}{I_C} = \frac{I_B}{I_C} + 1 \implies \frac{1}{\alpha} = \frac{1}{\beta} + 1 = \frac{1 + \beta}{\beta}$. Inverting yields $\alpha = \frac{\beta}{1 + \beta}$. Solving for $\beta$ gives $\beta = \frac{\alpha}{1 - \alpha}$.
formulas.description: Common-base current gain $\alpha$ and common-emitter current gain $\beta$ relations.
formulas.explanation: Small variations in base current produce large amplified collector current swings.

formulas.latex: V_{ripple} = \frac{I_{dc}}{2 f C} \quad (\text{Full-Wave Rectifier with Capacitor Filter})
formulas.title: Rectifier Ripple Voltage
formulas.derivation: Capacitor discharges through load resistor $R_L$ between successive rectification peaks for duration $\Delta t \approx T/2 = \frac{1}{2f}$. Charge lost is $\Delta Q = I_{dc} \Delta t = \frac{I_{dc}}{2f}$. Ripple voltage is $\Delta V = \frac{\Delta Q}{C} = \frac{I_{dc}}{2f C} = \frac{V_{dc}}{2f R_L C}$.
formulas.description: Peak-to-peak AC ripple voltage across capacitor filter in full-wave rectifier.
formulas.explanation: Ripple is halved compared to half-wave rectifier ($\frac{I_{dc}}{f C}$); higher capacitance yields smoother DC output.

formulas.title: Duane-Hunt Law for Continuous X-Ray Cutoff
formulas.derivation: Electrons strike heavy metal target (Tungsten/Molybdenum) after gaining kinetic energy $K = e V_a$. When an incoming electron loses 100% of its kinetic energy in a single braking deceleration impact with target nucleus, the emitted Bremsstrahlung photon carries maximum energy: $h\nu_{max} = \frac{hc}{\lambda_{min}} = e V_a$. Solving for $\lambda_{min}$ yields $\lambda_{min} = \frac{hc}{e V_a} = \frac{1240}{V_a}\text{ nm}$.
formulas.description: Shortest wavelength limit of Bremsstrahlung continuous X-ray spectrum at accelerating potential $V_a$.
formulas.explanation: Depends strictly on accelerating tube voltage $V_a$ and is completely independent of target anode material.

formulas.latex: \sqrt{\nu} = a(Z - b) \quad (\text{Moseley's Law for Characteristic X-Rays})
formulas.title: Moseley's Law
formulas.derivation: Henry Moseley (1913) analyzed characteristic X-ray transitions: an inner $K$-shell vacancy is screened by remaining electron, so effective nuclear charge seen by transition electron is $Z_{eff} = Z - 1$. Applying Bohr formula: $\nu = R_H c (Z - 1)^2 \left(\frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{2^2}\right) = \frac{3}{4}R_H c (Z - 1)^2$. Taking square root: $\sqrt{\nu} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{4}R_H c}(Z - 1) = a(Z - 1)$.
formulas.description: Linear relationship between square root of characteristic X-ray line frequency and nuclear atomic number Z.
formulas.explanation: Historical breakthrough proving the periodic table must be ordered by atomic number $Z$ (nuclear proton count), not atomic weight.

formulas.title: Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction and Lenz's Law
formulas.derivation: Empirical discovery by Michael Faraday (1831). The negative sign (Lenz's Law, Heinrich Lenz 1834) enforces energy conservation: the induced current flows in such a direction that its own magnetic field opposes the original flux change that produced it.
formulas.description: Induced electromotive force in a circuit equals negative rate of change of magnetic flux through loop.
formulas.explanation: If flux increases, induced magnetic field points opposite to applied field; if flux decreases, induced field reinforces it.

formulas.title: Motional EMF in a Moving Conductor
formulas.derivation: Mobile conduction electrons inside rod experience magnetic Lorentz force $\vec{F}_B = -e(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$. Work done moving an electron through length $\vec{l}$ is $W = \int \vec{F}_B \cdot d\vec{l} = -e \int (\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot d\vec{l}$. Induced EMF is work done per unit positive charge: $\mathcal{E} = W/(-e) = (\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot\vec{l} = B v l\sin\theta$.
formulas.description: Electromotive force induced across ends of a conducting rod of length l translating with speed v through magnetic field B.
formulas.explanation: Forms the foundation of electrical power generation in alternators and dynamos.

formulas.title: Rotational Motional EMF of a Rotating Rod
formulas.derivation: Consider element $dr$ at distance $r$ from pivot: linear velocity is $v(r) = r\omega$. Motional EMF generated across element is $d\mathcal{E} = B v(r) dr = B(r\omega)dr$. Integrating from pivot $r=0$ to tip $r=l$: $\mathcal{E} = B\omega \int_0^l r dr = B\omega \left[\frac{r^2}{2}\right]_0^l = \frac{1}{2}B\omega l^2$.
formulas.description: EMF induced between pivot and tip of a conducting rod of length l rotating with angular speed $\omega$ in perpendicular field B.
formulas.explanation: Also equals $B\left(\frac{dA}{dt}\right) = B\left(\frac{1}{2}l^2\omega\right)$, matching rate of area swept.

formulas.latex: Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}, \quad X_L = \omega L, \quad X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C}

formulas.derivation: Phasor analysis: current phasor $\tilde{I}$ is common in series loop. Resistor voltage $\tilde{V}_R = I R$ is in phase with current. formulas.description: Total opposition to sinusoidal alternating current flow combining resistance, inductive reactance, and capacitive reactance.
formulas.explanation: Phase angle between voltage and current is $\tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R}$.

formulas.title: Resonant Frequency and Quality Factor (Q) of Series LCR
formulas.derivation: Current amplitude is $I_0 = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{R^2 + (\omega L - 1/\omega C)^2}}$. At resonance, impedance is purely resistive ($Z_{min} = R$) and current is in phase with voltage ($\cos\phi = 1$). formulas.description: Condition for minimum impedance, maximum current resonance, and sharpness factor of resonance curve.
formulas.explanation: High $Q$ produces extremely sharp tuning selectivity in radio receivers and RF filter circuits.

formulas.title: Average AC Power and Power Factor
formulas.derivation: Instantaneous power is $p(t) = v(t)i(t) = [V_0 \sin(\omega t)][I_0 \sin(\omega t - \phi)] = V_0 I_0 \sin(\omega t)[\sin\omega t\cos\phi - \cos\omega t\sin\phi] = V_0 I_0 [\sin^2\omega t\cos\phi - \sin\omega t\cos\omega t\sin\phi]$. Hence $P_{avg} = \frac{1}{2}V_0 I_0 \cos\phi = \left(\frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\left(\frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\cos\phi = V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos\phi$. From impedance triangle, $\cos\phi = R/Z$.
formulas.description: Real active power dissipated in AC circuit over complete cycle governed by phase angle $\phi$.
formulas.explanation: For purely reactive circuits (pure $L$ or pure $C$), $\phi = \pm 90^\circ \implies \cos\phi = 0$, giving zero real power dissipation (wattless current).

formulas.title: Ideal Transformer Voltage, Current and Turns Ratio
formulas.derivation: Assuming ideal core with zero flux leakage: common flux $\Phi$ links both windings. Induced EMFs are $V_p = -N_p \frac{d\Phi}{dt}$ and $V_s = -N_s \frac{d\Phi}{dt}$. formulas.explanation: Step-up transformer ($N_s > N_p$): voltage increases and current decreases proportionately, minimizing $I^2 R$ transmission line losses.

formulas.explanation: Displacement current between plates exactly equals conduction current in the connecting wires ($I_d = I_c$), ensuring continuity.

An equivalent DC current $I_{rms}$ dissipates identical heat: $I_{rms}^2 R T = R \int_0^T I_0^2 \sin^2(\omega t) dt$. formulas.latex: Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}, \quad X_L = \omega L, \quad X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C}

formulas.derivation: Phasor analysis: current phasor $\tilde{I}$ is common in series loop. Resistor voltage $\tilde{V}_R = I R$ is in phase with current. Total complex voltage is $\tilde{V} = \tilde{V}_R + \tilde{V}_L + \tilde{V}_C = I [R + i(X_L - X_C)]$. Impedance magnitude is $Z = |\tilde{V}|/I = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$.
formulas.description: Total opposition to sinusoidal alternating current flow combining resistance, inductive reactance, and capacitive reactance.
formulas.explanation: Phase angle between voltage and current is $\tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R}$.

formulas.title: Resonant Frequency and Quality Factor (Q) of Series LCR
formulas.derivation: Current amplitude is $I_0 = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{R^2 + (\omega L - 1/\omega C)^2}}$. Current is maximized when reactive term vanishes: $\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C} = 0 \implies \omega_0^2 = \frac{1}{LC} \implies \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$. At resonance, impedance is purely resistive ($Z_{min} = R$) and current is in phase with voltage ($\cos\phi = 1$). Quality factor is $Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} = \frac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega}$ where $\Delta\omega$ is bandwidth at half-power points.
formulas.description: Condition for minimum impedance, maximum current resonance, and sharpness factor of resonance curve.
formulas.explanation: High $Q$ produces extremely sharp tuning selectivity in radio receivers and RF filter circuits.

formulas.title: Average AC Power and Power Factor
formulas.derivation: Instantaneous power is $p(t) = v(t)i(t) = [V_0 \sin(\omega t)][I_0 \sin(\omega t - \phi)] = V_0 I_0 \sin(\omega t)[\sin\omega t\cos\phi - \cos\omega t\sin\phi] = V_0 I_0 [\sin^2\omega t\cos\phi - \sin\omega t\cos\omega t\sin\phi]$. Hence $P_{avg} = \frac{1}{2}V_0 I_0 \cos\phi = \left(\frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\left(\frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\cos\phi = V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos\phi$. From impedance triangle, $\cos\phi = R/Z$.
formulas.description: Real active power dissipated in AC circuit over complete cycle governed by phase angle $\phi$.
formulas.explanation: For purely reactive circuits (pure $L$ or pure $C$), $\phi = \pm 90^\circ \implies \cos\phi = 0$, giving zero real power dissipation (wattless current).

formulas.title: Ideal Transformer Voltage, Current and Turns Ratio
formulas.derivation: Assuming ideal core with zero flux leakage: common flux $\Phi$ links both windings. Induced EMFs are $V_p = -N_p \frac{d\Phi}{dt}$ and $V_s = -N_s \frac{d\Phi}{dt}$. formulas.description: Transformation of AC voltage and current in magnetically coupled primary and secondary windings.
formulas.explanation: Step-up transformer ($N_s > N_p$): voltage increases and current decreases proportionately, minimizing $I^2 R$ transmission line losses.

formulas.explanation: Displacement current between plates exactly equals conduction current in the connecting wires ($I_d = I_c$), ensuring continuity.

formulas.explanation: Also equals $B\left(\frac{dA}{dt}\right) = B\left(\frac{1}{2}l^2\omega\right)$, matching rate of area swept.

formulas.latex: L = \frac{N \Phi_B}{I} = \mu_0 n^2 A l, \quad U_B = \frac{1}{2}L I^2, \quad u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}
formulas.title: Self-Inductance and Magnetic Energy Density
formulas.derivation: Inside solenoid, field is $B = \mu_0 n I$. Flux per turn is $\Phi = B A = \mu_0 n I A$. Total linkage is $\lambda = N\Phi = (nl)(\mu_0 n I A) = (\mu_0 n^2 A l)I$. By definition $L = \lambda / I = \mu_0 n^2 A l$. Work required to establish current $I$ against back-EMF $\mathcal{E}_L = -L\frac{di}{dt}$ is $U = \int P\,dt = \int (L\frac{di}{dt} i)dt = L \int_0^I i\,di = \frac{1}{2}LI^2$. Dividing by volume $V = Al$ and using $B = \mu_0 n I$ yields $u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$.
formulas.description: Self-inductance of solenoid, total energy stored in inductor magnetic field, and volume energy density.
formulas.explanation: Analogous to kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ and electrostatic energy density $\frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0 E^2$.

formulas.latex: M = \frac{N_2 \Phi_{21}}{I_1} = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l, \quad M \le \sqrt{L_1 L_2}
formulas.title: Mutual Inductance and Coupling Coefficient
formulas.derivation: Current $I_1$ in outer coil produces uniform field $B_1 = \mu_0 n_1 I_1$. Flux passing through each turn of inner coil of area $A$ is $\Phi_{21} = B_1 A = \mu_0 n_1 I_1 A$. Total linkage with coil 2 ($N_2 = n_2 l$ turns) is $\lambda_2 = N_2 \Phi_{21} = (n_2 l)(\mu_0 n_1 I_1 A) = (\mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l)I_1$. Mutual inductance is $M = \lambda_2 / I_1 = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l$. By reciprocity theorem, $M_{12} = M_{21} = M$.
formulas.description: Mutual inductance between two co-axial solenoids and coupling coefficient $k = M/\sqrt{L_1 L_2} \le 1$.
formulas.explanation: For perfectly coupled coils with zero flux leakage, $k = 1$ and $M = \sqrt{L_1 L_2}$.

formulas.latex: i(t) = I_0 (1 - e^{-t / \tau_L}) \quad (\text{Growth}), \quad i(t) = I_0 e^{-t / \tau_L} \quad (\text{Decay}), \quad \tau_L = \frac{L}{R}
formulas.title: Transient LR Circuit Growth and Decay
formulas.derivation: KVL during growth: $\mathcal{E} - L\frac{di}{dt} - iR = 0 \implies L\frac{di}{dt} = \mathcal{E} - iR$. Separating variables: $\frac{di}{\mathcal{E} - iR} = \frac{dt}{L}$. Integrating with $i(0) = 0$: $-\frac{1}{R}\ln\left(1 - \frac{iR}{\mathcal{E}}\right) = \frac{t}{L} \implies i(t) = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R}\left(1 - e^{-Rt/L}\right)$.
formulas.description: Time-dependent current build-up and decay in inductive RL circuit with inductive time constant $\tau_L = L/R$.
formulas.explanation: At $t = \tau_L = L/R$, current reaches $63.2\%$ of steady value $I_0$; inductor acts as open-circuit at $t=0^+$ and short-circuit as $t \to \infty$.

formulas.title: Root-Mean-Square (RMS) Values of Sinusoidal AC
formulas.derivation: For $i(t) = I_0 \sin(\omega t)$, Joule heat generated in resistor $R$ over one period $T = 2\pi/\omega$ is $H = \int_0^T i^2(t) R dt$. An equivalent DC current $I_{rms}$ dissipates identical heat: $I_{rms}^2 R T = R \int_0^T I_0^2 \sin^2(\omega t) dt$. Since the average of $\sin^2(\omega t)$ over full period is $\frac{1}{2}$: $I_{rms}^2 T = I_0^2 \left(\frac{T}{2}\right) \implies I_{rms} = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}$.
formulas.description: Effective heating value of alternating sinusoidal current and voltage over full periodic cycle.
formulas.explanation: Standard wall outlet voltages (e.g., $230\text{ V}$ or $120\text{ V}$) always quote RMS values; peak voltage is $V_0 = \sqrt{2}V_{rms}$ ($325\text{ V}$ for $230\text{ V}$).

formulas.latex: Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}, \quad X_L = \omega L, \quad X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C}
formulas.title: Impedance of Series LCR Circuit
formulas.derivation: Phasor analysis: current phasor $\tilde{I}$ is common in series loop. Resistor voltage $\tilde{V}_R = I R$ is in phase with current. Inductor voltage $\tilde{V}_L = I X_L$ leads current by $+90^\circ (+i)$. Capacitor voltage $\tilde{V}_C = I X_C$ lags current by $-90^\circ (-i)$. Total complex voltage is $\tilde{V} = \tilde{V}_R + \tilde{V}_L + \tilde{V}_C = I [R + i(X_L - X_C)]$. Impedance magnitude is $Z = |\tilde{V}|/I = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$.
formulas.description: Total opposition to sinusoidal alternating current flow combining resistance, inductive reactance, and capacitive reactance.
formulas.explanation: Phase angle between voltage and current is $\tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R}$.

formulas.title: Resonant Frequency and Quality Factor (Q) of Series LCR
formulas.derivation: Current amplitude is $I_0 = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{R^2 + (\omega L - 1/\omega C)^2}}$. Current is maximized when reactive term vanishes: $\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C} = 0 \implies \omega_0^2 = \frac{1}{LC} \implies \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$. At resonance, impedance is purely resistive ($Z_{min} = R$) and current is in phase with voltage ($\cos\phi = 1$). Quality factor is $Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} = \frac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega}$ where $\Delta\omega$ is bandwidth at half-power points.
formulas.description: Condition for minimum impedance, maximum current resonance, and sharpness factor of resonance curve.
formulas.explanation: High $Q$ produces extremely sharp tuning selectivity in radio receivers and RF filter circuits.

formulas.title: Average AC Power and Power Factor
formulas.derivation: Instantaneous power is $p(t) = v(t)i(t) = [V_0 \sin(\omega t)][I_0 \sin(\omega t - \phi)] = V_0 I_0 \sin(\omega t)[\sin\omega t\cos\phi - \cos\omega t\sin\phi] = V_0 I_0 [\sin^2\omega t\cos\phi - \sin\omega t\cos\omega t\sin\phi]$. Averaging over a full cycle: $\langle \sin^2\omega t \rangle = 1/2$ and $\langle \sin\omega t\cos\omega t \rangle = 0$. Hence $P_{avg} = \frac{1}{2}V_0 I_0 \cos\phi = \left(\frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\left(\frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\cos\phi = V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos\phi$. From impedance triangle, $\cos\phi = R/Z$.
formulas.description: Real active power dissipated in AC circuit over complete cycle governed by phase angle $\phi$.
formulas.explanation: For purely reactive circuits (pure $L$ or pure $C$), $\phi = \pm 90^\circ \implies \cos\phi = 0$, giving zero real power dissipation (wattless current).

formulas.title: Ideal Transformer Voltage, Current and Turns Ratio
formulas.derivation: Assuming ideal core with zero flux leakage: common flux $\Phi$ links both windings. Induced EMFs are $V_p = -N_p \frac{d\Phi}{dt}$ and $V_s = -N_s \frac{d\Phi}{dt}$. Dividing gives $\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$. For an ideal lossless transformer (100% efficiency), input power equals output power: $V_p I_p = V_s I_s \implies \frac{I_p}{I_s} = \frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$.
formulas.description: Transformation of AC voltage and current in magnetically coupled primary and secondary windings.
formulas.explanation: Step-up transformer ($N_s > N_p$): voltage increases and current decreases proportionately, minimizing $I^2 R$ transmission line losses.

formulas.latex: \omega_{LC} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}, \quad q(t) = Q_0 \cos(\omega_{LC} t), \quad i(t) = -\omega_{LC} Q_0 \sin(\omega_{LC} t)
formulas.title: LC Tank Circuit Oscillations
formulas.derivation: Total circuit energy is $E = U_E + U_B = \frac{q^2}{2C} + \frac{1}{2}Li^2$. In lossless circuit, $\frac{dE}{dt} = 0$: $\frac{q}{C}\frac{dq}{dt} + L i \frac{di}{dt} = 0$. Since $i = \frac{dq}{dt}$, dividing by $i$ gives $\frac{q}{C} + L\frac{d^2q}{dt^2} = 0 \implies \frac{d^2q}{dt^2} + \frac{1}{LC}q = 0$. This is standard SHM equation with $\omega_{LC} = 1/\sqrt{LC}$. Solution with initial charge $Q_0$ is $q(t) = Q_0\cos(\omega t)$.
formulas.description: Undamped harmonic exchange of energy between electric field of capacitor and magnetic field of inductor.
formulas.explanation: Energy sloshes sinusoidally between all-electric state ($U_E = Q_0^2/2C$) and all-magnetic state ($U_B = \frac{1}{2}L I_{max}^2$).

formulas.title: Maxwell's Displacement Current
formulas.derivation: Between capacitor plates during charging, no conduction electrons flow, yet magnetic field exists. Electric field is $E = \frac{Q}{\epsilon_0 A} \implies Q = \epsilon_0 E A = \epsilon_0 \Phi_E$. Differentiating charge with respect to time: $I_c = \frac{dQ}{dt} = \epsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$. Maxwell recognized this time-varying flux term acts as an effective displacement current $I_d = \epsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$, restoring Ampere's law to $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 (I_c + I_d)$.
formulas.description: Equivalent current arising from time-varying electric flux, completing Ampere-Maxwell law.
formulas.explanation: Displacement current between plates exactly equals conduction current in the connecting wires ($I_d = I_c$), ensuring continuity.

formulas.title: Speed of Electromagnetic Waves in Vacuum and Field Ratio
formulas.description: Propagation velocity of light from Maxwell's equations and relation between electric and magnetic field amplitudes.
formulas.explanation: Proved that light is an electromagnetic transverse wave propagating at universal speed $c$.

content_json.derivation: Empirical discovery by Michael Faraday (1831). The negative sign (Lenz's Law, Heinrich Lenz 1834) enforces energy conservation: the induced current flows in such a direction that its own magnetic field opposes the original flux change that produced it.
content_json.explanation: If flux increases, induced magnetic field points opposite to applied field; if flux decreases, induced field reinforces it.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: JEE Master: Solutions & Colligative Properties
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: Francois-Marie Raoult (1887) observed that escaping tendency of volatile solvent molecules from liquid surface into vapor phase is directly proportional to surface fraction of that component. In an ideal solution with identical intermolecular forces ($A-A \approx B-B \approx A-B$), surface mole fraction equals bulk liquid mole fraction $x_A$, giving $P_A = P_A^\circ x_A$. Dalton's law of partial pressures gives $P_{total} = P_A + P_B = P_A^\circ x_A + P_B^\circ(1 - x_A) = P_B^\circ + (P_A^\circ - P_B^\circ)x_A$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Vapor phase mole fraction $y_A$ is enriched in more volatile component: $y_A = \frac{P_A}{P_{total}} = \frac{P_A^\circ x_A}{P_{total}}$ (Konovalov's rule).

content_json.title: JEE Master: Solutions & Colligative Properties

sections.title: JEE Master: Solutions & Colligative Properties - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.latex: P_A = P_A^\circ x_A, \quad P_{total} = P_A^\circ x_A + P_B^\circ x_B = P_B^\circ + (P_A^\circ - P_B^\circ)x_A
formulas.title: Raoult's Law for Ideal Binary Liquid Mixtures

variables.P_A, P_B: Partial vapor pressures of components A and B
variables.P_A^\\circ, P_B^\\circ: Vapor pressures of pure components A and B

formulas.derivation: Francois-Marie Raoult (1887) observed that escaping tendency of volatile solvent molecules from liquid surface into vapor phase is directly proportional to surface fraction of that component. In an ideal solution with identical intermolecular forces ($A-A \approx B-B \approx A-B$), surface mole fraction equals bulk liquid mole fraction $x_A$, giving $P_A = P_A^\circ x_A$. Dalton's law of partial pressures gives $P_{total} = P_A + P_B = P_A^\circ x_A + P_B^\circ(1 - x_A) = P_B^\circ + (P_A^\circ - P_B^\circ)x_A$.
formulas.description: Partial vapor pressure of volatile liquid component proportional to its liquid mole fraction.
formulas.explanation: Vapor phase mole fraction $y_A$ is enriched in more volatile component: $y_A = \frac{P_A}{P_{total}} = \frac{P_A^\circ x_A}{P_{total}}$ (Konovalov's rule).

formulas.latex: P = K_H \cdot x, \quad m = K_H' \cdot P
formulas.title: Henry's Law for Gas Solubility in Liquids

variables.m: Mass of dissolved gas per unit volume
variables.x: Mole fraction of gas in liquid solution

formulas.derivation: William Henry (1803) showed that at dynamic equilibrium, rate of gas dissolution equals rate of gas escape. Since rate of gas condensation into solvent is proportional to collision frequency with liquid surface ($r_{in} \propto P$), dynamic balance requires $x \propto P \implies P = K_H x$.
formulas.description: Solubility of sparingly soluble gas in liquid is directly proportional to partial pressure of gas above liquid.
formulas.explanation: Henry's constant $K_H$ increases with rising temperature, explaining why gas solubility in water decreases as temperature rises (thermal pollution harms aquatic life).

formulas.latex: \frac{P_1^\circ - P_1}{P_1^\circ} = i \cdot x_2 \approx i \cdot \frac{n_2}{n_1} = i \cdot \frac{w_2 M_1}{M_2 w_1}
formulas.title: Relative Lowering of Vapor Pressure (RLVP)
formulas.derivation: From Raoult's law for non-volatile solute ($P_2 = 0$): $P_1 = P_1^\circ x_1 = P_1^\circ(1 - x_2)$. Rearranging: $P_1^\circ - P_1 = P_1^\circ x_2 \implies \frac{P_1^\circ - P_1}{P_1^\circ} = x_2$. For electrolyte solute, multiply by van 't Hoff factor $i$. In dilute solution ($n_2 \ll n_1$): $x_2 = \frac{n_2}{n_1 + n_2} \approx \frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{w_2 / M_2}{w_1 / M_1} = \frac{w_2 M_1}{M_2 w_1}$.
formulas.description: First colligative property: proportional vapor pressure reduction caused by dissolving non-volatile solute.
formulas.explanation: Accurately measures solute molar mass $M_2 = \frac{w_2 M_1}{w_1 \cdot (\Delta P / P_1^\circ)}$ via Ostwald-Walker dynamic method.

formulas.latex: \Delta T_b = i \cdot K_b \cdot m, \quad K_b = \frac{R M_1 T_b^2}{1000 \Delta H_{vap}}
formulas.title: Elevation of Boiling Point (Ebullioscopy)

variables.K_b: Molal boiling point elevation constant ($0.512\text{ K kg/mol for water}$)

formulas.derivation: Boiling occurs when solution vapor pressure reaches external atmospheric pressure. Lowering of vapor pressure shifts boiling curve to higher temperature: from Clausius-Clapeyron equation $\frac{\Delta P}{P^\circ} \approx \frac{\Delta H_{vap} \Delta T_b}{R (T_b^\circ)^2}$. By Raoult's law, $\frac{\Delta P}{P^\circ} = x_2 = \frac{n_2}{w_1 / M_1} = \frac{M_1}{1000}m$. Equating gives $\Delta T_b = \left(\frac{R M_1 (T_b^\circ)^2}{1000 \Delta H_{vap}}\right) m = K_b m$. Accounting for ion dissociation gives $\Delta T_b = i K_b m$.
formulas.description: Boiling point rise proportional to solution molality m and ebullioscopic constant $K_b$.
formulas.explanation: Depends strictly on solvent properties and number of solute particles, not on solute chemical identity.

formulas.latex: \Delta T_f = i \cdot K_f \cdot m, \quad K_f = \frac{R M_1 T_f^2}{1000 \Delta H_{fus}}
formulas.title: Depression of Freezing Point (Cryoscopy)

variables.K_f: Molal freezing point depression constant ($1.86\text{ K kg/mol for water}$)

formulas.derivation: Freezing occurs when liquid solvent chemical potential matches solid ice chemical potential: $\mu_{solvent}(l) = \mu_{solid}(s)$. Presence of solute lowers solvent chemical potential by $-RT\ln x_1 \approx RT x_2$. Equating to chemical potential shift from cooling: $\Delta T_f \frac{\Delta H_{fus}}{T_f^\circ} = R T_f^\circ x_2 = R T_f^\circ \left(\frac{M_1}{1000}m\right) \implies \Delta T_f = \left(\frac{R M_1 (T_f^\circ)^2}{1000 \Delta H_{fus}}\right)m = K_f m$. For ionizing solute, $\Delta T_f = i K_f m$.
formulas.description: Freezing point depression proportional to molality m and cryoscopic constant $K_f$.
formulas.explanation: Applied in road de-icing using rock salt ($NaCl$) or calcium chloride ($CaCl_2$) and ethylene glycol anti-freeze in vehicle radiators.

formulas.latex: \Pi = i \cdot C R T = i \cdot \frac{n_2}{V} R T = i \cdot \frac{w_2}{M_2 V} R T
formulas.title: van 't Hoff Equation for Osmotic Pressure
formulas.derivation: Jacobus Henricus van 't Hoff (1887) recognized thermodynamic equivalence between dilute solute molecules in solvent and ideal gas molecules in vacuum: chemical potential of pure solvent across membrane at pressure $P + \Pi$ must equal solution chemical potential at pressure $P$: $\mu_1^\circ(P + \Pi) = \mu_1(P) = \mu_1^\circ(P) + RT\ln x_1$. Expanding $\mu_1^\circ(P + \Pi) - \mu_1^\circ(P) = \int_P^{P+\Pi} V_m dP = \Pi V_m$. Using $\ln x_1 = \ln(1 - x_2) \approx -x_2 = -n_2 / n_1$: $\Pi V_m = RT(n_2 / n_1) \implies \Pi (n_1 V_m) = n_2 RT$. Since $n_1 V_m = V$ (total solution volume): $\Pi V = n_2 RT \implies \Pi = CRT$. Multiplying by $i$ for electrolytes gives $\Pi = iCRT$.
formulas.description: Hydrostatic excess pressure required to halt osmosis across semipermeable membrane.
formulas.explanation: The most sensitive colligative property for determining high molar masses of macromolecules, proteins, and synthetic polymers.

formulas.title: van 't Hoff Factor (i) Relations for Dissociation and Association

variables.n: Number of ions produced per formula unit

formulas.derivation: Dissociation: 1 mole of $A_n$ dissociates to give $(1-\alpha)$ moles of reactant and $n\alpha$ moles of ions. Total particles in solution is $N_{total} = (1-\alpha) + n\alpha = 1 + (n-1)\alpha$. By definition $i = \frac{\text{Actual moles}}{\text{Theoretical moles}} = \frac{1 + (n-1)\alpha}{1} = 1 + (n-1)\alpha$. Association: $n A \rightleftharpoons A_n$. Starting with 1 mole: remaining monomer is $1-\beta$, associated cluster is $\beta/n$. Total particles: $N_{total} = (1-\beta) + \beta/n = 1 - \left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)\beta \implies i = 1 - \left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)\beta$.
formulas.description: Calculates experimental van 't Hoff factor from degree of dissociation $\alpha$ or degree of dimerization/association $\beta$.
formulas.explanation: For benzoic acid dimerizing in benzene ($n=2$), $i = 1 - \beta/2 < 1$. For $K_4[Fe(CN)_6]$ completely dissociated ($n=5, \alpha=1$), $i = 5$.

formulas.title: Abnormal Molecular Mass and van 't Hoff Factor
formulas.derivation: Colligative properties $\Delta$ scale inversely with observed molar mass: $\Delta_{obs} \propto \frac{1}{M_{obs}}$. By definition of $i$: $\Delta_{obs} = i \Delta_{theor} \propto i \frac{1}{M_{theor}}$. Therefore $\frac{1}{M_{obs}} = \frac{i}{M_{theor}} \implies M_{obs} = \frac{M_{theor}}{i}$.
formulas.description: Relationship between apparent experimental molar mass from colligative properties and true formula weight.
formulas.explanation: If substance dissociates ($i > 1$), $M_{obs} < M_{theor}$; if substance associates ($i < 1$), $M_{obs} > M_{theor}$ (e.g., acetic acid in benzene shows molar mass $\sim 120$ instead of $60$).

formulas.title: Total Vapor Pressure in Terms of Vapor Phase Mole Fraction
formulas.derivation: From Dalton's law: $y_A = P_A / P_{total} = (P_A^\circ x_A) / P_{total} \implies x_A = \frac{y_A P_{total}}{P_A^\circ}$. Similarly $x_B = \frac{y_B P_{total}}{P_B^\circ}$. Since liquid mole fractions sum to unity: $x_A + x_B = 1 \implies \frac{y_A P_{total}}{P_A^\circ} + \frac{y_B P_{total}}{P_B^\circ} = 1$. Factoring $P_{total}$: $P_{total}\left(\frac{y_A}{P_A^\circ} + \frac{1 - y_A}{P_B^\circ}\right) = 1 \implies P_{total} = \frac{P_A^\circ P_B^\circ}{P_B^\circ y_A + P_A^\circ(1 - y_A)}$.
formulas.description: Calculates total equilibrium vapor pressure directly from vapor composition $y_A$.
formulas.explanation: Constructs the bubble-point and dew-point curves essential for fractional distillation column design.

formulas.latex: I = \frac{1}{2}\sum c_i z_i^2, \quad \log_{10} \gamma_\pm = -0.509 |z_+ z_-| \sqrt{I} \quad (\text{Debye-Huckel Limiting Law})
formulas.title: Ionic Strength and Debye-Huckel Limiting Law for Mean Activity Coefficients
formulas.derivation: Gilbert Lewis introduced ionic strength $I = \frac{1}{2}\sum c_i z_i^2$ to quantify the electrostatic field intensity generated by all ions. Debye and Huckel (1923) solved the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann equation for the ion cloud screening potential: the electrostatic free energy lowering yields $\ln\gamma_\pm = -\frac{e^2 \kappa}{8\pi\epsilon_r\epsilon_0 k_B T} |z_+ z_-|$. Since Debye screening parameter $\kappa \propto \sqrt{I}$, converting to base-10 log in aqueous solution at $25^\circ\text{C}$ gives $\log_{10}\gamma_\pm = -0.509 |z_+ z_-|\sqrt{I}$.
formulas.description: Measures total ionic electric field in solution and calculates deviation from ideal solution behavior.
formulas.explanation: Valid in dilute solutions ($I < 0.01\text{ M}$); explains why chemical equilibrium positions shift in presence of inert spectator salts.

formulas.latex: ppm = \frac{\text{Mass of Solute}}{\text{Total Mass of Solution}} \times 10^6, \quad ppb = \frac{\text{Mass of Solute}}{\text{Total Mass of Solution}} \times 10^9
formulas.title: Parts Per Million (ppm) and Parts Per Billion (ppb)

variables.ppm: Parts per million ($1\text{ mg/kg}$ or $1\text{ mg/L}$ for water)

formulas.derivation: Defined as mass fraction normalized to $10^6$ or $10^9$ parts: $\text{ppm} = \frac{m_{solute}}{m_{solution}} \times 10^6$. Since water density is $\rho \approx 1.0\text{ g/mL} = 1000\text{ g/L}$: $1\text{ liter}$ weighs $10^6\text{ mg}$, meaning $1\text{ mg of solute in 1 L of water} = 1\text{ ppm}$.
formulas.description: Dimensionless concentration units used for ultra-trace pollutants, atmospheric gases, and water hardness.
formulas.explanation: Standard environmental engineering metric for quoting water contaminants (e.g. arsenic, lead limits) and air particulates ($PM_{2.5}$).

formulas.latex: M = \frac{\% \text{ by mass} \times 10 \times d}{M_{solute}}, \quad m = \frac{1000 M}{1000 d - M \cdot M_{solute}}
formulas.title: Interconversion Between Molarity, Molality and Mass Percentage
formulas.derivation: Consider $100\text{ g}$ of solution: mass of solute is $x = \%\text{ by mass}$. Moles of solute is $n = x / M_{solute}$. Volume of $100\text{ g}$ solution is $V = \frac{100}{d}\text{ mL} = \frac{100}{1000 d}\text{ L} = \frac{1}{10 d}\text{ L}$. Molarity is $M = \frac{n}{V} = \frac{x / M_{solute}}{1 / (10 d)} = \frac{x \times 10 \times d}{M_{solute}}$. For molality: mass of solvent in $1\text{ L}$ solution is $w_1 = (1000 d - M \cdot M_{solute})\text{ g}$. Molality is $m = \frac{M}{w_1 / 1000} = \frac{1000 M}{1000 d - M \cdot M_{solute}}$.
formulas.description: Direct formulas converting mass percentage and solution density d into molarity M and molality m.
formulas.explanation: Molality is temperature-independent; molarity varies with temperature due to liquid thermal expansion.

content_json.derivation: Francois-Marie Raoult (1887) observed that escaping tendency of volatile solvent molecules from liquid surface into vapor phase is directly proportional to surface fraction of that component. In an ideal solution with identical intermolecular forces ($A-A \approx B-B \approx A-B$), surface mole fraction equals bulk liquid mole fraction $x_A$, giving $P_A = P_A^\circ x_A$. Dalton's law of partial pressures gives $P_{total} = P_A + P_B = P_A^\circ x_A + P_B^\circ(1 - x_A) = P_B^\circ + (P_A^\circ - P_B^\circ)x_A$.
content_json.explanation: Vapor phase mole fraction $y_A$ is enriched in more volatile component: $y_A = \frac{P_A}{P_{total}} = \frac{P_A^\circ x_A}{P_{total}}$ (Konovalov's rule).

catalog_formula_sheets.name: JEE Master: Coordination Compounds & Crystal Field Splitting
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: Hans Bethe (1929) developed Crystal Field Theory: in octahedral ligand field, 6 ligands approach along Cartesian axes ($x, y, z$). Orbitals with lobes pointing directly along axes ($d_{x^2-y^2}, d_{z^2}$) experience strong electrostatic repulsion and are destabilized by $+0.6\Delta_o$ ($e_g$). Orbitals directed between axes ($d_{xy}, d_{yz}, d_{xz}$) experience less repulsion and are stabilized by $-0.4\Delta_o$ ($t_{2g}$). In tetrahedral geometry, 4 ligands approach corners of cube (between axes), inverting splitting pattern and reducing splitting magnitude by factor $\Delta_t = \frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$ because fewer ligands are present and none point directly at d-orbitals.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Because $\Delta_t < P$ (pairing energy) always, tetrahedral complexes are almost exclusively high-spin.

formulas.title: Crystal Field Splitting in Octahedral and Tetrahedral Fields
formulas.derivation: Hans Bethe (1929) developed Crystal Field Theory: in octahedral ligand field, 6 ligands approach along Cartesian axes ($x, y, z$). Orbitals with lobes pointing directly along axes ($d_{x^2-y^2}, d_{z^2}$) experience strong electrostatic repulsion and are destabilized by $+0.6\Delta_o$ ($e_g$). Orbitals directed between axes ($d_{xy}, d_{yz}, d_{xz}$) experience less repulsion and are stabilized by $-0.4\Delta_o$ ($t_{2g}$). In tetrahedral geometry, 4 ligands approach corners of cube (between axes), inverting splitting pattern and reducing splitting magnitude by factor $\Delta_t = \frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$ because fewer ligands are present and none point directly at d-orbitals.
formulas.description: Splitting of degenerate d-orbitals into $t_{2g}/e_g$ and $e/t_2$ manifolds in electrostatic ligand fields.
formulas.explanation: Because $\Delta_t < P$ (pairing energy) always, tetrahedral complexes are almost exclusively high-spin.

formulas.title: Crystal Field Stabilization Energy (CFSE) for Octahedral Complexes

variables.m: Number of extra electron pairs formed relative to free ion

formulas.derivation: Barycenter rule requires total energy shift of the 5 degenerate orbitals to sum to zero: $3(-0.4\Delta_o) + 2(+0.6\Delta_o) = -1.2\Delta_o + 1.2\Delta_o = 0$. Each electron occupying lower $t_{2g}$ level stabilizes complex by $-0.4\Delta_o$, while each electron occupying upper $e_g$ level destabilizes complex by $+0.6\Delta_o$. Summing contributions gives $CFSE = (-0.4 n_{t_{2g}} + 0.6 n_{e_g})\Delta_o$. When electrons pair in same orbital against Coulomb repulsion, pairing energy $+mP$ is added.
formulas.description: Net energetic stabilization of d-electron configuration relative to spherical barycenter.
formulas.explanation: If $\Delta_o > P$ (strong field ligands like $CN^-, CO$), pairing occurs producing low-spin complex. If $\Delta_o < P$ (weak field ligands like $F^-, Cl^-$), Hund's rule dominates producing high-spin complex.

formulas.latex: I^- < Br^- < S^{2-} < SCN^- < Cl^- < NO_3^- < N_3^- < F^- < OH^- < C_2O_4^{2-} < H_2O < NCS^- < CH_3CN < py < NH_3 < en < bipy < phen < NO_2^- < PPh_3 < CN^- < CO
formulas.title: Spectrochemical Series of Ligands
formulas.derivation: Derived from UV-visible absorption spectra ($d-d$ transition band wavenumbers $\Delta_o = h c \bar{\nu}$). Ligands fall into three classes based on metal-ligand bonding: (1) Halides and oxygen donors are $\pi$-donors: ligand filled p-orbitals donate electron density into metal $t_{2g}$, destabilizing $t_{2g}$ and shrinking $\Delta_o$ (weak field). (2) Ammonia and amines are pure $\sigma$-donors: intermediate $\Delta_o$. (3) $CN^-$ and $CO$ are strong $\pi$-acceptors (back-bonding): empty $\pi^*$ orbitals accept electron density from metal $t_{2g}$, dramatically stabilizing $t_{2g}$ and expanding $\Delta_o$ (strong field).
formulas.description: Empirical ranking of ligands according to increasing magnitude of crystal field splitting $\Delta_o$.
formulas.explanation: Enables predicting whether transition metal complex is high-spin or low-spin, and determines magnetic and color properties.

formulas.title: Magnetic Moments of Coordination Complexes

variables.\\mu_{eff}: Effective magnetic moment in Bohr Magnetons (BM)

formulas.derivation: In first-row ($3d$) transition metal complexes, non-spherical electrostatic crystal field of surrounding ligands quenches orbital angular momentum ($L \approx 0$) by breaking spatial rotational symmetry. Magnetic moment reduces to spin-only expression: $\mu_s = g\sqrt{S(S+1)}\mu_B$. With electron g-factor $g \approx 2.00$ and $S = n/2$: $\mu_s = 2\sqrt{\frac{n}{2}\left(\frac{n+2}{2}\right)} = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\mu_B$.
formulas.description: Spin-only magnetic moment and complete spin-plus-orbital magnetic moment for first-row transition ions.
formulas.explanation: Guouy balance magnetic measurement directly diagnoses high-spin vs low-spin states (e.g. $[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}$ has $n=1, \mu = 1.73\text{ BM}$ while $[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{3+}$ has $n=5, \mu = 5.92\text{ BM}$).

formulas.title: Sidgwick's Effective Atomic Number (EAN) Rule / 18-Electron Rule
formulas.derivation: Nevild Sidgwick (1927) proposed that coordinate covalent bonds donate 2 electrons per coordination bond. The total effective electrons surrounding metal core is $EAN = Z - (\text{oxidation state}) + 2 \times (\text{ligand pairs})$. If $EAN$ equals the atomic number of the next noble gas ($Kr=36, Xe=54, Rn=86$), the complex possesses a completely filled valence shell of 18 electrons ($ns^2 (n-1)d^{10} np^6$), conferring high kinetic and thermodynamic stability.
formulas.description: Predicts stability of coordination and organometallic complexes by mimicking next noble gas configuration.
formulas.explanation: Explains stoichiometry of metal carbonyls: $Ni(CO)_4$ ($28 - 0 + 8 = 36$, $18e^-$), $Fe(CO)_5$ ($26 - 0 + 10 = 36$), $Cr(CO)_6$ ($24 - 0 + 12 = 36$).

formulas.title: Stepwise and Overall Formation Constants of Complexes
formulas.derivation: Ligand complexation occurs in sequential stepwise equilibria: $M + L \rightleftharpoons ML$ ($k_1 = \frac{[ML]}{[M][L]}$); $ML + L \rightleftharpoons ML_2$ ($k_2 = \frac{[ML_2]}{[ML][L]}$); $\dots$ $ML_{n-1} + L \rightleftharpoons ML_n$ ($k_n = \frac{[ML_n]}{[ML_{n-1}][L]}$). Overall reaction is $M + n L \rightleftharpoons ML_n$ with equilibrium constant $\beta_n = \frac{[ML_n]}{[M][L]^n}$. Multiplying stepwise constants gives $k_1 \cdot k_2 \dots k_n = \frac{[ML]}{[M][L]} \frac{[ML_2]}{[ML][L]} \dots \frac{[ML_n]}{[ML_{n-1}][L]} = \frac{[ML_n]}{[M][L]^n} = \beta_n$.
formulas.description: Thermodynamic stability constants for stepwise ligand addition equilibrium $ML_{n-1} + L \rightleftharpoons ML_n$.
formulas.explanation: Typically $k_1 > k_2 > k_3 > \dots > k_n$ due to statistical factors and steric hindrance.

formulas.latex: \Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ \quad (\Delta S^\circ > 0 \implies \text{Chelate Effect})
formulas.title: The Chelate Effect
formulas.derivation: Consider substitution of 6 monodentate ligands by 3 bidentate ligands: $[Ni(NH_3)_6]^{2+} + 3 en \rightleftharpoons [Ni(en)_3]^{2+} + 6 NH_3$. Reactant count is $1 + 3 = 4$ species; product count is $1 + 6 = 7$ species. Net increase of 3 independent dissolved particles generates substantial positive entropy of reaction: $\Delta S^\circ \gg 0$. Since $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$, this large positive entropy makes $\Delta G^\circ$ significantly more negative, driving formation constant higher by several orders of magnitude.
formulas.description: Enhanced thermodynamic stability of polydentate chelate complexes over monodentate analogues driven by positive entropy.
formulas.explanation: EDTA ($hexadentate$) forms extremely stable complexes with almost all metal cations ($1 + 1 \to 1 + 6$ displacement release).

formulas.latex: t_{2g}^3 e_g^1, \quad t_{2g}^6 e_g^1, \quad t_{2g}^6 e_g^3 \implies \text{Jahn-Teller Distortion}
formulas.title: Jahn-Teller Theorem Distortion

variables.d^9, d^4, d^7: Electronic configurations exhibiting strong Jahn-Teller effect

formulas.derivation: Hermann Jahn and Edward Teller (1937) proved mathematically that any non-linear molecular system in an electronically degenerate ground state is inherently unstable and will undergo geometric distortion to lower its symmetry, remove orbital degeneracy, and lower overall energy. In octahedral $d^9$ complexes (e.g. $Cu^{2+}$: $t_{2g}^6 e_g^3$), the odd electron can reside in either $d_{z^2}$ or $d_{x^2-y^2}$. Elongating along z-axis lowers energy of $d_{z^2}$ and destabilizes $d_{x^2-y^2}$, yielding 4 short equatorial bonds and 2 elongated axial bonds (tetragonal distortion).
formulas.description: Geometric distortion of non-linear degenerate electronic states to remove orbital degeneracy and lower energy.
formulas.explanation: Explains why $Cu(II)$ octahedral complexes are never perfectly regular octahedra, displaying pronounced axial elongation.

formulas.latex: r_{tet} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a - r_{anion} \approx 0.225 r_A, \quad r_{oct} = \frac{a}{2} - r_{anion} \approx 0.414 r_A
formulas.title: Radius Ratio Rules for Coordination Polyhedra in Solid State
formulas.derivation: Geometric contact condition requires central cation to touch all surrounding anions without anions overlapping: Linear ($CN=2$): $r_+/r_- < 0.155$. Trigonal planar ($CN=3$): $0.155 \le r_+/r_- < 0.225$. Tetrahedral ($CN=4$): geometry gives $\cos(109.5^\circ/2) = \frac{r_-}{r_+ + r_-} \implies r_+/r_- = \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2} - 1 = 0.225$. Octahedral ($CN=6$): square in-plane diagonal gives $2(r_+ + r_-) = \sqrt{2}(2r_-) \implies r_+/r_- = \sqrt{2} - 1 = 0.414$. Cubic ($CN=8$): body diagonal gives $2(r_+ + r_-) = \sqrt{3}(2r_-) \implies r_+/r_- = \sqrt{3} - 1 = 0.732$.
formulas.description: Limiting radius ratios determining stable coordination numbers (tetrahedral, octahedral, cubic) in ionic crystals.
formulas.explanation: Example: $NaCl$ ($r_{Na+}/r_{Cl-} = 0.525$, in $0.414 - 0.732$ range $\implies CN=6$ octahedral); $CsCl$ ($0.93 > 0.732 \implies CN=8$ cubic).

formulas.title: Crystalline Unit Cell Density Formula

variables.Z: Number of formula units per unit cell

formulas.derivation: Density is mass divided by volume: $\rho = \frac{m_{cell}}{V_{cell}}$. Volume of cubic unit cell is $V = a^3$. Mass of unit cell is mass of $Z$ formula units: $m_{cell} = Z \times m_{atom} = Z \times \left(\frac{M}{N_A}\right)$. Substituting yields $\rho = \frac{Z \cdot M}{N_A \cdot a^3}$. Lattice parameters: Simple cubic ($Z=1, a=2R$); Body-centered cubic ($Z=2, \sqrt{3}a = 4R$); Face-centered cubic ($Z=4, \sqrt{2}a = 4R$).
formulas.description: Calculates macroscopic solid crystal density directly from unit cell edge length a and lattice particle count Z.
formulas.explanation: Fundamental crystallographic formula connecting atomic micro-structure to macroscopic laboratory density.

formulas.latex: 2 d \sin\theta = n \lambda \quad (\text{Bragg's Law of X-Ray Diffraction})
formulas.title: Bragg's Law of Crystal X-Ray Diffraction
formulas.derivation: William Henry Bragg and William Lawrence Bragg (1913) treated crystal planes as specular semi-reflecting mirrors. Path difference between rays reflected from two adjacent parallel planes separated by distance $d$ is $\Delta x = 2 d\sin\theta$. Constructive interference produces sharp diffraction peaks when path difference is an integer number of wavelengths: $2d\sin\theta = n\lambda$. For cubic crystal with Miller indices $(h, k, l)$: $d_{hkl} = \frac{a}{\sqrt{h^2 + k^2 + l^2}}$.
formulas.description: Constructive interference condition for X-rays reflected from parallel lattice planes separated by spacing d.
formulas.explanation: Primary experimental technique for solving 3D atomic structures of crystalline solids, proteins, and DNA.

formulas.title: Freundlich Adsorption Isotherm

variables.x/m: Mass of gas adsorbed per unit mass of solid adsorbent
variables.k, n: Freundlich empirical constants depending on adsorbent and gas

formulas.derivation: Herbert Freundlich (1909) deduced an empirical isotherm for multilayer/heterogeneous adsorption: $x/m = k P^{1/n}$. Taking base-10 logarithm: $\log(x/m) = \log k + \frac{1}{n}\log P$. Plotting $\log(x/m)$ versus $\log P$ yields straight line of slope $1/n$ ($0 \le 1/n \le 1$) and y-intercept $\log k$.
formulas.description: Empirical power-law relation for gas adsorption on solid heterogeneous surface at constant temperature.
formulas.explanation: At low pressure ($1/n = 1$): $x/m \propto P$. At high pressure ($1/n = 0$): $x/m = \text{constant}$ (adsorption saturation).

Multiplying by modulus $r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ gives $z = r e^{i\theta}$.
