formulas.title: Torque and Angular Momentum Equation
formulas.derivation: Angular momentum is $\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$. Differentiating: $\frac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt} \times \vec{p} + \vec{r} \times \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \vec{v} \times (m\vec{v}) + \vec{r} \times \vec{F}_{net} = 0 + \vec{\tau}_{net}$. For rigid bodies rotating about fixed axis, $\vec{L} = I\vec{\omega}$, so $\vec{\tau} = I\frac{d\vec{\omega}}{dt} = I\vec{\alpha}$.
formulas.description: Rotational analog of Newton's second law relating net torque to moment of inertia and angular acceleration.
formulas.explanation: If net external torque about an origin is zero, angular momentum $\vec{L}$ about that origin is conserved.

formulas.title: Parallel Axis Theorem (Steiner's Theorem)

variables.I_{cm}: Moment of inertia about parallel axis through center of mass
variables.I_{parallel}: Moment of inertia about arbitrary parallel axis

formulas.derivation: Let origin be CM. Coordinate along new axis is $(x + d, y)$. Then $I = \int [(x+d)^2 + y^2] dm = \int (x^2 + y^2) dm + 2d \int x dm + d^2 \int dm$. Since origin is CM, first moment $\int x dm = 0$. Hence $I = I_{cm} + Md^2$.
formulas.description: Moment of inertia about any axis parallel to a centroidal axis at perpendicular distance d.
formulas.explanation: Applies to rigid bodies of arbitrary 3D geometry; must always start from the center-of-mass axis.

formulas.title: Perpendicular Axis Theorem

variables.I_z: Moment of inertia about axis perpendicular to lamina plane
variables.I_x, I_y: Moments of inertia about in-plane orthogonal axes

formulas.derivation: For a planar lamina in xy-plane ($z=0$), distance of mass element $dm$ to z-axis is $r_z^2 = x^2 + y^2$. Integrating: $I_z = \int (x^2 + y^2) dm = \int y^2 dm + \int x^2 dm = I_x + I_y$.
formulas.description: Relates moments of inertia of a planar laminar body about three mutually perpendicular intersecting axes.
formulas.explanation: Valid strictly for flat 2D planar laminas, never for 3D volumetric bodies like spheres or cylinders.

formulas.title: Kinetic Energy of Pure Rolling Body
formulas.derivation: In rolling without slipping, $v_{cm} = R\omega$. Substituting $I_{cm} = Mk^2$: $K = \frac{1}{2}M v_{cm}^2 + \frac{1}{2}(Mk^2)\left(\frac{v_{cm}}{R}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2}M v_{cm}^2\left(1 + \frac{k^2}{R^2}\right)$.
formulas.description: Total kinetic energy decomposed into translational motion of CM and rotation about CM.
formulas.explanation: Fraction of kinetic energy in rotation is $\frac{K_{rot}}{K_{total}} = \frac{k^2/R^2}{1 + k^2/R^2}$ (e.g., $2/7$ for solid sphere, $1/3$ for solid cylinder).

formulas.title: Acceleration of Body Rolling Down an Incline
formulas.derivation: Equations of motion: along incline $Mg\sin\theta - f = Ma$; torque about CM $f R = I_{cm}\alpha = I_{cm}\frac{a}{R} \implies f = \frac{I_{cm}a}{R^2}$. Substituting friction into force equation: $Mg\sin\theta - \frac{I_{cm}a}{R^2} = Ma \implies a\left(M + \frac{I_{cm}}{R^2}\right) = Mg\sin\theta \implies a = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1 + \frac{I_{cm}}{MR^2}}$.
formulas.description: Linear acceleration of a circular symmetric body rolling without slipping down an angle $\theta$.
formulas.explanation: A solid sphere ($k^2/R^2 = 2/5$) reaches the bottom fastest, followed by spherical shell ($2/3$), disc ($1/2$), and hoop/ring ($1$).

formulas.title: Minimum Friction Coefficient for Pure Rolling
formulas.derivation: Friction force is $f = \frac{I_{cm}a}{R^2} = \frac{Mg\sin\theta}{1 + MR^2/I_{cm}}$. Normal force is $N = Mg\cos\theta$. Pure rolling requires $f \le \mu_s N \implies \frac{Mg\sin\theta}{1 + MR^2/I_{cm}} \le \mu_s Mg\cos\theta \implies \mu_s \ge \frac{\tan\theta}{1 + MR^2/I_{cm}}$.
formulas.description: Threshold static friction coefficient required to prevent slipping on an incline.
formulas.explanation: If surface friction $\mu < \mu_{min}$, the body rolls with forward slipping ($v_{cm} \ne R\omega$).

formulas.title: Standard Moments of Inertia of Common Geometries
formulas.derivation: For disc: divide into concentric thin rings of radius $r$, width $dr$, mass $dm = \frac{M}{\pi R^2} 2\pi r dr = \frac{2M}{R^2} r dr$. Ring inertia is $dI = r^2 dm = \frac{2M}{R^2} r^3 dr$. Integrating: $I = \frac{2M}{R^2}\int_0^R r^3 dr = \frac{2M}{R^2}\frac{R^4}{4} = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$. Solid sphere: integrate spherical shells of $dm = 4\pi r^2 \rho dr$ with $I = \frac{2}{5}MR^2$.
formulas.description: Centroidal moments of inertia for standard rigid bodies rotating about symmetry axis.
formulas.explanation: Essential reference constants for rigid body rotational dynamics.

formulas.title: Moment of Inertia of Thin Uniform Rod
formulas.derivation: Linear mass density $\lambda = M/L$. For CM axis: $I_{cm} = \int_{-L/2}^{L/2} x^2 (\lambda dx) = \lambda \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-L/2}^{L/2} = \frac{M}{L}\left(\frac{L^3}{24} - \left(-\frac{L^3}{24}\right)\right) = \frac{1}{12}ML^2$. For end axis, parallel axis theorem gives $I_{end} = I_{cm} + M(L/2)^2 = \frac{1}{12}ML^2 + \frac{1}{4}ML^2 = \frac{1}{3}ML^2$.
formulas.description: Inertia about transverse axes passing through center of mass and one end.
formulas.explanation: Rotating about the end takes 4 times more torque for same angular acceleration as rotating about the center.

formulas.latex: v_c = \frac{m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2}{m_1 + m_2}, \quad L_O = \vec{r}_{cm} \times M\vec{v}_{cm} + \vec{L}_{cm}
formulas.title: Center of Mass Velocity and Koenig's Theorem for Angular Momentum
formulas.derivation: Let $\vec{r}_i = \vec{r}_{cm} + \vec{r}'_i$ and $\vec{v}_i = \vec{v}_{cm} + \vec{v}'_i$. Total angular momentum $\vec{L}_O = \sum m_i (\vec{r}_{cm} + \vec{r}'_i) \times (\vec{v}_{cm} + \vec{v}'_i) = \vec{r}_{cm} \times M\vec{v}_{cm} + \sum m_i \vec{r}'_i \times \vec{v}'_i + \vec{r}_{cm} \times \sum m_i \vec{v}'_i + (\sum m_i \vec{r}'_i) \times \vec{v}_{cm}$. By definition of CM, cross terms vanish, giving $\vec{L}_O = \vec{r}_{cm} \times M\vec{v}_{cm} + I_{cm}\vec{\omega}$.
formulas.description: Decomposition of total angular momentum about origin O into CM orbital part and intrinsic spin part.
formulas.explanation: Allows decoupling orbital angular momentum of planetary motion from planetary axial spin.

formulas.title: Condition for Toppling Before Sliding

variables.\\mu: Coefficient of friction between block and floor

formulas.derivation: Let horizontal force $F$ be applied at top height $h$. Sliding occurs when $F = \mu mg$. Toppling occurs about front edge when overturning torque exceeds stabilizing torque: $F h > mg (b/2) \implies F > mg \frac{b}{2h}$. Toppling occurs prior to sliding if $F_{topple} < F_{slide} \implies mg \frac{b}{2h} < \mu mg \implies \mu > \frac{b}{2h}$.
formulas.description: Threshold coefficient of friction determining whether a rectangular block of width b and height h topples or slips.
formulas.explanation: Tall, narrow blocks (large $h$, small $b$) topple easily on rough floors; squat blocks slide first.

formulas.title: Time Period of Physical (Compound) Pendulum
formulas.derivation: Restoring torque about pivot for deflection $\theta$ is $\tau = -mgd\sin\theta \approx -mgd\theta$. Equation of motion: $I\alpha = -mgd\theta \implies \frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} + \frac{mgd}{I}\theta = 0$. Angular frequency is $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{mgd}{I}}$. Period $T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{mgd}}$. Using parallel axis theorem $I = m(k^2 + d^2)$ gives $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{k^2 + d^2}{gd}}$.
formulas.description: Small-angle oscillation period of a rigid body pivoted at distance d from its center of mass.
formulas.explanation: Equivalent simple pendulum length is $L_{eq} = \frac{k^2 + d^2}{d}$. Minimum period occurs when $d = k$.

formulas.latex: x_{cm} = \frac{\int x \, dm}{\int dm}, \quad x_{cm, hem} = \frac{3}{8}R, \quad y_{cm, cone} = \frac{h}{4}
formulas.title: Center of Mass of Continuous Bodies
formulas.derivation: Solid hemisphere of radius $R$: slice into thin circular discs of thickness $dy$ at distance $y$ from base. Disc radius is $r = \sqrt{R^2 - y^2}$, mass $dm = \rho \pi (R^2 - y^2) dy$. Centroid is $y_{cm} = \frac{\int_0^R y \rho \pi (R^2 - y^2) dy}{\frac{2}{3}\pi R^3 \rho} = \frac{\pi [\frac{R^2 y^2}{2} - \frac{y^4}{4}]_0^R}{\frac{2}{3}\pi R^3} = \frac{R^4 / 4}{\frac{2}{3}R^3} = \frac{3}{8}R$.
formulas.description: Centroid coordinates for hemisphere, solid cone, and semicircular disc.
formulas.explanation: For hollow hemisphere, $y_{cm} = R/2$. For semicircular wire loop, $y_{cm} = 2R/\pi$.

content_json.derivation: Angular momentum is $\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$. Differentiating: $\frac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt} \times \vec{p} + \vec{r} \times \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \vec{v} \times (m\vec{v}) + \vec{r} \times \vec{F}_{net} = 0 + \vec{\tau}_{net}$. For rigid bodies rotating about fixed axis, $\vec{L} = I\vec{\omega}$, so $\vec{\tau} = I\frac{d\vec{\omega}}{dt} = I\vec{\alpha}$.
content_json.explanation: If net external torque about an origin is zero, angular momentum $\vec{L}$ about that origin is conserved.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: AP Statistics: Inference, Confidence Intervals & Hypothesis Testing
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: By definition of conditional probability: $P(E_i | A) = \frac{P(E_i \cap A)}{P(A)} = \frac{P(E_i) P(A | E_i)}{P(A)}$. By the Law of Total Probability, since $E_1, \dots, E_n$ partition the sample space $S$: $A = A \cap S = A \cap (\bigcup E_j) = \bigcup (A \cap E_j)$. Since $E_j$ are mutually disjoint: $P(A) = \sum_{j=1}^n P(A \cap E_j) = \sum_{j=1}^n P(E_j) P(A | E_j)$. Substituting $P(A)$ yields Bayes' theorem.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Calculates the updated probability of hypothesis E_i after observing experimental evidence A.

content_json.title: AP Statistics: Inference, Confidence Intervals & Hypothesis Testing

sections.title: AP Statistics: Inference, Confidence Intervals & Hypothesis Testing - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.latex: P(E_i | A) = \frac{P(E_i) P(A | E_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^n P(E_j) P(A | E_j)}
formulas.title: Bayes' Theorem for Conditional Posterior Probability
formulas.derivation: By definition of conditional probability: $P(E_i | A) = \frac{P(E_i \cap A)}{P(A)} = \frac{P(E_i) P(A | E_i)}{P(A)}$. By the Law of Total Probability, since $E_1, \dots, E_n$ partition the sample space $S$: $A = A \cap S = A \cap (\bigcup E_j) = \bigcup (A \cap E_j)$. Since $E_j$ are mutually disjoint: $P(A) = \sum_{j=1}^n P(A \cap E_j) = \sum_{j=1}^n P(E_j) P(A | E_j)$. Substituting $P(A)$ yields Bayes' theorem.
formulas.description: Bayes' Theorem for Conditional Posterior Probability
formulas.explanation: Calculates the updated probability of hypothesis E_i after observing experimental evidence A.

formulas.latex: P(X = r) = \binom{n}{r} p^r q^{n - r} \quad (q = 1 - p), \quad \mu = n p, \quad \sigma^2 = n p q
formulas.title: Binomial Distribution Probability Mass Function, Mean and Variance
formulas.derivation: In $n$ independent trials, the probability of any specific sequence with $r$ successes and $n-r$ failures is $p^r q^{n-r}$. The number of distinct sequences is the combinations of choosing $r$ trials out of $n$: $\binom{n}{r}$. Hence $P(X = r) = \binom{n}{r} p^r q^{n-r}$. Expectation: $E[X] = \sum r \binom{n}{r} p^r q^{n-r} = n p \sum \binom{n-1}{r-1} p^{r-1} q^{(n-1)-(r-1)} = n p (p+q)^{n-1} = n p$. Variance: $\text{Var}(X) = E[X(X-1)] + E[X] - (E[X])^2 = n(n-1)p^2 + np - n^2 p^2 = np(1-p) = npq$.
formulas.description: Binomial Distribution Probability Mass Function, Mean and Variance
formulas.explanation: Models the number of successes in n independent identical Bernoulli trials.

formulas.latex: P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)
formulas.title: Addition Theorem of Probability

variables.P(A \\cup B): probability of occurrence of at least one event

formulas.derivation: From set theory cardinality: $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$. Dividing both sides by the total number of outcomes in the finite sample space $n(S)$: $\frac{n(A \cup B)}{n(S)} = \frac{n(A)}{n(S)} + \frac{n(B)}{n(S)} - \frac{n(A \cap B)}{n(S)} \implies P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$. If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive ($A \cap B = \emptyset$), $P(A \cap B) = 0 \implies P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$.
formulas.description: Addition Theorem of Probability
formulas.explanation: Fundamental probability union identity for calculating the likelihood of either event A or B occurring.

formulas.latex: P(A \cap B) = P(A) P(B) \iff A, B \text{ are Independent}
formulas.title: Condition for Independence of Two Events
formulas.derivation: By definition of conditional probability: $P(A | B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$. Two events are independent if the occurrence of event $B$ has no influence on the probability of event $A$: $P(A | B) = P(A)$. Equating: $P(A) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \implies P(A \cap B) = P(A) P(B)$.
formulas.description: Condition for Independence of Two Events
formulas.explanation: Mathematically defines stochastic independence: joint probability equals product of marginal probabilities.

formulas.title: Expectation and Variance of a Discrete Random Variable
formulas.derivation: Expand variance definition: $\text{Var}(X) = E[(X - \mu)^2] = E[X^2 - 2\mu X + \mu^2] = E[X^2] - 2\mu E[X] + \mu^2$. Since $E[X] = \mu$: $\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - 2\mu^2 + \mu^2 = E[X^2] - \mu^2 = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2$. In summation form: $\sigma^2 = \sum x_i^2 P(x_i) - \left(\sum x_i P(x_i)\right)^2$.
formulas.description: Expectation and Variance of a Discrete Random Variable
formulas.explanation: Expectation gives the long-run probability-weighted average; Variance measures the squared dispersion about the mean.

formulas.latex: E[a X + b] = a E[X] + b, \quad \text{Var}(a X + b) = a^2 \text{Var}(X), \quad \sigma_{aX+b} = |a| \sigma_X
formulas.title: Effect of Linear Transformation on Mean and Variance
formulas.derivation: By linearity of summation: $E[aX + b] = \sum (a x_i + b) P(x_i) = a \sum x_i P(x_i) + b \sum P(x_i) = a E[X] + b(1) = a E[X] + b$. Variance: $\text{Var}(aX + b) = E[((aX + b) - E[aX + b])^2] = E[(aX + b - a\mu - b)^2] = E[(a(X - \mu))^2] = a^2 E[(X - \mu)^2] = a^2 \text{Var}(X)$. Taking square root gives $\sigma = |a|\sigma_X$.
formulas.description: Effect of Linear Transformation on Mean and Variance
formulas.explanation: Adding a constant shifts the mean but does not change the spread; multiplying scales the standard deviation by |a|.

formulas.title: Standard Deviation of a Data Set
formulas.derivation: Expand sum of squared deviations: $\frac{1}{N}\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 = \frac{1}{N}\sum (x_i^2 - 2x_i \bar{x} + \bar{x}^2) = \frac{1}{N}\sum x_i^2 - 2\bar{x}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum x_i\right) + \frac{1}{N}(N \bar{x}^2) = \frac{\sum x_i^2}{N} - 2\bar{x}^2 + \bar{x}^2 = \frac{\sum x_i^2}{N} - \bar{x}^2$. Taking square root gives standard deviation $\sigma$.
formulas.description: Standard Deviation of a Data Set
formulas.explanation: The most widely used statistical measure of variation and dispersion in data.

formulas.title: Coefficient of Variation (Relative Dispersion)
formulas.derivation: Standard deviation is scale-dependent. To compare variability between two data sets with different units or widely different means, divide standard deviation by arithmetic mean: $CV = \frac{\sigma}{\bar{x}} \times 100\%$. The data series with a lower CV is more consistent and stable.
formulas.description: Coefficient of Variation (Relative Dispersion)
formulas.explanation: Dimensionless ratio used to compare consistency between data series with different scales or measurement units.

formulas.title: Mean Deviation About Mean and Median
formulas.derivation: By definition, mean deviation is the average absolute difference of all observations from a measure of central tendency. Differentiating $\sum |x_i - c|$ with respect to $c$ changes sign at each point; the derivative is zero when the number of points below $c$ equals points above $c$, which occurs exactly at the median $M$. Hence, Mean Deviation is minimal when measured about the Median.
formulas.description: Mean Deviation About Mean and Median
formulas.explanation: Robust measure of dispersion; mathematically guaranteed to be minimized when calculated about the median.

formulas.title: Poisson Distribution for Rare Events

variables.\\lambda = n p: average rate of occurrences per interval

formulas.derivation: Take Poisson limit of binomial distribution as $n \to \infty, p \to 0$ with $np = \lambda$: $P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1 - p)^{n - k} = \frac{n(n-1)\dots(n-k+1)}{k!} \left(\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^k \left(1 - \frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^n \left(1 - \frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{-k}$. As $n \to \infty$: $\frac{n(n-1)\dots(n-k+1)}{n^k} \to 1$, $(1 - \lambda/n)^n \to e^{-\lambda}$, and $(1 - \lambda/n)^{-k} \to 1$. Hence $P(X = k) = \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}$.
formulas.description: Poisson Distribution for Rare Events
formulas.explanation: Models counts of rare independent events occurring in fixed time or space intervals (e.g. radioactive decays, server requests).

formulas.title: Karl Pearson's Empirical Relation for Moderately Skewed Distributions
formulas.derivation: In a symmetric distribution: Mean = Median = Mode. In a moderately skewed unimodal frequency distribution, the median approximately divides the distance from mean to mode in a 2:1 ratio: $\text{Mean} - \text{Median} \approx \frac{1}{3}(\text{Mean} - \text{Mode}) \implies 3(\text{Mean} - \text{Median}) \approx \text{Mean} - \text{Mode} \implies \text{Mode} \approx 3\text{Median} - 2\text{Mean}$.
formulas.description: Karl Pearson's Empirical Relation for Moderately Skewed Distributions
formulas.explanation: Empirical relationship connecting the three measures of central tendency in moderately asymmetric data.

formulas.latex: P(A | B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \implies P(A \cap B) = P(B) P(A | B) = P(A) P(B | A)
formulas.title: Multiplication Rule of Probability
formulas.derivation: Follows from definition of conditional probability: the probability that event $A$ occurs given that event $B$ has already occurred is the proportion of outcomes in $B$ that also belong to $A$: $P(A | B) = \frac{n(A \cap B)}{n(B)} = \frac{n(A \cap B)/n(S)}{n(B)/n(S)} = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$. Multiplying both sides by $P(B)$ gives $P(A \cap B) = P(B) P(A | B)$.
formulas.description: Multiplication Rule of Probability
formulas.explanation: Used for sequential probability calculation where earlier outcomes affect the likelihood of subsequent events.

content_json.derivation: By definition of conditional probability: $P(E_i | A) = \frac{P(E_i \cap A)}{P(A)} = \frac{P(E_i) P(A | E_i)}{P(A)}$. By the Law of Total Probability, since $E_1, \dots, E_n$ partition the sample space $S$: $A = A \cap S = A \cap (\bigcup E_j) = \bigcup (A \cap E_j)$. Since $E_j$ are mutually disjoint: $P(A) = \sum_{j=1}^n P(A \cap E_j) = \sum_{j=1}^n P(E_j) P(A | E_j)$. Substituting $P(A)$ yields Bayes' theorem.
content_json.explanation: Calculates the updated probability of hypothesis E_i after observing experimental evidence A.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: Olympiad Math: Number Theory, Modular Arithmetic & Diophantine Equations
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: Divide $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ by $a$: $x^2 + \frac{b}{a}x = -\frac{c}{a}$. Complete square by adding $\left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2$: $\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 = \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}$. Taking square roots gives $x + \frac{b}{2a} = \pm \frac{\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} \implies x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Yields the two exact roots of any general quadratic polynomial. The term $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$ governs the nature of the roots.

formulas.title: Quadratic Formula for roots of ax^2 + bx + c = 0
formulas.derivation: Divide $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ by $a$: $x^2 + \frac{b}{a}x = -\frac{c}{a}$. Complete square by adding $\left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2$: $\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 = \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}$. Taking square roots gives $x + \frac{b}{2a} = \pm \frac{\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} \implies x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$.
formulas.description: Quadratic Formula for roots of ax^2 + bx + c = 0
formulas.explanation: Yields the two exact roots of any general quadratic polynomial. The term $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$ governs the nature of the roots.

formulas.title: Vieta's Formulas for Quadratic Equations
formulas.derivation: Since $\alpha, \beta$ are roots: $a(x - \alpha)(x - \beta) = a(x^2 - (\alpha + \beta)x + \alpha\beta) = ax^2 - a(\alpha + \beta)x + a\alpha\beta = ax^2 + bx + c$. Equating coefficients: $-a(\alpha + \beta) = b \implies \alpha + \beta = -b/a$, and $a\alpha\beta = c \implies \alpha\beta = c/a$.
formulas.description: Vieta's Formulas for Quadratic Equations
formulas.explanation: Directly links polynomial coefficients to root sums and products without solving the equation explicitly.

formulas.title: Difference of Roots Formula
formulas.derivation: Using identity $(\alpha - \beta)^2 = (\alpha + \beta)^2 - 4\alpha\beta = \left(-\frac{b}{a}\right)^2 - 4\frac{c}{a} = \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{a^2} = \frac{\Delta}{a^2}$. Taking principal square root gives $|\alpha - \beta| = \frac{\sqrt{\Delta}}{|a|}$.
formulas.description: Difference of Roots Formula
formulas.explanation: Measures the horizontal distance between the x-intercepts of the parabola $y = ax^2 + bx + c$.

formulas.title: Discriminant Characterization of Roots
formulas.derivation: Follows directly from the radical term $\sqrt{\Delta}$ in the quadratic formula. If $\Delta > 0$, $\sqrt{\Delta} \in \mathbb{R}^+$, yielding two distinct real values. If $\Delta = 0$, $\sqrt{\Delta} = 0$, giving coincident root $-b/(2a)$. If $\Delta < 0$, $\sqrt{\Delta} = i\sqrt{-\Delta}$, producing non-real conjugate pair $\frac{-b \pm i\sqrt{4ac - b^2}}{2a}$.
formulas.description: Discriminant Characterization of Roots
formulas.explanation: Determines whether the parabola intersects the x-axis at 2 points, touches at 1 vertex, or never intersects.

formulas.title: Condition for Exactly One Common Root Between Two Quadratics

variables.a_i, b_i, c_i: coefficients of a1 x^2 + b1 x + c1 = 0 and a2 x^2 + b2 x + c2 = 0

formulas.derivation: Let $\alpha$ be common root: $a_1 \alpha^2 + b_1 \alpha + c_1 = 0$ and $a_2 \alpha^2 + b_2 \alpha + c_2 = 0$. By cross-multiplication: $\frac{\alpha^2}{b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1} = \frac{\alpha}{c_1 a_2 - c_2 a_1} = \frac{1}{a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1}$. Eliminating $\alpha$: $\alpha = \frac{c_1 a_2 - c_2 a_1}{a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1}$, so $\alpha^2 = \frac{(c_1 a_2 - c_2 a_1)^2}{(a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1)^2} = \frac{b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1}{a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1} \implies (c_1 a_2 - c_2 a_1)^2 = (a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1)(b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1)$.
formulas.description: Condition for Exactly One Common Root Between Two Quadratics
formulas.explanation: Necessary and sufficient algebraic condition for two distinct quadratic equations to share a common solution.

formulas.latex: \Delta \ge 0, \quad a \cdot f(k) > 0, \quad -\frac{b}{2a} > k \implies \text{Both roots greater than } k
formulas.title: Location of Roots: Both roots greater than real number k
formulas.derivation: For both roots $\alpha, \beta > k$: (1) Real roots require $\Delta \ge 0$. (2) Parabola opens up ($a>0$) means $f(k) > 0$; opens down ($a<0$) means $f(k) < 0$, unified as $a \cdot f(k) > 0$. (3) The vertex $x = -b/(2a) = (\alpha + \beta)/2$ must lie strictly to the right of $k$: $-b/(2a) > k$.
formulas.description: Location of Roots: Both roots greater than real number k
formulas.explanation: Standard IIT-JEE test for restricting both roots of a quadratic polynomial to the right of a given real value k.

formulas.latex: a \cdot f(k) < 0 \implies k \text{ lies strictly between the roots}
formulas.title: Location of Roots: Number k lies strictly between roots
formulas.derivation: If $k$ lies between $\alpha$ and $\beta$, the vertex value must have opposite sign to $f(k)$ compared to $a$. If $a > 0$, parabola is below x-axis between roots $\implies f(k) < 0 \implies a f(k) < 0$. If $a < 0$, parabola is above x-axis between roots $\implies f(k) > 0 \implies a f(k) < 0$. Note: $\Delta > 0$ is automatically guaranteed since $a f(k) < 0 \implies b^2 - 4ac > 0$.
formulas.description: Location of Roots: Number k lies strictly between roots
formulas.explanation: Simplest root-location check: a single inequality $a f(k) < 0$ guarantees real distinct roots with k strictly between them.

formulas.title: Maximum or Minimum Value of Quadratic Function

variables.a: lead coefficient (min if a > 0, max if a < 0)

formulas.derivation: Let $f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$. Setting derivative to zero: $f'(x) = 2ax + b = 0 \implies x = -b/(2a)$. Evaluating at critical point: $f(-b/2a) = a\left(\frac{b^2}{4a^2}\right) + b\left(-\frac{b}{2a}\right) + c = \frac{b^2 - 2b^2 + 4ac}{4a} = -\frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a} = -\frac{\Delta}{4a}$. Second derivative $f''(x) = 2a$, so minimum if $a > 0$, maximum if $a < 0$.
formulas.description: Maximum or Minimum Value of Quadratic Function
formulas.explanation: Gives the absolute extremum of a quadratic polynomial. Range of $f(x)$ is $[-\Delta/4a, \infty)$ if $a > 0$ and $(-\infty, -\Delta/4a]$ if $a < 0$.

formulas.latex: a S_n + b S_{n-1} + c S_{n-2} = 0 \quad \text{where } S_n = p \alpha^n + q \beta^n
formulas.title: Newton's Sums Theorem for Powers of Roots

variables.S_n: linear combination of n-th powers of roots

formulas.derivation: Since $\alpha$ and $\beta$ satisfy $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$: $a\alpha^2 + b\alpha + c = 0$ and $a\beta^2 + b\beta + c = 0$. Multiply by $p\alpha^{n-2}$ and $q\beta^{n-2}$ respectively: $a(p\alpha^n) + b(p\alpha^{n-1}) + c(p\alpha^{n-2}) = 0$ and $a(q\beta^n) + b(q\beta^{n-1}) + c(q\beta^{n-2}) = 0$. Adding both equations yields $a(p\alpha^n + q\beta^n) + b(p\alpha^{n-1} + q\beta^{n-1}) + c(p\alpha^{n-2} + q\beta^{n-2}) = 0 \implies aS_n + bS_{n-1} + cS_{n-2} = 0$.
formulas.description: Newton's Sums Theorem for Powers of Roots
formulas.explanation: Extremely powerful JEE Advanced shortcut for computing high-power root expressions like $\alpha^{10} -  eta^{10}$ without calculating roots.

formulas.title: Sum of Cubes of Quadratic Roots
formulas.derivation: From algebraic identity $(\alpha+\beta)^3 = \alpha^3 + \beta^3 + 3\alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta)$, rearrange: $\alpha^3 + \beta^3 = (\alpha+\beta)^3 - 3\alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta)$. Substitute $\alpha+\beta = -b/a$ and $\alpha\beta = c/a$: $\alpha^3 + \beta^3 = (-b/a)^3 - 3(c/a)(-b/a) = -\frac{b^3}{a^3} + \frac{3bc}{a^2} = \frac{3abc - b^3}{a^3}$.
formulas.description: Sum of Cubes of Quadratic Roots
formulas.explanation: Allows fast computation of third-order symmetric root expressions using solely equation coefficients.

formulas.title: Condition for Positive Definite Quadratic Expression
formulas.derivation: Completing square: $f(x) = a\left[\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 - \frac{\Delta}{4a^2}\right]$. The squared term is $\ge 0$. For $f(x)$ to remain strictly positive for all $x$, the parabola must open upwards ($a > 0$) and its minimum vertex value $-\Delta/(4a)$ must be strictly positive, which requires $-\Delta > 0 \implies \Delta < 0$.
formulas.description: Condition for Positive Definite Quadratic Expression
formulas.explanation: Guarantees that a quadratic expression never crosses or touches zero, remaining strictly positive across all real numbers.

formulas.latex: c x^2 + b x + a = 0 \implies \text{roots are } \frac{1}{\alpha}, \frac{1}{\beta}
formulas.title: Transformation of Equations: Reciprocal Roots
formulas.derivation: Let $y = 1/x \implies x = 1/y$. Substitute into $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$: $a(1/y)^2 + b(1/y) + c = 0 \implies \frac{a}{y^2} + \frac{b}{y} + c = 0$. Multiply through by $y^2$: $c y^2 + b y + a = 0$. The roots of this transformed equation are $y_1 = 1/\alpha$ and $y_2 = 1/\beta$.
formulas.description: Transformation of Equations: Reciprocal Roots
formulas.explanation: Reversing the coefficients of a polynomial immediately inverts all its roots.

content_json.derivation: Divide $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ by $a$: $x^2 + \frac{b}{a}x = -\frac{c}{a}$. Complete square by adding $\left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2$: $\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 = \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}$. Taking square roots gives $x + \frac{b}{2a} = \pm \frac{\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} \implies x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$.
content_json.explanation: Yields the two exact roots of any general quadratic polynomial. The term $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$ governs the nature of the roots.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: Olympiad Math: Classical Inequalities (AM-GM, Cauchy-Schwarz, Jensen)
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: Entry $(i, j)$ of $A \cdot \text{adj}(A)$ is $\sum_{k=1}^n A_{ik} [\text{adj}(A)]_{kj} = \sum_{k=1}^n A_{ik} C_{jk}$ where $C_{jk}$ is cofactor. By Laplace expansion: If $i = j$, $\sum A_{ik} C_{ik} = |A|$. If $i \ne j$, $\sum A_{ik} C_{jk} = 0$ (expansion of determinant with two identical rows). Thus $A \cdot \text{adj}(A) = |A| I_n$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: The core theorem of matrix algebra connecting matrix multiplication, adjoints, determinants, and inverses.

sections.title: Olympiad Math: Classical Inequalities (AM-GM, Cauchy-Schwarz, Jensen) - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.title: Fundamental Adjoint Theorem for Square Matrix
formulas.derivation: Entry $(i, j)$ of $A \cdot \text{adj}(A)$ is $\sum_{k=1}^n A_{ik} [\text{adj}(A)]_{kj} = \sum_{k=1}^n A_{ik} C_{jk}$ where $C_{jk}$ is cofactor. By Laplace expansion: If $i = j$, $\sum A_{ik} C_{ik} = |A|$. If $i \ne j$, $\sum A_{ik} C_{jk} = 0$ (expansion of determinant with two identical rows). Thus $A \cdot \text{adj}(A) = |A| I_n$.
formulas.description: Fundamental Adjoint Theorem for Square Matrix
formulas.explanation: The core theorem of matrix algebra connecting matrix multiplication, adjoints, determinants, and inverses.

formulas.title: Matrix Inversion Formula

variables.A^{-1}: multiplicative inverse satisfying A * A^{-1} = I

formulas.derivation: From $A \cdot \text{adj}(A) = |A| I_n$. For non-singular matrix $|A| \ne 0$, divide both sides by scalar $|A|$: $A \cdot \left(\frac{1}{|A|} \text{adj}(A)\right) = I_n$. By uniqueness of matrix inverse: $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|} \text{adj}(A)$.
formulas.description: Matrix Inversion Formula
formulas.explanation: Provides explicit analytical inverse for any non-singular square matrix.

formulas.title: Determinant of Adjoint Matrix
formulas.derivation: Take determinant of both sides of $A \cdot \text{adj}(A) = |A| I_n$: $|A \cdot \text{adj}(A)| = ||A| I_n|$. Using properties $|XY| = |X||Y|$ and $|k I_n| = k^n$: $|A| \cdot |\text{adj}(A)| = |A|^n$. For $|A| \ne 0$, divide by $|A|$: $|\text{adj}(A)| = |A|^{n-1}$. Holds by continuity for $|A| = 0$ as well.
formulas.description: Determinant of Adjoint Matrix
formulas.explanation: Direct power relation: for a 3x3 matrix ($n=3$), $|\text{adj}(A)| = |A|^2$.

formulas.title: Double Adjoint Matrix Identities
formulas.derivation: Replace $A$ with $B = \text{adj}(A)$ in adjoint formula: $B \cdot \text{adj}(B) = |B| I \implies \text{adj}(A) \cdot \text{adj}(\text{adj}(A)) = |\text{adj}(A)| I = |A|^{n-1} I$. Multiply on left by $A$: $A \cdot \text{adj}(A) \cdot \text{adj}(\text{adj}(A)) = A |A|^{n-1} I \implies |A| I \cdot \text{adj}(\text{adj}(A)) = |A|^{n-1} A \implies \text{adj}(\text{adj}(A)) = |A|^{n-2} A$. Taking determinant gives $|A|^{(n-1)^2}$.
formulas.description: Double Adjoint Matrix Identities
formulas.explanation: High-frequency JEE Advanced question evaluating compound adjoint operations.

formulas.title: Reversal Law for Inverses and Transposes
formulas.derivation: For transpose: $[(AB)^T]_{ij} = [AB]_{ji} = \sum A_{jk} B_{ki} = \sum B^T_{ik} A^T_{kj} = [B^T A^T]_{ij}$. For inverse: $(AB)(B^{-1} A^{-1}) = A(B B^{-1})A^{-1} = A I A^{-1} = A A^{-1} = I$. Thus by inverse uniqueness $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1} A^{-1}$.
formulas.description: Reversal Law for Inverses and Transposes
formulas.explanation: Multiplication order reverses whenever taking transposes, inverses, or adjoints of products.

formulas.title: Unique Decomposition into Symmetric and Skew-Symmetric Matrices
formulas.derivation: Direct algebra: $\frac{1}{2}(A + A^T) + \frac{1}{2}(A - A^T) = \frac{1}{2}A + \frac{1}{2}A^T + \frac{1}{2}A - \frac{1}{2}A^T = A$. Test symmetry of $P$: $P^T = [\frac{1}{2}(A+A^T)]^T = \frac{1}{2}(A^T+A) = P$. Test skew-symmetry of $Q$: $Q^T = [\frac{1}{2}(A-A^T)]^T = \frac{1}{2}(A^T-A) = -Q$. Diagonal elements of $Q$ must be zero.
formulas.description: Unique Decomposition into Symmetric and Skew-Symmetric Matrices
formulas.explanation: Any square matrix can be uniquely split into a symmetric part and a skew-symmetric part.

formulas.title: Cramer's Rule for System of 3 Linear Equations

variables.\\Delta_x, \\Delta_y, \\Delta_z: determinants with column replaced by constants vector

formulas.derivation: In matrix form $A X = B$. Multiply both sides by adjoint: $\text{adj}(A) A X = \text{adj}(A) B \implies |A| I X = \text{adj}(A) B \implies \Delta X = \text{adj}(A) B$. The first row of $\text{adj}(A) B$ is $C_{11}d_1 + C_{21}d_2 + C_{31}d_3$, which is the cofactor expansion of determinant $\Delta_x$. Thus $\Delta x = \Delta_x \implies x = \Delta_x / \Delta$.
formulas.description: Cramer's Rule for System of 3 Linear Equations
formulas.explanation: Explicit solution formula for non-singular linear systems using determinants.

formulas.latex: \Delta = 0 \text{ and at least one } \Delta_i \ne 0 \implies \text{No Solution (Inconsistent)}; \quad \Delta = \Delta_x = \Delta_y = \Delta_z = 0 \implies \text{Infinite Solutions or Inconsistent}
formulas.title: Consistency Criteria for Non-Homogeneous Linear Systems
formulas.derivation: If $\Delta = 0$, the planes are either parallel or intersect in a line or form a triangular prism. If at least one $\Delta_i \ne 0$, we have $0 \cdot x = \Delta_i \ne 0$, which is algebraically impossible $\implies$ no solution. If all $\Delta_i = 0$, equations may represent coincident or collinear planes (infinitely many solutions), or parallel distinct planes.
formulas.description: Consistency Criteria for Non-Homogeneous Linear Systems
formulas.explanation: Classifies whether a 3D linear system represents intersecting planes, parallel planes, or coincident planes.

formulas.title: Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
formulas.derivation: From matrix identity $(A - \lambda I) \cdot \text{adj}(A - \lambda I) = \det(A - \lambda I) I = p(\lambda) I$. The matrix $\text{adj}(A - \lambda I)$ is a polynomial in $\lambda$ of degree $n-1$: $B_{n-1} \lambda^{n-1} + \dots + B_1 \lambda + B_0$. Equating powers of $\lambda$ and summing matrix products eliminates intermediate matrices $B_k$, proving $p(A) = A^n + c_{n-1} A^{n-1} + \dots + c_0 I = 0$.
formulas.description: Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
formulas.explanation: Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial equation. Allows computing $A^{-1}$ and high powers $A^m$ linearly.

formulas.latex: A A^T = A^T A = I \implies A^{-1} = A^T, \quad |A| = \pm 1
formulas.title: Orthogonal Matrix Definition and Properties
formulas.derivation: By definition $A A^T = I$. Taking determinants: $|A A^T| = |I| \implies |A| |A^T| = 1$. Since $|A^T| = |A|$: $|A|^2 = 1 \implies |A| = \pm 1$. Multiplying $A A^T = I$ by $A^{-1}$ from left: $A^T = A^{-1}$. Columns and rows of orthogonal matrix form an orthonormal basis ($\vec{v}_i \cdot \vec{v}_j = \delta_{ij}$).
formulas.description: Orthogonal Matrix Definition and Properties
formulas.explanation: Represents rigid rotations ($|A| = +1$) and reflections ($|A| = -1$) that preserve lengths and angles in Euclidean space.

formulas.title: Scalar Multiplication Property of Determinants
formulas.derivation: Multiplying matrix $A$ by scalar $k$ multiplies every entry in every row by $k$. Determinant property: factoring $k$ out of a single row scales determinant by $k$. Since there are $n$ rows in an $n \times n$ matrix, factoring $k$ out of all $n$ rows gives $k \times k \times \dots \times k = k^n$. Thus $|kA| = k^n |A|$.
formulas.description: Scalar Multiplication Property of Determinants
formulas.explanation: Common trap in JEE: for 3x3 matrix, $|2A| = 2^3 |A| = 8|A|$, not $2|A|$.

formulas.latex: \begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \\ 1 & b & b^2 \\ 1 & c & c^2 \end{vmatrix} = (a - b)(b - c)(c - a)
formulas.title: Vandermonde Determinant Identity
formulas.derivation: Perform row operations $R_2 \rightarrow R_2 - R_1$ and $R_3 \rightarrow R_3 - R_1$: $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \\ 0 & b-a & b^2-a^2 \\ 0 & c-a & c^2-a^2 \end{vmatrix}$. Factor $(b-a)$ from row 2 and $(c-a)$ from row 3: $(b-a)(c-a) \begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \\ 0 & 1 & b+a \\ 0 & 1 & c+a \end{vmatrix}$. Expanding along first column: $(b-a)(c-a)[(c+a) - (b+a)] = (b-a)(c-a)(c-b) = (a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$.
formulas.description: Vandermonde Determinant Identity
formulas.explanation: Standard polynomial determinant; vanishes if and only if any two of a, b, c are identical.

By Laplace expansion: If $i = j$, $\sum A_{ik} C_{ik} = |A|$. If $i \ne j$, $\sum A_{ik} C_{jk} = 0$ (expansion of determinant with two identical rows). Thus $A \cdot \text{adj}(A) = |A| I_n$.
content_json.explanation: The core theorem of matrix algebra connecting matrix multiplication, adjoints, determinants, and inverses.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: NSEP Physics: Advanced Analytical Mechanics & Rotating Frames
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: Angular momentum is $\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$. Differentiating: $\frac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt} \times \vec{p} + \vec{r} \times \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \vec{v} \times (m\vec{v}) + \vec{r} \times \vec{F}_{net} = 0 + \vec{\tau}_{net}$. For rigid bodies rotating about fixed axis, $\vec{L} = I\vec{\omega}$, so $\vec{\tau} = I\frac{d\vec{\omega}}{dt} = I\vec{\alpha}$.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: If net external torque about an origin is zero, angular momentum $\vec{L}$ about that origin is conserved.

content_json.title: NSEP Physics: Advanced Analytical Mechanics & Rotating Frames

sections.title: NSEP Physics: Advanced Analytical Mechanics & Rotating Frames - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.title: Torque and Angular Momentum Equation
formulas.derivation: Angular momentum is $\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$. Differentiating: $\frac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt} \times \vec{p} + \vec{r} \times \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \vec{v} \times (m\vec{v}) + \vec{r} \times \vec{F}_{net} = 0 + \vec{\tau}_{net}$. For rigid bodies rotating about fixed axis, $\vec{L} = I\vec{\omega}$, so $\vec{\tau} = I\frac{d\vec{\omega}}{dt} = I\vec{\alpha}$.
formulas.description: Rotational analog of Newton's second law relating net torque to moment of inertia and angular acceleration.
formulas.explanation: If net external torque about an origin is zero, angular momentum $\vec{L}$ about that origin is conserved.

formulas.title: Parallel Axis Theorem (Steiner's Theorem)

variables.I_{cm}: Moment of inertia about parallel axis through center of mass
variables.I_{parallel}: Moment of inertia about arbitrary parallel axis

formulas.derivation: Let origin be CM. Coordinate along new axis is $(x + d, y)$. Then $I = \int [(x+d)^2 + y^2] dm = \int (x^2 + y^2) dm + 2d \int x dm + d^2 \int dm$. Since origin is CM, first moment $\int x dm = 0$. Hence $I = I_{cm} + Md^2$.
formulas.description: Moment of inertia about any axis parallel to a centroidal axis at perpendicular distance d.
formulas.explanation: Applies to rigid bodies of arbitrary 3D geometry; must always start from the center-of-mass axis.

formulas.title: Perpendicular Axis Theorem

variables.I_z: Moment of inertia about axis perpendicular to lamina plane
variables.I_x, I_y: Moments of inertia about in-plane orthogonal axes

formulas.derivation: For a planar lamina in xy-plane ($z=0$), distance of mass element $dm$ to z-axis is $r_z^2 = x^2 + y^2$. Integrating: $I_z = \int (x^2 + y^2) dm = \int y^2 dm + \int x^2 dm = I_x + I_y$.
formulas.description: Relates moments of inertia of a planar laminar body about three mutually perpendicular intersecting axes.
formulas.explanation: Valid strictly for flat 2D planar laminas, never for 3D volumetric bodies like spheres or cylinders.

formulas.title: Kinetic Energy of Pure Rolling Body
formulas.derivation: In rolling without slipping, $v_{cm} = R\omega$. Substituting $I_{cm} = Mk^2$: $K = \frac{1}{2}M v_{cm}^2 + \frac{1}{2}(Mk^2)\left(\frac{v_{cm}}{R}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2}M v_{cm}^2\left(1 + \frac{k^2}{R^2}\right)$.
formulas.description: Total kinetic energy decomposed into translational motion of CM and rotation about CM.
formulas.explanation: Fraction of kinetic energy in rotation is $\frac{K_{rot}}{K_{total}} = \frac{k^2/R^2}{1 + k^2/R^2}$ (e.g., $2/7$ for solid sphere, $1/3$ for solid cylinder).

formulas.title: Acceleration of Body Rolling Down an Incline
formulas.derivation: Equations of motion: along incline $Mg\sin\theta - f = Ma$; torque about CM $f R = I_{cm}\alpha = I_{cm}\frac{a}{R} \implies f = \frac{I_{cm}a}{R^2}$. Substituting friction into force equation: $Mg\sin\theta - \frac{I_{cm}a}{R^2} = Ma \implies a\left(M + \frac{I_{cm}}{R^2}\right) = Mg\sin\theta \implies a = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1 + \frac{I_{cm}}{MR^2}}$.
formulas.description: Linear acceleration of a circular symmetric body rolling without slipping down an angle $\theta$.
formulas.explanation: A solid sphere ($k^2/R^2 = 2/5$) reaches the bottom fastest, followed by spherical shell ($2/3$), disc ($1/2$), and hoop/ring ($1$).

formulas.title: Minimum Friction Coefficient for Pure Rolling
formulas.derivation: Friction force is $f = \frac{I_{cm}a}{R^2} = \frac{Mg\sin\theta}{1 + MR^2/I_{cm}}$. Normal force is $N = Mg\cos\theta$. Pure rolling requires $f \le \mu_s N \implies \frac{Mg\sin\theta}{1 + MR^2/I_{cm}} \le \mu_s Mg\cos\theta \implies \mu_s \ge \frac{\tan\theta}{1 + MR^2/I_{cm}}$.
formulas.description: Threshold static friction coefficient required to prevent slipping on an incline.
formulas.explanation: If surface friction $\mu < \mu_{min}$, the body rolls with forward slipping ($v_{cm} \ne R\omega$).

formulas.title: Standard Moments of Inertia of Common Geometries
formulas.derivation: For disc: divide into concentric thin rings of radius $r$, width $dr$, mass $dm = \frac{M}{\pi R^2} 2\pi r dr = \frac{2M}{R^2} r dr$. Ring inertia is $dI = r^2 dm = \frac{2M}{R^2} r^3 dr$. Integrating: $I = \frac{2M}{R^2}\int_0^R r^3 dr = \frac{2M}{R^2}\frac{R^4}{4} = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$. Solid sphere: integrate spherical shells of $dm = 4\pi r^2 \rho dr$ with $I = \frac{2}{5}MR^2$.
formulas.description: Centroidal moments of inertia for standard rigid bodies rotating about symmetry axis.
formulas.explanation: Essential reference constants for rigid body rotational dynamics.

formulas.title: Moment of Inertia of Thin Uniform Rod
formulas.derivation: Linear mass density $\lambda = M/L$. For CM axis: $I_{cm} = \int_{-L/2}^{L/2} x^2 (\lambda dx) = \lambda \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-L/2}^{L/2} = \frac{M}{L}\left(\frac{L^3}{24} - \left(-\frac{L^3}{24}\right)\right) = \frac{1}{12}ML^2$. For end axis, parallel axis theorem gives $I_{end} = I_{cm} + M(L/2)^2 = \frac{1}{12}ML^2 + \frac{1}{4}ML^2 = \frac{1}{3}ML^2$.
formulas.description: Inertia about transverse axes passing through center of mass and one end.
formulas.explanation: Rotating about the end takes 4 times more torque for same angular acceleration as rotating about the center.

formulas.latex: v_c = \frac{m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2}{m_1 + m_2}, \quad L_O = \vec{r}_{cm} \times M\vec{v}_{cm} + \vec{L}_{cm}
formulas.title: Center of Mass Velocity and Koenig's Theorem for Angular Momentum
formulas.derivation: Let $\vec{r}_i = \vec{r}_{cm} + \vec{r}'_i$ and $\vec{v}_i = \vec{v}_{cm} + \vec{v}'_i$. Total angular momentum $\vec{L}_O = \sum m_i (\vec{r}_{cm} + \vec{r}'_i) \times (\vec{v}_{cm} + \vec{v}'_i) = \vec{r}_{cm} \times M\vec{v}_{cm} + \sum m_i \vec{r}'_i \times \vec{v}'_i + \vec{r}_{cm} \times \sum m_i \vec{v}'_i + (\sum m_i \vec{r}'_i) \times \vec{v}_{cm}$. By definition of CM, cross terms vanish, giving $\vec{L}_O = \vec{r}_{cm} \times M\vec{v}_{cm} + I_{cm}\vec{\omega}$.
formulas.description: Decomposition of total angular momentum about origin O into CM orbital part and intrinsic spin part.
formulas.explanation: Allows decoupling orbital angular momentum of planetary motion from planetary axial spin.

formulas.title: Condition for Toppling Before Sliding

variables.\\mu: Coefficient of friction between block and floor

formulas.derivation: Let horizontal force $F$ be applied at top height $h$. Sliding occurs when $F = \mu mg$. Toppling occurs about front edge when overturning torque exceeds stabilizing torque: $F h > mg (b/2) \implies F > mg \frac{b}{2h}$. Toppling occurs prior to sliding if $F_{topple} < F_{slide} \implies mg \frac{b}{2h} < \mu mg \implies \mu > \frac{b}{2h}$.
formulas.description: Threshold coefficient of friction determining whether a rectangular block of width b and height h topples or slips.
formulas.explanation: Tall, narrow blocks (large $h$, small $b$) topple easily on rough floors; squat blocks slide first.

formulas.title: Time Period of Physical (Compound) Pendulum
formulas.derivation: Restoring torque about pivot for deflection $\theta$ is $\tau = -mgd\sin\theta \approx -mgd\theta$. Equation of motion: $I\alpha = -mgd\theta \implies \frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} + \frac{mgd}{I}\theta = 0$. Angular frequency is $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{mgd}{I}}$. Period $T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{mgd}}$. Using parallel axis theorem $I = m(k^2 + d^2)$ gives $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{k^2 + d^2}{gd}}$.
formulas.description: Small-angle oscillation period of a rigid body pivoted at distance d from its center of mass.
formulas.explanation: Equivalent simple pendulum length is $L_{eq} = \frac{k^2 + d^2}{d}$. Minimum period occurs when $d = k$.

formulas.latex: x_{cm} = \frac{\int x \, dm}{\int dm}, \quad x_{cm, hem} = \frac{3}{8}R, \quad y_{cm, cone} = \frac{h}{4}
formulas.title: Center of Mass of Continuous Bodies
formulas.derivation: Solid hemisphere of radius $R$: slice into thin circular discs of thickness $dy$ at distance $y$ from base. Disc radius is $r = \sqrt{R^2 - y^2}$, mass $dm = \rho \pi (R^2 - y^2) dy$. Centroid is $y_{cm} = \frac{\int_0^R y \rho \pi (R^2 - y^2) dy}{\frac{2}{3}\pi R^3 \rho} = \frac{\pi [\frac{R^2 y^2}{2} - \frac{y^4}{4}]_0^R}{\frac{2}{3}\pi R^3} = \frac{R^4 / 4}{\frac{2}{3}R^3} = \frac{3}{8}R$.
formulas.description: Centroid coordinates for hemisphere, solid cone, and semicircular disc.
formulas.explanation: For hollow hemisphere, $y_{cm} = R/2$. For semicircular wire loop, $y_{cm} = 2R/\pi$.

content_json.derivation: Angular momentum is $\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$. Differentiating: $\frac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt} \times \vec{p} + \vec{r} \times \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \vec{v} \times (m\vec{v}) + \vec{r} \times \vec{F}_{net} = 0 + \vec{\tau}_{net}$. For rigid bodies rotating about fixed axis, $\vec{L} = I\vec{\omega}$, so $\vec{\tau} = I\frac{d\vec{\omega}}{dt} = I\vec{\alpha}$.
content_json.explanation: If net external torque about an origin is zero, angular momentum $\vec{L}$ about that origin is conserved.

formulas.latex: A + AB = A, \quad A(A + B) = A
formulas.title: Absorption Laws of Boolean Algebra
formulas.derivation: $A + AB = A \cdot 1 + AB = A(1 + B)$. By dominance law, $1 + B = 1$. Thus $A(1) = A$. Dual identity: $A(A + B) = AA + AB = A + AB = A$.
formulas.description: Fundamental algebraic reduction identity eliminating redundant literals.
formulas.explanation: Crucial for simplifying logic circuits and minimizing logic gate counts.

formulas.title: De Morgan's Laws
formulas.derivation: Augustus De Morgan (1847) proved set complement duality $(A \cup B)^c = A^c \cap B^c$. Verifiable via truth table: for all 4 combinations of $(A, B)$, the output of $\overline{A + B}$ exactly matches $\overline{A} \cdot \overline{B}$.
formulas.description: Dual laws converting NOR to AND with inverted inputs and NAND to OR with inverted inputs.
formulas.explanation: Enables universal NAND/NOR logic realization and compiler conditional expression optimization.

formulas.latex: A + \overline{A}B = A + B, \quad A(\overline{A} + B) = AB
formulas.title: Boolean Redundancy (Simplification) Theorem
formulas.derivation: Apply distributive law: $A + \overline{A}B = (A + \overline{A})(A + B)$. By complement law, $A + \overline{A} = 1$. Thus $1 \cdot (A + B) = A + B$. Dual: $A(\overline{A} + B) = A\overline{A} + AB = 0 + AB = AB$.
formulas.description: Removes complemented literal from adjacent product term.
formulas.explanation: Frequently used in digital electronics Karnaugh map minimization.

formulas.title: Consensus Theorem
formulas.derivation: Expand third term using $A + \overline{A} = 1$: $AB + \overline{A}C + BC(A + \overline{A}) = AB + \overline{A}C + ABC + \overline{A}BC = AB(1 + C) + \overline{A}C(1 + B) = AB(1) + \overline{A}C(1) = AB + \overline{A}C$.
formulas.description: Eliminates redundant consensus term BC in sum-of-products expressions.
formulas.explanation: The term $BC$ is the consensus term of $AB$ and $\overline{A}C$ and can be eliminated without altering logical equivalence.

formulas.latex: f(x_1, \dots, x_n) = x_1 f(1, x_2, \dots, x_n) + \overline{x}_1 f(0, x_2, \dots, x_n)
formulas.title: Shannon's Expansion Theorem
formulas.derivation: Claude Shannon (1938) proved that setting $x_1=1$ or $x_1=0$ evaluates the function conditionally: when $x_1=1$, second term vanishes and first term evaluates to $f(1, \dots)$; when $x_1=0$, first term vanishes and second term evaluates to $f(0, \dots)$.
formulas.description: Decomposes any boolean function into sum of cofactor functions for multiplexer implementation.
formulas.explanation: Foundation of Binary Decision Diagrams (BDD) and FPGA Look-Up Table (LUT) architectures.

formulas.title: Exclusive-OR (XOR) Logic Properties
formulas.derivation: XOR evaluates to true when inputs are strictly distinct: $(A=1, B=0)$ or $(A=0, B=1)$. In sum-of-products form: $A\overline{B} + \overline{A}B$. Applying boolean factoring yields product-of-sums form $(A+B)(\overline{A}+\overline{B})$.
formulas.description: Modulo-2 addition truth table producing 1 if and only if inputs differ.
formulas.explanation: Key properties: $A \oplus 0 = A$; $A \oplus 1 = \overline{A}$; $A \oplus A = 0$; $A \oplus \overline{A} = 1$; self-inverse $((A \oplus B) \oplus B = A)$ used in cryptography.

formulas.latex: S = A \oplus B \oplus C_{in}, \quad C_{out} = AB + BC_{in} + AC_{in} = AB + C_{in}(A \oplus B)
formulas.title: Full Adder Circuit Equations
formulas.derivation: Full adder sums 3 binary bits: $S = A + B + C_{in} \pmod 2 = A \oplus B \oplus C_{in}$. Carry out occurs when at least 2 of the 3 inputs are 1: $C_{out} = AB + BC_{in} + AC_{in}$. Factoring: $AB + C_{in}(A + B) = AB + C_{in}(A \oplus B)$ (since $A B$ term already covers overlap).
formulas.description: Calculates sum bit S and carry-out bit $C_{out}$ for addition of three binary bits.
formulas.explanation: Core functional unit of arithmetic logic units (ALU) in microprocessors.

formulas.latex: C_{i+1} = G_i + P_i C_i, \quad G_i = A_i B_i, \quad P_i = A_i \oplus B_i
formulas.title: Carry Lookahead Adder (CLA) Generator and Propagator
formulas.derivation: Bit stage $i$ generates a carry unconditionally if $A_i = B_i = 1$ ($G_i = A_i B_i$). It propagates an incoming carry if either $A_i=1$ or $B_i=1$ ($P_i = A_i \oplus B_i$). The carry recurrence is $C_{i+1} = G_i + P_i C_i$. Unrolling recursively: $C_1 = G_0 + P_0 C_0$; $C_2 = G_1 + P_1 G_0 + P_1 P_0 C_0$; $C_3 = G_2 + P_2 G_1 + P_2 P_1 G_0 + P_2 P_1 P_0 C_0$.
formulas.description: Computes carries in $O(1)$ constant circuit delay by precomputing carry generation and propagation.
formulas.explanation: Eliminates ripple carry delay, reducing n-bit addition latency from $O(n)$ to $O(\log n)$.

formulas.latex: T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n) \implies T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a}) \quad (\text{if } f(n) = O(n^{\log_b a - \epsilon}))
formulas.title: Master Theorem for Divide-and-Conquer Recurrences

variables.f(n): Cost of divide and combine steps

formulas.derivation: Recurrence tree analysis: at depth $k$, number of nodes is $a^k$, each of size $n/b^k$. Total tree depth is $\log_b n$. Total leaf nodes is $a^{\log_b n} = n^{\log_b a}$. Case 1: If leaf work dominates ($f(n) = O(n^{\log_b a - \epsilon})$), $T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a})$. Case 2: If work is uniformly distributed at each level ($f(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a} \log^k n)$), $T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a} \log^{k+1} n)$. Case 3: If root work dominates ($f(n) = \Omega(n^{\log_b a + \epsilon})$ and regularity condition holds), $T(n) = \Theta(f(n))$.
formulas.description: Closed-form asymptotic Big-O runtime analysis for recursive algorithmic recurrences.
formulas.explanation: Examples: Merge Sort ($a=2, b=2, f(n)=n \implies T(n) = \Theta(n\log n)$); Strassen Matrix Multiplication ($a=7, b=2 \implies O(n^{\log_2 7}) \approx O(n^{2.81})$).

formulas.title: Gradient Descent with Momentum Optimization

variables.w_t: Model parameter weights at step t

formulas.derivation:
Standard gradient descent updates along instantaneous negative gradient: $w_{t+1} = w_t - \eta 
abla L$. Polyak (1964) introduced heavy-ball momentum to accelerate along flat ravines and dampen high-frequency oscillations: velocity vector updates as $v_t =  eta v_{t-1} + \eta 
abla L(w_t)$, and parameter updates as $w_{t+1} = w_t - v_t$. Unrolling reveals $v_t = \eta \sum_{	au=0}^t  eta^{t-	au} 
abla L(w_	au)$.
formulas.description: Accelerates gradient descent by incorporating an exponentially decaying moving average of past gradients.
formulas.explanation: Dramatically speeds up deep neural network training across narrow valleys and saddle points.

formulas.title: Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation) Optimizer
formulas.derivation: Diederik Kingma and Jimmy Ba (2014) combined Momentum and RMSprop: bias-corrected first and second moments are $\hat{m}_t = \frac{m_t}{1 - \beta_1^t}$ and $\hat{v}_t = \frac{v_t}{1 - \beta_2^t}$. The parameter update is $w_{t+1} = w_t - \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{\hat{v}_t} + \epsilon}\hat{m}_t$.
formulas.description: Computes individual adaptive learning rates for different parameters from estimates of first and second gradient moments.
formulas.explanation: State-of-the-art default optimizer for transformers (BERT, GPT, Llama) and deep learning models.

formulas.title: Binary Cross-Entropy Loss (Log Loss)
formulas.derivation: Assuming Bernoulli distribution for class probability: $P(y|x) = \hat{y}^y (1 - \hat{y})^{1-y}$. Likelihood over $N$ independent samples is $L = \prod_{i=1}^N \hat{y}_i^{y_i}(1 - \hat{y}_i)^{1 - y_i}$. Taking natural logarithm: $\ln L = \sum [y_i \ln\hat{y}_i + (1 - y_i)\ln(1 - \hat{y}_i)]$. Minimizing negative log-likelihood per sample yields Binary Cross-Entropy loss $L_{BCE} = -\frac{1}{N}\sum [y_i\ln\hat{y}_i + (1 - y_i)\ln(1 - \hat{y}_i)]$.
formulas.description: Negative log-likelihood loss function for binary classification models with sigmoid output probabilities.
formulas.explanation: When paired with sigmoid output $\hat{y} = \sigma(z)$, gradient is linear and free of vanishing gradients: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial z} = \hat{y} - y$.

formulas.derivation: Apply distributive law: $A + \overline{A}B = (A + \overline{A})(A + B)$. By complement law, $A + \overline{A} = 1$. Thus $1 \cdot (A + B) = A + B$. Dual: $A(\overline{A} + B) = A\overline{A} + AB = 0 + AB = AB$.
formulas.description: Removes complemented literal from adjacent product term.
formulas.explanation: Frequently used in digital electronics Karnaugh map minimization.

formulas.title: Consensus Theorem
formulas.derivation: Expand third term using $A + \overline{A} = 1$: $AB + \overline{A}C + BC(A + \overline{A}) = AB + \overline{A}C + ABC + \overline{A}BC = AB(1 + C) + \overline{A}C(1 + B) = AB(1) + \overline{A}C(1) = AB + \overline{A}C$.
formulas.description: Eliminates redundant consensus term BC in sum-of-products expressions.
formulas.explanation: The term $BC$ is the consensus term of $AB$ and $\overline{A}C$ and can be eliminated without altering logical equivalence.

formulas.latex: f(x_1, \dots, x_n) = x_1 f(1, x_2, \dots, x_n) + \overline{x}_1 f(0, x_2, \dots, x_n)
formulas.title: Shannon's Expansion Theorem
formulas.derivation: Claude Shannon (1938) proved that setting $x_1=1$ or $x_1=0$ evaluates the function conditionally: when $x_1=1$, second term vanishes and first term evaluates to $f(1, \dots)$; when $x_1=0$, first term vanishes and second term evaluates to $f(0, \dots)$.
formulas.description: Decomposes any boolean function into sum of cofactor functions for multiplexer implementation.
formulas.explanation: Foundation of Binary Decision Diagrams (BDD) and FPGA Look-Up Table (LUT) architectures.

formulas.title: Exclusive-OR (XOR) Logic Properties
formulas.derivation: XOR evaluates to true when inputs are strictly distinct: $(A=1, B=0)$ or $(A=0, B=1)$. In sum-of-products form: $A\overline{B} + \overline{A}B$. Applying boolean factoring yields product-of-sums form $(A+B)(\overline{A}+\overline{B})$.
formulas.description: Modulo-2 addition truth table producing 1 if and only if inputs differ.
formulas.explanation: Key properties: $A \oplus 0 = A$; $A \oplus 1 = \overline{A}$; $A \oplus A = 0$; $A \oplus \overline{A} = 1$; self-inverse $((A \oplus B) \oplus B = A)$ used in cryptography.

formulas.latex: S = A \oplus B \oplus C_{in}, \quad C_{out} = AB + BC_{in} + AC_{in} = AB + C_{in}(A \oplus B)
formulas.title: Full Adder Circuit Equations
formulas.derivation: Full adder sums 3 binary bits: $S = A + B + C_{in} \pmod 2 = A \oplus B \oplus C_{in}$. Carry out occurs when at least 2 of the 3 inputs are 1: $C_{out} = AB + BC_{in} + AC_{in}$. Factoring: $AB + C_{in}(A + B) = AB + C_{in}(A \oplus B)$ (since $A B$ term already covers overlap).
formulas.description: Calculates sum bit S and carry-out bit $C_{out}$ for addition of three binary bits.
formulas.explanation: Core functional unit of arithmetic logic units (ALU) in microprocessors.

formulas.latex: C_{i+1} = G_i + P_i C_i, \quad G_i = A_i B_i, \quad P_i = A_i \oplus B_i
formulas.title: Carry Lookahead Adder (CLA) Generator and Propagator
formulas.derivation: Bit stage $i$ generates a carry unconditionally if $A_i = B_i = 1$ ($G_i = A_i B_i$). It propagates an incoming carry if either $A_i=1$ or $B_i=1$ ($P_i = A_i \oplus B_i$). The carry recurrence is $C_{i+1} = G_i + P_i C_i$. Unrolling recursively: $C_1 = G_0 + P_0 C_0$; $C_2 = G_1 + P_1 G_0 + P_1 P_0 C_0$; $C_3 = G_2 + P_2 G_1 + P_2 P_1 G_0 + P_2 P_1 P_0 C_0$.
formulas.description: Computes carries in $O(1)$ constant circuit delay by precomputing carry generation and propagation.
formulas.explanation: Eliminates ripple carry delay, reducing n-bit addition latency from $O(n)$ to $O(\log n)$.

formulas.latex: T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n) \implies T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a}) \quad (\text{if } f(n) = O(n^{\log_b a - \epsilon}))
formulas.title: Master Theorem for Divide-and-Conquer Recurrences

variables.f(n): Cost of divide and combine steps

formulas.derivation: Recurrence tree analysis: at depth $k$, number of nodes is $a^k$, each of size $n/b^k$. Total tree depth is $\log_b n$. Total leaf nodes is $a^{\log_b n} = n^{\log_b a}$. Case 1: If leaf work dominates ($f(n) = O(n^{\log_b a - \epsilon})$), $T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a})$. Case 2: If work is uniformly distributed at each level ($f(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a} \log^k n)$), $T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a} \log^{k+1} n)$. Case 3: If root work dominates ($f(n) = \Omega(n^{\log_b a + \epsilon})$ and regularity condition holds), $T(n) = \Theta(f(n))$.
formulas.description: Closed-form asymptotic Big-O runtime analysis for recursive algorithmic recurrences.
formulas.explanation: Examples: Merge Sort ($a=2, b=2, f(n)=n \implies T(n) = \Theta(n\log n)$); Strassen Matrix Multiplication ($a=7, b=2 \implies O(n^{\log_2 7}) \approx O(n^{2.81})$).

formulas.title: Gradient Descent with Momentum Optimization

variables.w_t: Model parameter weights at step t

formulas.derivation:
Standard gradient descent updates along instantaneous negative gradient: $w_{t+1} = w_t - \eta 
abla L$. Polyak (1964) introduced heavy-ball momentum to accelerate along flat ravines and dampen high-frequency oscillations: velocity vector updates as $v_t =  eta v_{t-1} + \eta 
abla L(w_t)$, and parameter updates as $w_{t+1} = w_t - v_t$. Unrolling reveals $v_t = \eta \sum_{	au=0}^t  eta^{t-	au} 
abla L(w_	au)$.
formulas.description: Accelerates gradient descent by incorporating an exponentially decaying moving average of past gradients.
formulas.explanation: Dramatically speeds up deep neural network training across narrow valleys and saddle points.

formulas.title: Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation) Optimizer
formulas.derivation: Diederik Kingma and Jimmy Ba (2014) combined Momentum and RMSprop: bias-corrected first and second moments are $\hat{m}_t = \frac{m_t}{1 - \beta_1^t}$ and $\hat{v}_t = \frac{v_t}{1 - \beta_2^t}$. The parameter update is $w_{t+1} = w_t - \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{\hat{v}_t} + \epsilon}\hat{m}_t$.
formulas.description: Computes individual adaptive learning rates for different parameters from estimates of first and second gradient moments.
formulas.explanation: State-of-the-art default optimizer for transformers (BERT, GPT, Llama) and deep learning models.

formulas.title: Binary Cross-Entropy Loss (Log Loss)
formulas.derivation: Assuming Bernoulli distribution for class probability: $P(y|x) = \hat{y}^y (1 - \hat{y})^{1-y}$. Likelihood over $N$ independent samples is $L = \prod_{i=1}^N \hat{y}_i^{y_i}(1 - \hat{y}_i)^{1 - y_i}$. Taking natural logarithm: $\ln L = \sum [y_i \ln\hat{y}_i + (1 - y_i)\ln(1 - \hat{y}_i)]$. Minimizing negative log-likelihood per sample yields Binary Cross-Entropy loss $L_{BCE} = -\frac{1}{N}\sum [y_i\ln\hat{y}_i + (1 - y_i)\ln(1 - \hat{y}_i)]$.
formulas.description: Negative log-likelihood loss function for binary classification models with sigmoid output probabilities.
formulas.explanation: When paired with sigmoid output $\hat{y} = \sigma(z)$, gradient is linear and free of vanishing gradients: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial z} = \hat{y} - y$.

content_json.derivation: $A + AB = A \cdot 1 + AB = A(1 + B)$. By dominance law, $1 + B = 1$. Thus $A(1) = A$. Dual identity: $A(A + B) = AA + AB = A + AB = A$.
content_json.explanation: Crucial for simplifying logic circuits and minimizing logic gate counts.

formulas.title: Quadratic Formula for roots of ax^2 + bx + c = 0
formulas.derivation: Divide $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ by $a$: $x^2 + \frac{b}{a}x = -\frac{c}{a}$. Complete square by adding $\left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2$: $\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 = \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}$. Taking square roots gives $x + \frac{b}{2a} = \pm \frac{\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} \implies x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$.
formulas.description: Quadratic Formula for roots of ax^2 + bx + c = 0
formulas.explanation: Yields the two exact roots of any general quadratic polynomial. The term $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$ governs the nature of the roots.

formulas.title: Vieta's Formulas for Quadratic Equations
formulas.derivation: Since $\alpha, \beta$ are roots: $a(x - \alpha)(x - \beta) = a(x^2 - (\alpha + \beta)x + \alpha\beta) = ax^2 - a(\alpha + \beta)x + a\alpha\beta = ax^2 + bx + c$. Equating coefficients: $-a(\alpha + \beta) = b \implies \alpha + \beta = -b/a$, and $a\alpha\beta = c \implies \alpha\beta = c/a$.
formulas.description: Vieta's Formulas for Quadratic Equations
formulas.explanation: Directly links polynomial coefficients to root sums and products without solving the equation explicitly.

formulas.title: Difference of Roots Formula
formulas.derivation: Using identity $(\alpha - \beta)^2 = (\alpha + \beta)^2 - 4\alpha\beta = \left(-\frac{b}{a}\right)^2 - 4\frac{c}{a} = \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{a^2} = \frac{\Delta}{a^2}$. Taking principal square root gives $|\alpha - \beta| = \frac{\sqrt{\Delta}}{|a|}$.
formulas.description: Difference of Roots Formula
formulas.explanation: Measures the horizontal distance between the x-intercepts of the parabola $y = ax^2 + bx + c$.

formulas.title: Discriminant Characterization of Roots
formulas.derivation: Follows directly from the radical term $\sqrt{\Delta}$ in the quadratic formula. If $\Delta > 0$, $\sqrt{\Delta} \in \mathbb{R}^+$, yielding two distinct real values. If $\Delta = 0$, $\sqrt{\Delta} = 0$, giving coincident root $-b/(2a)$. If $\Delta < 0$, $\sqrt{\Delta} = i\sqrt{-\Delta}$, producing non-real conjugate pair $\frac{-b \pm i\sqrt{4ac - b^2}}{2a}$.
formulas.description: Discriminant Characterization of Roots
formulas.explanation: Determines whether the parabola intersects the x-axis at 2 points, touches at 1 vertex, or never intersects.

formulas.title: Condition for Exactly One Common Root Between Two Quadratics

variables.a_i, b_i, c_i: coefficients of a1 x^2 + b1 x + c1 = 0 and a2 x^2 + b2 x + c2 = 0

formulas.derivation: Let $\alpha$ be common root: $a_1 \alpha^2 + b_1 \alpha + c_1 = 0$ and $a_2 \alpha^2 + b_2 \alpha + c_2 = 0$. By cross-multiplication: $\frac{\alpha^2}{b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1} = \frac{\alpha}{c_1 a_2 - c_2 a_1} = \frac{1}{a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1}$. Eliminating $\alpha$: $\alpha = \frac{c_1 a_2 - c_2 a_1}{a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1}$, so $\alpha^2 = \frac{(c_1 a_2 - c_2 a_1)^2}{(a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1)^2} = \frac{b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1}{a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1} \implies (c_1 a_2 - c_2 a_1)^2 = (a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1)(b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1)$.
formulas.description: Condition for Exactly One Common Root Between Two Quadratics
formulas.explanation: Necessary and sufficient algebraic condition for two distinct quadratic equations to share a common solution.

formulas.latex: \Delta \ge 0, \quad a \cdot f(k) > 0, \quad -\frac{b}{2a} > k \implies \text{Both roots greater than } k
formulas.title: Location of Roots: Both roots greater than real number k
formulas.derivation: For both roots $\alpha, \beta > k$: (1) Real roots require $\Delta \ge 0$. (2) Parabola opens up ($a>0$) means $f(k) > 0$; opens down ($a<0$) means $f(k) < 0$, unified as $a \cdot f(k) > 0$. (3) The vertex $x = -b/(2a) = (\alpha + \beta)/2$ must lie strictly to the right of $k$: $-b/(2a) > k$.
formulas.description: Location of Roots: Both roots greater than real number k
formulas.explanation: Standard IIT-JEE test for restricting both roots of a quadratic polynomial to the right of a given real value k.

formulas.latex: a \cdot f(k) < 0 \implies k \text{ lies strictly between the roots}
formulas.title: Location of Roots: Number k lies strictly between roots
formulas.derivation: If $k$ lies between $\alpha$ and $\beta$, the vertex value must have opposite sign to $f(k)$ compared to $a$. If $a > 0$, parabola is below x-axis between roots $\implies f(k) < 0 \implies a f(k) < 0$. If $a < 0$, parabola is above x-axis between roots $\implies f(k) > 0 \implies a f(k) < 0$. Note: $\Delta > 0$ is automatically guaranteed since $a f(k) < 0 \implies b^2 - 4ac > 0$.
formulas.description: Location of Roots: Number k lies strictly between roots
formulas.explanation: Simplest root-location check: a single inequality $a f(k) < 0$ guarantees real distinct roots with k strictly between them.

formulas.title: Maximum or Minimum Value of Quadratic Function

variables.a: lead coefficient (min if a > 0, max if a < 0)

formulas.derivation: Let $f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$. Setting derivative to zero: $f'(x) = 2ax + b = 0 \implies x = -b/(2a)$. Evaluating at critical point: $f(-b/2a) = a\left(\frac{b^2}{4a^2}\right) + b\left(-\frac{b}{2a}\right) + c = \frac{b^2 - 2b^2 + 4ac}{4a} = -\frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a} = -\frac{\Delta}{4a}$. Second derivative $f''(x) = 2a$, so minimum if $a > 0$, maximum if $a < 0$.
formulas.description: Maximum or Minimum Value of Quadratic Function
formulas.explanation: Gives the absolute extremum of a quadratic polynomial. Range of $f(x)$ is $[-\Delta/4a, \infty)$ if $a > 0$ and $(-\infty, -\Delta/4a]$ if $a < 0$.

formulas.latex: a S_n + b S_{n-1} + c S_{n-2} = 0 \quad \text{where } S_n = p \alpha^n + q \beta^n
formulas.title: Newton's Sums Theorem for Powers of Roots

variables.S_n: linear combination of n-th powers of roots

formulas.derivation: Since $\alpha$ and $\beta$ satisfy $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$: $a\alpha^2 + b\alpha + c = 0$ and $a\beta^2 + b\beta + c = 0$. Multiply by $p\alpha^{n-2}$ and $q\beta^{n-2}$ respectively: $a(p\alpha^n) + b(p\alpha^{n-1}) + c(p\alpha^{n-2}) = 0$ and $a(q\beta^n) + b(q\beta^{n-1}) + c(q\beta^{n-2}) = 0$. Adding both equations yields $a(p\alpha^n + q\beta^n) + b(p\alpha^{n-1} + q\beta^{n-1}) + c(p\alpha^{n-2} + q\beta^{n-2}) = 0 \implies aS_n + bS_{n-1} + cS_{n-2} = 0$.
formulas.description: Newton's Sums Theorem for Powers of Roots
formulas.explanation: Extremely powerful JEE Advanced shortcut for computing high-power root expressions like $\alpha^{10} -  eta^{10}$ without calculating roots.

formulas.title: Sum of Cubes of Quadratic Roots
formulas.derivation: From algebraic identity $(\alpha+\beta)^3 = \alpha^3 + \beta^3 + 3\alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta)$, rearrange: $\alpha^3 + \beta^3 = (\alpha+\beta)^3 - 3\alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta)$. Substitute $\alpha+\beta = -b/a$ and $\alpha\beta = c/a$: $\alpha^3 + \beta^3 = (-b/a)^3 - 3(c/a)(-b/a) = -\frac{b^3}{a^3} + \frac{3bc}{a^2} = \frac{3abc - b^3}{a^3}$.
formulas.description: Sum of Cubes of Quadratic Roots
formulas.explanation: Allows fast computation of third-order symmetric root expressions using solely equation coefficients.

formulas.title: Condition for Positive Definite Quadratic Expression
formulas.derivation: Completing square: $f(x) = a\left[\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 - \frac{\Delta}{4a^2}\right]$. The squared term is $\ge 0$. For $f(x)$ to remain strictly positive for all $x$, the parabola must open upwards ($a > 0$) and its minimum vertex value $-\Delta/(4a)$ must be strictly positive, which requires $-\Delta > 0 \implies \Delta < 0$.
formulas.description: Condition for Positive Definite Quadratic Expression
formulas.explanation: Guarantees that a quadratic expression never crosses or touches zero, remaining strictly positive across all real numbers.

formulas.latex: c x^2 + b x + a = 0 \implies \text{roots are } \frac{1}{\alpha}, \frac{1}{\beta}
formulas.title: Transformation of Equations: Reciprocal Roots
formulas.derivation: Let $y = 1/x \implies x = 1/y$. Substitute into $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$: $a(1/y)^2 + b(1/y) + c = 0 \implies \frac{a}{y^2} + \frac{b}{y} + c = 0$. Multiply through by $y^2$: $c y^2 + b y + a = 0$. The roots of this transformed equation are $y_1 = 1/\alpha$ and $y_2 = 1/\beta$.
formulas.description: Transformation of Equations: Reciprocal Roots
formulas.explanation: Reversing the coefficients of a polynomial immediately inverts all its roots.

Second derivative $f''(x) = 2a$, so minimum if $a > 0$, maximum if $a < 0$.
formulas.description: Maximum or Minimum Value of Quadratic Function
formulas.explanation: Gives the absolute extremum of a quadratic polynomial. Range of $f(x)$ is $[-\Delta/4a, \infty)$ if $a > 0$ and $(-\infty, -\Delta/4a]$ if $a < 0$.

formulas.latex: a S_n + b S_{n-1} + c S_{n-2} = 0 \quad \text{where } S_n = p \alpha^n + q \beta^n
formulas.title: Newton's Sums Theorem for Powers of Roots

variables.S_n: linear combination of n-th powers of roots

formulas.derivation: Since $\alpha$ and $\beta$ satisfy $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$: $a\alpha^2 + b\alpha + c = 0$ and $a\beta^2 + b\beta + c = 0$. Multiply by $p\alpha^{n-2}$ and $q\beta^{n-2}$ respectively: $a(p\alpha^n) + b(p\alpha^{n-1}) + c(p\alpha^{n-2}) = 0$ and $a(q\beta^n) + b(q\beta^{n-1}) + c(q\beta^{n-2}) = 0$. Adding both equations yields $a(p\alpha^n + q\beta^n) + b(p\alpha^{n-1} + q\beta^{n-1}) + c(p\alpha^{n-2} + q\beta^{n-2}) = 0 \implies aS_n + bS_{n-1} + cS_{n-2} = 0$.
formulas.description: Newton's Sums Theorem for Powers of Roots
formulas.explanation: Extremely powerful JEE Advanced shortcut for computing high-power root expressions like $\alpha^{10} -  eta^{10}$ without calculating roots.

formulas.title: Sum of Cubes of Quadratic Roots
formulas.derivation: From algebraic identity $(\alpha+\beta)^3 = \alpha^3 + \beta^3 + 3\alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta)$, rearrange: $\alpha^3 + \beta^3 = (\alpha+\beta)^3 - 3\alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta)$. Substitute $\alpha+\beta = -b/a$ and $\alpha\beta = c/a$: $\alpha^3 + \beta^3 = (-b/a)^3 - 3(c/a)(-b/a) = -\frac{b^3}{a^3} + \frac{3bc}{a^2} = \frac{3abc - b^3}{a^3}$.
formulas.description: Sum of Cubes of Quadratic Roots
formulas.explanation: Allows fast computation of third-order symmetric root expressions using solely equation coefficients.

formulas.title: Condition for Positive Definite Quadratic Expression
formulas.derivation: Completing square: $f(x) = a\left[\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 - \frac{\Delta}{4a^2}\right]$. The squared term is $\ge 0$. For $f(x)$ to remain strictly positive for all $x$, the parabola must open upwards ($a > 0$) and its minimum vertex value $-\Delta/(4a)$ must be strictly positive, which requires $-\Delta > 0 \implies \Delta < 0$.
formulas.description: Condition for Positive Definite Quadratic Expression
formulas.explanation: Guarantees that a quadratic expression never crosses or touches zero, remaining strictly positive across all real numbers.

formulas.latex: c x^2 + b x + a = 0 \implies \text{roots are } \frac{1}{\alpha}, \frac{1}{\beta}
formulas.title: Transformation of Equations: Reciprocal Roots
formulas.derivation: Let $y = 1/x \implies x = 1/y$. Substitute into $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$: $a(1/y)^2 + b(1/y) + c = 0 \implies \frac{a}{y^2} + \frac{b}{y} + c = 0$. Multiply through by $y^2$: $c y^2 + b y + a = 0$. The roots of this transformed equation are $y_1 = 1/\alpha$ and $y_2 = 1/\beta$.
formulas.description: Transformation of Equations: Reciprocal Roots
formulas.explanation: Reversing the coefficients of a polynomial immediately inverts all its roots.

content_json.derivation: Divide $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ by $a$: $x^2 + \frac{b}{a}x = -\frac{c}{a}$. Complete square by adding $\left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2$: $\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 = \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}$. Taking square roots gives $x + \frac{b}{2a} = \pm \frac{\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} \implies x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$.
content_json.explanation: Yields the two exact roots of any general quadratic polynomial. The term $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$ governs the nature of the roots.

formulas.title: Quadratic Formula for roots of ax^2 + bx + c = 0
formulas.derivation: Divide $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ by $a$: $x^2 + \frac{b}{a}x = -\frac{c}{a}$. Complete square by adding $\left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2$: $\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 = \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}$. Taking square roots gives $x + \frac{b}{2a} = \pm \frac{\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} \implies x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$.

formulas.explanation: Yields the two exact roots of any general quadratic polynomial. The term $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$ governs the nature of the roots.

formulas.title: Vieta's Formulas for Quadratic Equations
formulas.derivation: Since $\alpha, \beta$ are roots: $a(x - \alpha)(x - \beta) = a(x^2 - (\alpha + \beta)x + \alpha\beta) = ax^2 - a(\alpha + \beta)x + a\alpha\beta = ax^2 + bx + c$. Equating coefficients: $-a(\alpha + \beta) = b \implies \alpha + \beta = -b/a$, and $a\alpha\beta = c \implies \alpha\beta = c/a$.
formulas.description: Vieta's Formulas for Quadratic Equations
formulas.explanation: Directly links polynomial coefficients to root sums and products without solving the equation explicitly.

formulas.title: Difference of Roots Formula
formulas.derivation: Using identity $(\alpha - \beta)^2 = (\alpha + \beta)^2 - 4\alpha\beta = \left(-\frac{b}{a}\right)^2 - 4\frac{c}{a} = \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{a^2} = \frac{\Delta}{a^2}$. Taking principal square root gives $|\alpha - \beta| = \frac{\sqrt{\Delta}}{|a|}$.
formulas.description: Difference of Roots Formula
formulas.explanation: Measures the horizontal distance between the x-intercepts of the parabola $y = ax^2 + bx + c$.

formulas.title: Discriminant Characterization of Roots
formulas.derivation: Follows directly from the radical term $\sqrt{\Delta}$ in the quadratic formula. If $\Delta > 0$, $\sqrt{\Delta} \in \mathbb{R}^+$, yielding two distinct real values. If $\Delta = 0$, $\sqrt{\Delta} = 0$, giving coincident root $-b/(2a)$. If $\Delta < 0$, $\sqrt{\Delta} = i\sqrt{-\Delta}$, producing non-real conjugate pair $\frac{-b \pm i\sqrt{4ac - b^2}}{2a}$.
formulas.description: Discriminant Characterization of Roots
formulas.explanation: Determines whether the parabola intersects the x-axis at 2 points, touches at 1 vertex, or never intersects.

formulas.title: Condition for Exactly One Common Root Between Two Quadratics

variables.a_i, b_i, c_i: coefficients of a1 x^2 + b1 x + c1 = 0 and a2 x^2 + b2 x + c2 = 0

formulas.derivation: Let $\alpha$ be common root: $a_1 \alpha^2 + b_1 \alpha + c_1 = 0$ and $a_2 \alpha^2 + b_2 \alpha + c_2 = 0$. By cross-multiplication: $\frac{\alpha^2}{b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1} = \frac{\alpha}{c_1 a_2 - c_2 a_1} = \frac{1}{a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1}$. Eliminating $\alpha$: $\alpha = \frac{c_1 a_2 - c_2 a_1}{a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1}$, so $\alpha^2 = \frac{(c_1 a_2 - c_2 a_1)^2}{(a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1)^2} = \frac{b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1}{a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1} \implies (c_1 a_2 - c_2 a_1)^2 = (a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1)(b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1)$.
formulas.description: Condition for Exactly One Common Root Between Two Quadratics
formulas.explanation: Necessary and sufficient algebraic condition for two distinct quadratic equations to share a common solution.

formulas.latex: \Delta \ge 0, \quad a \cdot f(k) > 0, \quad -\frac{b}{2a} > k \implies \text{Both roots greater than } k
formulas.title: Location of Roots: Both roots greater than real number k
formulas.derivation: For both roots $\alpha, \beta > k$: (1) Real roots require $\Delta \ge 0$. (2) Parabola opens up ($a>0$) means $f(k) > 0$; opens down ($a<0$) means $f(k) < 0$, unified as $a \cdot f(k) > 0$. (3) The vertex $x = -b/(2a) = (\alpha + \beta)/2$ must lie strictly to the right of $k$: $-b/(2a) > k$.
formulas.description: Location of Roots: Both roots greater than real number k
formulas.explanation: Standard IIT-JEE test for restricting both roots of a quadratic polynomial to the right of a given real value k.

formulas.latex: a \cdot f(k) < 0 \implies k \text{ lies strictly between the roots}
formulas.title: Location of Roots: Number k lies strictly between roots
formulas.derivation: If $k$ lies between $\alpha$ and $\beta$, the vertex value must have opposite sign to $f(k)$ compared to $a$. If $a > 0$, parabola is below x-axis between roots $\implies f(k) < 0 \implies a f(k) < 0$. If $a < 0$, parabola is above x-axis between roots $\implies f(k) > 0 \implies a f(k) < 0$. Note: $\Delta > 0$ is automatically guaranteed since $a f(k) < 0 \implies b^2 - 4ac > 0$.
formulas.description: Location of Roots: Number k lies strictly between roots
formulas.explanation: Simplest root-location check: a single inequality $a f(k) < 0$ guarantees real distinct roots with k strictly between them.

Albert Einstein postulated light energy arrives in discrete quantized packets (photons) of energy $E = h
