formulas.title: de Broglie Wavelength of Matter Waves
formulas.derivation: Louis de Broglie hypothesized nature is symmetric: if photons have momentum $p = E/c = h\nu/c = h/\lambda$, matter particles must carry wavelength $\lambda = h/p$. For non-relativistic particle accelerated through voltage $V$: $K = qV = \frac{p^2}{2m} \implies p = \sqrt{2mqV}$. Hence $\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$. For electron ($m = 9.109 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}, q = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$), this evaluates to $\lambda = \frac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}\text{ nm}$.
formulas.description: Wave-particle duality wavelength associated with any material particle of momentum p.
formulas.explanation: Confirmed experimentally by Davisson-Germer electron diffraction on nickel crystals; forms the basis of electron microscopy.

formulas.title: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle
formulas.derivation: Follows from Fourier transform properties of wavepackets: spatial width $\Delta x$ and wavenumber spread $\Delta k$ obey $\Delta x \Delta k \ge 1/2$. Using de Broglie relation $p = \hbar k \implies \Delta p = \hbar \Delta k$, multiplying by $\hbar$ yields $\Delta x \Delta p_x \ge \hbar / 2$.
formulas.description: Fundamental quantum limit on simultaneous measurement precision of conjugate variables.
formulas.explanation: Strict quantum mechanical property; proves why electrons cannot exist inside atomic nuclei.

formulas.latex: r_n = \frac{n^2 h^2 \epsilon_0}{\pi m e^2 Z} = \frac{n^2}{Z} a_0, \quad a_0 \approx 0.529 \text{ \AA}
formulas.title: Bohr Atomic Model: Orbital Radii
formulas.derivation: Bohr's quantization postulate: $m v r = \frac{n h}{2\pi} \implies v = \frac{n h}{2\pi m r}$. Coulomb force supplies centripetal force: $\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Z e^2}{r^2} = \frac{m v^2}{r} = \frac{m}{r}\left(\frac{n h}{2\pi m r}\right)^2 = \frac{n^2 h^2}{4\pi^2 m r^3}$. Solving for $r$: $r_n = \frac{\epsilon_0 n^2 h^2}{\pi m Z e^2} = \frac{n^2}{Z} a_0$.
formulas.description: Quantized orbital radii of hydrogen-like single-electron atoms.
formulas.explanation: Orbital radius scales as $n^2 / Z$.

formulas.latex: E_n = -\frac{m Z^2 e^4}{8 \epsilon_0^2 h^2 n^2} = -13.6 \frac{Z^2}{n^2} \text{ eV}
formulas.title: Bohr Atomic Model: Quantized Energy Levels
formulas.derivation: Kinetic energy: $K = \frac{1}{2}m v^2 = \frac{1}{8\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Z e^2}{r}$. Potential energy: $U = -\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Z e^2}{r}$. Total energy: $E = K + U = -\frac{1}{8\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Z e^2}{r} = -K = \frac{1}{2}U$. Substituting orbital radius $r_n$: $E_n = -\frac{m Z^2 e^4}{8\epsilon_0^2 h^2 n^2} = -13.6 \frac{Z^2}{n^2}\text{ eV}$.
formulas.description: Total discrete energy levels of bound electron in hydrogenic atom.
formulas.explanation: Negative sign signifies bound state. Ground state of hydrogen ($n=1, Z=1$) has ionization energy $13.6\text{ eV}$.

formulas.title: Rydberg Formula for Hydrogen Spectral Series

variables.n_1, n_2: Lower and higher energy quantum numbers ($n_2 > n_1$)

formulas.derivation: Conservation of energy: $E_{photon} = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = E_{n_2} - E_{n_1} = \frac{m Z^2 e^4}{8\epsilon_0^2 h^2}\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$. Dividing by $hc$: $\frac{1}{\lambda} = \left(\frac{m e^4}{8\epsilon_0^2 h^3 c}\right) Z^2 \left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right) = R_H Z^2 \left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$.
formulas.description: Wavenumber of photon emitted or absorbed during electron transition between quantum states $n_2 \to n_1$.
formulas.explanation: Lyman series ($n_1=1$, Ultraviolet); Balmer series ($n_1=2$, Visible); Paschen series ($n_1=3$, Infrared); Brackett ($n_1=4$); Pfund ($n_1=5$).

formulas.latex: N(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda t} = N_0 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t / T_{1/2}}, \quad T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda} \approx \frac{0.693}{\lambda}, \quad \tau = \frac{1}{\lambda}
formulas.title: Law of Radioactive Decay
formulas.derivation: Rate of disintegration is directly proportional to present population: $-\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N \implies \frac{dN}{N} = -\lambda dt$. Integrating from $t=0$ ($N=N_0$) to $t$: $\ln(N/N_0) = -\lambda t \implies N(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$. At half-life $t = T_{1/2}$, $N = N_0 / 2$: $e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}} = 1/2 \implies \lambda T_{1/2} = \ln 2 \implies T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda} \approx \frac{0.693}{\lambda}$. Mean life is $\tau = \frac{1}{N_0}\int_0^\infty N(t)dt = \frac{1}{\lambda}$.
formulas.description: Exponential disintegration of unstable radionuclides, half-life $T_{1/2}$, and mean lifetime $\tau$.
formulas.explanation: Activity is $A(t) = -dN/dt = \lambda N(t) = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$; 1 Becquerel (Bq) $= 1\text{ decay/sec}$, 1 Curie (Ci) $= 3.7 \times 10^{10}\text{ Bq}$.

formulas.latex: \Delta m = [Z m_p + (A - Z)m_n] - M_{nucleus}, \quad E_b = \Delta m \cdot c^2 = \Delta m (931.5 \text{ MeV/u})
formulas.title: Nuclear Mass Defect and Binding Energy
formulas.derivation: Free nucleons have greater combined rest mass than the bound composite nucleus. The missing mass $\Delta m = Z m_p + (A-Z)m_n - M$ was liberated as binding energy during nucleosynthesis following Einstein's mass-energy equivalence $E = \Delta m \cdot c^2$. Using $1\text{ u} = 1.6605 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$ and $c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$ yields $1\text{ u} \equiv 931.5\text{ MeV}$.
formulas.description: Mass converted into binding energy holding nucleons together within the nucleus.
formulas.explanation: Binding energy per nucleon curve peaks near Iron-56 ($E_b/A \approx 8.8\text{ MeV/nucleon}$), explaining why light nuclei undergo nuclear fusion and heavy nuclei undergo nuclear fission.

formulas.latex: R = R_0 A^{1/3}, \quad R_0 \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \text{ m} = 1.2 \text{ fm}, \quad \rho_{nuclear} \approx 2.3 \times 10^{17} \text{ kg/m}^3
formulas.title: Nuclear Radius and Constant Nuclear Density
formulas.derivation: High-energy electron scattering experiments demonstrate nuclear volume is directly proportional to number of nucleons $A$: $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \propto A \implies R = R_0 A^{1/3}$. Nuclear mass is $M \approx A m_N$. Density is $\rho = \frac{M}{V} = \frac{A m_N}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \frac{3 m_N}{4\pi R_0^3} = \text{constant} \approx 2.3 \times 10^{17}\text{ kg/m}^3$.
formulas.description: Nuclear size scaling with mass number A and universal nuclear matter density.
formulas.explanation: Nuclear density is invariant across the entire periodic table, independent of atomic number.

formulas.latex: n_i^2 = n_e n_h \quad (\text{Mass Action Law}), \quad I = I_0 (e^{e V / \eta k_B T} - 1) \quad (\text{Diode Equation})
formulas.title: Semiconductor Mass Action Law and Shockley Diode Equation
formulas.derivation: Law of Mass Action: thermal generation rate of electron-hole pairs equals recombination rate $R = r n_e n_h$. In thermal equilibrium, generation equals recombination, yielding $n_e n_h = n_i^2$, valid for both intrinsic and doped extrinsic semiconductors. Shockley diode equation follows from Boltzmann diffusion of majority carriers across depletion barrier: $I = I_0(e^{eV / \eta k_B T} - 1)$.
formulas.description: Carrier concentration product in thermal equilibrium and I-V characteristic of p-n junction diode.
formulas.explanation: For n-type semiconductor ($n_e \approx N_D$), minority hole density drops to $n_h = n_i^2 / N_D$.

formulas.title: Bipolar Junction Transistor (BJT) Current Gains
formulas.derivation: By Kirchhoff's law on transistor: $I_E = I_B + I_C$. Dividing by $I_C$: $\frac{I_E}{I_C} = \frac{I_B}{I_C} + 1 \implies \frac{1}{\alpha} = \frac{1}{\beta} + 1 = \frac{1 + \beta}{\beta}$. Inverting yields $\alpha = \frac{\beta}{1 + \beta}$. Solving for $\beta$ gives $\beta = \frac{\alpha}{1 - \alpha}$.
formulas.description: Common-base current gain $\alpha$ and common-emitter current gain $\beta$ relations.
formulas.explanation: Small variations in base current produce large amplified collector current swings.

formulas.latex: V_{ripple} = \frac{I_{dc}}{2 f C} \quad (\text{Full-Wave Rectifier with Capacitor Filter})
formulas.title: Rectifier Ripple Voltage
formulas.derivation: Capacitor discharges through load resistor $R_L$ between successive rectification peaks for duration $\Delta t \approx T/2 = \frac{1}{2f}$. Charge lost is $\Delta Q = I_{dc} \Delta t = \frac{I_{dc}}{2f}$. Ripple voltage is $\Delta V = \frac{\Delta Q}{C} = \frac{I_{dc}}{2f C} = \frac{V_{dc}}{2f R_L C}$.
formulas.description: Peak-to-peak AC ripple voltage across capacitor filter in full-wave rectifier.
formulas.explanation: Ripple is halved compared to half-wave rectifier ($\frac{I_{dc}}{f C}$); higher capacitance yields smoother DC output.

formulas.title: Duane-Hunt Law for Continuous X-Ray Cutoff
formulas.derivation: Electrons strike heavy metal target (Tungsten/Molybdenum) after gaining kinetic energy $K = e V_a$. When an incoming electron loses 100% of its kinetic energy in a single braking deceleration impact with target nucleus, the emitted Bremsstrahlung photon carries maximum energy: $h\nu_{max} = \frac{hc}{\lambda_{min}} = e V_a$. Solving for $\lambda_{min}$ yields $\lambda_{min} = \frac{hc}{e V_a} = \frac{1240}{V_a}\text{ nm}$.
formulas.description: Shortest wavelength limit of Bremsstrahlung continuous X-ray spectrum at accelerating potential $V_a$.
formulas.explanation: Depends strictly on accelerating tube voltage $V_a$ and is completely independent of target anode material.

formulas.latex: \sqrt{\nu} = a(Z - b) \quad (\text{Moseley's Law for Characteristic X-Rays})
formulas.title: Moseley's Law
formulas.derivation: Henry Moseley (1913) analyzed characteristic X-ray transitions: an inner $K$-shell vacancy is screened by remaining electron, so effective nuclear charge seen by transition electron is $Z_{eff} = Z - 1$. Applying Bohr formula: $\nu = R_H c (Z - 1)^2 \left(\frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{2^2}\right) = \frac{3}{4}R_H c (Z - 1)^2$. Taking square root: $\sqrt{\nu} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{4}R_H c}(Z - 1) = a(Z - 1)$.
formulas.description: Linear relationship between square root of characteristic X-ray line frequency and nuclear atomic number Z.
formulas.explanation: Historical breakthrough proving the periodic table must be ordered by atomic number $Z$ (nuclear proton count), not atomic weight.

content_json.derivation:
Albert Einstein postulated light energy arrives in discrete quantized packets (photons) of energy $E = h
u$. An electron absorbs a single photon: portion of energy $\phi$ overcomes surface binding potential barrier (work function); remainder appears as maximum kinetic energy: $h
u = \phi + K_{max} \implies K_{max} = h
u - \phi$. Applying retarding potential $V_0$ stops fastest electrons: $K_{max} = e V_0$.
content_json.explanation: Explains why photoelectron emission occurs with zero detectable time lag ($< 10^{-9}\text{ s}$) and why emission stops entirely below threshold frequency $\nu_0$ regardless of light intensity.

formulas.title: Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction and Lenz's Law
formulas.derivation: Empirical discovery by Michael Faraday (1831). The negative sign (Lenz's Law, Heinrich Lenz 1834) enforces energy conservation: the induced current flows in such a direction that its own magnetic field opposes the original flux change that produced it.
formulas.description: Induced electromotive force in a circuit equals negative rate of change of magnetic flux through loop.
formulas.explanation: If flux increases, induced magnetic field points opposite to applied field; if flux decreases, induced field reinforces it.

formulas.title: Motional EMF in a Moving Conductor
formulas.derivation: Mobile conduction electrons inside rod experience magnetic Lorentz force $\vec{F}_B = -e(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$. Work done moving an electron through length $\vec{l}$ is $W = \int \vec{F}_B \cdot d\vec{l} = -e \int (\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot d\vec{l}$. Induced EMF is work done per unit positive charge: $\mathcal{E} = W/(-e) = (\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot\vec{l} = B v l\sin\theta$.
formulas.description: Electromotive force induced across ends of a conducting rod of length l translating with speed v through magnetic field B.
formulas.explanation: Forms the foundation of electrical power generation in alternators and dynamos.

formulas.title: Rotational Motional EMF of a Rotating Rod
formulas.derivation: Consider element $dr$ at distance $r$ from pivot: linear velocity is $v(r) = r\omega$. Motional EMF generated across element is $d\mathcal{E} = B v(r) dr = B(r\omega)dr$. Integrating from pivot $r=0$ to tip $r=l$: $\mathcal{E} = B\omega \int_0^l r dr = B\omega \left[\frac{r^2}{2}\right]_0^l = \frac{1}{2}B\omega l^2$.
formulas.description: EMF induced between pivot and tip of a conducting rod of length l rotating with angular speed $\omega$ in perpendicular field B.
formulas.explanation: Also equals $B\left(\frac{dA}{dt}\right) = B\left(\frac{1}{2}l^2\omega\right)$, matching rate of area swept.

formulas.latex: L = \frac{N \Phi_B}{I} = \mu_0 n^2 A l, \quad U_B = \frac{1}{2}L I^2, \quad u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}
formulas.title: Self-Inductance and Magnetic Energy Density
formulas.derivation: Inside solenoid, field is $B = \mu_0 n I$. Flux per turn is $\Phi = B A = \mu_0 n I A$. Total linkage is $\lambda = N\Phi = (nl)(\mu_0 n I A) = (\mu_0 n^2 A l)I$. By definition $L = \lambda / I = \mu_0 n^2 A l$. Work required to establish current $I$ against back-EMF $\mathcal{E}_L = -L\frac{di}{dt}$ is $U = \int P\,dt = \int (L\frac{di}{dt} i)dt = L \int_0^I i\,di = \frac{1}{2}LI^2$. Dividing by volume $V = Al$ and using $B = \mu_0 n I$ yields $u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$.
formulas.description: Self-inductance of solenoid, total energy stored in inductor magnetic field, and volume energy density.
formulas.explanation: Analogous to kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ and electrostatic energy density $\frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0 E^2$.

formulas.latex: M = \frac{N_2 \Phi_{21}}{I_1} = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l, \quad M \le \sqrt{L_1 L_2}
formulas.title: Mutual Inductance and Coupling Coefficient
formulas.derivation: Current $I_1$ in outer coil produces uniform field $B_1 = \mu_0 n_1 I_1$. Flux passing through each turn of inner coil of area $A$ is $\Phi_{21} = B_1 A = \mu_0 n_1 I_1 A$. Total linkage with coil 2 ($N_2 = n_2 l$ turns) is $\lambda_2 = N_2 \Phi_{21} = (n_2 l)(\mu_0 n_1 I_1 A) = (\mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l)I_1$. Mutual inductance is $M = \lambda_2 / I_1 = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l$. By reciprocity theorem, $M_{12} = M_{21} = M$.
formulas.description: Mutual inductance between two co-axial solenoids and coupling coefficient $k = M/\sqrt{L_1 L_2} \le 1$.
formulas.explanation: For perfectly coupled coils with zero flux leakage, $k = 1$ and $M = \sqrt{L_1 L_2}$.

formulas.latex: i(t) = I_0 (1 - e^{-t / \tau_L}) \quad (\text{Growth}), \quad i(t) = I_0 e^{-t / \tau_L} \quad (\text{Decay}), \quad \tau_L = \frac{L}{R}
formulas.title: Transient LR Circuit Growth and Decay
formulas.derivation: KVL during growth: $\mathcal{E} - L\frac{di}{dt} - iR = 0 \implies L\frac{di}{dt} = \mathcal{E} - iR$. Separating variables: $\frac{di}{\mathcal{E} - iR} = \frac{dt}{L}$. Integrating with $i(0) = 0$: $-\frac{1}{R}\ln\left(1 - \frac{iR}{\mathcal{E}}\right) = \frac{t}{L} \implies i(t) = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R}\left(1 - e^{-Rt/L}\right)$.
formulas.description: Time-dependent current build-up and decay in inductive RL circuit with inductive time constant $\tau_L = L/R$.
formulas.explanation: At $t = \tau_L = L/R$, current reaches $63.2\%$ of steady value $I_0$; inductor acts as open-circuit at $t=0^+$ and short-circuit as $t \to \infty$.

formulas.title: Root-Mean-Square (RMS) Values of Sinusoidal AC
formulas.derivation: For $i(t) = I_0 \sin(\omega t)$, Joule heat generated in resistor $R$ over one period $T = 2\pi/\omega$ is $H = \int_0^T i^2(t) R dt$. An equivalent DC current $I_{rms}$ dissipates identical heat: $I_{rms}^2 R T = R \int_0^T I_0^2 \sin^2(\omega t) dt$. Since the average of $\sin^2(\omega t)$ over full period is $\frac{1}{2}$: $I_{rms}^2 T = I_0^2 \left(\frac{T}{2}\right) \implies I_{rms} = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}$.
formulas.description: Effective heating value of alternating sinusoidal current and voltage over full periodic cycle.
formulas.explanation: Standard wall outlet voltages (e.g., $230\text{ V}$ or $120\text{ V}$) always quote RMS values; peak voltage is $V_0 = \sqrt{2}V_{rms}$ ($325\text{ V}$ for $230\text{ V}$).

formulas.latex: Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}, \quad X_L = \omega L, \quad X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C}
formulas.title: Impedance of Series LCR Circuit
formulas.derivation: Phasor analysis: current phasor $\tilde{I}$ is common in series loop. Resistor voltage $\tilde{V}_R = I R$ is in phase with current. Inductor voltage $\tilde{V}_L = I X_L$ leads current by $+90^\circ (+i)$. Capacitor voltage $\tilde{V}_C = I X_C$ lags current by $-90^\circ (-i)$. Total complex voltage is $\tilde{V} = \tilde{V}_R + \tilde{V}_L + \tilde{V}_C = I [R + i(X_L - X_C)]$. Impedance magnitude is $Z = |\tilde{V}|/I = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$.
formulas.description: Total opposition to sinusoidal alternating current flow combining resistance, inductive reactance, and capacitive reactance.
formulas.explanation: Phase angle between voltage and current is $\tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R}$.

formulas.title: Resonant Frequency and Quality Factor (Q) of Series LCR
formulas.derivation: Current amplitude is $I_0 = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{R^2 + (\omega L - 1/\omega C)^2}}$. Current is maximized when reactive term vanishes: $\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C} = 0 \implies \omega_0^2 = \frac{1}{LC} \implies \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$. At resonance, impedance is purely resistive ($Z_{min} = R$) and current is in phase with voltage ($\cos\phi = 1$). Quality factor is $Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} = \frac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega}$ where $\Delta\omega$ is bandwidth at half-power points.
formulas.description: Condition for minimum impedance, maximum current resonance, and sharpness factor of resonance curve.
formulas.explanation: High $Q$ produces extremely sharp tuning selectivity in radio receivers and RF filter circuits.

formulas.title: Average AC Power and Power Factor
formulas.derivation: Instantaneous power is $p(t) = v(t)i(t) = [V_0 \sin(\omega t)][I_0 \sin(\omega t - \phi)] = V_0 I_0 \sin(\omega t)[\sin\omega t\cos\phi - \cos\omega t\sin\phi] = V_0 I_0 [\sin^2\omega t\cos\phi - \sin\omega t\cos\omega t\sin\phi]$. Averaging over a full cycle: $\langle \sin^2\omega t \rangle = 1/2$ and $\langle \sin\omega t\cos\omega t \rangle = 0$. Hence $P_{avg} = \frac{1}{2}V_0 I_0 \cos\phi = \left(\frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\left(\frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\cos\phi = V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos\phi$. From impedance triangle, $\cos\phi = R/Z$.
formulas.description: Real active power dissipated in AC circuit over complete cycle governed by phase angle $\phi$.
formulas.explanation: For purely reactive circuits (pure $L$ or pure $C$), $\phi = \pm 90^\circ \implies \cos\phi = 0$, giving zero real power dissipation (wattless current).

formulas.title: Ideal Transformer Voltage, Current and Turns Ratio
formulas.derivation: Assuming ideal core with zero flux leakage: common flux $\Phi$ links both windings. Induced EMFs are $V_p = -N_p \frac{d\Phi}{dt}$ and $V_s = -N_s \frac{d\Phi}{dt}$. Dividing gives $\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$. For an ideal lossless transformer (100% efficiency), input power equals output power: $V_p I_p = V_s I_s \implies \frac{I_p}{I_s} = \frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$.
formulas.description: Transformation of AC voltage and current in magnetically coupled primary and secondary windings.
formulas.explanation: Step-up transformer ($N_s > N_p$): voltage increases and current decreases proportionately, minimizing $I^2 R$ transmission line losses.

formulas.latex: \omega_{LC} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}, \quad q(t) = Q_0 \cos(\omega_{LC} t), \quad i(t) = -\omega_{LC} Q_0 \sin(\omega_{LC} t)
formulas.title: LC Tank Circuit Oscillations
formulas.derivation: Total circuit energy is $E = U_E + U_B = \frac{q^2}{2C} + \frac{1}{2}Li^2$. In lossless circuit, $\frac{dE}{dt} = 0$: $\frac{q}{C}\frac{dq}{dt} + L i \frac{di}{dt} = 0$. Since $i = \frac{dq}{dt}$, dividing by $i$ gives $\frac{q}{C} + L\frac{d^2q}{dt^2} = 0 \implies \frac{d^2q}{dt^2} + \frac{1}{LC}q = 0$. This is standard SHM equation with $\omega_{LC} = 1/\sqrt{LC}$. Solution with initial charge $Q_0$ is $q(t) = Q_0\cos(\omega t)$.
formulas.description: Undamped harmonic exchange of energy between electric field of capacitor and magnetic field of inductor.
formulas.explanation: Energy sloshes sinusoidally between all-electric state ($U_E = Q_0^2/2C$) and all-magnetic state ($U_B = \frac{1}{2}L I_{max}^2$).

formulas.title: Maxwell's Displacement Current
formulas.derivation: Between capacitor plates during charging, no conduction electrons flow, yet magnetic field exists. Electric field is $E = \frac{Q}{\epsilon_0 A} \implies Q = \epsilon_0 E A = \epsilon_0 \Phi_E$. Differentiating charge with respect to time: $I_c = \frac{dQ}{dt} = \epsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$. Maxwell recognized this time-varying flux term acts as an effective displacement current $I_d = \epsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$, restoring Ampere's law to $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 (I_c + I_d)$.
formulas.description: Equivalent current arising from time-varying electric flux, completing Ampere-Maxwell law.
formulas.explanation: Displacement current between plates exactly equals conduction current in the connecting wires ($I_d = I_c$), ensuring continuity.

formulas.title: Speed of Electromagnetic Waves in Vacuum and Field Ratio
formulas.description: Propagation velocity of light from Maxwell's equations and relation between electric and magnetic field amplitudes.
formulas.explanation: Proved that light is an electromagnetic transverse wave propagating at universal speed $c$.

content_json.derivation: Empirical discovery by Michael Faraday (1831). The negative sign (Lenz's Law, Heinrich Lenz 1834) enforces energy conservation: the induced current flows in such a direction that its own magnetic field opposes the original flux change that produced it.
content_json.explanation: If flux increases, induced magnetic field points opposite to applied field; if flux decreases, induced field reinforces it.

catalog_formula_sheets.name: Probability Formula Sheet
catalog_formula_sheets.derivation: By definition of conditional probability: $P(E_i | A) = \frac{P(E_i \cap A)}{P(A)} = \frac{P(E_i) P(A | E_i)}{P(A)}$. By the Law of Total Probability, since $E_1, \dots, E_n$ partition the sample space $S$: $A = A \cap S = A \cap (\bigcup E_j) = \bigcup (A \cap E_j)$. Since $E_j$ are mutually disjoint: $P(A) = \sum_{j=1}^n P(A \cap E_j) = \sum_{j=1}^n P(E_j) P(A | E_j)$. Substituting $P(A)$ yields Bayes' theorem.
catalog_formula_sheets.explanation: Calculates the updated probability of hypothesis E_i after observing experimental evidence A.

sections.title: Probability Formula Sheet - High-Yield Formulas

formulas.latex: P(E_i | A) = \frac{P(E_i) P(A | E_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^n P(E_j) P(A | E_j)}
formulas.title: Bayes' Theorem for Conditional Posterior Probability
formulas.derivation: By definition of conditional probability: $P(E_i | A) = \frac{P(E_i \cap A)}{P(A)} = \frac{P(E_i) P(A | E_i)}{P(A)}$. By the Law of Total Probability, since $E_1, \dots, E_n$ partition the sample space $S$: $A = A \cap S = A \cap (\bigcup E_j) = \bigcup (A \cap E_j)$. Since $E_j$ are mutually disjoint: $P(A) = \sum_{j=1}^n P(A \cap E_j) = \sum_{j=1}^n P(E_j) P(A | E_j)$. Substituting $P(A)$ yields Bayes' theorem.
formulas.description: Bayes' Theorem for Conditional Posterior Probability
formulas.explanation: Calculates the updated probability of hypothesis E_i after observing experimental evidence A.

formulas.latex: P(X = r) = \binom{n}{r} p^r q^{n - r} \quad (q = 1 - p), \quad \mu = n p, \quad \sigma^2 = n p q
formulas.title: Binomial Distribution Probability Mass Function, Mean and Variance
formulas.derivation: In $n$ independent trials, the probability of any specific sequence with $r$ successes and $n-r$ failures is $p^r q^{n-r}$. The number of distinct sequences is the combinations of choosing $r$ trials out of $n$: $\binom{n}{r}$. Hence $P(X = r) = \binom{n}{r} p^r q^{n-r}$. Expectation: $E[X] = \sum r \binom{n}{r} p^r q^{n-r} = n p \sum \binom{n-1}{r-1} p^{r-1} q^{(n-1)-(r-1)} = n p (p+q)^{n-1} = n p$. Variance: $\text{Var}(X) = E[X(X-1)] + E[X] - (E[X])^2 = n(n-1)p^2 + np - n^2 p^2 = np(1-p) = npq$.
formulas.description: Binomial Distribution Probability Mass Function, Mean and Variance
formulas.explanation: Models the number of successes in n independent identical Bernoulli trials.

formulas.latex: P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)
formulas.title: Addition Theorem of Probability

variables.P(A \\cup B): probability of occurrence of at least one event

formulas.derivation: From set theory cardinality: $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$. Dividing both sides by the total number of outcomes in the finite sample space $n(S)$: $\frac{n(A \cup B)}{n(S)} = \frac{n(A)}{n(S)} + \frac{n(B)}{n(S)} - \frac{n(A \cap B)}{n(S)} \implies P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$. If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive ($A \cap B = \emptyset$), $P(A \cap B) = 0 \implies P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$.
formulas.description: Addition Theorem of Probability
formulas.explanation: Fundamental probability union identity for calculating the likelihood of either event A or B occurring.

formulas.latex: P(A \cap B) = P(A) P(B) \iff A, B \text{ are Independent}
formulas.title: Condition for Independence of Two Events
formulas.derivation: By definition of conditional probability: $P(A | B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$. Two events are independent if the occurrence of event $B$ has no influence on the probability of event $A$: $P(A | B) = P(A)$. Equating: $P(A) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \implies P(A \cap B) = P(A) P(B)$.
formulas.description: Condition for Independence of Two Events
formulas.explanation: Mathematically defines stochastic independence: joint probability equals product of marginal probabilities.

formulas.title: Expectation and Variance of a Discrete Random Variable
formulas.derivation: Expand variance definition: $\text{Var}(X) = E[(X - \mu)^2] = E[X^2 - 2\mu X + \mu^2] = E[X^2] - 2\mu E[X] + \mu^2$. Since $E[X] = \mu$: $\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - 2\mu^2 + \mu^2 = E[X^2] - \mu^2 = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2$. In summation form: $\sigma^2 = \sum x_i^2 P(x_i) - \left(\sum x_i P(x_i)\right)^2$.
formulas.description: Expectation and Variance of a Discrete Random Variable
formulas.explanation: Expectation gives the long-run probability-weighted average; Variance measures the squared dispersion about the mean.

formulas.latex: E[a X + b] = a E[X] + b, \quad \text{Var}(a X + b) = a^2 \text{Var}(X), \quad \sigma_{aX+b} = |a| \sigma_X
formulas.title: Effect of Linear Transformation on Mean and Variance
formulas.derivation: By linearity of summation: $E[aX + b] = \sum (a x_i + b) P(x_i) = a \sum x_i P(x_i) + b \sum P(x_i) = a E[X] + b(1) = a E[X] + b$. Variance: $\text{Var}(aX + b) = E[((aX + b) - E[aX + b])^2] = E[(aX + b - a\mu - b)^2] = E[(a(X - \mu))^2] = a^2 E[(X - \mu)^2] = a^2 \text{Var}(X)$. Taking square root gives $\sigma = |a|\sigma_X$.
formulas.description: Effect of Linear Transformation on Mean and Variance
formulas.explanation: Adding a constant shifts the mean but does not change the spread; multiplying scales the standard deviation by |a|.

formulas.title: Standard Deviation of a Data Set
formulas.derivation: Expand sum of squared deviations: $\frac{1}{N}\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 = \frac{1}{N}\sum (x_i^2 - 2x_i \bar{x} + \bar{x}^2) = \frac{1}{N}\sum x_i^2 - 2\bar{x}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum x_i\right) + \frac{1}{N}(N \bar{x}^2) = \frac{\sum x_i^2}{N} - 2\bar{x}^2 + \bar{x}^2 = \frac{\sum x_i^2}{N} - \bar{x}^2$. Taking square root gives standard deviation $\sigma$.
formulas.description: Standard Deviation of a Data Set
formulas.explanation: The most widely used statistical measure of variation and dispersion in data.

formulas.title: Coefficient of Variation (Relative Dispersion)
formulas.derivation: Standard deviation is scale-dependent. To compare variability between two data sets with different units or widely different means, divide standard deviation by arithmetic mean: $CV = \frac{\sigma}{\bar{x}} \times 100\%$. The data series with a lower CV is more consistent and stable.
formulas.description: Coefficient of Variation (Relative Dispersion)
formulas.explanation: Dimensionless ratio used to compare consistency between data series with different scales or measurement units.

formulas.title: Mean Deviation About Mean and Median
formulas.derivation: By definition, mean deviation is the average absolute difference of all observations from a measure of central tendency. Differentiating $\sum |x_i - c|$ with respect to $c$ changes sign at each point; the derivative is zero when the number of points below $c$ equals points above $c$, which occurs exactly at the median $M$. Hence, Mean Deviation is minimal when measured about the Median.
formulas.description: Mean Deviation About Mean and Median
formulas.explanation: Robust measure of dispersion; mathematically guaranteed to be minimized when calculated about the median.

formulas.title: Poisson Distribution for Rare Events

variables.\\lambda = n p: average rate of occurrences per interval

formulas.derivation: Take Poisson limit of binomial distribution as $n \to \infty, p \to 0$ with $np = \lambda$: $P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1 - p)^{n - k} = \frac{n(n-1)\dots(n-k+1)}{k!} \left(\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^k \left(1 - \frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^n \left(1 - \frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{-k}$. As $n \to \infty$: $\frac{n(n-1)\dots(n-k+1)}{n^k} \to 1$, $(1 - \lambda/n)^n \to e^{-\lambda}$, and $(1 - \lambda/n)^{-k} \to 1$. Hence $P(X = k) = \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}$.
formulas.description: Poisson Distribution for Rare Events
formulas.explanation: Models counts of rare independent events occurring in fixed time or space intervals (e.g. radioactive decays, server requests).

formulas.title: Karl Pearson's Empirical Relation for Moderately Skewed Distributions
formulas.derivation: In a symmetric distribution: Mean = Median = Mode. In a moderately skewed unimodal frequency distribution, the median approximately divides the distance from mean to mode in a 2:1 ratio: $\text{Mean} - \text{Median} \approx \frac{1}{3}(\text{Mean} - \text{Mode}) \implies 3(\text{Mean} - \text{Median}) \approx \text{Mean} - \text{Mode} \implies \text{Mode} \approx 3\text{Median} - 2\text{Mean}$.
formulas.description: Karl Pearson's Empirical Relation for Moderately Skewed Distributions
formulas.explanation: Empirical relationship connecting the three measures of central tendency in moderately asymmetric data.

formulas.latex: P(A | B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \implies P(A \cap B) = P(B) P(A | B) = P(A) P(B | A)
formulas.title: Multiplication Rule of Probability
formulas.derivation: Follows from definition of conditional probability: the probability that event $A$ occurs given that event $B$ has already occurred is the proportion of outcomes in $B$ that also belong to $A$: $P(A | B) = \frac{n(A \cap B)}{n(B)} = \frac{n(A \cap B)/n(S)}{n(B)/n(S)} = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$. Multiplying both sides by $P(B)$ gives $P(A \cap B) = P(B) P(A | B)$.
formulas.description: Multiplication Rule of Probability

content_json.derivation: By definition of conditional probability: $P(E_i | A) = \frac{P(E_i \cap A)}{P(A)} = \frac{P(E_i) P(A | E_i)}{P(A)}$. By the Law of Total Probability, since $E_1, \dots, E_n$ partition the sample space $S$: $A = A \cap S = A \cap (\bigcup E_j) = \bigcup (A \cap E_j)$. Since $E_j$ are mutually disjoint: $P(A) = \sum_{j=1}^n P(A \cap E_j) = \sum_{j=1}^n P(E_j) P(A | E_j)$. Substituting $P(A)$ yields Bayes' theorem.
